translations.text: An instructive discourse on the way of monastic life, composed by Mar Isaac, bishop of Nineveh.
With the strength of our Lord Jesus Christ, we begin to write the first part of the instructive discourse of the holy Mar Isaac of Qatar,
bishop of the city of Nineveh. Our Lord, help me through his prayer. Amen. First discourse.
The fear of God is the beginning of virtue, for it is called the offspring of faith.
It is sown in the heart when a person gives his mind respite from the distractions of the world,
so that he may confine its wandering movements within reflections on the restoration that is to come.
For laying the foundation of virtue, none of its particular practices takes precedence
over this: that we gather ourselves together by withdrawing from affairs
to the illuminating word concerning the straightness of the holy paths, which the psalmist, through the Spirit, called a guide.
A person who can endure honors is scarcely to be found—or perhaps cannot be found at all.
This is because of his readiness to undergo changes, as one might put it, even if he is angelic in character.
The beginning of the way of life is to occupy the mind with the words of God and to practice patient endurance.
The nourishment drawn from the former helps bring the latter to perfection.
Likewise, receiving nourishment for growth toward perfection in the latter gives greater scope to the need for the former.
The help that comes from both swiftly brings about the raising of the whole building.
No one has been able to draw near to God except the person who has withdrawn from the world.
By withdrawal I do not mean a bodily journey, but withdrawal from the world's affairs.
Virtue is this: that a person should be free of the world in his mind.
As long as the senses occupy themselves with things, the heart cannot rest from thinking about them.
Neither do the passions cease nor do evil thoughts come to an end without the wilderness and solitude.
For until the soul acquires intoxication with faith in God
through perceptibly receiving its power, it neither heals the weakness of the senses
nor is it able forcefully to trample upon visible matter, which is a barrier to what is inward and imperceptible.
Rationality is the cause of freedom, and the fruit of both is the capacity to turn in either direction. Without the first, there is no second.
And where the second is lacking, there the third is bound as though in shackles.
When grace increases in a person, then, through love of righteousness, the fear of death is despised.
He finds many reasons within himself why it is right for a person to endure afflictions for the sake of the fear of God.
And those things regarded as [?]—bodily things, that is—and that press forcibly upon nature,
and necessarily entail suffering, are already considered nothing in his eyes compared with what he awaits.
And that it is impossible to know the truth without undergoing the experience of sufferings—
he finds firm assurance of this within his own mind.
And God takes great care of the human being, who has not been abandoned to chance.
Those who have gone out in search of him and have borne suffering for his sake see this especially clearly, as though it were pointed out with a finger.
But when lack of faith takes root in our hearts, then everything appears in the opposite light.
“It is not for the sake of testing,” and, “Trusting in God does not always succeed,”
and, “God does not care for you as much as people suppose”—
these things are repeatedly insinuated by those who lie in ambush and shoot their arrows in the darkness.
The beginning of a person's true life is the fear of God.
This cannot remain in the soul alongside distraction with worldly affairs. For there is distraction
of the heart from delight in God through the activity of the senses.
The inward impulses are bound, in their perception, to the senses that serve them.
Doubt in the heart brings fear upon the soul.
But faith can strengthen the mind even when the limbs are being cut off.
As long as love of the body is strong within you, you cannot be courageous and free from fear,
because of the many adversities that continually lie in wait for what is loved.
Anyone who pursues honor cannot fail to find causes of distress.
There is no one whose mind does not undergo a corresponding change, in one direction or another, as circumstances change.
If, indeed, sensation is the nurse of the senses, from which desire is naturally born,
according to the saying of Evagrius, then let those who promise to keep their minds at peace amid distractions be silent.
This is the chaste person: one whom foul impulses have ceased to confront, though not as a result of a struggle,
Rather, the sincerity of his heart makes the gaze of his mind modest, so that it does not boldly attach itself to shameful thoughts.
And while the holiness of his conscience is attested by the gaze of his faithfully guarded eyes,
modest reserve hangs like the panels of a door in the hidden place of his thoughts,
so that, like a modest virgin, its purity may be faithfully guarded for Christ.
Nothing is so capable of removing shameful habits from the soul
and checking the disturbing memories that kindle turbulent flames in the body
as absorption in the love of learning and the pursuit of the roots of the meanings
of the sayings of the Scriptures. When the mind's movements plunge delightfully into the pursuit of the wisdom stored in these words,
through the power of the sweetness that understanding draws from there, the mind leaves its body entirely behind.
It forgets the world and everything in it, and wipes from the soul all the memories that raise up images of the world's material things.
And how often the soul itself, in its meditation, remains in wonder, free from concern with habitual thoughts and the workings of nature,
at the new things that meet it from the sea of their mysteries! Even if the mind is swimming only in its upper waters,
unable to send its movements down into this whole depth to see all the treasures in its abysses,
study, through love of it, is powerful enough to bind thoughts firmly by means of thoughts of wonder,
so that they cease pondering and running after the body's nature, as one of those clothed in God said.
“For because the heart is weak,” he says, “it cannot endure the troubles that meet it from outside and the warfare from within.
You know,” he says, “that the evil love of the body is burdensome.
And unless the heart occupies itself with learning, it cannot endure the turmoil of the body's onslaught.”
For just as the heaviness of a weight checks the swift movement of a balance against the disturbance of gusts,
so modest reserve and fear check the mind's tendency to incline.
The degree of deficiency there corresponds exactly to the excess of freedom's power here.
The greater the deficiency there, the greater the cause of the pans' easy, unsteady swaying.
And here, the greater the freedom resulting from the removal of fear from the soul,
the more swiftly the balance of the mind swings in every direction.
Instability, then, is the counterpart of freedom.
And mental wanderings: the second after turning aside.
Be wise in laying a foundation for your journey on God's path, and in a few days it will bring you to the gate of the kingdom,
without a roundabout journey. Do not lag behind those who travel according to the order established by the teachers,
through words drawn from experience and set down to train your conduct, so that your soul may grow through the greatness of the insights they contain.
Discern the purpose of the words in every subject you encounter in the writings,
so that your soul may go deep and dwell with the great [?] contained in the writings of enlightened people.
Those who are guided by grace in their conduct toward enlightenment
constantly perceive something like an intelligible ray of light running between the sentences.
It distinguishes for the mind ordinary speech from subjects expressed with greatness of understanding for the opening of the soul.
A person who reads great sayings in an ordinary way—
his heart too becomes ordinary and dull, and is deprived of the holy power that gives the heart a sweet taste through insights
that fill the soul with wonder. Everything naturally runs toward what is akin to it. And a soul that has a share of the Spirit,
when it hears something in which spiritual power is hidden, eagerly clings to the account of it,
even though a subject expressed spiritually, with great power hidden in it, does not awaken wonder in everyone.
Teaching about virtue requires a heart emptied of the world and its concerns.
For a person whose mind is occupied with concern for passing things, discussions of virtue do not stir his thought
to a loving desire to acquire it. In the natural order, release from material things precedes the bonds that unite us to God.
Yet, through the workings of grace, in certain individuals the latter sometimes precedes the former, so that one love may cover over another.
But in the customary order of providence, the general sequence is different.
You, however, should keep to the general order. If grace comes to meet you beforehand, that is its own doing.
Otherwise, follow the path everyone travels in succession, and climb the ascent of the spiritual tower.
Everything practiced in contemplation, for whose sake a commandment is fulfilled, is itself entirely invisible to the [?] of the flesh.
And everything belonging to action is entirely composite.
For there is only one commandment that requires both—that is, both contemplation and practice.
For embodiment, freedom from embodiment, and the harmonizing of the two—this is [?].
For this reason, the enlightened mind understands both the thing and its purpose, in a twofold way, as was previously commanded through the blessed Moses.
Its simplicity is understood, and so is its twofold character.
As for something blameworthy that happened previously, the labors undertaken by the pure do not remove awareness of its memory.
Rather, they remove the painfulness of its remembrance from the mind, so that the passage through the mind that has already taken place may serve a more virtuous purpose [?].
The soul’s eagerness to acquire virtue overcomes its partner’s share of desire for visible things.
Moderation adorns everything. But without it, even things intended to help
turn into harm, and their usefulness is checked and reduced to nothing. Do you wish to commune with God in your mind,
with a heightened awareness of that delight which is not subject to the senses? Cling to mercy.
For when something resembling him is found within you, that holy beauty is depicted in you through it.
The whole range of deeds of mercy, without any intervening time,
brings the soul into communion with the unity of the radiant glory of the Godhead.
Spiritual union is an imageless remembrance that shines inseparably in the heart with a flame of love.
This remembrance, through perseverance in the commandments, gains strength
to bind fast; and neither by borrowing nor by nature
is material found there on which the soul’s vision can rest in a concrete form.
For this reason it is drawn into wonder, with the closing of both sets of senses, bodily and those of the soul.
There is no other path to spiritual love, which depicts the invisible image,
unless a person first begins with mercy, according to the words of our Lord,
who commands his hearers to make this the foundation for attaining the Father’s perfection.
A word grounded in action is one thing; beautiful words are another.
Even without experience of things, wisdom knows how to adorn its words,
to speak the truth without being acquainted with it, and to boast about virtue without ever having experienced its practice.
A word that comes from practice is a treasure of confidence. But idle wisdom is a deceptive deposit.
It is like an artist who paints water on walls, though it cannot relieve his thirst,
and like someone who sees pleasant dreams. But the person who speaks about virtue from the experience of his own labor,
As though from the profits of his trade, he brings a word to his hearers.
And as though from his own possessions, he sows his teaching in the ears of those who listen to him.
He opens his mouth boldly with his spiritual children, like the aged Jacob speaking to Joseph the chaste:
“And I, behold, have given you one portion more than your brothers, which I took from the hand of the Amorites with my sword and my bow.”
Therefore, everyone whose conduct is stained holds this temporal life dear.
The second such person is the one who lacks knowledge.
Someone has rightly said, “The fear of death torments the fleshly man.”
But someone who has a good testimony within his soul longs for death as he would for life.
Do not consider someone truly wise if he subjects his mind to fear for the sake of this temporal life.
Consider all the good and bad things that happen to the body to be dreams.
For it is not only through death that you will be released from them; often, even before death, they leave you and pass away.
But if there are things in which your soul shares, consider those your everlasting possessions,
for they will go with you into the world to come. If they are good, rejoice and thank God in your mind.
But if they are bad, grieve and sigh, and seek relief from them while you are still in the body.
As for every good thing done for you, openly or secretly, be certain
that baptism and faith have been the means through which it came to you—those through which you were called in Jesus Christ to good works.
To him, his Father, and the Holy Spirit be glory, honor, and worship, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.
The first discourse is finished.
The second discourse.
The recipient’s gratitude encourages the giver to give gifts greater than the first.
Whoever is ungrateful for small things is also dishonest and unjust in great things.
A sick person who recognizes his illness is easily treated, and someone who acknowledges his pain is close to recovery.
The pains of a hard heart will multiply, and the suffering of a sick person who rebels against the physician will increase.
There is no sin without forgiveness except the one that remains without repentance.
And there is no gift that remains without increase except the one that lacks thanksgiving.
The fool, it is said, sees his portion as small.
Always remember those who surpass you in virtue, so that you may always see yourself as inferior in comparison with them.
And always consider the severe afflictions of those whose troubles are harsh and grievous,
so that you may give thanks for the small troubles that come your way and be able to endure them joyfully.
When you are overcome, brought low, and weary,
and are bound and shackled to your enemy in miserable wretchedness and in the wearisome service of sin,
bring to mind your former times of diligence, and how you showed care even in the smallest things,
and were stirred with zeal against the obstacles to your progress, and poured out sighs over
the small things you happened to neglect; and you would crown your whole self with victory over them.
Then, through these and similar memories, your soul will awaken as though from the depths,
and clothe itself in the flame of zeal. It will rise from its submerged state as though from the dead,
raise itself up, and return to its former position in the fervent struggle against Satan and sin.
Remember the fall of the mighty, so that you may be humble about your virtues.
And remember the gravity of the sins of those who fell and repented, and the exaltation and honor they received afterward,
so that you may take courage in your repentance. Persecute yourself, and your enemy will be driven from your presence.
Make peace with yourself, and heaven and earth will be at peace with you.
Strive to enter the treasury within you, and you will see the one in heaven.
This one and that one are one, and through a single entrance you will see them both.
The ladder to that kingdom is hidden within you, within your soul.
Dive into yourself, away from sin, and there you will find the steps by which you may ascend.
The Scriptures have not explained what the things of the world to come are.
But how we may receive a sense of their delight even now,
without a change of nature or a change of place, they have plainly taught us.
And although, to encourage us, they have given them the beloved names of glorious things that we find pleasant and beautiful,
by saying, “The eye has not seen, and the ear has not heard,” and so on—but [?] resemblance
Without mentioning any of the things here, he made known to us the things to come.
Spiritual enjoyment, that is, is not the use of independently existing things
that exist outside the selves of those who receive them and are to be received in the state prepared for us.
Otherwise, what of the sayings, “The kingdom of heaven is within you,” and “Your kingdom come”?
Do we then possess within ourselves the substance of sensible things as a pledge of the enjoyment found in them?
For the pledge must necessarily bear a resemblance to those things, even if here it is only partial, while there it is entirely complete.
For even the expression “as in a mirror” necessarily indicates a resemblance, though not an actual substantial presence.
But if, according to the reliable testimonies of the interpreters of Scripture,
it is an intelligible activity of the Holy Spirit, and this is a part of that activity in its entirety,
then nothing but spiritual activity, known through intellectual perception, comes between it and them.
And there is nothing sensible there that mediates the enjoyment of the saints between the senses and those who perceive,
apart from the spaces that contain everything within limits. For even if we speak of an outpouring of light, it is not endowed with understanding.
A lover of virtue is not someone who diligently does good things,
but someone who joyfully accepts the troubles that accompany them.
It is not so great a thing for someone to endure afflictions for the sake of virtue
as it is for the mind not to be turned aside from its good and freely chosen purpose by seductive enticements.
For every repentance that follows an arrogant exercise of freedom
produces no joy, nor is it counted as recompense for the deeds that preceded it.
Cover the sinner, provided you suffer no harm through him. Rather, encourage him toward life, so that the mercy of the Lord may carry you.
Support the weak and the distressed in spirit with words, as far as you are able, so that the right hand that carries all things may support you.
Share with the sorrowful in the suffering of prayer and heartfelt grief, and the fountain of compassion will open before your petitions.
Exert yourself in constant supplication before God, with a heart bearing a pure thought full of sorrow,
and he will guard your mind from filthy thoughts, so that the way of God may not become contemptible in your eyes.
Occupy your sight with constant attention to discerning reading, lest through idleness some alien image be imprinted on your vision.
Do not put your mind to the test, as though conducting an experiment, by contemplating the shameful thoughts that tempt you.
While you think that you cannot be defeated, even the wise have become confused at this point and gone astray.
Do not carry a flame in your lap, as has been said. Without severe bodily hardships,
it is difficult for the undisciplined nature of youth to submit to the yoke of chastity.
When a sign of the beginning of the mind’s darkening appears in the soul, this is what it is:
it begins first with listlessness toward worship and prayer.
For there is no other way for a path toward confusion to be opened in the soul unless it first falls away from these things, so that,
when it is deprived of divine help, which flows to it from there,
it easily falls into the hands of its enemies. And another thing:
when it no longer cares about the things of virtue, it will inevitably be swept toward their opposites.
Departure from either side is the beginning of movement toward the opposite side.
The practice of virtue will become hard for the soul, and you will reflect on it, and so on. Show your weakness before God at all times,
so that strangers do not test your strength when you are left alone, away from your helper. The work of the cross is twofold.
This corresponds to the twofold character of our nature, which is divided into two parts:
the endurance of bodily hardships, which is accomplished through the activity of the soul’s spirited part and is called [?] practical action;
and the subtle work of the understanding in divine matters, persistence in prayer, and so on,
which is carried out through the desiring part and is called contemplation.
The one purifies the part subject to passions through the power of zeal.
The other clarifies the understanding part through the activity of the soul’s love, which is its natural longing.
Therefore, anyone who, before being trained in the first part, steps into the second because of its sweetness,
eagerly—not to say lazily—should expect wrath to blow against him. For, without first
putting to death his members that are on earth—that is, healing the sickness of his thoughts by enduring the toil and [?] of the cross—
he has dared to contemplate in his mind the glory of the cross [?]. This is what was said by the saints of old:
if the mind wishes to ascend the cross before the senses themselves have ceased to be weak,
the wrath of God comes upon it. By the ascent to the cross that brings about wrath,
he does not mean that first part, the endurance of hardships, which is the crucifixion of the body;
But to the ascent of contemplation, which is the second part, the one that comes after the healing of the soul.
For, it is said, anyone whose mind is stained with shameful passions,
yet rushes to ponder in his heart the glittering images of thoughts about things to come, is silenced by a blow to the head.
For without first purifying his mind through the hardships of subduing the desires of the flesh,
he has rushed ahead, on the strength of hearsay and ink, to travel a road full of darkness while the pupils of his eyes are blind.
Even those whose sight is healthy and full of light, and who have grace as their guide, are in danger of [?].
Their eyes are filled with tears, and they join night to day in prayer and weeping because of the danger of the journey,
the formidable cliffs they encounter, and the forms of truth that are found in abundance along the road together with their imitations.
The things of God, it is said, come of their own accord, without your being aware,
if the place of the heart is pure and undefiled. If you have not purified
the little pupil of your soul, do not dare to stare at the sun’s disk, lest you be deprived even of your ordinary sight,
which is simple faith, humility, heartfelt thanksgiving,
and the little work that is within your strength, and be thrown into one of the spiritual regions:
the darkness outside God, like the man who dared to enter the banquet in filthy clothes.
From toil and vigilance—and vigilance—springs purity of thoughts.
And from purity of thoughts comes illumination of the mind.
From there, the intellect is guided by grace toward something that the senses have no power either to teach or to learn.
Think of virtue as the body, and contemplation as the soul.
Together they are one complete spiritual person, united from perceptible and intelligible parts.
And just as [?] the soul cannot come into existence and be born without the body’s formation being completed with all its organs,
so contemplation, the second soul, which is the spirit of revelations, cannot
be formed in the womb of the mind that receives the substance of the spiritual seed,
without the bodily practice of virtue, the dwelling of the knowledge that receives revelations.
Contemplation is the perception of the divine mysteries hidden in the things being spoken of.
But whenever you hear of withdrawal from the world, or abandonment of the world, or purity from the world, you must first learn
And know—not superficially, but through thoughtful reflection—what the designation “world” means and how many distinct elements make up this name.
Then you will be able to know for yourself how far you are removed from the world or how closely you are involved with it.
Unless a person first knows what the world is, he cannot even understand in how many of his members he is distant from it and in how many he is entangled in it.
There are many who, because they have restrained themselves from the world in two or three things,
have imagined themselves to be entirely outside it in their way of life,
because they have not understood and wisely recognized that, although they are dead to the world in one or two members,
the rest of their members are alive within the body of the world. Consequently, they have not even been able to recognize their passions.
And because they have not recognized them, they have not concerned themselves with curing them.
From the standpoint of contemplative examination, “world” is a collective name applied to the various passions.
When we wish to name the passions collectively, we call them “the world.”
But when we speak of them individually, we call them “passions,” distinguishing them by their particular names. The passions are parts of the ongoing course of the world.
Where the passions have ceased, there the world has stopped its course. These passions are: love of wealth;
accumulating possessions; fattening the body, from which comes the impulse of sexual passion;
love of honors, which is the source of envy; exercising leadership; the arrogance and pride of power;
self-adornment; human praise, which is a cause of resentment; fear for the body.
Where these have stopped their course, there, to the extent that a person has withdrawn from them, the world has ceased to exist and come to a stop.
It is so with each of the saints: while alive, they are dead.
They are indeed alive in the body, but they do not live according to the flesh. See which of these things you are alive in,
and then you will know in how many respects you are alive to the world and in how many you are dead.
Once you have learned what the world is, these distinctions will also teach you how deeply you are entangled in it or how free you are from it.
In short, the world is a bodily way of life and a fleshly mindset.
For rising above it is also recognized by these two things: a change in one's way of life and a difference in one's inner impulses.
From the promptings of your mind concerning the things among which its impulses wander, you can discern the measure of your way of life:
what your nature longs for without effort, which promptings are constant, and which are stirred by chance circumstances;
and whether your mind has fully acquired awareness of immaterial impulses or moves entirely on a material level.
And its material character is [?]; or rather, they are impressions of bodily activity,
through which the mind is drawn, against its will, to the things by means of which it practices the virtues.
And from these it readily takes an occasion for fervor and for the gathering
of thoughts, which the mind, with a good intention, knows how to carry out bodily—bodily—because of its lack of training, even if not passionately.
And if the mind does not [?] in its hidden encounters with the impressions of thoughts because of its intense fervor in God,
which habitually cuts off idle memories. These few indications in this chapter
are enough to enlighten a person, if he is mature and discerning, in place of many books. Fear for the body is powerful in a person,
so much so that he often holds back from glorious and honorable things because of it.
But when fear for the soul presses upon this fear, it is overcome before it, like wax before the power of a flame.
The second discourse is ended.
The third discourse.
Every soul that does not add the further anxiety of accumulating possessions to its natural concerns
needs little attention to discover, from itself and within itself, intimations of wisdom concerning God.
Its withdrawal from the world naturally awakens a stirring of insights within the soul,
through which you will rise toward God, and we will remain in wonder.
When waters from outside do not enter the soul’s spring, the waters that well up from its own nature will be
wondrous insights, continually stirred toward God. Whenever,
therefore, you find yourself outside this state, either the soul has taken its prompting from an alien memory,
or the senses have stirred up disturbance within it through encounters with things.
But when the senses have been fenced in by uninterrupted stillness, and memories fade with the help this provides,
then you will see what the natural character of the soul’s thoughts is,
and what the soul’s nature is, and what treasures are stored within it.
These treasures are immaterial insights that spring up of themselves, without attention or labor being devoted to them.
A person does not even know that thoughts like these can be stirred within human nature,
or who became his teacher, or how he discovered something that he cannot even describe to his companion, though he knows it.
And who was his guide in what he did not learn from another? This is the nature of the soul.
The passions, then, are an addition to the soul arising from external causes. By its nature, however, it is not subject to passions.
Whenever you find bodily and spiritual passions mentioned somewhere in the writings, they are described according to their causes.
The soul, for its part, has no passions by nature. The pagan philosophers, however, do not believe this.
Likewise, neither do those who follow their way of thinking.
But we believe this: God did not make his image subject to passions.
By his image I do not mean the body, but the soul, which is not
visible. In every image, the likeness of its model is depicted.
A visible image cannot depict the likeness of something invisible.
Therefore we believe that the passions of the soul are not natural, as they claim.
But if anyone disputes this, we ask him to tell us:
Which condition is natural to the soul: to be free of passions and full of light,
or to be stirred by passions and darkened? Now, if there was a time when the soul’s nature was clear
and receptive to the blessed light, then whenever it returns to its original created state, it will be found in this same condition.
But when it is stirred by passions, all the members of the church acknowledge that it has departed from its natural state.
The passions, then, entered the soul’s nature afterward. It is not right to regard them as passions belonging to the soul at all.
For although the soul is stirred by them, it has become clear that it is stirred by something external to itself, not by something of its own.
And if these things are considered natural to it because it is stirred by them on account of the body,
then hunger, thirst, and sleep also belong to the soul, because through them it suffers and finds rest along with the body.
So too do the severing of limbs, fevers, pains, illnesses, and the rest, because the body suffers these things in its union with the soul,
and the soul suffers with it, is moved to joy by the body’s experiences, and receives distress from its afflictions.
What is natural to the soul, what is outside its nature, and what is above its nature.
What belongs naturally to the soul is the understanding of all created things, both those perceived by the senses and those apprehended by the mind.
Above its nature is its soaring in divine contemplation.
Outside its nature is its being stirred by passions.
Look, Basil too, the light of the world, clothed in victory, says this: “When the soul is in its natural order [?],
it is found above. But when it is [?] its nature, it is below and on earth.
There are therefore no passions above, where the soul’s dwelling place is also said to be.
But when nature descends below its proper order, then it becomes subject to passions.”
Where, then, are the soul’s passions, since it has become clear that they do not belong to its nature?
Thus the soul is stirred by the blameworthy passions in the body, just as it also experiences hunger and thirst because of the body.
But because no laws have been laid down concerning these, it is not blameworthy.
Even among those things that are subject to condemnation, there are times when a person is commanded by God to do them.
And instead of condemnation and blame, he receives a good reward. So it was with the prophet Hosea, who entered into an unlawful marriage,
and with Elijah, who resorted to killing out of zeal for God, and with those who, at Moses’ command, stabbed their relatives with swords.
But they say again: “Anger and fury belong naturally to the soul,
apart from those things that belong to the body’s nature; these,” they say, “are its passions.” Second Question.
And we ask: When the soul’s desire is set ablaze by divine things, is this the desire that belongs to its nature, or is it rather
desire for earthly and bodily things? And on behalf of what must the soul’s nature be zealous for this to be called anger, or natural anger?
Is it when it acts on behalf of bodily desire, envy, glory, and the rest, or, rather, when it acts against these things?
Let whoever disputes this answer us about these things, and we too will follow him.
For holy Scripture says many things with reference to a particular subject.
And it often applies figurative names to the soul that properly belong to the body.
And it often applies to the body things that belong to the soul, without distinguishing them, so that the discussion will not become lengthy.
But discerning people understand what they read—that is, the intention of Scripture.
For example, it applies things belonging to our Lord’s divinity to his humanity in an exalted and lofty manner:
things that are not appropriate to human nature, and things that are not appropriate to his divinity.
And many who did not understand the intention of Scripture’s words have stumbled here into a [?] from which there is no rising.
The same applies to these things concerning soul and body. Now, if virtue is the soul’s natural health,
then the passions are like diseases that assail its nature, afflicting it and depriving it of its health:
It is well known that health is naturally prior to the onset of illnesses.
And if this is so, as indeed it truly is, then virtue
is necessarily natural to the soul, while its afflictions are contrary to nature.
For it is impossible that what is [?] should not be natural.
Third question. Are bodily passions placed in the body naturally, or are they borrowed?
And in the soul [?], are those that arise because of the body borrowed or natural?
But we cannot say that the passions of the body are contrary to nature.
As for the soul, since it is known and acknowledged by everyone that purity is natural to it,
no one dares to say here that it is subject to passions otherwise than by borrowing them.
For illness is acknowledged to be secondary to health. And it is impossible for one and the same nature to be both good and evil.
For one of the two must necessarily precede the other. Whichever is older is the natural one.
Anything accidental is not said to arise from nature itself and does not belong to it, but intrudes from outside.
And every accidental condition and intrusion is eventually accompanied by alteration and change.
Nature, however, does not change or alter. All the passions that exist are given for the benefit of each of the natures,
to which they belong naturally, and were given by God for their growth.
Bodily passions were placed in the body by God for its benefit and growth.
And the passions of the soul—that is, the powers of the soul—are for the soul’s growth and benefit.
Whenever the body is forced to leave its own susceptibility to passions, by being deprived of them, and to follow those of the soul, it is harmed.
And whenever the soul abandons what belongs to it and follows what belongs to the body, it is harmed.
For, as the apostle says, the spirit desires what harms the body,
and the body desires what harms the spirit. The two are opposed to one another in their natural properties.
Therefore, let no one blaspheme against God by saying that he placed passions and sin in our nature.
For in each of the natures that he fashioned, he placed what promotes its growth.
And whenever one desires the other, it finds itself not in what belongs to it, but in what does not belong to it.
And if these passions belong naturally to the soul, why is it harmed whenever it makes use of them?
The properties belonging to a nature do not harm that nature.
And why does satisfying the bodily passions bring growth and strength to the body?
And why do those of the soul harm the soul, if they belong to it?
And why does virtue torment the body but nourish the soul?
You have seen how something outside nature [?] harms each of these natures.
For each nature rejoices when it draws near to what belongs to it.
Do you want to know what properties belong to each of these natures?
Observe each of them: the things that benefit it when it uses them belong to it.
And where it suffers, know that it is involved with things that do not belong to it. This is the rule.
If, then, you have learned [?] that the passions of these two natures are opposed to one another,
then whatever benefits and comforts the body, when the soul uses it, should not be considered proper to the soul’s own nature [?].
For the things belonging to the soul’s nature are death to the body. Rather, these bodily things are imposed on the soul as borrowed things. Because of
the weakness of the flesh, however, the soul cannot free itself from them completely as long as it is clothed in the flesh.
For its nature shares in the flesh’s afflictions because its impulses are united with it,
woven into its bodily senses by that wisdom which cannot be fathomed.
Nevertheless, even though they are mingled in this way, their impulses remain distinct from one another, and one will remains distinct from the other.
That is, the flesh’s will is distinct from the spirit’s. Nature is not confused at all, nor does it [?] what belongs to it.
Rather, even if someone brings these two into very close agreement through sin or virtue,
each of them, at times, stirs its own will and flutters toward what belongs to it.
But when concern for the body is lifted in some measure, then the soul’s impulses awaken wholly and entirely in the spirit,
and swim in the heart of heaven among things beyond comprehension.
Yet the body does not cease remembering what belongs to it. Even so, just as not even when they are in sin
do the good things of the soul cease stirring in the mind. What purity of mind is.
A person pure in mind is not someone who knows nothing of evil. Otherwise, he would be an animal.
Nor do we call those whom nature has left at the level of childhood pure in mind.
Otherwise, we do not even demand from people the standard of outsiders.
Rather, purity of mind is absorption in divine things, which comes after the many virtues a person has practiced.
We do not even dare to say that such a person has acquired this without experiencing opposing thoughts.
Otherwise, he would not even be clothed in a body. But we do not remove opposing forces from
nature before the world to come. By the experience of thoughts,
I do not mean surrendering to them, but the beginning of the struggle with thoughts that is stirred up in the mind
by the four general causes appointed to stir up every kind of passion.
Thus no one can be found in this life who is above base recollections.
These may be only the beginnings of struggles, even if, like Paul, he considers himself perfect.
But while the body acts through its impulses according to the natural order, and the world through its natural objects by the operation of the senses,
and the soul through thoughts, recollections, and its powers of inclination, and demons through stirring up the things just mentioned,
through these four the provocation of the passions clamors at him; yet he, though slightly disturbed,
is carried away toward higher and higher things perceived in the understanding.
Judge for yourself whether any one of these four can cease before the world passes away, or before departure through death.
Or whether the body can rise completely above its needs, so that nature does not compel it to seek any of the things here.
But if it is absurd to think this while these things remain,
then passions must also be stirred up in everyone clothed in a body, and everyone is obliged to be vigilant.
By passions I do not mean just one or two, but every variety of passion, as is fitting for those clothed in flesh.
Unless, however, someone dares, because of the weakness of
his impulses and the scarcity of his struggles—whoever he may be—to say that there is no need for toil and great vigilance.
What is the difference between purity of mind and purity of heart?
Purity of mind is one thing, and purity of heart is another.
It is like the difference between one part of the whole body and the entire body.
The mind is one of the soul’s senses. The heart, however, holds the inner senses together.
That is, it is the sense of the senses, which is the root. And if the root is holy, so are all the branches.
But it is not so when it is sanctified, even in one of its branches.
The mind, however, through a little engagement with the Scriptures and a little effort in fasting and stillness,
forgets its former preoccupation and becomes clear when it keeps away from alien concerns.
Yet it is also easily defiled. The heart, however, through great afflictions
and withdrawal from all involvement with the world, together with complete deadness to everything, is purified.
Once it has been purified, its purity is not defiled by encounters with trivial things.
That is, its purity is not afraid even of fierce battles. For it has acquired a healthy stomach,
which easily digests all foods that are difficult for others whose consciences are sick.
For physicians say that any meat-based food that is difficult to digest
gives greater strength to a healthy body when it is taken into a strong stomach.
Likewise, every purification that comes about easily and in a
short time, with little effort, is also easily defiled.
But purity that is acquired through great afflictions and over a long time,
and in each part of the soul, is not afraid of minor encounters with things.
Restrained senses bring peace to the soul, because they do not allow it to experience combat.
For as long as it receives no sensation of anything, it has victory [?] without a struggle.
But neglecting to persevere in not knowing, and then, after a sensation has entered, struggling to be free of it,
destroys the former things: the serenity and innocence that belong to nature.
For most people—or perhaps even the whole world—leave that place with this intention.
One among many is found who has returned to his place by the second way.
But simplicity is far better than the various forms of forgiveness.
Fear is useful to human nature for keeping it from crossing the boundary of the commandment.
Love, however, serves to stir in it a longing for good things, for whose sake it is urged on to practice good deeds.
Spiritual knowledge comes into being after the practice of virtue.
But love and fear precede both of them. Fear also precedes love.
But anyone who rashly tries to acquire the later things before the earlier ones undoubtedly lays within himself a foundation for destruction.
For God has arranged them in this sequence, so that these should be born from those.
Do not exchange love for your neighbor for love of things, for the One who is more precious than everything is hidden within him. What a physical object
is to bodily eyes, a passion-driven need is to inward vision.
And what the order of the dark clouds of the passions is to the second natural contemplation, the same
is this contemplation to natural integrity. And so they stand in relation to one another, up to that in which the succession of contemplations ends.
When the mind stands in natural integrity, it is engaged in contemplation of the angels,
which is the first natural contemplation. This same contemplation is also called the naked mind.
But when it is engaged in the second natural knowledge, it sucks milk from bodily breasts and is nourished by it.
This is called the outermost garment of the order mentioned earlier, which is placed after purification,
so that the mind should enter it first. It is itself earlier in coming into being, for it is the first order of knowledge,
but last in honor. For this reason it is also called secondary. It is like the outlines of letters,
through which the mind is purified and trained to ascend to that second order,
which is the perfection of the movements of the understanding and the order nearest to divine contemplation.
The senses are the mind’s outermost garment. Its nakedness is its activity in contemplations without material objects.
Let go of small things so that you may find precious things. Be dead while alive, and do not live in death.
Give yourself over to dying in diligence, and not to living under condemnation.
It is not only those who accept death for faith in Christ who are martyrs,
but also those who die for keeping his commandments.
Do not be petty in your requests, lest you dishonor God without knowing it.
Learn to pray wisely, so that you may be found worthy of glorious things. Ask for precious things from the One who does not withhold,
so that you may receive honor from him because of the wise choice of your will.
Solomon asked for wisdom, and received earthly kingship along with it,
because he wisely knew how to ask—that is, to ask a king for great things.
Elisha asked for twice as much of the spirit that was upon his master, and his request was not withheld from him.
Israel sought contemptible things and received God's wrath.
He gave up marveling at God's works and the wonders of his deeds, and asked for what his belly craved.
While their food was still in their mouths, God's wrath rose against them.
Present your requests to God in keeping with his glory, so that your honor before him may increase and he may rejoice in you.
Just as someone who asks a man, a king[?], for a measure full of dung will not only be despised himself because of the contemptible nature of his request,
since he has condemned himself as ignorant, but has also offered an insult to the king through his foolish petition,
so it is with anyone who asks God for bodily things in prayer.
Look: the angels and archangels, who are the king's high officials,
watch you at the time of prayer to see what petition you will present to their Lord.
They marvel at you when they see a bodily being who has abandoned his filth and asked for heavenly things. Do not ask God for that
which he takes care to give us even without our petitioning him.
He gives not only to the members of his household, but even to those who are complete strangers to the knowledge of him,
and does not withhold it from those who do not even know that he exists. “Do not babble like the pagans,” he says.
What does “like the pagans” mean? “It is the nations of the earth,” he says, “that seek these bodily things.”
“But you,” he says, “must not worry about what we will eat, what we will drink, or what we will wear.”
“Your Father,” he says, “knows that you too need these things.” A son never asks his father for bread;
rather, he presents a petition for the great portions that are his in his father's house.
As for our Lord's command to ask in prayer for daily bread, this is a request he handed down for people in general because of the weakness of their understanding.
But look at what he commands those who are mature in knowledge and sound in soul: “Do not even worry,” he says, “about food or clothing.”
“If God takes care of the bird that does not toil,” he says, “how much more will he take care of you!”
But seek the kingdom and righteousness from God, and he will give you these other things as extras.
If he is slow to grant your request, so that you ask and do not readily receive, do not be distressed.
For you are not wiser than God. But whenever you remain in such a condition,
it is either because your conduct does not match your requests, or because the ways of your heart differ from the aim of your prayer,
not because of your hidden stature, which is that of a child compared with the greatness of the matter.
It is not right that great things should easily
fall into our hands, lest God's gift be undervalued because of the ease of obtaining it.
Whatever is easy to obtain is also easily lost.
Whatever is obtained through toil is guarded carefully. Thirst for Jesus, so that he may make you drunk with his love.
Close your eyes to the world's honors, so that you may be worthy for the peace that comes from God to reign in your heart.
Fast from enticing things that delight the eyes, so that you may be worthy of joy in the Spirit.
If your conduct is not worthy of God, do not ask him for glorious things, lest you appear like someone who puts God to the test.
Prayer, properly speaking, corresponds to one's conduct.
No one longs for heavenly things while bound by self-chosen bonds for the body's sake.
And no one asks for these divine things while preoccupied with earthly things. Everyone's desire is known from their deeds.
And whatever concerns someone, they are also eager to ask for it in prayer.
And whatever someone prays for, they are also eager to express in their outward actions.
Whoever is intent on great things does not concern himself with lesser things. Be free even while you are bound in the body,
and in your freedom show yourself a servant for Christ's sake. Be shrewd in your innocence, so that you are not deceived.
Love humility in your conduct, so that you may escape the unseen snares
that are always found outside the paths along which the humble walk.
Do not reject afflictions, for through them you will enter into knowledge.
Do not fear trials, for through them you will find precious things.
Pray that you may not enter into trials affecting the soul. But prepare yourself with all your strength for those affecting the body,
and swim through them with all your limbs. For without them you cannot draw near to God.
For divine rest lies within them. Whoever flees from trials flees from virtue.
Not from temptations involving desires, but from afflictions.
And how does the saying, “Pray that you may not enter into temptation,” agree with the saying, “Strive to enter through the narrow gate,”
and, “Do not fear those who kill the body,” and, “Whoever loses his life for my sake will find it”?
Everywhere our Lord urges us toward trials, yet here he commands us to pray that we may not enter them.
What virtue is perfected without trials? Or what trial is more severe than destruction,
which he commands us to undergo for his sake? “Whoever does not take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me.”
And he says, “Pray that you do not enter into temptation.” Yet throughout his teaching, entering into trials is woven everywhere.
And he said that without trials the kingdom of [?] cannot be found. Oh, how narrow is the path of your teaching, our Lord!
Anyone who does not read with knowledgeable discernment always remains outside it in his understanding.
When the sons of Zebedee and their mother asked him for seats beside him in the kingdom, this was what he required of them:
whether they could joyfully accept the cup of trials. “Can you drink
the cup that I drink, and be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized?” How, then, do you command here, “Pray that you do not enter,”
our Lord? What trials should we pray not to enter? Pray that you do not enter into a trial of your faith.
Pray that you do not enter into temptation through presumption in your mind, together with the demon of blasphemy and pride.
Pray that you are not abandoned to enter into outward trials affecting the senses, which Satan knows how to bring upon you
when God gives him permission because of the foolish thoughts you have entertained.
Pray that the witness of chastity does not depart from you, leaving you to be tempted by the flames of sin without him.
Pray that you do not enter into a temptation to blaspheme anything. Pray, then, that you do not enter into trials of the soul,
that is, those that place the soul amid struggle, doubts, and provocations.
But prepare yourself with your whole body for bodily trials.
Plunge into them with all your limbs, your eyes full of tears, so that you may be found in them together with your guardian.
Without trials, however, God's providential care is not experienced, and confidence before him is not acquired;
the wisdom of the Spirit is not learned, and the love of God is not established in the soul.
Before trials, a person prays to God like a stranger.
But once he has entered into afflictions out of love for him and has not changed,
then, like someone who has placed God under some obligation, he is regarded as a member of his household
and a friend who has fought for his will against the power of his enemies. This is the meaning of
“Pray that you do not enter—enter into temptation.” And again, pray that you do not enter into trials because of your arrogance,
but because you love God, so that his power may triumph in you.
Pray that you do not enter into these things because of the folly of your thoughts and deeds,
but rather so that you may be shown to be a lover of God, and so that his power may be glorified through your endurance.
On our Lord’s compassion in this matter: how he measured his words according to human weakness.
Again, in this matter he spoke compassionately, if you consider it, even concerning bodily things,
taking account of the weakness of human nature, lest, because of the frailty of the body,
a person should be unable to stand firm against the onslaught of trials when caught in their midst, and because of this should even fall away from the truth, overcome by afflictions.
Therefore he commands us that, as far as possible, no one should willingly give himself over to entering into trial.
And not only this, but also: “Pray earnestly that you may not find yourselves in it even under compulsion, if it is possible for you to please God without it.”
But if a very great virtue becomes imperative, and trials accompany it, even if they are terribly frightening,
and that virtue[?] cannot be brought to completion unless a person accepts them, at such a time we must not show partiality to ourselves or to anyone else.
Nor should you abandon out of fear that great deed in which the life of your soul lies, and take as a cover
for slackness the saying, “Pray that you do not enter into trial.” These are the people of whom it is said that they sin against the commandments contemptuously.
And again, if a situation arises in which one of God’s commandments is about to be broken by someone—whether a covenant of chastity,
or the way of life of holiness, or the confession of faith, or bearing witness to the word of God,
or carefully observing the other boundaries of the law—and there is no way for him to avoid falling if he shrinks from trials,
then let him, with complete confidence, disregard the body, entrust himself to God, and enter in the name of the Lord.
And he who was with Joseph in the land of Egypt and was a witness to chastity,
and with Daniel in the lions’ den, and with Hananiah and his companions in the fiery furnace,
and beside Jeremiah in the muddy pit, and rescued him and granted him mercy in the midst of the Chaldean camp,
and with Peter in prison, and brought him out through locked gates, and with Paul in the gatherings of the Jews,
and, in short, who was with his servants in every generation, in every place and [?],
and showed his power through them, made them victorious, and protected them in a greatly wondrous way, so that they plainly saw his deliverance at the time of their afflictions—
he will strengthen and protect this person in the midst of the storms that surround him.
Let him therefore take into himself the zeal of the Maccabees against the invisible enemy and his servants,
and be like the rest of the holy prophets, apostles, martyrs, confessors, and solitary monks;
who upheld the divine laws and the commandments of the Spirit in fearsome places and in difficult trials
and grievous ones, and cast the world and the body behind them.
They persevered in their steadfastness and did not succumb to the oppression that bore down on body and soul alike, but triumphed courageously.
And look, the names of a few out of many are recorded in the book of life until the coming of our Lord.
Their histories are preserved in writing at God's command, for our instruction and encouragement,
according to the testimony of the blessed apostle, so that through them we may become wise and learn God's way,
as we place their stories like pictures of life before the eyes of our minds,
and take an example from them, patterning the ways of our conduct after them, with those of old as our model.
Divine speech is pleasant to the discerning soul, like rich food that transforms the body is to the palate of the healthy.
The stories of the righteous are delightful to the ears of the blameless, like constant watering to new plants.
Let the account of God's providence, which he exercised toward the people of old, be precious to you,
like costly medicines for eyes with impaired sight. Keep their memory with you at every hour of the day.
Study them, reflect on them, and gain wisdom through them, so that you may learn to hold the memory of God's greatness in honor within your soul.
And you will find eternal life for yourself in Jesus Christ, the mediator between God and humanity, united in both his natures.
Although the legions of angels cannot gaze upon the glory surrounding the throne of his majesty,
he appeared to the world for your sake, despised and lowly as a man, having neither beauty nor splendor. He
whose invisibility does not fall within the perception of created and made beings,
carried out his saving plan through the doorway made from our bodily members, for the salvation of the life of all.
This is the one through whom he purified many nations. And the Lord laid upon him the sins of us all, according to the word of Isaiah.
And the Lord wished to humble him and make him suffer. Sin was laid upon his soul, though he knew no sin.
For his saving work throughout all generations for our sake,
to him be glory, praise, thanksgiving, and worship from all, now and always, and forever and ever. Amen.
The third discourse is finished.
The fourth discourse.
The soul that loves God finds its rest in God alone.
First release yourself from outward bonds, and then strive to bind your heart to God.
Release from material things comes before attachment to God.
After a child is weaned from milk, it is then offered bread to eat.
Likewise, a person who wishes to grow in virtue before God must first wean himself from the world, like a child weaned from its mother's breasts.
Bodily labors come before the work of the soul, just as, in coming into being,
the creation of the body comes before that of the soul. For whoever has no bodily labors has no
labors of the soul either. These are born from those, just as an ear of grain grows from bare seeds.
Whoever has no work of the soul is also deprived of the gifts of the Spirit.
Temporary sufferings endured for the truth cannot compare with the delight prepared for those who labor in virtue.
Just as joyful sheaves follow the tears of sowing, so joy follows labors undertaken for God's sake.
Bread earned by sweat is sweet to the farmer, and labors undertaken for righteousness are sweet to the heart that has received the knowledge of Christ.
Endure contempt humbly, with a virtuous attitude, for the sake of confidence of heart before God.
For every hardship that someone endures with discernment, without its being caused by his own wrongdoing,
he receives a crown of thorns on his head for Christ's sake, and blessed is he. He too is crowned at a time he does not know.
Whoever knowingly flees from praise has felt within himself the hope of the world to come.
Whoever professes renunciation of the world to come, to feel within himself [?].
Whoever professes renunciation of the world but quarrels with people over things,
so that his comfort [?] may not be diminished, is completely blind.
He has willingly abandoned the whole world, yet quarrels over one part of it.
Whoever flees from the comforts of this world directs his mind toward the world to come. Whoever clings to possessions is a slave to the passions.
Do not regard only gold and silver as possessions, but also everything you cling to because your will desires it.
Whoever cuts off entanglements out of fear of the passions is truly wise.
Without constant practice of virtue, knowledge of the truth cannot
be found. Knowledge [?] of life is not acquired through bodily labors alone,
but when the aim set for those labors is to cut off the passions of the mind.
Anyone who labors without discernment easily falls when occasions for sin confront him.
Never praise someone who labors with his body but leaves his senses loose and unrestrained:
that is, his hearing, his unguarded mouth, and his wandering eyes.
When you set yourself the goal of practicing mercy in your actions,
train yourself not to insist on justice in other matters,
so that you are not seen working with one hand and scattering with the other.
For the former calls for compassion, and the latter for generosity of mind.
In these matters, let forgiving your debtors count as an act of righteousness for you.
Then you will see peace rejoicing in your mind from both sides—that is,
when you rise above obligation and justice in your conduct and make room for freedom in everything.
For one of the saints, speaking about these things, says, “A merciful person who is not just is blind.”
This means that he should provide for others out of his honest endeavors and his own labor,
and not out of possessions acquired through deceit, extortion, oppression, and trickery.
As this same man also explains elsewhere, “If you sow among the poor, sow from what is your own.
But what comes from others is more bitter than tares.” But I
say that unless a merciful person also rises above justice, he is not merciful.
That is, he should not only show mercy to people from his own possessions, but also willingly and gladly endure injustice.
He should not uphold and demand the full measure of justice in his dealings with his fellow, but should have mercy on him,
so that, by overcoming justice through mercy, he may weave himself
not the crown of the righteous under the law, but that of the perfect under the new covenant.
For a person to give to the poor from his own possessions, to clothe someone when he sees him naked,
to love his neighbor as himself, and neither to wrong anyone nor to deceive—these things were commanded even by the old law.
The perfection of conduct under the new covenant commands this: “If someone takes what is yours, do not demand it back.
And give to everyone who asks you.” You are not only to endure joyfully the wrongful taking of your possessions and other things external to you,
but also to give your life for your fellow human being. A merciful person is one who shows mercy to his neighbor not only through gifts:
But even when he hears or sees something that causes someone pain, his heart cannot bear the burning.
And even when he receives a blow from his brother, he does not dare repay him even with a word and cause his mind pain.
Value the labors of keeping vigil, so that you may find consolation close at hand within your soul.
Practice reading in stillness, so that you may be drawn toward wonder at all times.
Love poverty with perseverance, so that your mind may be gathered back from distraction.
Hate luxury, so that you may be protected from confusion of mind.
Withdraw from the company of many people and take care over your conduct, so that your soul may be delivered from disturbance of its inner stillness.
Love chastity, so that you will not be ashamed at the time of petition before the one who appoints the contest.
Acquire purity in your conduct, so that your soul may rejoice in prayer, and joy may shine in your mind at the remembrance of death.
Be steadfast in small things, so that you will not be driven away from great things.
Do not be lazy about your labors, so that you will not be ashamed when you are gathered with all your companions.
Bear your toil with understanding, so that [?] from your entire course.
Do not be without provisions, lest they leave you alone halfway along the road and depart.
Acquire freedom in your conduct, so that you may be freed from anxiety.
Do not use your freedom as a pretext for [?], lest you become a slave of slaves.
Love humiliation in your conduct, so that the thoughts that oppress you with pride and frivolity alike may be beaten back.
One who avoids dishonor cannot acquire a humble mind.
For the inward heart necessarily moves in step with outward forms of behavior.
Who has ever indulged in luxury and managed to acquire modesty of mind? Or who devises ways to win praise from outside,
yet acquires humble thoughts within himself? And who is frivolous in his outward behavior and unrestrained in his bodily movements,
yet is gentle in his heart and holy in his thoughts?
When the mind is led by the senses, it shares with them the food of animals.
But when the senses are led by the mind, they share with it the nourishment of angels.
Vainglory is the servant of sexual immorality. But when it concerns one's way of life, it is the servant of pride.
Reserve accompanies humility, while lack of restraint accompanies the love of praise.
The former, through constant recollection, encounters contemplations and equips the soul for chastity.
The latter, however, through the mind’s constant distraction, gathers filth through encounters with things and defiles the heart.
For the latter encounters the very natures of things in a base way and inflames the mind with base thoughts.
The former, however, gathers itself inward spiritually through contemplation of them and stirs its wings toward praise.
Therefore, do not compare all the miracles and signs performed throughout the whole world with someone sitting in stillness with understanding.
Love inactivity in stillness more than feeding the hungry of the world and turning a multitude of nations from error to the worship of God.
Let freeing yourself from the bonds of sin be more valuable in your eyes
than releasing captives into freedom from those who enslave their bodies.
Make peace with yourself through the harmony of the threefold nature within you:
body, soul, and spirit, rather than making peace between angry people through your teaching.
Love ignorance of words together with the knowledge of inward experience more than pouring forth
a torrent of teaching from sharpness of mind and a store of learning acquired through hearing and ink.
Be concerned to bring your soul, dead through the passions, back to life, so that it is stirred by insights into God,
rather than raising from death those who are physically dead.
There were many who performed miracles, raised the dead, labored among those in error, and performed great signs.
Through the wonder they inspired, they drew many toward God by the things that happened through their hands.
Yet afterward these people who had brought others to life fell into vile and contemptible passions.
While they gave life to others, they put themselves to death,
and in turn caused those others to stumble through the contradiction revealed in their deeds.
For while they were still sick in their own souls, they took no care for their own healing.
Instead, they gave themselves over to plunging into the sea of the world to heal the souls of others, while they themselves were still sick.
Through this purpose I have described, they lost their own hope in God,
because their weak senses could not withstand the glitter of things,
which commonly arouse the violence of the passions in those who still need watchfulness.
I mean the sight of women, comforts, money, possessions, and the passion for leadership and superiority over others.
Be despised by fools for your ignorance, rather than by the wise for your shamelessness.
Become poor for the sake of humility, and do not become wealthy through shamelessness.
Refute those who dispute with you through the power [?] of your virtues, not through words.
And through the peacefulness of your lips, silence the [?] of those who will not be persuaded, rather than through shouting.
Put the frivolous to shame by the dignity of your conduct, and those whose senses are shameless by the modesty of your eyes,
which are quietly gathered toward you. Consider yourself a stranger wherever you enter, all your days,
so that you may escape the great harms that arise from excessive familiarity.
Always give the impression that you know nothing,
so that you may be saved from the reproaches that presumption stirs up against you when you think you are capable of correcting others.
Let your mouth be constantly occupied with blessings, and no abuse from anyone will ever come upon you.
Insult produces insult, and blessing produces blessing.
Always consider yourself in need of instruction, so that you may be found wise throughout your life.
Do not pass on to others, as though it were your own, a way of life that you have not yet attained,
lest you be ashamed of yourself and your falsehood be exposed by comparison with your conduct [?].
Rather, even when you speak about what is right, speak as a student, not authoritatively,
first reproaching yourself and showing that you fall short of it,
so that you may also give your listeners an example of humility, and hearing your words may encourage them all the more
to hasten to put them into practice, and you may be honored in their eyes. As far as possible, about
such matters speak with tears, so that you may benefit both yourself and your companions and draw grace toward you.
If, by the grace of Christ, you have attained the enjoyment of the mysteries of visible created things,
which is the first stage of knowledge, arm yourself against the spirit of blasphemy.
Do not stand unarmed in this place, lest you be easily killed in secret by those who lead astray.
Let your armor be fasting and the tears you shed with continual groaning.
And beware of reading books that explain the teachings of religions with the intention, that is, of refuting them,
for this especially arms the spirit of blasphemy against the soul.
When your belly is full, do not presume to investigate, lest you regret it.
Understand what I am saying: in a full belly there is no knowledge of the mysteries of God.
Devote yourself tirelessly and without ever having enough to the writings about God’s providence composed by holy people,
which reveal the purpose of his varied works in the ordering of the world’s different natures,
so that your understanding may be strengthened by them and you may acquire luminous thoughts from their subtlety,
and your mind may travel its path clearly toward the purpose of the right ordering of the world’s creation,
in keeping with the glorious wisdom of the plan of the Creator of all natures.
Read both Testaments, which God established for the instruction of the whole inhabited world,
so that you may be supplied with strength from his guidance in every generation and be swallowed up in wonder.
These readings and others like them are especially suited to this purpose. Let your reading take place in stillness, away from everything,
free from excessive concern for the body and the disturbance of affairs, so that it may impart a delightful taste to your soul
through sweet insights beyond the senses, which the soul perceives through its constant attention to them.
Do not treat words that come from experience as though they were the inventions of word merchants,
lest you remain in darkness until the end of your life, deprived of their benefit,
and stumble about as though at night in times of battle—not to mention falling into one of the pits disguised as truth.
This will be a sign to you when you have come close to entering beyond that place:
when grace begins to open your eyes to perceive things with an accurate vision of what they are,
at that very moment your eyes begin to shed tears, until their abundance washes your cheeks,
and the agitation of the senses will grow calm, and they will withdraw pleasantly within you.
If anyone teaches you something contrary to this, do not believe him.
Apart from tears, you are not permitted to seek anything else from the body as an outward sign indicating the perception of truth,
except only the stilling of the activity of the bodily members. That is, when the mind is raised above created things,
the body will cease even from tears, from sensation, and from movement, except for its natural life.
For that knowledge does not descend to allow the forms of things belonging to the sensory world a place alongside it,
even figuratively, in the mind’s vision. “Whether in the body,” he says, “or outside the body, I do not
“I do not know; God knows,” and that he “heard words that cannot be spoken.” Yet everything heard with the ears can be spoken.
But he did not [?] through sounds perceptible to the senses, nor through a vision of bodily forms belonging to perceptible things.
Rather, it was through movements of the mind, in a rapture away from the body, without the will participating in it.
“The eye,” it says, “has never seen anything like it, and the ear has not heard its equal.”
Nor has the heart longed to recall through memory forms of its knowledge resembling that vision,
of what God has prepared to show the pure in heart when they die to the world.
It is not a bodily vision whose distinct features are received materially through eyes of flesh,
nor, again, thoughts derived from these and formed in the mind by analogy,
but the undivided contemplation of things understood and believed,
which rejects being broken into parts and distinct divisions displaying images composed of elements.
When facing the sphere of the sun, direct your gaze according to the strength of your sight, merely to enjoy its rays,
and not also to investigate the course of its orb, lest even your limited sight be taken from you.
If you find honey, eat only as much as you need, lest you become full and vomit it up.
The soul is agile by nature, and from time to time it steps beyond its bounds, longing to learn things above its nature.
And often, through the course of reading and contemplation
of things, it grasps various matters. When these are compared, the measure of its knowledge is far smaller than the extent of what it has discovered.
And how far its knowledge penetrates—until it is clothed in shaking and trembling in its thoughts!
Then it hastens to turn back out of fear, when it ventures to approach fiery things.
Fear, on the one hand, restrains it because of the terrifying nature of these things.
Discernment, on the other hand, silently signals to the soul’s understanding: “Do not venture forward, lest you die.”
Do not seek things too difficult for you, and do not investigate things beyond your strength.
“Understand,” it says, “what you have been authorized to understand; it is not for you to venture into hidden things.”
So bow down and give praise in silence, and acknowledge what cannot be comprehended.
For much that is beyond you has been shown to you; do not trouble yourself over the rest of his works.
And “it is not good to eat much honey,” nor, it says, to investigate glorious words.
Lest, when we wish to see from a high mountain, but have not yet reached its vicinity,
we grow faint from the immeasurable length of the road, and also suffer harm from the power of the sight.
For sometimes it presents mirages in place of the truth.
For when the mind grows weary from trying to comprehend, it also loses its precision.
And Solomon the wise rightly said, “Like a breached city without a wall, so is a man who lacks patience.”
There is no need to wander after God in heaven and on earth, or to strain our minds searching for him in different places. Purify your soul, human being,
and remove from yourself thoughts of memories contrary to nature. Set the doors of modesty and humility over your impulses.
Through these you can find him who is within you. For it is said, “Mysteries are revealed to the humble.”
If you have devoted yourself to the practice of prayer that purifies the mind, and to keeping continual vigil at night,
so that you may acquire a mind clothed in light, shelter your soul from the sights of the world, and cut yourself off from conversation.
Do not be willing to receive an ordinary friend inside your enclosure, not even with the intention of pursuing virtue,
except someone who shares your purpose and is your confidant in your way of life.
If you fear disturbance and the soul’s hidden inner conversation,
which habitually arises on its own without our seeking it, then cut yourself off from outward conversation as well.
Join virtues to your prayers, so that your soul may see the radiance of the dawning of truth.
The more the heart becomes still from outward memories, the more your mind will receive wonder through understanding the words.
The soul can readily exchange one occupation for another, if we show a little care and take the trouble.
Impose on it the labor of reading books that make known the subtleties of the paths of conduct,
and of contemplation, and the accounts of the saints—even if at first it feels no delight,
because of the darkness and confusion arising from recent memories—so that it may exchange one occupation for another. And when you stand for prayer
and worship, instead of dwelling on worldly matters, reflections drawn from the books will be imprinted on your mind.
Through these, the memory drawn from the books is forgotten and erased from it.
Through these, the memory of what it saw and heard a short time ago is forgotten and erased from it.
And in this way your mind will attain purity. This is what is meant by the saying:
“The soul draws its labor from reading when it comes to prayer,” and, “Through reading it will be enlightened in prayer.”
That is, instead of outward distraction, let us find nourishment for the soul through the different forms of prayer:
Precise insights flash in the mind from the wondrous recollections that come from there,
so that often they silence the mind and leave it astonished, even taking it away from prayer itself.
At these times, the power of contemplation arising from the Scriptures holds it motionless.
As I have said, this commonly interrupts prayer through its sweetness and brings stillness upon the heart,
silencing the heart’s movements by bringing the faculties of soul and body to rest.
Those who have experienced this matter in their own souls and have entered into its mysteries know what I am saying,
not through instruction received from others or things gleaned from writings, which can often misrepresent the truth.
For a full belly, investigating spiritual matters is as unfitting as speaking about chastity is for a prostitute.
A conscience full of sickness recoils from wholesome food.
And for a mind filled with the world, approaching the investigation of divine activities
is impossible. Fire does not burn in wet wood, and fervor for God does not blaze up in a heart far from comforts.
