A prostitute does not remain in love with one man, nor does a soul bound to many things persist in its love of spiritual instruction.
Just as someone who has never seen the sun with his own eyes, merely from hearing about it and pondering its light in his mind,
cannot form an image of it within himself and perceive the beauty of its rays,
so someone who has not personally tasted spiritual practice, and whose way of life has not brought him into the experience of its mysteries,
cannot, through human instruction and the study of writings, form in his mind an image resembling the truth,
find true assurance within himself, or grasp the reality of the matter.
If you possess anything beyond the day’s sustenance [?], go and give it to the poor,
and come and offer prayer with confidence. That is, speak with God as a son speaks with his father.
Nothing brings the heart close to God like compassion, and nothing gives peace to the mind like voluntary poverty.
Let many reproach you as ignorant because of your openhandedness and your boundless generosity,
practiced out of reverence for God, rather than call you wise and sensible because of your stinginess.
If someone is riding a horse and stretches out his hand, do not close your hand against him
in anything that his need truly requires. For at that moment he is in need, like any other needy person.
When you give, give generously, and let your face brighten toward the recipient.
Besides what he asked for, give him something he did not ask for as well.
“Cast your bread upon the waters,” it is said, “and after a long time you will find a reward.”
Do not distinguish between rich and poor, or between the deserving and the undeserving.
For your part, consider all people worthy of kindness.
Especially since, through these things, you draw them toward the truth.
Through bodily things, the soul is easily drawn toward a disposition of reverence for God.
He even welcomed tax collectors and prostitutes to share his table,
without setting them apart as undeserving, so that through this he might draw them toward reverence for God.
Through sharing bodily things, he sought to bring them into spiritual fellowship.
Therefore, consider all people worthy of kindness and honor, whether someone is a Jew, an unbeliever, or a murderer.
All the more so because he is your brother and shares your nature, and strays from the truth through ignorance.
Whenever you do good, do not set your mind on the goal of an immediate reward, and you will be rewarded by God in both respects.
If possible, do not do it even for the sake of a reward hereafter, so that you may advance all the more in divine love.
The degree of love is more inward even than service to God itself.
In its mystery, it is more inward than that service, even more than the soul is inward in relation to the body.
If you have already set yourself the goal of renunciation,
and by God's grace have been freed from anxiety and risen above the world through your renunciation,
take care that love for the poor does not entice you to fall into anxiety over possessions and material things,
supposedly to give alms, and to throw yourself back into turmoil:
taking from one person and giving to another, and cheapening your dignity by stooping to approach people with pleas
in pursuit of such things, falling from the height of your liberated mind back into concern for earthly things.
Your standing is higher than that of those who give alms. I beg you, do not make yourself an object of ridicule.
That is a stage in the training of childhood; this, however, is the way of perfection.
If you have anything, distribute it all at once. If you have nothing, do not long to possess anything.
Cleanse your way of life of luxuries and excess, for this will necessarily lead you to ascetic discipline.
For necessity endures many things that we are unwilling to endure voluntarily when we have the opportunity.
Those who have overcome the outward battle have also removed the inward fear.
There is no longer any compulsion driving them by force and troubling them with fighting from the front and from behind.
By the outward battle I mean the one that a person foolishly stirs up against himself through the senses.
That is, through taking and giving, hearing and seeing,
speaking and eating, and continually multiplying activities for himself, one after another, so that his soul becomes blind,
and, because of the disturbances that arise from outside, cannot see itself in the hidden struggle that is being stirred up,
or, through quiet, overcome the things that erupt from within.
But if a person secures the outskirts of the city, the fighting from then on takes place face to face.
He does not fear ambushes from behind the city.
Blessed is the person who understands these things and perseveres in stillness, without multiplying work for himself even there,
but replaces all bodily work with the labor of prayer, if he is able,
and who, between one service and the next, alongside the work of God, which is prayer and reading,
mixes nothing else with it, and believes that, while he works with God and meditates on him night and day,
God will not leave him lacking any of the necessities he needs, since it is for God's sake that he does not work.
If someone cannot persevere in stillness without working, he must work.
But he should take it up as a helper, not as something that consumes him, and as secondary to these things, not as the primary commandment.
This concession is for the weak. Evagrius calls manual work a hindrance to the remembrance of God.
The fathers prescribed work for the needy and the fainthearted, not as a binding legal obligation for the diligent.
When God opens your understanding from within, and you devote yourself to frequent kneeling, do not give your heart over to anxiety
about anything, as the demons secretly urge you to do. Then see and marvel at what these things bring forth in you.
Do not compare any other practice with lying face down before the cross night and day, with your hands turned behind your back.
Do you want your fervor never to cool and your tears never to run dry? Practice these things.
Blessed are you, O human being, if you meditate on these things I have told you and seek nothing else alongside them, night or day.
Then your light will break out like the dawn, and your righteousness will quickly shine forth.
And you will be like a flourishing garden, and like a spring of water whose waters never fail.
See how many good things a person gains through diligence.
Sometimes a person is kneeling at the time of prayer, with his hands spread out or stretched toward heaven,
and his head turned toward the cross, and, so to speak, all his inner activity and thought directed toward God in supplication.
And while a person—a person—is engaged in these supplications and sighs at that time,
suddenly a spring of delight wells up from his heart, his limbs grow weak, and his eyes close.
He lowers his face, and his thoughts are transported, so that even his knees cannot remain braced against the ground,
because of the joy of that goodness which flows through his whole body. Consider, O human being, what you are reading.
Can these things really be learned from ink? Or does the taste of honey pass into the reader’s mouth through written words? If you do not make an effort,
you will not find. And if you do not knock fervently and keep watch at the door for a long time, you will not be answered.
Who would hear these things and long for outward righteousness, except someone who cannot endure the bonds of the cell?
But if someone is incapable of these things, since being inside the door is a gift from God,
at least let him not neglect that other portion, so that he is not deprived of both portions of life.
For until the outer person dies to the affairs of the world, not only to sin,
but also to every bodily activity, and the inner person dies to the troubling memories of shameful things,
and natural impulses are also stripped away, and the body all but dies through its labors,
so that the sweetness of sin no longer flows through the heart, the Spirit of God does not work her sweetness in a person.
His limbs are not opened to life, and divine stirrings do not appear in his soul.
And until the heart ceases to concern itself with things here, apart from the necessities that nature itself demands of it in its time of need,
while leaving even these to God to provide, intoxication in the Spirit is not awakened within it.
Nor does it experience that madness for which the apostle was reproached: “Your great learning has driven you mad.”
But I do not say this to cause despair, as though, unless someone has reached the depths of perfection,
grace from God is not given to him, or consolation does not come to him.
Truly, when a person has rejected evil things, has become completely estranged from them, and has joined
for good things, he soon becomes aware of help. And if he makes a little effort,
he finds within himself the comfort of forgiveness of sins, is counted worthy of grace, and receives many good things.
Yet he is inferior, by comparison, to the person who has become completely estranged from the world
and has found within himself the mystery of the blessings of the world to come, and has attained that for which Christ took hold of us.
To him, his Father, and the Holy Spirit be glory and praise forever and ever. Amen.
The fourth discourse is finished.
The fifth discourse.
God has greatly honored the human being through the twofold instruction he has given him.
From every direction he has opened a door for him to enter into knowledge.
Seek a trustworthy witness from nature for yourself, and you will not go astray.
But if you have departed from there, learn from a second witness, and it will set you on the path from which you strayed.
A distracted heart cannot escape error, and wisdom does not open her door before it.
Anyone who can understand with certain knowledge the equal state to which the end of all human beings will bring them
needs no other teacher besides this concerning the worthlessness of the world
. The first book given by God to rational beings is the nature of created things.
Instruction in ink was added after the turning aside.
Anyone who does not willingly distance himself from the causes of sin is dragged into sin unwillingly.
The causes of sins are wine, a woman, wealth, and bodily vigor.
This is not to say that these things, in and of themselves, are called sin,
but because of human weakness and the unlawful use of them. That is, through these things more than anything else,
human nature can easily incline toward various sins, and in these matters it needs greater vigilance.
If you constantly remember and know for certain that you are weak, you will never step beyond the bounds of caution.
Among human beings, poverty [?] is despised more than anything else.
But before God, pride of heart and a contemptuous mind are even more despised.
Among human beings, wealth is honored; but before God, a humble soul.
Whenever you wish to begin practicing one of the virtues, first prepare yourself,
so that the hardships that come because of it do not make you doubt the truth. Whenever the evil one sees that someone
is beginning to practice one of the virtues with the fervor of faith, he habitually brings fierce and terrible trials upon him,
so that, frightened by these things, the love in his mind may immediately grow cold,
and he may no longer be eager to approach the works of God.
Thus, because of fear of the trials that accompany good deeds, no one would practice good deeds.
But prepare yourself to meet the hardships that accompany the virtues courageously and vigorously, and then begin.
If you do not expect hardships, do not begin practicing virtue.
The man who doubts the Lord is pursued by his own shadow. In a time of plenty, he will go hungry,
and in a time of peace, his ruin will grow severe. But the heart of the one who trusts in God will be strengthened,
and his honor will be revealed before the crowds, and his glory before his enemies.
God’s commandments are better than the treasures of the whole earth.
Whoever acquires his laws in his heart will find the Lord within them.
Whoever toils in meditation gains God as a member of his household. Whoever longs for his will will find the heavenly watchers as his teachers.
Whoever fears sins will pass without stumbling even through a dangerous place.
In a time of darkness, he will find light within himself.
The Lord guards the steps of the one who fears sins, and mercy comes before his stumbles.
But whoever considers his offenses small falls into worse ones than his earlier offenses,
and he is repaid sevenfold. Sow acts of charity in humility, and you will reap mercy at the judgment seat.
By the same means through which you lost good things, you will acquire them again.
If you owe God a small coin in some matter, he will not accept a pearl from you in its place.
For that is what is needed there. If you have lost your chastity, do not leave sexual immorality in its place
and give alms in exchange for it: he will not accept this from you. In place of holiness, he demands holiness.
Or if you have wronged the poor, do not leave the property gained through oppression in your home while you abstain from bread.
Do not leave wrongdoing in its place while you struggle against something else. Oppression is uprooted through compassion and giving away your possessions.
You have left the plant in its place and are fighting something else, as the great teacher Mar Ephrem said.
“See,” he says, “in summertime you do not fight the heat with winter clothes.”
Likewise, whatever a person has sown in wrongdoing, let him reap it by its opposite.
Meet every illness with its own medicine. You are now being killed by envy, yet you are fighting against sleep.
Uproot sin while it is still a weed, so that it does not cover the whole ground.
Anyone who turns a blind eye to evil as though it were insignificant will eventually find it a harsh master and will run before it in chains.
Anyone who boldly confronts it at the outset will easily rule over it. Whoever endures injustice with joy,
when victory is within his power, has received from God a consolation for his faith that he can actually feel.
And anyone who endures oppression with humility
has attained perfection. The angels will marvel at this person. There is no virtue harder or greater than this.
Do not believe yourself strong until you have entered into trials and found your mind unchanged amid them.
In every matter, assess yourself in this way. Take pride in the faith of your heart,
so that you may tread on the necks of your enemies and find your mind humble.
Do not rely on your strength, lest you be abandoned to the weakness of your nature and learn your weakness through your fall.
Nor rely on your knowledge, lest you become caught among thoughts of hidden stratagems and be thrown into confusion.
Acquire a humble tongue, and dishonor will never befall you. Acquire gracious lips, and you will be found to be everyone's friend.
Do not boast aloud about anything, because nothing in creation is immune to change.
Otherwise your shame may be doubled when you find yourself in the opposite condition. Whatever you boast about before other people,
God providentially changes, so that it may become an occasion for humility for you.
Thus you should attribute everything to God's knowledge and not assert that anything in creation is secure.
When you discover this, let your eyes always be fixed on him.
Providence surrounds all people at all times. Yet it is not visible
except to those who have purified themselves from sins and meditate on God at every moment. To these people it is then revealed
clearly: when they enter great trials for the sake of the truth,
then they receive an actual perception of it, as though with bodily eyes.
And when necessary, even in a way perceptible to the senses, according to the kind of trial and its cause, for greater encouragement.
As happened with Jacob, Joshua son of Nun, Hananiah and his companions, Peter, and the others:
the likeness of a man appeared to them, to encourage them and comfort them in their faith.
And if you say that these were acts of divine providence and matters of common concern, let the holy martyrs serve as encouragement for you.
These sometimes suffered for God in large groups together, and sometimes individually in various places.
Along with the hidden power through which they were strengthened in their bodily limbs,
to withstand mutilation with iron instruments and tortures of every kind—deeds beyond nature—
at times holy angels also appeared to them openly,
so that everyone might know that God's providential care is with those who endure sufferings for his sake under all circumstances,
for their own encouragement and the shame of their persecutors.
For the more the sufferers were strengthened to triumph by such a vision, the more their persecutors were tormented by their endurance.
And what shall we say about the many solitaries, strangers, and true mourners,
who made the wilderness a peaceful dwelling [?] and a place for the companies of angels who gathered with them,
because of the similarity of their ways of life? And like true fellow servants of one Lord, at all times
the heavenly companies mingled with the community [?] of these men, who loved solitude throughout their lives,
made caves and clefts in the rocks their dwellings, and readily endured desolation and wilderness for the love of God.
And because they forsook the earth and loved heaven, in imitation of the angels, the angels themselves did not withhold themselves from their sight.
Instead, at times they taught them about how to live.
At times they answered the questions they asked them about various matters.
At times, when they lost their way in the wilderness, they showed them the way. And at times they delivered them from trials.
And at times, from some onslaught of danger, [?] without their knowing, some danger suddenly assails:
when it suddenly assailed them without their knowing, they brought them out from its midst.
For example, some snake, or a fall from a cliff, or a blow from a stone that suddenly plunged down violently from some height.
And at times, amid the intensity of Satan's open attacks, they openly showed themselves to them,
clearly making known that they had been sent to help them, and offering them encouragement through their words.
And sometimes they would also provide healing for their pains and for injuries that had arisen from various causes.
By the touch of their hands they would heal them. And at other times, even to their bodies, which had been deprived of all
nourishment, they would give bodily strength through their words or through a sudden touch of the hand.
And in the weakened constitution they would secretly receive strength.
And into the weakened constitution they would secretly pour strength.
And sometimes they would bring them food: hot bread and olives.
To some they would bring various fruits, while to others they would reveal the time of their death.
And how much I have to recount about the love of the holy angels for our race,
and the extraordinary care they show toward the [?], like older brothers who tend and protect their younger brothers.
All these things are so that everyone may be assured how close God is to those who love him,
and how much care he shows toward those who entrust their lives into his hand and follow him with a pure heart.
If you are certain and believe that God watches over you,
you should not worry about your body, nor should you anxiously devise ways to provide for yourself.
But if you doubt this and seek to take care of yourself apart from God,
you are the most miserable of all people. What is the point of your even living [?]?
Cast your anxiety upon God, so that you may overcome every fear.
Whoever has once entrusted his life to God lives with peace of mind.
Without giving up possessions, the soul is not freed from the turmoil of thoughts.
And without stillness of the senses, peace of mind is not experienced. And without entering
into trials, spiritual wisdom is not acquired.
And without [?] in reading, subtlety of thought is not learned.
And without freedom from troubling thoughts, the mind is not stirred by hidden mysteries.
And without the confidence of faith, the soul does not dare to press forward amid terrors and hardships.
And without practical experience of God's care, the heart cannot trust in God.
And unless the soul tastes suffering for Christ's sake, it does not share in knowledge with him.
Consider this person a man of God: someone who, out of great compassion, constantly keeps himself in a state of need.
Whoever does good to the poor finds God caring for him, and whoever becomes needy for God's sake finds a great treasure.
God needs nothing, but he rejoices whenever someone gives relief to his image for his sake, or honors it.
Whenever someone asks you for something and you have it, do not say in your heart, “I will keep it for myself, so that I can enjoy greater comfort through it,”
or dismiss him for the moment, saying, “God will provide for this man through someone else; I will put this aside for myself.” Do not say this.
Let wicked men dwell on this, and let people who do not know God think this way and spend the night with these thoughts.
A righteous man does not give his honor to someone else, nor does he let the opportunity for kindness pass.
God will certainly make provision for that man from somewhere else, if he knows that he is in distress.
God abandons no one. But you, for the moment,
have turned God's honor away from yourself and driven his grace away from you.
Instead, [?] you have something and are giving, and say, “Glory to you, God, who have enabled me to give relief to another person as well!”
And when you have nothing, rejoice all the more, continually offering abundant thanks to God and saying:
“I thank you, God, for granting me this honor of becoming poor for your sake,
and for making me worthy to taste the suffering that you have placed on the path of your commandments,
in sickness and poverty, just as the saints who walked this path tasted it.”
And when you are sick, say, “Blessed are those who have been able, in accordance with God's appointed purpose,
to benefit from the things he brings upon us.” God brings sickness for the health of the soul.
One of the saints once said, “I have taken this as a sign: whenever a solitary does not serve God well
and is not diligent in his work, God certainly allows some trial to come upon him for him to think about,
so that he will not be entirely idle and, through his great idleness, his mind turn toward thoughts of things belonging to the left.
Rather, when he is unwilling to think about virtue, God lays upon him the task of trials,
so that he will think about it and not dwell on empty things. God does this for everyone he loves.
When he sees that someone has begun to neglect his work, he allows great suffering to come upon him to make him wise and discipline him.
For this reason, even when such people call upon him again, he holds back and does not
hurry to deliver them until they grow weary and realize that it was because of their negligence that they came to endure these things.”
“When you spread out your hands,” he says, “I will turn my eyes away from you. Even if you multiply your prayers, I will not listen.”
Even if this was spoken to others, it was certainly spoken to those who abandon the way.
And why, when God is so merciful, do we keep knocking at his door in distress and praying,
while he disregards our petition? He says, “Look, the Lord’s hand is not too short to save, nor is his ear too dull to hear.
Rather, your offenses have separated you from God, and your sins have turned his face away from you, so that he does not hear.”
Remember the Lord at all times, and he will remember you when trouble approaches you. He made your nature susceptible to misfortunes.
And in the world in which he created you and left you, he multiplied the causes of misfortunes and trials.
He made your nature readily susceptible to these things. Troubles are not far from you, not even a little.
For they spring up for you from within you whenever he gives the signal, and from beneath your feet and from the place where you stand.
Indeed, just as one eyelid is close to the other, so trials are close to human beings.
In his wisdom God arranged your circumstances in this way for your own benefit,
so that you would continually knock at his door and, through fear of painful things, plant the constant remembrance of him in your mind,
and be close to God through your continual petition, and be bound to him through the constant remembrance of him in your heart.
And when you call upon him and he answers you, you will know that your Savior
is God. You will become aware of your God, who created you, provides for you, and guards you, through his having made two worlds for your sake:
one for your instruction, like a school for a short time,
and the other like your Father’s house, your home forever and ever.
He did not make you incapable of suffering, lest you covet the rank of divinity and inherit what Satan inherited.
Nor did he make you inwardly incapable of change, lest you be like creatures whose natures are constrained,
and experience your good things and bad things without benefit or reward, like the other physical bodies on earth.
Everyone knows how many rebukes and humiliations, together with expressions of thanksgiving, arise from susceptibility to suffering and fear, and also from susceptibility to change.
Let it be known that both our diligence in righteousness and our turning away from evil are matters of our own will,
and that the honor and disgrace resulting from these are to be attributed to us, so that through disgrace we may feel shame and fear,
but through honor we may give thanks to God and strive for what is good. He has given you all these teachers in abundance,
lest, when you are free from these things because you have no needs and your nature is not susceptible to them,
And in your freedom from fear and suffering, you may forget God, turn away from him, and follow many gods.
This is what many people did, even though they were very vulnerable to suffering and in need,
and all these scourges were let loose upon them: with a little prosperity and power lasting only a short time,
and with even a little good health, they not only invented many gods,
but in their madness even dared to describe themselves by saying, “We are of the nature of God.”
For this reason he has kept you from all these things through the troubles that afflict you from time to time, lest you should turn away,
and he should become angry with you and wipe you away from his presence in punishment.
I leave aside also the wickedness and sins that spring from good health, freedom from fear, and ease,
even if what was mentioned first does not happen. For this reason, through sufferings and troubles he has increased the remembrance of himself in your heart.
Through the fear of adversities, he rouses you to approach the door of his mercy.
And by delivering you from them, he sows within you reasons to love him.
And when you have found love, he brings you near to the honor of being his children.
He shows you how rich his grace is, and how constant his care for you is.
Then he will also make you perceive the holiness of his glory and the hidden mysteries of the nature of his greatness.
How would you have come to know these things if you had not experienced adversities? For through these, the love of God is found to grow especially strong in the soul:
that is, through understanding his gracious gifts and remembering the various ways he cares for you.
All these good things are born for you out of sufferings, if you know how to give thanks.
Devote yourself, then, to God, so that he may remember you continually. And when he remembers you and delivers you, you will receive all these blessings.
Do not forget him in your empty distractions, lest he too reject you in your trials.
In times of ease, be close to him and obedient, so that in affliction you may have confidence before him,
because of your constant devotion to him in your heart through your prayers.
Sit before him at all times, thinking about him and remembering him in your heart,
lest, when you see him after a long absence, you lack the confidence to speak with him because of your estrangement.
Great confidence is born of constant companionship. Companionship with other people is bodily,
but companionship with God consists in the soul’s meditation and drawing near to him in prayer.
And through its great persistence, that meditation is mingled with wonder from time to time.
Let the hearts of those who seek the Lord rejoice. Seek the Lord, you sinners, and strengthen your thoughts with hope.
And seek his face through repentance at all times, and you will be sanctified by the holiness of his face and washed clean of your wrongdoing.
Run, you wrongdoers, to the Lord, who forgives wrongdoing and removes sins.
For he declared with oaths, “I do not desire the death of the sinner who dies, but rather that he should repent and live.”
“I stretched out my hands all day long,” he says, “toward a people who are quarrelsome and disobedient.”
“And why are you dying,” he says, “you household of Jacob? Turn to me, and I will turn toward you.”
And in Ezekiel he says, “On the day when the wrongdoer abandons his way and turns to the Lord
and practices justice and righteousness, the sins he committed will not be remembered against him, but he will surely live,” says
the Lord. “Likewise, if the righteous person abandons his righteousness and sins and does wrong, I will not remember the righteousness he practiced.
Instead, I will place a stumbling block before him, and he will die for the wrongdoing he committed, if he continues and persists in it.”
Why? Because the wrongdoer will not stumble because of his wrongdoing on the day when he turns to the Lord.
And the righteousness of the righteous person will not deliver him on the day when he sins, if he builds his building upon that foundation.
And to Jeremiah he said this: “Take a scroll for yourself,
and write on it everything I have said to you, from the days of Josiah king of Judah until today:
all the calamities I told you I would bring upon this people. Perhaps they will listen and be afraid,
and each person will abandon his evil way, repent, and turn to me, and I will forgive their sins.”
And the wise man says, “A person who conceals his wrongdoing will not prosper.
But whoever confesses his sins and turns away from them, God will have mercy on him.”
And Isaiah, rich in revelations, said, “Seek the Lord, and when you find him, call upon him.
And when he draws near, let the sinner abandon his way, and the wicked man his thoughts, and let him turn to me,
and I will have mercy on him, and to our God, who forgives abundantly. For my thoughts are not like your thoughts [?],
and my ways are not like your ways. Why do you not weigh out silver for what is not bread,
and your labor for what does not satisfy? Listen carefully to me, and you will eat good things. Come to me and listen to me, and
your soul will live.” When you keep the ways of the Lord and do his will, then you will delight in the Lord.
Then you will call him, and he will answer you; you will cry out, and he will say, “Here I am.”
When trouble comes upon a wicked person, he has no confidence to call upon God.
Nor can he wait for God's deliverance, because he kept far from God's will in the days of his ease.
Before you enter battle, secure a helper for yourself. Before you become ill, seek a physician for yourself.
Before distress reaches you, pray; then, in the time of distress, you will find your prayer, and it will answer you.
Before you stumble, pray and plead. Before you make a vow, prepare your vows—that is, your provisions.
The ark was built in a time of peace. Its trees were planted a hundred years beforehand.
When wrath came, the wicked, who had been occupied with wrongdoing, were thrown into confusion, but the ark became a shelter for the righteous man.
Wrongdoing shuts the mouth in prayer. The reproach that comes from conscience takes confidence away from the heart.
Integrity of heart brings down tears of joy during supplication.
Resolute endurance of willingly accepted injustice purifies the heart.
Endurance of injustice comes from disregard for the world.
If someone persists under oppression without distress, it is because his heart has begun to see the truth.
Joy in oppression and willingly accepted injustice lift up the heart.
No one can endure oppression and injustice with joyful willingness [?],
except those who, in their thoughts, have died completely to the world. But those in whose thoughts the whole scent of this life
is still present are driven by vainglory to flare up immediately in anger,
or they fall into sorrowful thoughts that arise from this.
Oh, how difficult this virtue is, and how much glory it has before God!
Anyone who longs for this way of life should give himself to living as a stranger and leave his own country.
It is difficult for someone to perfect this exalted virtue in his own country.
Only the bold and strong can endure the pain that this great way of life produces among their acquaintances,
and those who, while still alive, have died to this life and have given up hope of comfort in this present age.
Just as grace is close to humility, so difficult misfortunes are close to pride.
The Lord's heart is set on the humble, to do them good. The Lord's face is against the proud, to humble them.
Humility always receives mercy.
For hardness of heart and unbelief continually encounter severe, unexpected blows,
until evil suddenly rises against them and they are handed over to the destruction of final judgments.
Make yourself small in everything among people, and he will raise you even above the leaders of the people. You shall be.
Bow low before everyone, and be the first to offer your greeting. You will be honored more than someone who offers gold from Ophir.
Be despised and contemptible in your own eyes, and you will see the glory of God within yourself. Where humility blossoms, from
there praise springs up. If you openly strive to be despised, he increases your honor among people.
And if you are humble in your heart, he will show you his glory in your heart. In your greatness be [?], and do not be great in your lowliness.
Learn to be despised when you are filled with the Lord’s honor, and not to be honored when you are afflicted with sores within.
Reject honor so that you may be honored. Do not love it, so that you may not be despised. If you run after honor, it flees before you.
But if you flee from it, wherever you hide, it will spring up upon you there and become a herald of your humility to everyone.
If you belittle yourself in order to be honored, the Lord will expose you.
But if you despise yourself for the sake of truth, he will command created things to praise you.
They will unfold before you the glory of the Creator, who has spoken through them from eternity, and they will glorify you as they do the Creator, because you are his true image.
A person whose conduct is exalted, yet who is despised among people, radiant, set apart, and poor in spirit—
who can find such a person? Blessed is the one who humbles himself in everything, for he will be exalted in everything.
Whoever humbles himself and makes himself small for God’s sake is glorified by God.
And whoever hungers and thirsts for his sake, he makes drunk from his goodness with that wine whose drinkers’ intoxication never passes away.
And whoever goes naked for his sake, he clothes with a robe of glory. And whoever is poor and needy for his sake, through his
true wealth he makes that person’s consolation secure. Belittle yourself for God’s sake, so that your praise may increase even without your knowing it.
Throughout your life, consider yourself a sinner, so that throughout your life you may be found righteous.
Be despised even though you are wise, and do not become foolish in your wisdom.
Be unlearned in your wisdom, and do not present yourself as wise when you are unlearned.
If humility exalts the despised, how much more does it exalt the honored! Flee from glory, and you will be glorified.
Fear arrogance, and you will be exalted. For pride, it is said, was not allotted to human beings,
and exaltation willingly; do not quarrel with anyone over small portions of it.
If you have rejected praise, flee from those who hunt for glory. Flee from those who acquire possessions as you flee from possessions themselves.
Keep away from those who live in luxury as you keep away from luxuries. Flee from the dissolute as you flee from sexual immorality.
If remembering their conduct disturbs the mind, how much more will seeing them and associating closely with them!
Draw near to the virtuous, so that through them you may draw near to God. Associate with a humble person,
so that you may learn from his ways. If the sight of his conduct benefits those who see him, how much more the practices of his life
and the teaching from his mouth! Love the poor, so that through them you may find mercy.
Do not approach [?], lest you be forced to abandon your peaceful habits.
Do not recoil from the repulsiveness of the sickness of the sick, for you too are clothed in flesh. Do not rebuff those whose hearts are
bitter, lest you be struck with the rod that struck them, and seek a comforter but find none.
Do not despise those with natural defects, lest you enter Sheol with them. Love sinners, but reject their deeds.
Do not scorn them because of their failings, lest you too be tempted by those very same things.
Remember that you share in Adam’s corruption; you too are clothed in that weakness.
To someone who needs compassionate prayer and words of encouragement,
do not give rebuke instead, lest you destroy him and his life be required at your hands.
Imitate physicians, who use cooling remedies against fevers.
Compel yourself, whenever you meet your neighbor, to offer him honor beyond what is due to him.
Kiss his hand and his foot, and let your heart burn with pure love for him.
Frequently take his hands, place them over your eyes, and kiss them with great honor.
Attribute good qualities to him that he does not possess.
Even when he is absent, say good and beautiful things about him, and call him by distinguished titles of honor.
By these and similar things, you will not only compel him to aspire to good things,
as he feels ashamed of the title you have bestowed on him without the deeds to match it, and you sow in him the seed of virtues; but through these and similar forms of behavior,
in which you train yourself, you establish peaceful and humble habits in your soul,
and you are spared many difficult struggles, protection from which others acquire only through toil.
And not only this: even if the person who receives these honors from you has some shortcoming or a defect in his will,
when you point it out to him by example, with only a hint, he readily accepts healing from you,
out of shame before the honor you show him, and because of the evidence of love that he constantly sees in you.
Hold firmly to this purpose toward all people.
As for becoming angry with someone and being zealous over the faith or over his evil deeds,
or blaming him or rebuking him—guard yourself against this. We all have a righteous judge in heaven.
But if you have compassion and want to turn him toward the truth, suffer on his behalf.
With tears and love, say a word or two to him, and do not flare up against him.
Remove every sign of hostility from your face.
Love does not know how to become angry; it is not puffed up; it does not condemn passionately.
The sign of love and knowledge, wherever they are present, is deep humility arising from the inward mind.
The fifth discourse is finished.
The sixth discourse.
That a person falls into sinful lapses reveals the weakness of human nature, for our nature is necessarily susceptible to this.
God did not consider it beneficial for a person to rise entirely above this before his nature enters the second creation.
This susceptibility to lapses is beneficial for humbling the mind. But persistence in them is shamelessness.
There are three ways by which every rational soul draws near to God.
Some draw near through the fervor of faith, some through fear, and some through chastisement from God.
But the soul does not approach the state of love independently, by itself; rather, it takes one of these ways as its starting point.
Just as confusion of thoughts is born from an undisciplined stomach,
so ignorance and foolishness of mind arise from frivolous talk and disorderly conversations.
Concern about business confuses the soul.
An accumulation of tasks disturbs the mind, draws it out of tranquility, and drives peace away from it.
The solitary who has prepared himself and devoted himself to heavenly work ought always to be free from anxiety in his mind,
so that, when he examines himself and considers some affair belonging to this world,
And he sees in his soul no thought of any visible thing, so that through his
complete withdrawal from these passing things, he may be able to meditate on the law of the Lord night and day, without anything joining in.
Bodily labors without the beauties of the mind are a barren womb and dry breasts.
They do not bring one near to the knowledge of God. The body is worn out, but they take no care to uproot the passions from their minds.
And they too will reap nothing. Like someone who sows among thorns and cannot reap,
so is someone whose mind is corrupted by anxiety, resentment, and greed for accumulating possessions,
and who groans on his bed from his excessive vigils and abstinence.
Scripture bears witness when it says: “Like a people who practiced righteousness and did not abandon the judgment of their God,
they ask me for judgment and righteousness, and desire to draw near to God.
‘Why have we fasted, and you have not seen? Why have we humbled ourselves, and you have not noticed?’ Look, on the day of your fasting,
you do your own will and bring forward all your idols.”
That is, his evil thoughts and evil intentions—you keep them in your souls in place of God.
Every day you sacrifice to them your precious freedom, a sacrifice more precious than anything else,
which you ought to have set apart for me through your good deeds and a pure conscience of heart.
Good soil that gladdens its owner with a hundredfold crop is a soul that is purified
by meditation on God, through its wakeful vigil night and day. There the Lord will build, over its dwellings and its surroundings,
a cloud for shade by day and the brightness of a flame of fire by night. And from within its darkness, light will dawn.
Just as mist dims the rays of the moon, so the fumes of the belly obscure the wisdom of God from the soul.
And as a blaze of fire in dry wood, so is bodily desire in a full belly.
And just as oily substances stir up the flare of a flame, so the richness of foods stirs up sexual passion within the body.
The knowledge of God does not dwell in a body that loves comfort.
A person who loves his body is not deemed worthy of divine gifts.
Just as through labor pains a child is born who gladdens the pregnant woman,
so through labors knowledge of the mysteries of God is born in the soul.
But for the lazy and those who love comfort, the fruit brings shame.
For just as a father has compassion on his son, so Christ has compassion on the toiling body and is close to its mouth at all times.
The labor of wisdom has no equal. A stranger is someone whose mind is a stranger to every [?] of this world.
A mourner is someone who spends all his days in this life in hunger, thirst, and mourning,
because he awaits that heavenly hope. A solitary is someone who, having placed
his dwelling beyond the sights of the world, has a single request in prayer: the longing for the world to come.
The wealth of the solitary is this: either the comfort granted to him in the midst of mourning,
or the joy that dawns from faith within the treasury of his mind.
A merciful person is someone who, in his mind, makes no distinction between the different classes of humanity when showing mercy.
Virginity consists not merely in someone keeping his body from the defilement of sexual acts,
but also in feeling shame even before himself, even when he is alone.
If you long for chastity, restrain the flow of shameful thoughts by occupying yourself with reading
and with constant supplication to God. Then you will be armed against the impulses that arise inwardly from nature.
Without these things, no one can see purity within himself.
If you long to acquire mercy, first train yourself to acquire disregard for material things,
so that their importance does not draw your mind away from the goal it had previously set.
The sincerity of mercy is recognized through enduring injustice.
And humility reaches perfection when you rejoice at being wronged without cause. If you are truly merciful,
when you are unjustly and wrongfully deprived of what belongs to you, do not become angry inwardly.
And outwardly, do not display your patient endurance to others.
Instead, let the offenses committed against you be swallowed up in compassionate feelings, like the harshness of wine that is diluted
in a great deal of water. Rather, show a sign of the sincerity that comes from abundant mercy
through the further kindnesses you gladly bestow on those who wrong you. There is [?].
Just as the blessed Elisha also did to his enemies who came against him to capture him.
By praying and covering their eyes with dazzling blindness, he was revealing the power that was with him,
and that, if he wished, they were nothing before him. And by feeding them, giving them drink, and allowing them to go,
He made known the compassion he had acquired within himself. And if you are truly humble, do not become upset when you are wronged.
Do not vent your anger over the matter, but genuinely accept the unjust accusation made against you,
without being concerned to convince people that the matter was otherwise. Instead, ask all the more for forgiveness.
Others willingly attached to themselves the disgraceful reputation of sexual immorality.
Others took upon themselves acts of adultery that were beyond them,
and watered with tears the fruit of a sin that was not theirs, as though it were their own.
With weeping they asked their accuser for forgiveness for sins they had not committed, while their souls were crowned with all the purity of chastity.
Still others, so that they would not be praised for the wonderful way of life they practiced in secret,
presented themselves as madmen, though they were firmly grounded in complete good sense and serenity.
Thus, because of the marvelous nature of their deeds, the holy angels would be
the ones to proclaim the greatness of such people.
But you claim humility for yourself! While those others testified against themselves,
you do not even endure such accusations in silence when they are directed against you, yet you consider yourself humble.
If you are humble, test yourself by these things: see whether you remain untroubled.
By the many rooms in the Father's house, he means the different capacities of understanding among the inhabitants of that place.
That is, the differences in gifts and spiritual degrees in which they delight inwardly,
and the different ranks of spiritual gifts. It does not mean that, through a division into dwellings in different locations,
each individual is assigned a separate place to exist, with a plainly recognizable difference in the location of their individual dwellings.
Rather, just as, in the one common enjoyment of this visible sun,
each of us receives his own particular benefit from it in proportion to the purity of his sight,
according to how much the capacity of his pupils can contain of the uniform outpouring of its light;
and just as a lamp in a single house distributes the benefit of its light separately to each,
without itself being divided in its being, passing from the oneness of its radiance into multiplicity through differences in its appearance;
so too, they dwell in a single habitation that is not divided into many separate parts—
those who were found worthy to be there at the appointed time—from one sun perceived by the mind:
Each person, according to the rank of his way of life, will draw delight for his soul in one atmosphere and one place,
and one dwelling, one vision, and one form, without seeing the high degree of his companion’s rank when he is inferior to him.
That is, he will not be ashamed at the abundance of his companion’s gifts and the smallness of his own.
Otherwise, this would become a cause of sadness and torment to his mind. Far from it!
There is no thinking about these things in that place of delights. Each person, according to the gift of which he has been deemed worthy and the greatness of his rank,
takes delight within himself. But the outward vision is the same for everyone, and the place is one.
More precisely, it is like the way the angelic hosts dwell together in a single region of the air,
with the same outward vision, but with a hidden knowledge of their degrees, through differing revelations of contemplation belonging to their orders.
If, then, for beings that truly exist, there is nothing apart from active perception and movements of the mind,
not even in the world to come will anyone dare to introduce [?] a mode different from this,
that is, from the intellect onward, though with greater clarity because of the perfection of nature.
True, then, is the saying spoken by the fathers: some ignorance is defined as having no time limit,
while for some, a time is reserved for its removal to be revealed,
along with the rest of the mysteries belonging to the divine Being, which are bounded by silence.
For apart from the all-embracing height and the utter depth, there is no further
intermediate place between the two at the judgment to come. A person belongs entirely either to those above or to those below.
Within each of these, however, there are differing ranks of recompense.
And if this is true, as indeed it is, what is this foolishness of some people: “I do not seek to be in the kingdom,”
each of them says. “If only I can strive merely to be saved from Gehenna!”
Salvation from Gehenna is itself the kingdom, and falling away from the kingdom is itself Gehenna.
For the Scriptures have not taught us that there are three places.
What, then, do they say? “When the Son of Man comes in his glory, he will place the sheep at his right and the goats at his left.”
Here too he speaks not of three groups, but of two: those on the right,
and those on the left. The places where they dwell are distinctly separated.
Of the former he says that they will shine like the sun in the kingdom of the Father; the latter will go to everlasting fire.
And again, he says, “They will come from the east and from the west and recline at table with Abraham’s household in the kingdom.
But the children of the promise who were not persuaded will go out into the darkness outside the kingdom.
There will be weeping of the soul and gnashing of teeth”—that is, sorrow more painful than fire.
From this you understand that being left behind from that ascent is itself the torment of Gehenna.
It is good for someone to encourage people toward good things and, through his constant care, bring them from
error to the knowledge of life. This is the way of our Lord and the apostles, and it is very exalted.
But if he senses within himself that, through close association and constant involvement of this kind,
his conscience grows sick from seeing things, and the calm of his discernment is disturbed,
and his knowledge grows dark, because his mind still needs watchfulness and greater restraint of the senses,
then, before they are healed, he himself becomes sick. While he wishes to make them well, he loses the partial health of his own soul
and passes from the chaste freedom of his will into confusion of mind.
Let this person remember the apostle’s words: “Solid food is for the healthy.”
Let him turn back, lest he hear them say mockingly, “How can you be a physician to others
when you yourself are covered with wounds?” Let him therefore keep to himself and preserve his own health alone.
Instead of audible speech, let the beauty of his conduct serve others.
And instead of words from his mouth, let others, if possible, receive help while he keeps his own soul healthy.
Let them be made healthy through his health, even while he is far away, through emulation of his virtuous deeds. This is more fitting
than for him to serve them personally with mere words while he himself is sick, since he too needs healing even more than they do.
For if a blind person leads a blind person, both fall into a pit. “For the healthy,” he says, “is
solid food, and for those whose senses have been trained and strengthened to receive every kind of food.”
That is, through all encounters involving the senses, the heart does not become sick, because it has been thoroughly trained.
Whenever Satan wishes to defile a pure mind with thoughts of sexual immorality,
he first tests its endurance through vainglory, although the initial thought itself does not resemble passionate thoughts.
He does this to a guarded mind into which he cannot easily cast an evil thought openly.
But when that strong man has come out of his stronghold by grazing on the earlier thoughts,
And a little [?] from there, he brings him into contact with objects of sexual immorality, leading the mind toward base things.
At first, however, he is suddenly alarmed at encountering them, because his thoughts have become attached to these things,
from the sight of which the mind that guides them had previously abstained.
Nevertheless, it has descended from the height of its former contemplation, even if it has not been defiled.
But if he does not turn back, and vigorously pursues the first thoughts,
which are the cause of the second thoughts, when he encounters those things many times,
then habit itself blinds the soul’s discernment through these constant encounters.
Thus the degree and kind of bondage to the later passion correspond to the degree and kind of the first passion.
It is easier and better to evade the passions by remembering virtuous things than to overcome them in combat.
For when the passions come out of their place and stir themselves to appear in battle,
then they also imprint images and likenesses on the mind.
This manner of proceeding has great power to drain the mind’s strength, and it greatly agitates and disturbs one’s thinking.
But with the first approach I mentioned, not even the traces of the passions are perceptible in the mind after they have passed away.
Bodily labors and meditation on the Scriptures preserve purity, while hope and fear strengthen those labors.
Withdrawal from other people and constant supplication establish hope and fear in the mind.
Until a person receives the Comforter, he needs written marks in ink,
so that through these forms he may fix beneficial reminders in his heart,
and through constant meditation on them renew his impulses toward virtue,
and find within himself vigilance against the subtle paths of sin, since he does not yet possess the sustaining power of the Spirit,
which drives away the forgetfulness that snatches beneficial reminders from a person and brings negligence upon him through distraction of the mind.
But when the power of the Spirit enters and dwells in the intellectual faculties of the soul engaged in spiritual labor,
then, in place of laws written in ink, the commandments of the Spirit are fixed in the heart.
The heart itself learns these secretly from the Spirit, without needing the assistance of perceptible objects through the mediation of the senses.
As long as the mind learns from material things, error and forgetfulness accompany its learning.
But when its learning concerns things that do not perish,
And the remembrance of him also remains unextinguished in the awareness that is in them. There are good thoughts,
and there is a good will. There are evil thoughts, and there is an evil heart.
For the former, without the latter, count for little in determining recompense.
The former are movements that pass through the mind, like winds passing over the sea and raising waves.
The latter, however, are roots. And according to the purpose on which the foundation rests,
so the recompense will be good or bad, and not according to the stirring of thoughts.
For the soul never stops stirring up various thoughts.
But if you assign recompense to each of these, although they have no root beneath them,
then you are likely to change your blessings and your sentence a thousand times in a single day.
The mind that has only recently emerged from the thickets of the passions through the labors of repentance is a fledgling without wings.
At the time of prayer it forces itself to rise above earthly things, but cannot.
Instead, it still creeps along the surface of the earth, where the serpent crawls.
It gathers its thoughts through reading, labors, fear, and meditation on the various forms of virtue.
For it knows nothing else besides these. Yet even these keep the mind pure for only a short time.
Then memories come again and disturb and defile the heart. For it has not yet experienced the peaceful, free air
that keeps the mind recollected and serene for a long time, without any remembrance of things.
For it still has fleshy wings—that is, bodily virtues
that are practiced outwardly. As for the contemplation of the virtues it practices,
it has not yet seen it or perceived that it is the mind’s wings, by which it draws near to heavenly things and moves away from the earth.
As long as a person serves God through the senses and through material things,
the impressions of things creep through his thoughts, and his mind contemplates bodily forms in these divine matters.
But when he becomes aware of what lies within things, then, according to the measure of his awareness,
his mind itself is also raised above the forms of things from time to time.
The eyes of the Lord are upon the humble, and his ears are ready to hear them.
The prayer of the humble is as though from mouth to ear [?]. The Lord my God [?] will illuminate [?] my darkness.
When you are in solitude, engaged in the good practice of humility, and your soul is close to emerging from beneath the dark cloud,
this will be your sign: your heart will burn and seethe as though in fire, night and day,
so that you will consider all earthly things ashes and dung.
That is, you will not even find pleasure in approaching food, because of the sweetness of the fresh, ardent thoughts
that are constantly stirring in your soul. And suddenly a fountain of tears will be given to you,
so that they flow from your eyes like water in streams, without forcing, mingling with all your activities.
That is, with your reading and your prayer, with your worship and your meditation, with your eating and your drinking,
and with everything you do, tears will be mingled. When you see these things in yourself, take courage:
you have crossed the sea. Increase your labors and hold firmly to watchfulness, so that grace may increase day by day.
Until you encounter these things, you have not yet completed your journey to the mountain of God.
But if, after you have found them, they cease and that ardor subsides,
without being replaced by something else that you are to receive after them, alas for what you have lost! Either you have become proud or you have grown slack.
What, then, is the thing that comes after tears, which a person encounters upon passing beyond them?
And what else comes after that? We outline this below, in the chapters on the progression of the spiritual life,
according to the enlightenment we have received from the Scriptures and from the fathers who were entrusted with mysteries like these.
If you have no labors, do not speak about virtue.
Afflictions endured for righteousness are more precious to God than all vows and offerings,
and the scent of the sweat of their toil more than all sweet-smelling herbs and choice perfumes.
Consider every virtue in which the body suffers no hardship a stillborn child without a soul.
The offerings of the righteous are the tears of their eyes, and their acceptable sacrifices are the sighs of their vigils.
The saints cry out and sigh under the body's weight, and in sorrow they send their prayers up to God.
At the sound of their cries, the holy powers make their way
to meet them, to encourage them with hope and comfort them.
Through their closeness to the saints, the holy angels share in their trials and sufferings.
Labors and humility make a human being a god on earth.
Faith and mercy, however, quickly bring one near to serenity.
Fervor and brokenheartedness do not coexist in one soul, just as those who are drunk have no restraint of mind.
When fervor is given, sadness and mourning are taken away.
Wine is given for gladness, and fervor for the soul’s joy.
The former warms the body, but the word of God warms the mind.
Those who are set ablaze with fervor are carried away in their thoughts to the world to come through meditation on hope.
Just as various fantasies are pictured before those who are drunk with wine,
so too the person who is drunk and aflame with hope for things to come knows neither affliction
nor the world nor anything in it. These things happen to those who are simplehearted and fervent in hope.
And many things that are to come after long labors of purification for those who follow the traditional course of life—
these people taste them at the beginning of the road, through the soul’s faith alone. The Lord does whatever he pleases.
Blessed are those who have cast themselves into the sea of afflictions simply and without questioning, in fervor for God,
and have not turned back, for they quickly escape to the harbor of the promises
and rest in those dwellings that all who labor well reach.
They are comforted after their troubles and exult in the joy
of their hope. Those who run in hope do not see the dangers lying along the road, nor do they have time to investigate such things.
But when they have come out of the sea, then these things become visible to them, and they praise God
for how they were preserved amid all those waves and many rocks without knowing it themselves,
since they had not concerned themselves with devoting their attention to examining such things.
But those who ponder intricate ideas and want to become exceedingly wise,
and give themselves over to shifting thoughts and fear, and undertake many preparations,
and look for and consider causes of harm and thoughts that sap their strength—
these people are generally found continually at the doors of their own houses.
For when the lazy person is sent out, he says, “There is a lion on the road, and slaughter in the streets.”
They are also like those who said, “We saw descendants of giants there, and we were like grasshoppers in their eyes.”
And their cities are fortified, and their walls rise up to heaven.
These are the ones who, at the time of death, are found at the beginning of their journey.
These are the ones who continually grow wiser and wiser, but never begin.
But the unlearned man swam and crossed over with his first stroke.
He gave no thought to his body, nor to whether his profit might fail to come into his hands.
Do not let your excessive wisdom become a stumbling block to your soul and a snare before you, preventing you from beginning courageously and readily, with hope in God,
on your blood-spattered [?], so that you will not always remain needy and stripped of the knowledge of God.
Whoever watches the winds does not sow. Death in battle for God's sake is better for us than a life of shame and humiliation.
When you are about to begin one of God's works, first make your will,
as someone who has no life left in this world, and as someone who has prepared himself for death.
Approach it with no hope of survival, as someone whose end will come in that very undertaking, and for whom it is the last of his days,
and who will no longer see the days that follow it. Let this be firmly settled in your mind.
Otherwise, the expectation of life may rob you of victory by weakening your resolve.
Therefore, do not give wisdom complete control over your affairs. Give faith a little room in your mind as well.
Always remember the days after death, and slackness will never enter your soul.
As the wise man said: A thousand years in this world do not equal a single day in the world of the righteous.
Begin every virtuous deed courageously. As it is said, do not approach it with a divided heart.
Do not waver in your heart as you travel your way, trusting in the grace of God,
lest your [?] be in vain and the toil of your service become burdensome to you.
Instead, believe in your heart that God is merciful and gives grace to those who seek him, not according to our service,
but according to the love in our souls and our faith in him. As it is said, let it be done for you as you have believed.
There is someone whose bowing of his head throughout the day takes the place of his appointed times of worship.
And there is someone whose continual kneeling makes up the number of his prayers.
There is someone whose flow of tears takes the place of his prescribed observances. He seeks nothing else along with it, because it is better for him than anything.
And there is someone whose diligence in the meditations of his mind fulfills the rules prescribed for him.
For one who torments his belly, the pain of hunger that eats away at his flesh leaves him empty, keeping him from bringing his work to fulfillment.
There is another whose psalms never cease because of the fervor of his mind.
There is another whose heart burns with the Scriptures, and another who is taken captive by their meaning.
There is another for whom wonder at the words stops the movement of his lips from their customary flow.
There is another who tasted all these things and was satisfied, but turned back and stopped. And there is another who, after only a little of them, became puffed up and arrogant and went astray.
There is another whose body held him back from these things through the severity of its suffering and pains.
For another, it is desire for this or that; for another, a position of authority; and for others, human praise.
For others, it is attachment to possessions; for others, social interaction and frivolity.
And there is another who persevered and stood firm, and did not turn his back until he had obtained the pearl.
Joyfully begin every work that is for God's sake.
And if you are free from passions and a divided heart, God himself brings it to completion and helps you
and makes you wise; and according to his will it reaches completion in a wonderful way.
To him be glory, dominion, worship, and exaltation forever and ever. Amen.
The six discourses on the practice of virtue are finished.
Further, on other subjects, each chapter standing on its own, in short sections:
On the nature of trust in God, and who ought to trust in God,
and, when he trusts, receives what he intends; and who trusts foolishly and without understanding. 7.
There is a trust in God, grounded in the faith of the heart, that is good and comes from knowledgeable discernment.
And there is another that is insipid and foolish: it is a false trust.
Consider, then, someone who has absolutely no concern for any of these passing things,
and whose soul is devoted night and day to the works of God, who is not concerned with any business of this world
because of his great concern for virtue, and who has taken upon himself the entire care of these divine things.
Because of this, he neglects to provide clothing or food, or to arrange and prepare a place for his shelter, and so forth,
and trusts in God to provide everything he needs at the proper time and to care for him.
This is certainly true trust, and it is wise trust.
And indeed, it is also fitting for this man
to trust in God, because he is his servant.
He bears God's concerns and carries the burden of his works, without the negligence that comes from distractions.
And God, too, ought to show him a care different from that shown to the rest of humanity,
because he carefully holds fast in his own person to the word of our Lord, who said, “Seek God's kingdom and his righteousness, and do not worry about the body.”
And when you concern yourselves with this, the world itself, like a servant, prepares everything for you.
It submits to your words without hesitation, as to a master, opposing your will in nothing.
Therefore, so that distractions may not interrupt his constant standing before God, he does not devote himself to the pressing needs of the body.
For he is not concerned about other things either, but maintains the same freedom from involvement in them all,
from the smallest to the greatest, whether they offer comfort or recreation or distraction from the fear of God.
And he himself finds them in a wonderful way, without approaching any of them or laboring over them.
Another man, however, has his heart completely buried in the earth and constantly eats dust with the serpent.
He has no concern at all for anything befitting God, and in [?] he wallows in bodily things.
He is constantly lax and idle through socializing, recreation, and luxury, and seizes on all sorts of excuses.
While he lies in this laziness and neglect of virtue,
whenever he comes under pressure, lacks something, or is distressed in some matter by the fruit of his foolishness,
he says, “I will trust in God, and he will free me from worry and give me rest.”
You fool! Until now you have not remembered God, and you have dishonored him by the laxity of your conduct.
Because of you, his name was blasphemed among the nations, as it is written.
And now you boldly declare, “I trust in him to help me and take care of me.”
God, too, spoke well through the prophet when he rebuked people like these: “They seek me every day and wish to know my ways.
Like a people who practiced righteousness and did not abandon the judgment of their God, they ask me for judgment and righteousness.”
Among these is the fool who does not draw near to God even in his thoughts,
but when the thorns of affliction surround him, he raises his hands to him in trust.
Such a man deserves to be scorched many times, so that from then on he may grow wise.
When he has no deeds worthy of trust in God,
but instead deserves discipline because of his evil deeds and neglect of his duties, and is borne with in mercy,
he must not deceive himself, forget the character of his previous conduct, and say, “I trust in God.”
Let such a person be disciplined. When he has no deeds of faith, he must not stretch out his legs in idleness
and say, “I believe that God will give me food,” as though he had been laboring in God's work.
Or someone goes and falls into a well because of his recklessness,
and although God had never entered his thoughts at all before this, he now says, “I trust in God
to rescue me.” Do not be deceived, you fool! Labor for God's sake and the sweat of serving him come before trust in God.
You believe God: you do well. Yet faith also requires deeds,
and trust in him requires the testimony of conscience that arises from the labor of virtue.
Believe that God cares for his creation and is also all-powerful. But accompany your faith with deeds that are consistent with it, and then he will answer you.
Do not try to grasp the wind in your fist—that is, faith without deeds.
But if someone is unaware and travels along a road where there is a wild beast or murderous people,
or anything else of this kind, without knowing it, this is God's general providence:
how often he causes the danger to pass him by, delaying him where he is through various circumstances,
until the harmful event takes place, or someone meets him and turns him back.
Again, suppose a dangerous snake is lying in the road, and he does not see it.
God wishes him not to be caught in this danger, and suddenly that creature makes a sound, or leaves and moves elsewhere,
or crawls in front of him so that he will see it and take care. God rescues him, even though he does not deserve it,
for hidden reasons that he alone knows, and above all because of his mercy.
Again, there are times when a house, a wall, or a rock is about to fall
or slip out of its place and come crashing down, and sitting
there are a few people. God commands an angel, who delays the event and holds it back until they get up from there,
bringing them out through some circumstance so that not even one remains beneath it. Once they have gone out, it falls that very moment.
And if one of them happens to be caught beneath it, he suffers no harm.
By this he wishes to make known the greatness of his power. These things and others like them belong to general providence.
But the righteous person possesses this grace continually, and individually, not merely as part of the general provision.
As for everyone else, God has commanded them to conduct themselves with discernment,
and to combine knowledge with God's providence in their affairs.
But the righteous person does not seek this knowledge in order to manage his affairs by it.
Instead of this knowledge, he possesses faith, through which he conquers rebellious strongholds.
He fears none of the things we have listed, as it is written:
“The righteous person is confident like a lion,” and through faith he boldly faces everything.
He does not do this as someone testing God, but as someone holding firmly to his trust in him, armed and mightily clothed in the power of the Spirit.
Concerning the abundance of his constant care for him, God himself also said: “I am with him in distress;
and you will strengthen him, and I will honor him. I will satisfy him with length of days and show him my salvation.” Whoever
is feeble and slack in his deeds, or negligent, or whose actions are evil, cannot possess this hope.
Rather, it belongs to someone who remains constantly with God in everything and is close to him through his good deeds,
and constantly directs his heart's gaze toward his grace, as David said: “My eyes have failed while I wait for my God.”
On what helps a person draw near to God in his heart,
and what is the sure cause by which help secretly draws near to him, and what cause brings a person near to humility. 8.
Blessed is the person who knows his own weakness!
This knowledge becomes for him the foundation and beginning of all good and noble things.
When a person knows and perceives that he is certainly and truly weak,
then he draws himself back from dissipation, which scatters knowledge, and becomes more watchful over himself.
For unless he is left somewhat deprived, and a little negligence comes upon him, and trials surround him,
whether through bodily afflictions or the soul's susceptibility to passions, a person cannot perceive his own weakness.
Then, by comparison with his own weakness, he also understands how great the help from God is.
And again, when he sees that however much he devises plans and increases his vigilance, and withdraws and conceals himself
in ten thousand inner rooms, and however many grounds for confidence he devises for himself, his heart still does not cease to be afraid.
Then he recognizes and considers that all this agitation of the heart
shows him that he lacks something else, something more urgently needed: namely, that he needs further help.
For the heart itself bears witness from within through the fear that trembles in it, revealing that something is lacking.
For this reason, he cannot rest confidently. God's help, he realizes, is needed for deliverance.
When he knows that he needs divine help, he increases his prayer. And when he increases his supplications, his heart is humbled.
For no one who is distressed and asks for help is without humility. And God does not despise a broken and humble heart.
Until the heart is humbled, it does not cease wandering. Humility gathers the heart together.
When a person is humbled, mercy immediately surrounds and embraces him.
When mercy draws near, the heart immediately senses help, because a certain confidence and strength also stir within it.
When he senses divine help coming to him,
and that God is his supporter and helper, then his heart is immediately filled with faith.
From this point onward, he recognizes and understands that prayer is a harbor of help, a fountain of salvation,
a treasure of confidence, an ocean that brings deliverance amid the waves, a light for those in darkness,
a support for the weak, a shelter in times of trial, a healer in times of sickness,
a protective barrier of help in battle, and a sharp arrow against enemies.
He also understands that through prayer he has found access to all these good things. From then on, he delights in the prayer of faith,
while his heart rejoices in confidence, no longer praying blindly and merely with words from his mouth, as he had until now.
And when he knows [?], he now possesses prayer like a treasure within his soul.
In his joy, he changes the purpose of his prayer into words of thanksgiving.
This is the saying spoken by the wise man among the saints, Mar Evagrius,
who had established a definition for everything: “Prayer is joy that pours forth thanksgiving.”
He is speaking of this prayer that follows the reception of the knowledge of God. As for the expression “pours forth,”
this is because the person himself is not praying laboriously, as with the other prayer of suffering
that precedes the awareness of grace. Rather, the heart itself, filled with joy and wonder,
cries out continually with stirrings of thanksgiving and gratitude, in silence, as he kneels.
Rather, it comes from the inward impulse, which is deeply stirred with wonder at the meaning of God's gracious gifts.
Suddenly he raises his voice and praises without ever having enough, as that inward impulse pours out his thanksgiving through his tongue as well.
And he repeats at length and insistently: Whoever has experienced these things clearly and not dimly,
and has gained discerning knowledge of them, let him understand what I am saying—that there is no variation in it,
because of his extensive experience of the matter. From then on, therefore, he abstains from
empty things and remains steadfastly with God in constant prayer, afraid of being deprived of the stream of help it brings.
All these good things arise from a person's awareness of his weakness.
For this awareness, through his longing for help, drives him toward God with the entreaties of his prayer.
And the more he draws near to God in his mind, the more God draws near to him through his gifts.
And God never withdraws his protection from him, because of his great humility.
For like the widow before the judge, he cries out continually, “Give me justice against my adversary.”
This is so that he may have all the more reason to draw near to him,
and, because of his need, may remain constantly beside the fountain of help.
He answers some of his requests quickly, but others he does not.
That is, those things he knows the man cannot live without; the rest he delays.
At times he restrains the enemies' onslaught against him, and at times he allows him to be tested.
This is so that this very thing, as I have said, may give him a reason to draw near to God,
and so that he may gain wisdom from his trials. This is what is said in Scripture:
