The Lord left many nations and did not destroy them quickly or hand them over to Joshua,
to test Israel through them, and so that the generations of the Israelites might gain knowledge and learn warfare.
A righteous person who does not recognize his weakness is in danger in all his affairs.
He is not far from falling, nor is the destroying lion—the demon of pride—far from him.
Whoever lacks knowledge of his weakness lacks humility.
Whoever lacks humility lacks perfection. Whoever lacks perfection is still in danger.
And whenever this is the case, the enemy has an opening against him.
Because his city is not secured with iron bars and bronze thresholds.
For humility itself cannot be acquired without the things that bring it about:
through them, contrition of heart continually arises, and presumptuous thoughts are overthrown.
Without humility, a person's work is not brought to completion.
The seal of the Spirit has not yet been placed on the document of his freedom; he is still a slave,
and his work is not beyond fear. Without humbling himself, his work is not made secure.
Without trials he does not acquire wisdom, and without wisdom he does not attain humility.
For this reason, God necessarily allows the saints to encounter things that bring about humility, contrition of heart, and earnest, undistracted prayer.
Sometimes he strikes them through the assaults of natural passions and through lapses brought about by loathsome thoughts.
Sometimes it is through dishonor, the undeserved insults they endure from other people, and bodily pains.
Sometimes it is through poverty and deprivation arising from distressing circumstances; and sometimes through intense feelings of fear during the battles
openly waged by demons, which he allows to come upon them to shake them repeatedly,
and through terrifying changes, each more severe, distressing, and difficult than the last.
All these things are to give them a reason for humility and to keep them from sleeping in negligence,
whether because of present trials, in which the athlete is weak, or from fear of what is to come.
Trials, then, are necessarily beneficial to human beings.
I am not saying that, in order to have a reason to humble himself, a person ought therefore
to give himself over willingly to evil deeds, so that, that is, he may be humbled by remembering them,
or rush into these other trials. Rather, while working and laboring at good deeds, he ought
continually to keep himself alert and reflect that he is a created being and is clothed in the capacity to go astray.
Everything that is created also needs another power—that is, to support it.
Anyone who needs help from another reveals the deficiency of his own nature.
Everyone who knows that he is deficient ought also to humble himself, so that he may receive what he needs from the one who is able to give it to him.
If he had known all these things from the beginning and had kept his attention on them at all times, he would not have fallen asleep.
If he had not fallen asleep, he would not have been handed over to tormentors to awaken him.
Therefore, someone who walks in the way of God ought, in everything that comes
upon him, to give thanks and to blame and chastise himself, knowing that either, because he had become negligent,
the tempter stirred his soul at the command of the Ruler, or it was because he had become proud.
He should therefore not recoil and be shaken, or present himself as beyond reproach, lest his evil increase.
For there is no injustice with God—far be it!—who is the fountain of righteousness.
On sins committed with premeditation and an evil will, and on those committed under compulsion. 9.
There is sin that comes from weakness, in which a person becomes entangled under compulsion. And there is sin that comes from the will.
There is also sin that comes from ignorance; there is sin into which an unforeseen event brings a person; there is sin that comes from persistence; and there is sin that comes from habit.
Although all these classes and kinds of sins fall under condemnation,
the penalty for them varies, being lesser or greater.
There is someone whose repentance is accepted only with difficulty and whose blame is great; and there is someone who is close to receiving mercy.
God, too, although he exempted none of Adam, Eve, and the serpent from receiving punishment for their wrongdoing,
showed a great difference between his curse upon the serpent, the one upon Eve, and the one directed toward Adam. So it is also with their children.
For each person, the judgment against him becomes severe in proportion to his zeal and love for sin. But if there is someone
who does not love pursuing sin, yet is swept toward it through negligence in righteousness,
because of [?] in his diligence in righteousness, then even though involvement in sin is distressing to him, his judgment is severe.
But if temptations to sin meet him while he is zealous for righteousness, mercy is undoubtedly close at hand for his transgression.
For it is one thing when a person takes care over virtue,
perseveres in its deeds, and spends the night thinking about it, lest he fall short in any of its duties,
and goes about by day carrying its burden, with all his thought devoted to righteousness; and while he is occupied with these and similar things,
because of ignorance, or because of the pressure of opposing forces on that very path of virtue,
and the waves of pleasure constantly rising in his limbs, and the inclination placed within him to test his freedom,
the pan of the scales tips a little to the left, and through the weakness of the flesh he is swept into one of the kinds of sin,
while he is sorrowful and distressed over it and sighs with grief over himself because of his wretchedness in facing the mishaps that occur from time to time.
And it is another thing when a person is slack in practicing righteousness, or has abandoned the path altogether,
He runs like a slave, in complete obedience, to meet all the pleasures of sin;
and he takes pains to find ways to gratify it. Like a slave, he is ready
eagerly to do his enemy’s will, while his limbs stand ready as weapons for Satan in complete obedience.
He does not even look toward repentance, toward drawing near to virtue and putting an end to his ruinous way.
The slips and falls that lie on the path of the virtues are one thing,
and on the journey of righteousness, as the fathers say.
“On the path of the virtues,” they say, “there are falls, there are changes, there is distress,” and so on.
But the death of the soul, complete destruction, and total abandonment are another thing.
This distinction is recognized by the fact that, when he falls, he does not forget his Father’s love.
Though he experiences slips of every kind, his zeal for his good work is not hindered.
He does not stop running his course. Even in his defeat, he does not grow weary of standing up again to fight against them.
Though his building collapses, he does not cease making a fresh start on its foundation every day.
The prophet’s words remain in his mouth until the hour of his departure from this world: “Do not rejoice over me, my enemy; though I have fallen, I will rise again.
Though I sit in darkness, the Lord gives me light.” He does not cease fighting until death.
He does not surrender himself to defeat as long as there is breath in his nostrils.
Though his ship is wrecked every day, and the sweat of his trading sinks into the depths,
he does not cease borrowing, fitting out ships, and sailing in hope,
until the Lord sees his zeal, takes pity on his ruin, and extends his mercy to him.
He gives him powerful impulses to endure and to face the flaming arrows of the evil one.
This is the wisdom that comes from God, and this is the wise sick person. Despair brings no benefit.
For it is better for us to be judged for individual faults than for complete abandonment. Therefore the blessed Interpreter,
when warning us not to grow weary because of the many struggles and the frequent kinds of battles along the path of righteousness,
and turn back and give our enemy a complete victory through one kind of evil,
sets them out in outline and says: “For if you are truly eager to look toward virtue,
to cultivate serenity of mind toward God, and to do what is fitting in his sight,
You must necessarily endure all the battles that arise over these things:
those that continually tend to rise against you from natural passions, the entanglements of this world, and the malice of demons.
Do not grow slack because the struggle is constant and unrelenting,
and do not fear the intensity and violence of the battle.
Do not be terrified by the armies of the enemies,
and do not fall into despair if you happen to stumble somewhere and sin,
and receive wounds and bruises on your faces, as happens in so great a battle.
Nor should you abandon your resolve because of this.
Instead, persist in the way of life you have chosen, considering this something lovable and glorious:
that you should be seen in the battle drenched in the blood of your wounds,
without ever ceasing your struggle against the enemies.
These are the admonitions of the blessed Interpreter.
Nevertheless, we must not grow slack because of these things. Woe to the monk who is false to his covenant
and, trampling on his conscience, helps Satan gain access to him through both minor and major kinds of sin.
For he can no longer find the strength to defend the breach he has made in himself before his enemies.
With what face will he look when his chaste companions gather together,
those from whom he parted ways to follow the road to destruction? And how will he look upon the confidence that the holy have before God,
and that prayer which rises from a chaste heart, ascending and passing even beyond the [?] of the angels,
and is not held back until it enters before the majesty of God, holding keys in its hands, and is not held back
until it receives what it requests and returns joyfully to the mouth that sent it?
And the hardest thing of all is this: just as he parted ways with them here, Christ will separate him from them on that day,
when luminous clouds carry on their backs the bodies that have shone with purity, and they enter through the great gate of heaven.
Therefore the wicked will not stand in the judgment, because their conduct is already judged.
Nor will sinners stand in the assembly of the virtuous at the resurrection of judgment, nor the dissolute in the ranks of the holy.
On how the words of the Scriptures are spoken in measured terms, as to the [?] and the sick, lest they perish utterly away from the living God.
But let us not, on this account, take them as an aid to greater boldness in sin. 10.
The encouragements that our fathers give us in their writings, and the strengthening concerning repentance found in the books of the prophets and apostles:
let us not take them as an incentive to act shamelessly toward the threats of divine judgments,
and toward the punishment for breaking boundaries that must not be crossed,
concerning those things whose abolition, from ancient days, through the mouths of all his holy ones and through every kind of law,
God has firmly decreed. It is as though, because there is hope through repentance,
we have found opportunities to steal the sense of fear from our souls, so that we can sin more freely and without anxiety.
The sentence against these things, expressed in every form of warning, is confirmed by the seals of the word of God
in all the Scriptures of our salvation. He has also revealed some of them, among many people and among few,
through the punishments he brought upon them, to show that he hates sin.
For what reason were the generations in Noah’s days destroyed in the flood? Was it not through the impulse of lust, when they became infatuated with the beauty of the daughters of
Cain? There was no love of money at that time, nor worship of idols,
nor sorcery, nor wars in which people drew up against one another. And why were burned forever
the five cities of the Sodomites? Was it not because they gave lust room in their bodily members, and it ruled over them as it pleased,
in every kind of uncleanness? Was it not because of one man’s sexual immorality that there fell from Israel, God’s firstborn,
twenty-five thousand through a plague at a single command? Why was Samson, the mighty warrior, rejected by God,
a Nazirite from the womb and consecrated to God, who was announced by an angel like John son of Zechariah, and through whose hands God performed mighty deeds and signs,
who, by the supernatural strength poured into his body, slaughtered a thousand men with the jawbone of a donkey,
and became Israel’s deliverer and judge? Was it not because he defiled and polluted his consecrated bodily members through intercourse with a prostitute,
and because of this the Lord withdrew from him, and he was handed over to his enemies? David, who was after God’s heart,
because of whose virtue the promise to the righteous fathers was handed down through his offspring,
and from whom Christ arose for the salvation of the whole world—was it not through adultery with one woman and being overcome in a single hour
that, from a glance of his eye, he received an arrow in his soul, and God raised up evil against him from his own household,
and the son who came from his own loins pursued him? And this happened even though he had shown repentance, and the Lord had said to him, “I too have taken away
your sin; you shall not die”—despite that whole flood of his tears,
from their abundance he would soak his bed at night. I turn also to what came even before this.
Why? Why did calamities and the full force of the decreed judgments overtake the house of Eli the priest,
a righteous old man, a priest, and a judge of Israel for forty years? Was it not because of Phinehas and Hophni, his sons,
who were abusing the women who came to pray at the tent of meeting, although he himself had not sinned, nor was it his will?
Rather, it was solely because he remained passive and rebuked them only with words, and did not show zeal against his sons’ sexual immorality
and exact the Lord’s judgment from them. And so that no one should suppose that the Lord displays his zeal only against those who have been sinners all their lives,
because of this brazen sin, hateful to God, look: he displays his zeal against those close to him,
against his priests, the judges and leaders of the people, and those who are consecrated to him and through whose hands he has performed wonders.
For even when they transgress the laws he has established, he shows them no favoritism.
As it is written in Ezekiel, he said to the man whom he commanded to destroy the people of Jerusalem with a concealed sword:
“Begin in front of the altar, and have no pity on old man, child, or young man.”
This was to show that those who truly belong close to him are those who walk with fear and careful concern
before him and do his will. The Lord’s holy ones and those close to him are good deeds and a pure conscience.
But when they reject the paths of the Lord’s will, he too rejects them, casts them out of his presence, and withdraws his grace from them.
And why did the decree of the Most High fall upon Belshazzar for his insolence through the sign of a hand? Was it not
because he insolently violated the sacred vessels that he had brought from Jerusalem,
and he and his concubines drank from them? Likewise, anyone whose bodily members were once set apart for the Lord’s holiness,
but who insolently uses them for worldly deeds—with all this insolence, the decree of the Most High suddenly falls upon him,
just as it did upon Belshazzar, who insolently violated the consecrated vessels brought out of the Lord’s sanctuary.
Therefore, we must not, because of our confidence in repentance and the encouraging words of the Scriptures,
defy God’s words and threats, or dishonor him through our hateful deeds,
or dishonor the bodily members that we once presented as an offering, so that his holy rites might be performed through them
and they might be used for his work. Look, we are consecrated to God and abstain from women.
And like Elijah, [?] Elisha, the sons of the prophets, and the rest of the consecrated ascetics and holy virgins,
through whose hands great and marvelous things were done, and who spoke face to face with God.
And like those who came afterward, such as John the virgin, holy Simon, and the rest of the heralds of the new covenant, who consecrated themselves
to the Lord and received mysteries from him, some from his own mouth and others through revelation.
They became mediators between God and humanity, and heralds of his revelations,
and bearers of good news and bearers of good news of the kingdom to the inhabitants of the world.
11. By what means the beauties of the solitary life are preserved, and how it may become a cause for praising God.
The solitary ought, in every aspect of his conduct, to be an encouraging sight to those who see him,
so that through his many beauties, which shine like rays of sunlight from every aspect of his conduct,
even the enemies of the truth may acknowledge, against their will, that Christians have a sure hope.
And from every place people may run to them for refuge, and the head of the church may be raised above her enemies,
so that the glory of his deeds may inspire many with courage to leave the world,
and that he may be held in awe by everyone because of the splendor of his virtue,
so that, because of him, the members of the church may speak boldly and hold their heads high above all religions.
The way of life of solitaries is the pride of Christ’s church.
Therefore, the solitary ought to have the beauties of his appearance displayed pleasingly in every respect:
in the modesty of his limbs, in the [?] of his appearance, in his elevation above visible things,
in the thoroughness of his renunciation, in his complete disregard for the body,
in the strenuousness of his fasting, in his constant silence, in the discipline of his senses,
in the restraint of his gaze, in his lack of eagerness for any created thing,
in the fewness of his words, in his freedom from resentment, in the simplicity of his discernment.
And he should be known as one who is beyond this corruptible and fleeting life
and close to that true and spiritual life, through his constant attention to himself,
through his remaining unknown among people and his not being bound to anyone in companionship and intimacy,
through the quiet place where he lives, through the confinement of his dwelling, through the fewness and low value of his possessions,
through his flight from people, through his constancy in prayer, through his hatred and avoidance of honor,
through his lack of attachment to this temporal life, through the great depth of his patience, and through his perseverance in trials,
And from his restraint from listening to and investigating worldly affairs, and from his constant meditation and reflection on that true homeland of his.
This is revealed by the lack of cheerfulness in his expression and the scorched appearance of his face, and by his constant weeping by night and [?].
And above all, by his care to preserve his chastity and his freedom from greed, in matters ranging from the smallest to the greatest.
These, in brief outline, are the visible virtues of the solitary, which testify to his complete death
to the world and his closeness to God. We ought to meditate on these things constantly and acquire them.
But if someone asks, “Why was it necessary for these signs
to be described at such length?” I say, “It was very necessary.”
For when someone searches within himself for these signs one by one, if he is concerned about his life and lacks anything,
these distinctions will enable him to recognize his deficiency in each of the virtues.
These signs will serve him as reminders.
And when he has acquired in himself all these things that have been described, then, as for the remaining things that were left out,
knowledge of them is given to him, and he becomes a reason for human beings and the holy angels to praise God.
And already here he prepares a place of rest for his soul, before his departure from this world.
On why it is not fitting for a servant of God who has emptied himself of the world and gone out in search of God and of truth
to stop seeking truth because of fear—that is, lest he fail to find the truth—
or to abandon the burning fervor born of longing for divine things and of investigating their mysteries, which are depicted symbolically.
For through this search the mind rests from evil distraction and memories stirred by the passions. 12.
There are three stages through which the whole course of human life progresses:
the stage of beginning, the intermediate stage, and the stage of perfection.
In the first stage, all a person's occupation and recollection remain subject to passion, even if his mind is directed toward virtue.
The second is intermediate between being subject to the passions and being spiritual.
Thoughts from the right and from the left clamor within him equally.
The springs of light and darkness on either side never run dry, as has been said.
But if he stops, even briefly, his unceasing study of the writings of the Spirit and [?] concerning these divine things,
through meditation on which he may be set ablaze like fire, with his purpose directed toward truth, while also keeping outward watch according to his strength.
because of which even what is within, and the labor he is capable of, is swept toward the passions.
And if he nourishes his natural warmth with these things I have mentioned, and does not cease seeking and investigating,
and longs for them from afar, although they are not visible to him except through their indications in the Scriptures,
and nurtures his thoughts and disciplines them through these things so that they do not turn to the left,
or receive any seed of fantasies from demons in place of truth,
rather, let him yearn and watch over himself, and entreat God with heartfelt prayer arising from patient endurance.
When it pleases God to grant it to him, he opens a door before him,
especially because of his humility, for mysteries are revealed to the humble.
But if he dies in this very expectation, without having seen that land up close,
I think his inheritance will be with the righteous of old, who awaited perfection, according to the apostle’s words, and did not
see it, but labored all their days in hope of it and fell asleep.
But what shall we say? If someone does not attain the point of entering the promised land, which is the rank of the perfect,
and finding the truth plainly before his eyes, as far as nature is capable, should he then give this up too, remaining in that lower rank which is wholly occupied with words?
And because he has not found the whole truth, should he remain in a lowly state in which he does not even know how to desire these things,
or rise to this intermediate state that I mentioned, even if he does not see as in a mirror, but awaits it from afar,
and in this very expectation is gathered to his fathers? Even if he is not deemed worthy of all that grace here,
still, let him occupy his mind by engaging with it, even while far away.
And through its encouragements, as long as he lives, let him break away [?] from evil thoughts.
And in this hope, with his heart full of God, he departs from this world.
Everything that takes place in humility is good.
The mind’s immaterial meditations, directed toward the love of God through the meanings of the Scriptures,
fence off the entrances of the soul against foreign thoughts and protect the mind from recollections of things.
Through these, the warmth of its activity would slacken, and it would fall into lustful desires.
On the changes that occur in those practiced in stillness, and how this path is ordered by God for their benefit.
At times there is sadness and anguish of soul, and suddenly cheerfulness and joy, warm fervor, and unusual strength.
Glory [?] to the one who orders our way. Amen. 13.
But anyone who has resolved in his mind to establish himself in a solitary dwelling, alone with himself,
and to spend the rest of his life in the practice and discipline of the various forms of stillness, whenever, as commonly happens in stillness—
a practice wisely ordained by divine grace—his soul happens to be enveloped in gloom,
and, like the rays of the sun that are hidden from the inhabited world by a thick mass of clouds,
[?] he is briefly deprived of spiritual consolation and the radiance of grace by a cloud of passions,
and that joy-giving power withdraws from him a little, and an unfamiliar darkness gathers over his mind,
he should not let his thoughts become disturbed or give way to discouragement.
Instead, he should endure, occupying himself with the writings of godly men and persistent prayers, and waiting for help.
And suddenly it is given to him, without his knowing it. For just as the face of the inhabited world is brightened by the sun’s rays
when the thickness of the air clears, so the words of prayer can dissolve and scatter the fog of the passions from the soul
and gladden and illuminate the mind with the rays of joy and consolation that prayer produces in our thoughts.
This is especially so when it has [?] for assistance from the Holy Scriptures, and wakefulness that purifies the mind.
Constant meditation on the holy writings continually fills the soul with incomprehensible wonder and joy in God.
Again, concerning those who walk in stillness: when they begin to weep, even a little, how far they have advanced in their practice,
so that, in the unfathomable sea of the life of stillness, they may have a little confidence in their labor, which has begun to bear fruit. 14.
I will tell you something, and do not laugh, for I am telling the truth.
And do not doubt this statement, for those from whom I received it are trustworthy.
Even if you hang before God by your eyelids, until you attain tears, do not suppose that you have achieved anything in your way of life.
For your hidden depths still serve the world. That is, you remain at the level of the life of faithful people living in the world.
For it is with your outward self that you labor in the service of God, while your inward self is still without fruit.
Its fruit begins at the point I have mentioned. But when you reach the place of tears,
then understand that your mind has left the prison of this world and set foot on the road of the new world.
It has begun to breathe the wondrous air there, and it begins to shed tears,
because the pains of childbirth have now come upon it, for that spiritual child.
For grace, the mother within, hastens mystically to give birth to the soul, the image of God, into the light of the world to come.
And when the time of birth arrives, the mind now begins to perceive, little by little, something from that world,
like a faint breath that an infant receives within, from the organs in which it has grown.
And, unable to bear something so unfamiliar, it stirs the body to weeping mingled with a joy that surpasses the sweetness of honey.
The more that infant within grows, the more the tears increase.
The flow of tears begins when the mind starts to become clear.
But in speaking of the flow of tears belonging to this stage, I am not concerned with the intermittent kind that comes from time to time.
This consolation that comes from time to time happens to everyone who labors with God in stillness:
sometimes through the mind’s contemplation, sometimes through the words of the Scriptures, and sometimes through the communion of supplication.
My concern is to speak of the continuous kind, which goes on without interruption, night and day.
This happens to someone who, through exactness in his way of life, has found the truth in stillness: his eyes become springs of water
for a period of two years, more or less. This happens at the time of transition.
I mean a mystical transition. Then, after the tears, you enter into peace of thoughts.
And in this very peace of thoughts, you enter into that divine rest of which Paul spoke,
in part, as nature allows. From this place of peace, the intellect begins
to see hidden things. Then the Holy Spirit begins to reveal heavenly things before it,
as God dwells in you and stirs up the fruits of the Spirit within you.
And from this you perceive that transformation which all creation is to receive at the renewal of all things,
dimly, as through a hint. I have written these things for my own benefit and for the benefit of everyone who encounters this book,
as something I have grasped through contemplation of the Scriptures, from the mouths of trustworthy people, and a little from experience,
so that I too may receive help through the prayers of those who benefit from these things, because I have labored over them.
Listen also to something else I tell you, as I learned it from a mouth that does not lie:
when you have entered this peaceful region of thoughts, the continuous flow of tears is then taken away from you,
and you come to tears that have a limit and a measure. This, stated briefly, is the precise truth.
It is confirmed and trusted by the whole Church, and by the champions and foremost warriors among her children.
On the progression of the solitary way, briefly and with a little explanation.
And how, and in what manner, its virtues are born from one another. 15.
Clearly and explicitly, their progression is as follows.
From the labors of self-discipline in stillness is born that blazing fervor
which has no measure and flares up in the heart from the burning thoughts that flash forth anew in the mind.
These labors and watchfulness, through their heat, refine the intellect and give it vision.
That vision gives birth to the burning thoughts I mentioned, through the depth of spiritual seeing, which is called contemplation.
Contemplation gives birth to fervor, and from this fervor comes vision granted by grace.
Then the outpouring of tears is born: first, the kind that comes intermittently.
That is, tears break forth for a person many times in a single day.
From this he comes to uninterrupted tears. From tears the soul receives peace of thoughts.
From peace of thoughts it is raised to clarity of mind.
With a clear mind, a person comes to see hidden things.
For purity is contained in freedom from inner battles.
After these things, the intellect reaches something whose illustration is depicted in that stream in the prophet Ezekiel,
which portrays these three stages of souls drawing near to divine things; the third of them cannot be crossed.
The beginning of all these things is a good will directed toward God and varied labors in stillness,
and not that perversity which is born of excessive separation from the world.
It was not necessary to distinguish the different labors, since they are known to everyone.
Nevertheless, whenever a person encounters them, he certainly suffers no loss. As for benefiting,
I know that he will benefit. These are the labors: enduring hunger,
reading, and wakeful vigils at night, each according to his strength;
and the many prostrations a person makes at the appointed times during the day and many times during the night.
One person makes thirty prostrations at a time and finishes, and then leaves the presence of the cross.
Another adds even more to this number. Another lingers for three periods in a single prayer:
And he is drawn into his mind as he lies face down, with no compulsion there and no distraction of thoughts.
Both these different forms reveal the great abundance of grace, which visits each person differently, according to his measure.
Whether it is the form in which abundance, kindled by fervor, increases the number, or the form in which his soul receives it in stillness,
and encompasses in a single one the many repetitions of the former prayers.
But as for the cause of that other prayer, the lingering in it, and its freedom from compulsion,
I did not think it right to explain such things, bringing their various forms into spoken and written expression,
lest a reader who cannot grasp anything of it regard it as something foolish.
But if he is acquainted with these things, he despises someone who does not know how to set limits to such matters.
From this person comes blame, and from the other, laughter.
And in this matter I become a foreigner to that person, whoever he may be, according to the apostle’s statement about
the person who prophesies. But whoever longs to understand these things—the way leading to them has been outlined above.
Let him join action to thought, by the grace of our Lord. When he has experienced these things in practice, he learns for himself.
“Sit in your cell,” it is said, “and your cell will teach you everything.”
On how greatly freedom from activities helps the soul in stillness,
and how coming and going diminish the understanding of the beginner who has only recently begun to look within himself;
and how bodily activities plainly compel the solitary to fall short in doing the works of God. 16.
A person burdened with many concerns cannot be at rest and at peace.
For the necessary, necessary circumstances that accompany the matters in which you are occupied
force him into agitation and plunder his rest and tranquility.
Without points of contact, Satan has no opening through which to enter the soul.
The solitary ought to place himself continually before God and watch for his signal,
if he has truly resolved to guard his mind attentively and wishes to perceive keenly the little impulses that stir within it,
and to know how, with a peaceful mind, to distinguish what enters and what leaves. Encounters
that are frequent in a solitary’s life are a sign of his neglect of preparation for Christ’s service,
and indications revealing his deficiency in these divine things.
Without freedom from cares, do not expect illumination from your soul.
Nor expect rest and tranquility while your senses are scattered, or recollection of the senses amid involvement in affairs.
Do not multiply involvements for yourself, and you will not find confusion in your mind.
Without continual supplication, it is impossible to draw near to God.
To introduce another concern into the mind while laboring in supplication is a distraction of the heart.
The burning impulses that once came upon you through a taste of God, in the fierce ardor of things done for his sake—
when you returned and examined them again, you found that their taste had faded and that they had grown cold within your soul:
the attraction of human company has swept over you from somewhere,
or you have valued bodily activity more than them, and because of this the warmth of your thoughts has cooled.
But tears, touching your head to the ground in prayer, and fervent sighs awaken the warmth of their sweetness within the heart again.
And in a praiseworthy madness the heart flies after God, crying out:
“My soul thirsts for you, the living God. When shall I come and see your face?”
Only someone who has drunk this wine and then been deprived of it knows what torment he has been left in,
and what has been taken from him because of his negligence. Oh, how harmful seeing people and conversing with them is for someone
who lives in stillness—even more than for someone who is lax and undisciplined! Truly, alas! Like a violent blast of icy wind,
which suddenly strikes the branches of trees and scorches the little tips that have sprouted from the boughs,
so conversation with people, even if very brief, and even if their gathering seems to be for a good purpose,
withers the shoots of the virtues that have newly put out their tips in the mild air of stillness,
which cluster thickly around the tree of the soul planted beside the streams of repentance.
And like the force of frost, which overtakes the fresh shoots of plants,
strikes down their tips, and drives them into the ground, so human company acts upon the plant of the mind,
which has begun to grow green with the shoots of the virtues: it strikes down their tips, drives them back into their place, and covers their trembling growth.
And if conversation with those who exercise even a little self-restraint, merely because it interrupts one's customary practice,
does all this harm to the soul, how much more does speaking with and seeing frivolous and ignorant people,
not to mention worldly people! This is like fire to a forest.
And just as a respected and dignified man forgets himself through drinking a great deal of wine,
and his modesty is disturbed and his dignity debased, and through the alien thoughts that assail his mind under the influence of wine,
his self-restraint is disturbed, so too the soul’s modesty is disturbed through associating with people and seeing them.
It forgets the goal of its vigilance, and the entire aim of its will is erased from its mind.
The whole foundation of its praiseworthy conduct is uprooted by social intercourse, ease, and the practice of distraction.
Even if someone remains silent and is merely personally present at a gathering of such people, seeing and hearing,
what his eyes and ears alone bring in is enough to divert his mind from divine things and cause great disturbance.
That is, merely seeing people and hearing their idle talk.
And if this continues for some time, this alone can cause all kinds of harm to a solitary who guards himself.
What, then, shall we say about continual encounters or prolonged lingering?
Smoke rises from the belly against the knowledge of divine things, like the vapors that rise from the moisture of the earth before the sun.
Pride does not perceive that it walks in darkness, and it knows neither understanding nor wisdom.
It raises itself above everything in its thoughts, yet it is poorer and lower than everything. It cannot know the ways of God.
And the Lord hides his will from it, because it has not loved walking in the way of the humble.
On the short paths to God that are revealed to a person through the sweet labors of the night vigil,
and how those who labor in the practice of vigil are nourished on honey all their days. 17.
Do not suppose, O human being, that among all the labors of ascetics there is any practice greater or more excellent than the labor of vigil.
Truly, [?], if the ascetic is also free during the day from distraction over bodily matters and passing concerns,
but has even a little separation from the world and a little watchfulness along with his vigil, I have no difficulty telling you the truth:
within a short time his mind flies as though on wings and ascends to God to delight in him.
It readily contemplates that glory and swims lightly in that knowledge which is higher than human understanding.
Do not regard the solitary who perseveres in vigil with mental discernment as someone clothed in flesh.
Truly, this activity belongs to the order of angels. For it is impossible that those who labor in this practice
should be left without great gifts and [?] from God, because of the wakefulness and brightness of their hearts,
and because their thoughts continually meditate on him. Thus the soul that labors in this practice of vigil is trained:
She has the eyes of the cherubim, with swift perception and keenness, to gaze continually upon heavenly visions.
For my part, I think it impossible that someone who, with great understanding and discernment,
has chosen for himself this great and divine labor, and has taken care to bear this entire burden,
in this glorious portion he has chosen for himself, should not strive to guard himself even during the day from the disturbance of conversations and thoughts about tasks,
so that he may not be deprived of the wonderful fruits and great delights that he is to gather from it.
As for anyone who neglects this, I can confidently say, without speaking falsely,
that he does not even know what all this labor is for: the loss of sleep, the many repetitions, the weariness of the tongue,
and standing on his feet all night, since his mind is not even present where he is singing psalms and praying.
Rather, he is held by habit, as though engaged in something without discernment. If things were not as I say,
how could he bear to be deprived of, and cease reaping from his diligent mind, the excellent fruits of his labor? Instead of these things, he would labor
at the holy occupation of reading the Scriptures, which strengthens the mind
and, above all, provides water for prayer, assists the vigil, and is its fellow under the yoke,
a light for the ground, a path along the way, and a sower of material for contemplation in prayer.
It restrains the mind from wandering and going off to roam among empty things.
It sows in the soul continual remembrance of God and of the ways of the saints who pleased him.
And it gives the mind wisdom and subtle understanding. Why, then, diligent man, do you so
undiscerningly conduct your affairs? For you show such care for yourself
that you stand on your feet all night and weary yourself with praises, psalms, and prayers.
Is it a small thing to you that, through a little vigilance during the day, you should be found worthy of grace from God for your labor in everything else?
Why do you weary yourself and sow at night, but scatter your labors during the day
and end up without your fruits? You dissipate the alertness and warmth that you acquire during the vigil
through disturbing conversations with people and work that draws you away, and you destroy your gain by dissipating yourself over nothing.
If you joined your nightly meditation, O man, to your daytime work, and that warmth of the heart’s converse
you did not interrupt in between, in a short time you would be embracing the breast of Jesus.
But from this it is evident that you are afflicted with a lack of discernment.
Nor do you understand why keeping vigil is required of ascetics.
You suppose, then, that it is only for the hardship, and not because they look toward something else that comes from it.
But anyone whom grace has made worthy even to a small degree, and who knows what hope makes the wise struggle against sleep,
and put all this constraint upon their nature, so that, awake in body and in their thoughts, they may offer prayers throughout the night,
would also know the strength that comes from watchfulness during the day,
and what help it gives the mind in the solitude of the night, during its discerning vigil,
and what freedom from thoughts, alertness, and concentration of mind it brings him,
without compulsion or struggle, freely. I have digressed [?] in speaking at length.
But I also say this: even if the body happens to need rest from the labor of fasting because of weakness
and its great exhaustion, the labor of keeping vigil alone can bring the mind into a proper state for prayer,
and give the heart understanding to recognize spiritual powers.
This is so only if confusion does not enter it through giving free rein to distractions during the day.
Therefore I urge you, discerning person who longs to acquire wakefulness of mind in God and knowledge of the new life,
never throughout your life to despise this practice of keeping vigil.
Through it your eyes are opened to see all the glory of this way of life and the power of the path of righteousness.
And if at any time—God forbid—a thought of slackness should settle within you as a trial,
since your Helper is accustomed to train you and make you wise through such changes, through coldness as well as fervor,
or because of circumstances and distractions, or because your body is sick or grows weak, and because of it you come to this point:
because you do not want to tire your body, you intend to go to sleep in the evening, then I ask you in love:
even if you rest from all that sustained chanting, the labors of the service, and the many kneelings
in prayer that are your custom, at least sit, if you have any strength at all—I mean, remain awake—
without chanting or prostrating yourself. If you can, pray only in your heart. But do not sleep.
By every means, pass the night sitting, engaged in the good meditation to which you are accustomed.
Only do not let your heart become dull and darkened through sleep.
Then your former lightness, strength, and fervor will come to you again through grace, and you will be glad and rejoice and give thanks to God.
For heaviness and lightness of this kind are allowed to come upon a person as a test.
But if someone rouses himself fervently, shakes it off and casts it away, and makes himself exert a little effort, grace immediately draws near as before.
And another power comes to him, in which countless blessings and various forms of help are hidden.
The person is astonished and amazed when he remembers his former heaviness,
and his laxity and weakness then, and how he suddenly underwent such a change.
Thus he gains wisdom from this, so that at other times too, when that heaviness comes, he recognizes it.
And if he had not persevered boldly on the earlier occasions, he would not have acquired this knowledge.
Do you see how much wisdom a person gains when he rouses himself a little and takes courage in times of struggle?
Unless, that is, his bodily nature has simply become utterly exhausted, and it is not a struggle,
but an illness or an unavoidable weakness, against which fighting does no good.
But in all other cases, a person benefits in every way from making himself exert effort.
Constant stillness together with reading and a measured diet readily awaken wonder about things in the mind,
provided that circumstances do not create a break in the continuity of stillness.
The insights stirred up by labors in stillness, suddenly and of their own accord, without being sought,
make these two eyes into a kind of baptismal font, through the tears that stream down and drench the cheeks with their abundance.
But whenever, while you are humbling your body through ascetic discipline in watchful stillness, you feel in your body the intensity of a persistent passion for sexual immorality,
beyond the faint stirring usual to nature, know that you have been tempted by pride in your thinking.
Mix your food with ashes, press your belly to the dust, and examine what you have been thinking.
Recognize the changes in your nature and your practices that go beyond your nature.
Perhaps God will have mercy on you and send you light to learn how to humble yourself, so that your trouble does not grow worse.
Let us not cease being watchful until repentance dawns in our hearts, we find humility, and our hearts find rest in God.
Further things that I heard from elders, and accounts of holy people,
their devout words and their wonderful ways of life. May our Lord protect us through their prayers. Amen. 18.
One day I went to the cell of a certain holy brother and lay down in a corner because of an illness, so that
he might care for me for God's sake. For I had no one in those parts.
For I used to see this brother at night, getting up long before the appointed time.
He was accustomed to waking for the service before all the other brothers.
He would begin with the psalms and continue with them for a while.
Then suddenly he would leave off the service and fall on his face.
A little short of a hundred times, one might say, he would strike his head against the ground, repeatedly and vigorously,
with that fervor which grace kindled in his heart. Then he would stand up and salute the cross.
Again he would bow down, stand up, and salute it, and again fall on his face.
He would do this so many times that I could not say how many.
Who could have counted the many times that brother knelt down during the nights!
He would approach the cross [?] and give it twenty kisses,
eagerly and warmly, with love mingled with fear. Then he would resume the psalms.
And sometimes, because of the many surges of thoughts that set him ablaze with their warmth,
when he could no longer bear that blaze because of his joy,
he would suddenly be overcome and raise his voice, because he could not contain himself.
I marveled at the grace that was with that brother,
and I was amazed at how diligent and watchful he was in the works of God.
After the morning service, when he sat down to read, he seemed like someone caught up in a trance.
At every passage he read, he would fall on his face many times.
At most of the verses, he would stretch out his hands toward heaven [?] and offer praise many times.
He was a man of moderate stature, about forty years old.
He ate little, and he was lean and hot in constitution.
Because he forced himself even when his body could not bear it, he sometimes looked like a shadow,
so that one would pity him for the gauntness of his face, which wasted away until it was like two fingers.
I told him many times, “My brother, take care to preserve this upright discipline of your life,
and this beautiful path to which you hold fast. Do not disrupt and break this discipline of yours, which is like a spiritual chain.
Because of greed for a little, you add much toil and hold yourself back from your whole course.
Eat in moderation, so that you may keep eating. Do not travel farther than your strength allows, lest you come to a complete stop.
For he was compassionate and very bashful, and he showed mercy cheerfully.
He was gentle by nature, very easily persuaded, and wise in God.
Because of his gentleness and cheerfulness, he was dear to everyone, and everyone loved him.
He also worked clay with all the brothers in their cells whenever they had such work:
sometimes for three days, sometimes for four days. And from
evening to evening he would come to his cell, until the brother’s work was finished.
He was very willing to do this work. Whenever he had something, even if he needed it badly,
he was very bashful before people of every rank. He could not say, “I have nothing,” or, “I need it myself.”
His continually leaving his cell to work for the brothers was also
because of his bashfulness before others: he forced himself, although he was not comfortable going out,
and he often told me about the distress that leaving his cell caused him.

Such was the godly way of life of that wonderful brother.

About another elder.
Once I went to the cell of an elder, one of the men of old, a virtuous man who loved me dearly.
He was somewhat unpolished in his speech, but clear and profound in his thoughts.
Whatever came to him, he spoke as though it came from grace.
He did not readily leave his cell, except for the holy sacraments. He constantly kept to himself and remained quiet.
I said to him, “Father, the thought comes to me that I should go on Sunday and sit in the church porch
and eat early in the morning, so that everyone coming in and going out may see me, and I may be despised.”
The elder said to me, “It is written: ‘Whoever causes worldly people to stumble shall not see the light.’
“But no one knows you in these regions, nor do they know anything about you.
“They will say, ‘Monks eat early in the morning.’ Moreover, there are novice brothers
“whose thoughts are weak. Many of them are even now being built up by you.
“When they see you, they will turn back. The fathers of old used to do things like these:
Because of the signs and many miracles that were performed through their hands, and because of the reputation and great honor they enjoyed.
Each of them would do these things so that he might be despised and mistreated,
to bring the glory of his conduct into disrepute, so as to remove from himself any occasion for pride.
But as for you, what necessity compels you to do this? Do you not know
that even in practices such as these there is a measure for you? You have neither an exceptional way of life nor a reputation.
You live just like the rest of the brothers. Therefore, you do not benefit yourself by this, and you also harm others.
This way of life does not benefit everyone, but only people who are great and mature,
because it involves giving the senses freedom. But it greatly harms beginners and those at an intermediate stage,
since they have greater need of vigilance and restraint of the senses.
For the elders have passed the checkpoint, as the saying goes, and they trade in whatever they wish and know how to make a profit.
An inexperienced merchant incurs greater losses for himself in large transactions.
But in smaller ones, he often makes progress easily.
Therefore, as I said, there is a measure for every action, and for every
practice an appointed time. Anyone who begins something beyond his measure before its time heaps up harm, not benefit.
If you desire this, first endure the insults that come upon you providentially, against your will,

joyfully, without becoming disturbed or hating those who insult you.

By another elder.
Once I was in conversation with that diligent man who had tasted of the tree of life through the sweat of his soul,
from the morning of his youth until the evening of his old age.
After teaching me many things about virtue, he also said this to me: “Every prayer
in which the body does not toil and the heart does not suffer—consider that prayer a stillborn child without a soul.”
He also said to me: “Do not converse at all with anyone who loves to win arguments, is cunning in his thinking, and is shameless in his senses,
lest you drive away from yourself the serenity you acquired through toil, and he fill your heart with darkness and confusion.”
Once I went to the cell of one of the fathers. This holy man did not readily open his door to anyone.
When he saw through the window that it was I, he said to me, “Do you want to come in?” I said to him, “Yes.”
After I had entered and we had prayed and sat down, he spoke with me about many things.
Finally, I also asked him this: “What should I do, my lord? There are people who constantly come to see me, and I gain no benefit
from their conversation. Yet I feel embarrassed to tell them not to come.
Moreover, they often keep me from my customary prayer services.
I cannot tell them openly, and I am greatly worn down by this matter.”
That blessed man said to me, “Whenever people like these come to see you—lovers of idleness and talkers of empty things—
after they have sat for a little while, act as though you want to get up for the prayer service.
Bow to the person and say, ‘My brother, get up; let us perform the prayer service,
because the time for my own prayer service has arrived, and I cannot let it pass.
Otherwise, it becomes a burden for me to add another prayer period to the next one,
and this becomes a cause of confusion for me. I cannot leave any of them out except out of necessity.
But now we have no compelling reason to neglect the appointed time.’
Do not leave him alone at all until he gets up with you for the prayer service.
If he says, ‘Go ahead and pray yourself, for I am leaving,’ bow before him and say,
‘Show me this kindness and perform this one prayer service with me, so that I may be helped by your prayer.’
When he has agreed and you have stood up, make your prayer service longer than usual. Do this to them whenever they come.
When they see that you do not share their outlook and love idleness, they will no longer come near any place where they hear you are.
Take care not to show deference to anyone at the expense of neglecting the works of God.
But if it is one of the fathers, or a visiting brother who is weary, it will be counted as a great service
for you to spend time in conversation with him.
But if the visitor too is one of those who love idle talk, give him what comfort you can and send him on his way quickly.”
One of the holy men once said to me, “I am amazed to hear that there are people who do some work in their cells
and also fulfill the prayer rules of the cell without leaving anything out, and can do so without becoming distracted.” And he said something worthy of wonder:
“Truly I tell you, even going to draw water disrupts my customary order,
as though I had been hindered in my practice and in completing the portions assigned to me.”
An elder was asked by a brother, “What should I do? Often I have something that I need,
whether because of illness, or because of work, or for any other reason;
so that, with the help its use provides, I can manage to live in solitude, more or less.
Then I see someone who is in need as I am, and I am overcome by compassion and give it to him.
Or someone asks me for it, and I am compelled by love and by the commandment, and give it to him.
Afterward, I find myself needing the thing.
My need for it throws me into anxiety, distress, and confusion of thoughts,
and takes away my mental concentration and my meditation on the customary exercises of the solitary life.
As a result, I am often compelled even
to leave my solitude and go in search of the thing.
If, on the other hand, I persevere and do not go out, I suffer great distress and confusion of mind.
Because of the matter, I am constantly worn down and troubled.
I do not know which of the two I should choose: what disrupts and shatters my tranquility for the sake of my neighbors’ comfort,
or to neglect this so that I can persevere in solitude and freedom from distractions, attending only to my own small needs,
without being obliged to fall into many preoccupations and anxieties on anyone else’s account.
Concerning this, I want to learn what is good and more acceptable.
The elder answered and said: Any act of compassion or love or almsgiving or generosity, or any duty whatsoever,
or any action thought to be of God, that interrupts your solitude and takes away your detachment from the world,
throws you into anxiety, distracts you from meditation on God through concern about it, and interrupts the order of your prayers,
brings confusion of thoughts upon you, and takes away your concentrated attention to reading and your freedom from distraction,
loosens your vigilance, turns you from one who stays confined into a wanderer, and from a solitary into one who mingles with others,
rouses buried passions against you, undoes the restraint of your senses, and brings you back to life from being dead to the world,
and brings you down from the work of angels, which is solitary meditation on the One,
and assigns you a share in the service of people living in the world—let that righteousness perish.
Fulfilling the obligations of love toward one’s neighbor by providing bodily comforts is the work of people living in the world, or else
of those solitaries who fall short of the work practiced in solitude.
Or they maintain silence mixed with fellowship with [?], and constant coming and going.
But those solitaries who have firmly chosen withdrawal from the world in body and mind,
to establish in their minds solitary prayer, with deadness to passing things,
and to thinking about every affair, and to seeing and remembering things, directed toward Christ,
do not serve him through these bodily practices and the righteousness of outward [?], or through the mediation of other people,
as though they would be justified through them, but through putting to death their members that are on earth, according to the apostle’s words,
always offering the pure sacrifices of their thoughts as firstfruits, the firstfruits of their service,
and the sufferings of their bodies through enduring afflictions for the sake of the hope they await.
To abandon the service of heavenly things and to trade in righteousness through earthly things.
A brother was urged to provide, from what he possessed, for the needs of the poor.
He answered arrogantly, “Are solitaries concerned with almsgiving?”
The man who had urged him said to him, “It is well known which solitary is not concerned with almsgiving:
the one who can confidently say to our Lord, in accordance with what is written,
‘Look, we have left everything and followed you.’ That is, the one who possesses nothing
on earth, does not labor bodily at earthly things, does not burden his mind with concern for anything in the world among these visible things, and does not seek to acquire anything.
When something is offered to him by someone, he accepts only enough for his needs and does not even look at the rest.
He is like a bird in his way of life. This is the one who is not concerned with giving alms, because he has a service superior to almsgiving.
How can he give others something from which he himself is free? But as long as someone works with his hands
and also receives from others, he is also obliged to give alms.
Neglecting this is an open violation of God’s commandments.
But if he does not advance toward God in hidden things, and does not know how to serve God in spirit,
and also despises these outward things that he is capable of doing, what other hope does he still have by which to gain his life? Such a person is accursed.”
Another admonition from one of the fathers concerning proper stillness.
Another also said, “I am astonished at those who disturb themselves in the practice of stillness
because they want to provide others with bodily comforts.”
Again he says: One should not mix concern for anything in the world with the practice of stillness,
except for those things that have a place in the practice of stillness itself.
And each way of life should be honored in its proper place, so that we do not become confused in our way of life. He says, “Anyone who is concerned about many things
is a slave to many masters. Anyone who lets everything go and concerns himself with setting his soul right is a friend of God.”
See how many people there are in the world who give alms and fulfill the duty of love for their neighbor through material things.
But those who practice stillness well and devote themselves to God are scarcely to be found, and they are few.
Or who is there among those who practice righteousness through material things and are justified through earthly things,
whom one can find receiving even one of the gifts that those who labor in stillness receive from God?
Again the same man said: If you are a layperson, conduct yourself in the ways that are good for laypeople.
And if you are a solitary, grow in excellence through the labors by which solitaries grow in excellence.
But if you wish to practice both ways of life, you will fall away from both.
The labor of solitaries is this: to become free from things perceived by the senses,
and to devote themselves continually to God through the meditation of the heart and the body's toil in prayer.
Judge for yourself whether, when these things are neglected, worldly virtue can take their place.
Or can a solitary who labors in stillness really manage both ways of life, the outward and the inward:
that is, both concern for God and burdening his heart with concern for others as well?
For my part, I think that even when someone who wishes to live rightly before God abandons everything
and concerns himself only with his own soul in matters of conduct, even then he cannot manage all his duties without strain
in the practice of stillness. Rather, he still lacks the strength to carry his burden,
however completely he may rest from worldly needs and concerns—let alone add still other concerns.
Our Lord has those who minister to and care for his servants and his children; and he has also chosen those who minister before him personally.
It is not only in the affairs of earthly kings that we see how much more honored and elevated in rank
are those who remain continually before the king and are admitted to his secrets,
than those who undertake outward tasks out of love for the king. Rather, in the affairs of God's household too, it is easy to see
how much freedom of access is possessed by those who are admitted to intimacy with him through constant communion with him in prayer.
And over how much of the wealth of heaven and earth they have authority, and how their dominion is seen over all the beings in creation:
for these submit to their words without dispute, as they do to God.
And his likeness is clearly imprinted in them through the great honor they receive from all rational creatures and those without speech.
From those who serve God with earthly possessions and things, and give him comfort through their fellow human beings.
Although this is very good, it is fitting for us to take our example not from those whose ranks in God's service are lower,
but from the champions of our path and from the saints who share our way of life,
and from those who once and for all let go of the earth and abandoned it, and laid hold of the vault of heaven.
By what means did those early saints please God,
those who blazed the trail of our way of life, the illustrious among them? That holy John from the region of the Thebaid,
that treasury of virtue and fountain of prophecy—did he, from within his confinement, provide bodily comforts for his fellow human beings,
or did he please God through prayer? I acknowledge that there were also people who pleased God and excelled through these other things.
But they were inferior to those who pleased God through prayer and through withdrawal from everything.
It is well known what help those who excel in stillness give their fellow human beings.
It is to help them, when necessity calls, with a beneficial word, or to offer prayer on their behalf.
Apart from these things, however, for the recollection of anyone, or concern for these bodily matters,
to lodge in the heart of someone living in stillness is not wise. The saying, “Give Caesar what belongs to Caesar, and God what belongs to God,”
and “Give your neighbor what belongs to him, and God what belongs to him,” is not for those who live in stillness, but for those who lead their lives outside.
But someone who lives by the service of the angels—that is, by the soul's meditation—
has no business seeking to please through earthly things, that is, becoming caught up in concern for manual work,
or looking to receive from others and give to others. His own work, however, is in heaven.
It is not fitting for a solitary to let thought of anything disturb his mind and bring it down from its standing before God.
But if someone boldly brings up the case of Paul, saying, “Paul too used to work
and give alms,” we say to him in reply: Paul was a unique individual who was equal to everything.
We do not know whether there was another Paul who could be equal to everything as he was.
Show me another Paul, if you can, and I will be persuaded by you.
Therefore, do not bring these matters of outward administration into the midst of inward activities.
For the work of preachers is one thing, and the work of stillness is another.
But if you wish to embrace stillness, be like a cherub, who has no concern for anything earthly.
Consider that there is no other human being in creation except you alone,
and God, on whom you meditate, as your fathers who walked before you taught you.
For unless a person hardens his heart and forcibly restrains his compassion, so as to remain far from concern for anyone,
whether for God's sake or for bodily matters, except in prayer alone at the times appointed for him,
so that love and thought of anyone do not enter his heart, he cannot free himself from the disturbance of cares and live in stillness.
This is the goal. But whenever a thought comes to you to concern yourself with someone under the appearance of virtue,
so as to plunder from you the peace that habitually arises in your heart from the remembrance of God,
say to it, “Love and compassion for God's sake are a good way of life.
Nevertheless, it is precisely for God's sake that I do not want it.”
“Wait for me,” that solitary said, “for it is for God's sake that I am pursuing you.” He replied to him, “And it is for God's sake that I am fleeing
from you.” Thus Abba Arsenius, for God's sake, would not even open his mouth to speak, either about something beneficial or about some occupation.
Another, however, spoke all day long for God's sake and welcomed all the strangers who came there.
But the former chose silence and stillness instead. For this reason, he and the Spirit of God, amid the sea of this world,
were sailing in surpassing peace in the ship of the life of stillness,
as was shown in a revelation to the spiritual athletes who investigated this matter.
Indeed, this is the very meaning of the name “stillness”: quietness from everything. For if, even in stillness itself, you are full of disturbance,
with your body preoccupied with manual work and various activities, and your soul with concern for someone else,
what quietness do you have left? Judge for yourself whether you can concern yourself with many things and please God.
To speak of embracing the life of stillness without giving up everything and concern about everything is laughable to me.
Again, on the distinctions between revelations and the workings that occur among the saints in various forms. 19.
The order of revelation is distinct from a person's deepening his thoughts through the study of wisdom and the labor of the mind,
toward some understanding, inquiry, and contemplation concerning a subject, through wonder.
of the mind concerning them. For revelation is called the silence of the mind.
Nor does a person himself devise a representation through human effort and reflection in order to attain knowledge;
rather, it happens through spiritual activity. At that very moment, the person to whom the revelation comes
is not aware of any thought belonging to the soul or of what lies before the senses. He neither engages with these things nor perceives them.
We do not say this on the basis of our own thinking; rather, it can be learned more fully from the writings of the prophets:
at the times when revelations came to them, because they were in a state of astonishment,
at those very times they had none of their customary activity or use of voluntary thoughts, nor any involvement with what lay before their senses.
Rather, their minds were wholly and completely concentrated only on those things that appeared to them in revelation.
It was like what happened to blessed Peter when he was hungry and went up onto the roof to pray.
Once that revelation came upon him, he was no longer even aware of his hunger.
Even the memory of food was erased from his mind, because he was in a trance, as Scripture says.
One can learn the distinctions between all these things clearly from the writings of the blessed bishop Theodore, the light of the whole inhabited world.
He speaks about the manner and order of revelations especially in these books:
in the three volumes on Genesis, and in the two on Job,
and in the last volume on the Twelve Prophets, and in the commentary on Acts and the one on Matthew.
For Scripture speaks of six kinds of revelations. The first is through the senses.
The second is through a vision of the soul. The third is through intellectual [?] rapture.
The fourth is in the order of prophecy. The fifth is in a certain intelligible manner.
The sixth is as in a dream. Those that come through the senses are divided into two categories:
revelation through the elements, and revelations that occur without material substances.
Those through the elements include the revelation in the bush, in the cloud, on the tablets, and the rest, which were also seen by the people.
They also include the wonders that occur every day in this universe, whose causes and significance the saints grasp through revelations,
as well as hidden or distant deeds, events, and matters that are revealed to people while they are taking place and happening.
Those without material substances include the men who appeared to Abraham, Jacob’s ladder, and the revelation concerning the tabernacle.
“See,” he says, “and make it according to the pattern that was shown to you on the mountain,” together with the other things of this kind.
And like that divine light, with its exalted rays, which flashed upon Paul on the road and blinded his eyes.
For it is well known that, although this revelation was visible and was perceived through the senses,
so that even those with him saw [?] and heard, it was nevertheless not a material revelation,
nor was it a natural light composed of the elements, as the blessed Interpreter also makes known when explaining it in Acts,
in his explanation of the account where it says, “Those who were traveling with Paul on the road stood bewildered [?],
hearing a voice but seeing no one.”
He explains: “It says ‘astonished,’ that is, silent and speechless. They too were seized with terror,
because they perceived the sound of the voice that came to him, and they saw as much as they were able to see of the light that appeared to him,
so that Saul would not afterward be thought to have invented what had happened and taken place in his presence,
with none of his companions having heard or seen anything. But they saw no one, for they did not see Jesus.
For, as I said, what appeared was not even a light perceptible to the senses.
Rather, through divine action he experienced an incomprehensible perception in an incorporeal manner,
in the likeness of a vision of light, so that he thought the heavens had opened,” and so forth.
These are revelations that took place through the bodily senses,
although they transcend the mingling of the elements and the ways in which perceptible and human events occur.
Yet they do not impart mental ecstasy to those who receive them, as does the revelation that takes place through the eyes of the soul.
As for a vision of the soul, there is, for example: “I saw the Lord sitting on a lofty throne, and around him were seraphim, each with six wings.”
And there is that revelation of Ezekiel, of the wheels and the wondrous figures,
and the sound from within the wheels, like a sound resembling that of the sea, and the praises heard from
those many-eyed cherubim, who say, “Blessed is the glory of the Lord from his place.” [?]
How much subtler these aspects are than those earlier orders that were mentioned is known to the enlightened.
And there is the vessel that appeared to Peter, with the animals in it, along with other things that are recorded.
Anyone who wishes can learn about them from the Scriptures. As for being caught up in mind,
there is, for example, the statement: “He was caught up to the third heaven; whether in the body or outside the body, I do not know.
And he was caught up into paradise and heard inexpressible words, which a human being is not permitted to utter.”
As for prophecy: it is like those things that happened to the prophets, who spoke beforehand about future events, many generations [?] in advance.
Thus Balaam the diviner was also granted the ability to speak great things through the spirit of prophecy,
which surpass [?] in their abundance even what the prophets prophesied.
In an intellectual manner, as in these words spoken by the blessed Paul:
“I pray,” he says, “that you may be filled with the knowledge of God, in all wisdom and all spiritual understanding.”
And, he says, “May the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, give you a spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him.
May the eyes of your hearts be enlightened, so that you may know what is the hope of his calling, and what are the riches of his glory among the saints,
and what is the surpassing greatness of his power in us who believe.”
And the other things that were granted to the apostle himself through a revelation of knowledge concerning
the things of the world to come, the order of the resurrection, and the transformation of human bodies, along with the rest.
And again, concerning the order of exalted concepts, and also knowledge concerning the divine nature:
as in the statement, “He is the image of the invisible God,” and, “Through him,” he says, “he made the worlds.”
“God,” he says, “has revealed it to us through his Spirit.” And again: “We know only a little out of much, and we understand only a little out of much.”
And as in the statement, “In the beginning was the Word,” and the statement, “You are the Messiah, the Son of the living God,” and the rest.
And as in the statement, “No one has fathomed his judgments, and his ways cannot be traced out.” And, he says, “He does everything according to the counsel of his will.”
And the statement, “God has confined everyone in disobedience, so that he may have mercy on everyone,” and the rest.
These are kinds of conceptual knowledge concerning the divine nature, which they were granted through the Spirit to know and understand.
As for what comes through dreams: it is like what happened to Abimelech, Joseph, Pharaoh, and Nebuchadnezzar.
And the statement, “An angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph, Mary's husband,” and the rest. But it is also necessary to know this:
that all the revelations that God has made for the instruction of human beings and for knowledge concerning things
come through images, especially to those who are simple in knowledge and have little understanding of the truth.
For those that are for a person's own enjoyment and assurance, and for some consolation and assurance for an individual person,
come without images and through intellectual awareness.
The blessed Interpreter explains this clearly in the second volume on Job.
For see how great are the things given in the revelation of knowledge and concepts through the understanding mind:
And how much higher are these mysteries concerning the knowledge of everything about God than those other revelations!
This is the perfection of knowledge. Moreover, this too should be known:
Revelation and spiritual activity are one thing, while truth and knowledge are another.
For revelation [?] does not contain certainty about the truth; rather, it displays certain hints and signs in keeping with human capacity.
Nor are the activities and wonders that occur in revelations called knowledge and truth.
These are called the overshadowing of spiritual activity.
For as for anything concerning God's foreknowledge or the incomprehensibility of his nature,
or the distinctions between his attributes, or the meaning of the mysteries of his will toward all,
and the other things about him that can be grasped through sound knowledge—these things cannot be learned from these experiences.
Thus, the mysteries concerning the divine nature that the mind grasps through understanding [?] are one thing,
and a certain activity that [?] upon the mind for a time is another.
Therefore, not everyone to whom a revelation comes, or in whom some consoling spiritual activity is stirred,
necessarily also knows the truth and has certain knowledge
of God. Indeed, there have been many who experienced these things, yet knew God like little children.
Further, on the distinctions between the intelligible powers of the mind in the activity of revelations and visions of the Spirit. [?]
Divine vision is a revelation to the mind that is not perceived by the senses.
Divine revelation is the stirring of the mind with spiritual insights concerning the Godhead.
It is not even given to the nature of angels to be stirred in this way on their own, without revelation that comes from grace.
Being stirred by revelations concerning God's creative activity is one thing,
and being stirred by revelations concerning the nature of his being is another.
The former can receive an occasion for its reception from things perceived by the senses.
The latter, however, has no occasion anywhere, from the mind downward.
It is the threefold, highest purity, as they say.
Not even one in a thousand righteous people can be found worthy of this great perception.
For contemplation of our Lord's becoming human and his revelation in the flesh is also said to belong to divine contemplation itself.
The true vision of angels is a movement within the spiritual perceptions proper to them.
But as for the nature of the spiritual powers, outside the mind
