there is no possibility of seeing it. When someone is deemed worthy to see them in their own nature and their own realm,
and as they exist in their created spiritual state, grace moves his mind through the revelation of spiritual perceptions concerning them.
But when the soul has been purified to see its fellow beings, it receives the vision of them through these eyes.
They are not bodies, such that, apart from the soul's vision, which is true contemplation,
they could also be seen in some other way as they are, without being changed—that is, without being brought down from their nature in their appearances.
It is not possible for anyone to receive [?] this vision without the second purity of the mind.
But their appearing to people in visible forms is not a true vision;
rather, they carry out a providential arrangement in their mission.
Or they appear in a vision perceptible to the senses to comfort and encourage simple people.
Such appearances occur even to those who are not pure. But the first kind
belongs to enlightened and discerning people who, through the glorious practices of stillness, have been raised to the state of purity.
On the things that occur in prayer amid stillness. 21.
Who knows that delightful kneeling, when, with the tongue silent, the heart silently sings a certain song of praise,
whose movement never ceases in its delight, while the body kneels motionless upon its knees? Blessed is
the person who continually feeds on these things! But they depend on the will, not on whenever a person wishes.
This is the partial delight given as consolation to someone who lives blamelessly before God in a life of stillness.
But if he perseveres in it with complete simplicity, taking care to keep his service pure,
and his conduct is consistent, after a time he is also deemed worthy of those earlier things that were mentioned.
As for those who flourish in their way of life and whose purpose is upright, grace first gives them a taste of these and similar things through reading,
and draws their thoughts away from reflection on earthly things toward itself. They labor, keep vigil, and pray without growing weary.
But those who have been trained even a little in the mysteries of stillness experience this awareness in prayer and worship.
On the many distinctions within prayer, and on the limits of the mind's authority.
And how far it has authority to set its voluntary movements in motion in the different forms of prayer:
And what is the boundary set for human nature in prayer, up to which it is permitted to pray?
Once it passes beyond that point, it is no longer prayer, even if what happens then is called by the name of prayer. 22.
Glory to him whose gift is poured out abundantly upon human beings, who, although they are flesh,
has enabled them to perform on earth the service of incorporeal beings, and has made those whose nature is dust worthy to speak about mysteries
such as these. Especially sinners like us, who are not worthy even to hear talk about such things.
But in his grace he opened our blind heart to understand through contemplation of the Scriptures and the teaching of the great fathers,
although I have not been found worthy, through my own efforts, to gain experience of even one in a thousand of the things written by my hands,
especially in this discourse, which we have ventured to write for the enlightenment and encouragement of our soul and of those who encounter it,
so that perhaps our soul may be stirred, if only by its own longing, to approach actual practice.
What, then? The sweetness of prayer is one thing, and vision in prayer is another.
The second is superior to the first, as a fully grown man is to a little child.
Sometimes the very words become sweet in the mouth,
and a single phrase of prayer is repeated countless times, while the person knows no satisfaction that would allow him to leave it and pass on to another.
And sometimes contemplation [?] is born from prayer itself, and it cuts off even prayer from the lips.
The person who is gazing upon it becomes, in amazement, like a body without a soul.
This is what we call vision in prayer, not some image or shape that is pictured, as foolish people say.
Even within this contemplation in prayer there are degrees and differences of gifts.
But up to this point it is still prayer. For thought has not yet passed over into that which is no longer prayer, although it is superior
to prayer. For the movements of the tongue and heart in prayer are keys.
What comes after these is entry into the treasury. Here, then, let every mouth and tongue fall silent,
and the heart, the treasurer of thoughts, and the mind, the governor of the senses, and the understanding, that swift-flying, presumptuous thing;
and let all their means and their use, and their entreaties, cease here, for the master of the house has arrived.
For just as the entire force of the laws and commandments established by God for human beings
has purity of heart as its limit, according to the saying of the fathers,
so also all the kinds and forms of prayer that human beings offer to God:
The limit extends as far as pure prayer. Groans, sighs, entreaties, and heartfelt supplications,
and powerful tears, and all the other forms found in prayer, as I have said:
pure prayer is the limit of their scope and their power to act.
But beyond the purity of prayer, once the mind has crossed this boundary, it has
neither prayer, nor movements, nor tears, nor power, nor freedom, nor entreaties,
nor desire, nor longing for anything that is awaited in this world or in the world to come.
For this reason, after pure prayer there is no longer prayer.
All its movements and forms lead the mind only this far through the power of their freedom. For this reason, there is also
struggle in it. But beyond this boundary, there is wonder, not prayer.
From this point onward, the mind has ceased from prayer. There is vision, and the mind is no longer praying.
Every kind of prayer that exists operates through movements of the soul.
Once the intellect has entered into spiritual movements, it can no longer pray there.
Prayer is one thing, and the contemplation within it is another, even though they arise from one another.
The former is sowing; the latter is gathering sheaves.
The reaper stands in wonder at an indescribable vision: from the insignificant, bare grains that he sowed,
what glorious ears of grain have suddenly sprung up before him! And in his vision he ceases from every movement.
Every prayer that exists is a petition and a request, or praise, or thanksgiving.
Examine whether any one of these, or a petition for anything, exists once the intellect has crossed this boundary and entered that place.
It is those who know the truth whom one asks. Nor is it for everyone to investigate these distinctions,
but only for those who have personally been witnesses and ministers of this very reality,
or who were brought up in the presence of fathers like these and received the truth from their mouths,
and spent their days in these and similar discussions, asking questions and giving answers about the truth.
Just as scarcely one person in ten thousand can be found who has fulfilled the commandments and laws
with very little lacking, and has been found worthy of serenity of soul, so only one among many is found
who, through great vigilance, has been found worthy of pure prayer, has broken through this boundary, and has also been found worthy of that mystery.
Not many are considered worthy even of pure prayer, but only a few.
As for that other mystery beyond it, scarcely one person in each generation is found who has approached this knowledge by the grace of God.
Prayer is supplication, concern, and longing for something:
either escape from the evils of this world, or anticipation of the promises, or some request through which a person receives help in approaching God.
All forms of prayer are contained within these movements.
Its purity or impurity is determined as follows.
Whenever, at those times when the mind prepares to offer up one of these movements that we have listed,
some foreign thought or distraction about something becomes mixed with it, it is called impure.
For it has brought up onto the Lord’s altar—which is the heart, the spiritual sanctuary—one of those animals that are not permitted.
For when, at the time of supplication, the mind is intently occupied with one of these movements, according to the urgency of the matter,
and, because of its great longing, the gaze of its movement is drawn through the eye of faith inward, beyond the doorway of the heart,
through these things the entrances of the soul are now fenced off against those foreign thoughts that are called
strangers, whom the law does not permit to enter the Tabernacle of Testimony.
This is called the acceptable sacrifice of the heart and pure prayer.
Its limits, too, extend only this far. Beyond this, it can no longer be called prayer.
But if someone brings to mind what the fathers call spiritual prayer,
without understanding the meaning of the fathers’ words, and says that this too falls within the limits of prayer,
I think that, if he arrives at an exact understanding of the meaning, it is blasphemy to say that anyone among created beings can
pray spiritual prayer at all. Whatever can be prayed falls short of spirituality.
And whatever is spiritual belongs to an order beyond movement and prayer.
For if a person can scarcely even pray purely, what are we to say about praying spiritually? For the holy fathers have the custom
of calling all virtuous movements and all spiritual activity by the name of prayer.
And not only these: the blessed Interpreter even counts good deeds as prayer.
Yet it is clear that prayer is one thing, and the deeds that are performed are another.
But sometimes, in various places, they call this very thing spiritual prayer.
In some places they call it contemplation, and sometimes knowledge,
and sometimes revelations of intelligible things. Do you see how the Fathers vary
the names they use for spiritual things? Such precision in terminology, then, holds good for the things of this world.
But there is no true name for the things of the new world, only a single, simple knowledge
that is above every name, letter, form, color, shape, and compound designation.
Therefore, when the soul’s knowledge rises above this realm of visible things,
the Fathers use whatever expressions they wish concerning it.
No one knows their precise names; rather, these provide something for the soul’s thoughts to rest upon.
We use designations and figurative expressions, in accordance with the words of Saint Dionysius, who said:
“We use letters, syllables, established names, and words because of the senses.
But whenever our soul is moved toward divine things by the activity of the Spirit,
the senses and their activities are then superfluous to us,
just as the soul’s spiritual powers are also superfluous when our soul becomes a likeness of the Godhead
through an incomprehensible union, and shines with the rays of the light on high through those sightless movements.”
Therefore, my brother, let this be certain for you: the mind’s power to set distinct impulses in motion has its place up to the point of purity in prayer.
But when it reaches that point, it either turns back or ceases from prayer.
Prayer has thus become a kind of intermediary between the life of the soul [?] and the life of the spirit. But as long as it is in motion,
it remains in the realm of the soul. Once it has entered that other realm, prayer ceases.
Thus, just as the saints in the new world do not actually pray
when the mind is swallowed up in the Spirit, but dwell in wonder in that delightful glory,
so too, when the mind is deemed worthy to experience that blessedness which is to come,
it forgets itself and everything here, and can no longer be moved by thought of anything.
For this reason, one may confidently dare to say that every virtue that exists and every form of prayer that takes place,
whether in the body or in the mind, is directed and moved by free will, as is the intellect, which rules the senses.
But when the activity of the Spirit reigns over the intellect, which orders the senses and the thoughts,
Freedom is taken away from nature: at that point it is being led, rather than doing the leading.
And how can there be prayer at that time, when nature has no control over itself but is led by another power to a place it does not know?
It does not direct the movements of the mind toward whatever it wishes. Rather, captivity rules over nature at that moment,
and leads it where it is not aware, for at that time it does not even have a will.
This goes so far that the person does not even know whether he is in the body or outside the body, as Scripture testifies.
Can someone who is taken captive in this way, when he is not even aware of himself, really be praying? Therefore,
let no one blaspheme by daring to say that a human being can pray spiritual prayer. Such
boldness is claimed by arrogant people of prayer, ignorant in understanding, who spread reports about themselves
that whenever they wish, they can pray the prayer of the Spirit.
But the humble, who have understanding and bow down to learn from the fathers,
and who know the limits of nature, do not give their thoughts over to such boldness. And why,
when it is not prayer, is this inexpressible gift called by the name of prayer? The reason
is what we are saying: because it is bestowed at the time of prayer on those who are worthy.
And it takes its occasion from prayer, because there is no opportunity for this glory [?] to be bestowed
except at this time, as the fathers testify.
For this reason it is called prayer: because it was from prayer that the mind was led into that blessedness.
And because prayer is its occasion, and at other times there is no opportunity for it, as Mar Evagrius and the others testify.
We also see in the accounts of many of the saints that their minds were caught up while they stood in prayer.
But someone asks, “Why do these great and inexpressible gifts come only at this time?” We say, “Because at this time,
more than at all other hours, a person is recollected and ready to look toward God, longing for and awaiting mercy from him.”
To put it briefly, this is the time when he stands at the King's door and pleads. And the request
of someone who longs and implores should fittingly be answered at this time.
At what other time is a person so watchful, prepared, and ready
as at the time when he prays [?]? Or would it have been fitting that, while he was asleep or attending to some task,
or distracted in his mind, he should be found worthy of this? Indeed, even though the saints had no time of idleness,
For at all times they occupy themselves with spiritual things; but when they are not standing in readiness for prayer,
how often they either study some of the accounts in the Scriptures, or their minds meditate on the contemplation of created things,
along with the other things that are also beneficial subjects of meditation.
At the time of prayer, however, the mind fixes its gaze exclusively on God himself, and the whole range of its movements is directed toward him.
It continually and fervently offers him heartfelt appeals with pressing earnestness.
For this reason, at this time when the soul is occupied with a single meditation, it is fitting that divine mercies should also flow forth from him.
For we see that even the gift of the Spirit descends upon this visible offering that we present, when everyone stands prepared in prayer,
pleading and imploring, with their minds gathered toward God: it descends upon the bread and wine placed on the altar.
An angel also appeared to Zechariah at the time of prayer and announced to him the good news of John's conception. And to Peter, while he was praying
on the roof, at the prayer of the sixth hour, that revelation appeared which made known the admission of the nations,
through the vessel lowered from heaven and the animals within it. And to Cornelius, while he was praying, there appeared the things recorded [?] about him.
And God spoke with Joshua son of Nun while he lay face down in prayer.
And that cover placed above the ark, from which the priest learned from God through revelation whatever was needed—
at the time when the high priest entered once a year, at the awesome time of prayer, when all the tribes of the Israelites were assembled
and stood praying in trembling and fear in the outer tabernacle, the high priest would enter the inner sanctuary.
And while he lay face down, the sounds of God's voice could be heard
from within that cover above the ark, in an awesome revelation beyond words.
Oh, how awesome was the mystery enacted in this action!
Likewise, all the revelations and visions that came to the saints came to them at the time of prayer.
What time is as holy and as fitting for sanctification and the reception of gifts as the time of prayer, when a person speaks with God?
Therefore, because at this time a person is engaged in petitioning God, appealing to him, and speaking with him,
and all the person's mental activity and thought are forcibly gathered there from every direction, and on God himself
alone the person meditates and calls for mercy, with the whole mind absorbed in speaking to him and the heart filled with him,
from this point, then, certain incomprehensible insights—
the Holy Spirit, in order to stir them within a person according to that person's capacity, takes material from these very things for which the person prays, and stirs them within that person.
How, through these insights, prayer ceases to move.
The mind is absorbed in wonder, and the desire behind its petition is forgotten.
Its movements are submerged in deep intoxication, and it is no longer in this world.
From then on, there is no awareness there of either body or soul, nor any remembrance of anything, as Evagrius says.
“Prayer,” he says, “is a state of the mind that is interrupted only by the light of the Holy Trinity, through wonder.”
You see how prayer is interrupted: it is interrupted through wonder. These things are born in the mind from prayer itself,
as I said at the beginning of this discourse, and in many places up to this point.
Again he says: “The state of the mind is the height of intelligible things, resembling the color of the sky,
upon which the light of the Holy Trinity shines at the time of prayer.”
And when is a person deemed worthy of all this grace, so that at the time of prayer he is raised to such greatness?
He says: “When the mind puts off the old self and, through grace, puts on the new, then it also
sees its own state at the time of prayer, resembling sapphire or the color of the sky.
This was called ‘the place of God’ by the elders of Israel, to whom it appeared on the mountain.”
Therefore, as I said, this gift should not be called spiritual prayer.
What, then, should it be called? The offspring of pure prayer, which is absorbed in the Spirit.
There the understanding has now risen above prayer. Through finding something more excellent, prayer has ceased within it.
From this point on, it is not actually praying, but gazing in wonder at incomprehensible things that do not belong to the world of mortals.
It is still, unaware of everything here. This is the unknowing that has been spoken of,
and the saying, “Blessed is the one who has reached the unsurpassable unknowing that comes in prayer,” as Evagrius said.
On the purpose of speaking about the knowledge of truth. 23.
Everything perceptible, whether an action or a word, is a manifestation of something hidden within,
provided that its occurrence is not accidental, but its practice is habitual.
It is the latter that is taken into account for recompense; the former carries less weight in the reckoning.
That is, the strength or weakness of the will in doing evil or good
is not tested by an isolated occurrence. Rather, the habitual course of events provides the test of its freedom.
Authority is given to events, and at times they can go beyond freedom of choice. Events, whether good
or bad, happen to a person either for encouragement, for testing, as a consequence, or as repayment.
For encouragement, a good event; for testing, one that seems bad. For an outcome and repayment, both kinds of events.
There is no event that happens by chance. Nothing happens to a person by chance, whether good or bad.
There is a governor who governs the affairs of this world.
And there is a guardian with each one of us, from whom nothing escapes notice and who does not grow negligent.
Rather, every event is indeed managed by that guardian who has been appointed;
and his management serves our needs in these four ways. But heartfelt prayer,
accompanied by conduct that matches its earnestness, changes the character of these events and makes them beneficial.
It strengthens and confirms what is good, but changes what is bad into its opposite.
Therefore, do not doubt what I have said: that no event happens by chance or without a governor.
If indeed prayer accompanied by upright conduct can change or regulate events, then let us believe that every event has a governor.
Blessed is the person who compares every event that happens to him with his hidden inner life, investigates its cause, and sees the one who governs it.
Anyone who wants to become wise in the things of God has no way to do so
unless he scorns the world and hates the glory of [?].
Admirable is the person who conceals the greatness of his labor through a humble view of himself.
The angels marvel at this. Let the failings that are not
intentional, in which even the vigilant are sometimes found, be regarded by you as guardians of righteousness.
No prayer is accepted as readily as a person's request for reconciliation with those who are angry with him.
For when he judges himself to be at fault, this request is answered without delay.
For whenever, while fulfilling your duty and being watchful over your own conduct, you see yourself as weak and regard yourself as contemptible,
and human praise is hateful to you, know that you truly stand on God's path.
But whenever you sense within yourself a departure from this, and moreover, when you examine yourself, you find that even thoughts of criticism cause you pain,
know that you are empty of truth and have been stolen away into falsehood.
On the things provided for a brother within his cell. 24.
It often happens in the middle of the daytime that, even if an earthly kingdom were offered to a brother,
he would not agree at that hour to leave his cell, or to have anyone knock at his door. A time for gain has suddenly come upon him.
And this often happens on days considered days of relaxation and coming and going.
Grace suddenly visits him through tears beyond measure,
or through the intensity of sorrow that troubles his heart, or through some joy without an apparent cause, or
through the delight of kneeling. I know a brother who put the key into the door of his cell to lock it,
intending to go out and pursue the wind, as Scripture says; but grace visited him there, and he immediately turned back.
Our masters, let no one blame a brother if, on days when he is not observing the prescribed stillness,
he sometimes happens to miss the communal service.
Especially if he is not one of those notorious for negligence,
or someone who rushes into empty conversations, and has not neglected it because of bodily distractions.
You know, my brothers, that our work is not only what is performed before human eyes;
we also have work hidden from human eyes, unknown to beginners and people of the world.
For you understand that the solitary is under providential direction and is not his own master.
Likewise, if one of his brothers happens to come to visit him and he does not answer,
let him turn back immediately without blaming his brother, for he does not know what state he is in at that moment.
The solitary’s cell is the cave in the rock, as the fathers say, where God spoke with Moses.
Solitaries who have no experience in the practice of truly tasting stillness do not understand these things.
They despise their brothers and judge them, demanding that they be just like themselves in everything.
There are also times when a certain unavoidable struggle is brought
upon a brother suddenly, and he is in danger, holding his hands over his heart lest it fly away.
He lies on his face, pleading with God, and cannot listen to anyone’s voice.
Those who have made a crossing on this sea know these changes and understand the winds that blow.
Sometimes a thought of repentance wells up in him, and his past deeds suddenly gather together, along with the remembrance of his death, which stands before him.
This bright sun grows dark before his face, and all remembrance of the world is forgotten in his heart.
And sometimes waves suddenly rose against him, and his ship sank in hidden shipwrecks.
These things are not known to everyone: what unexpectedly befalls the solitary in the midst of stillness,
through Satan’s fierce battles, so that his cell becomes a house of weeping. Many are the changes of this sea,
and who knows its hardships, the abundance of its merchandise, and the wonderful pearls within its depths,
and the creatures that rise from within it? Blessed is the one who does not fall asleep throughout his voyage, until he reaches the harbor of departure from this life.
There is no one who loves something without also cultivating the things that bring it about.
No one can occupy himself with divine things unless he distances himself from temporal things and despises them,
becoming a stranger to the world’s honor and pleasures and attaching himself to the disgrace of the cross,
while every day he drinks vinegar and bitter gall from sufferings, people, demons, and poverty.
Be diligent, my brother, and be like a wise merchant, as you carry
your pearl and wander about in the world, so that the beauty of its brilliance is not marred.
Take care that it is not stolen from you through your negligence, and that you do not enter Sheol in sorrow.
Run after the little consolation acquired through toil at its proper time, so that you may be worthy of that great consolation
which relieves those who have found it of distress in this life of afflictions.
Do not despise small things, lest you be deprived of great ones.
No one has ever seen a child who is still nursing on milk put meat into his mouth.
Through small things, the door to great things is opened.
You dishonor God, my brother, when you desire him to lead you without following the proper order.
No one has been entrusted with great things unless he has first been tested in lesser things.
Lay this to heart, my brother, and remember me when its time comes:
every chamber you reach tomorrow along this path of virtue and knowledge of the truth,
you will find more glorious and excellent than those in which you lodged yesterday.
You were indeed beside yourself and marveled at the beauties of the chamber you entered today.
Yet its beauty is swallowed up by that which you are going to encounter tomorrow.
Who has experienced the delightful changes of the mind? Only pray that the door may be opened before you.
Guard against despair. You are not working for a tyrant; your service is to a kind master.
He has given you everything without taking anything from you. When you did not exist at all, he made you into what you are.
Even for this alone—that he brought us into being—who can repay his goodness? Oh,
what immeasurable goodness! Who can adequately praise him,
who has given us knowledge of everything—not only of visible things, but also of hidden things?
So that we may know that there is something which, although we do not know it, we need to ask him for.
And who taught you, mortal human being, that something the knowledge of which is not in your nature
should stir you with love to seek it? Never seek consolation that lies outside the heart, namely, knowledge of distinctions.
Rise above every consolation served by the senses, so that you may be worthy of the consolation acquired inwardly, beyond them.
A solitary who has become a stranger to the world's consolation but does not look each day for Christ's consolation is dead while still alive.
For God is merciful and loves to give, but he wants us to provide the occasion.
For he rejoices whenever someone offers him a wise prayer.
It is a sign that he is beginning to recover from [?] when he longs for hidden things. But he delays, looking for his complete recovery.
Someone who becomes discouraged when there is a delay is the companion of someone who grows weary of asking.
Weariness removes the petition from prayer—that is, it prevents you from asking.
Discouragement, however, cuts it short, so that you do not prolong the petition and persist in it. It fosters perseverance
and encourages us to persist in prayer. Hope lightens the burden of weariness on the body's limbs.
It also knows how to give the heart rest in its afflictions.
There is no load whose weight is more pleasant than the toil undertaken with it. There is no traveling companion whose conversation is more desirable than
its own. Even a prison is pleasant to live in with it. Make it your companion,
O repentant brother, and you will not feel all the hardships of your struggle.
If you are in your cell, let it be with you. And if you find yourself among other people, keep your mind fixed on it.
Then your heart will never be distracted by anything in the world; the world and everything in it will become foreign to you.
And if you lie down to sleep, make it your bedfellow, and converse with it until you sink into sleep.
Then no shameful thought will approach your heart, because your conversation is free of material things.
Anything bearing the form of material things, whose appearance stirs the mind, cannot appear there.
And a demonic thought does not know how to show itself except through a material appearance.
Patience in prayer—the fruit of life peeks out from it. And perseverance helps those who hold to it in prayer.
When you pray, remember the farmer who sows in hope,
and the one who returns many times over the seed of the farmer who sows in faith,
and who has given greater importance to asking for his kingdom and his righteousness than to temporal things: he answers our requests according to his promise. Amen.
Subjects for the soul that seeks deep contemplation in which to immerse itself, away from bodily thoughts arising from memories of things. 25.
Everything that is above something is hidden from what is at its own level and below it. This, however, is not through being covered by other bodies,
but it possesses this by nature, as well as the ability, whenever it wishes, to bring what is hidden in it into the open.
Thus, for every intelligible essence, the distinctions of its rank do not lie outside it,
but are defined within its movements. To put this more clearly:
it is a matter of being further inward and receiving the primal light without any intermediary, or of being last in rank.
This is not spatial, but depends on the degree of clarity or density of the intellects, in relation to their capacity to receive indications from above.
For every intelligible nature, in relation to those at its own level and below it,
their hiddenness from one another is not a matter of nature, but of the superiority of their movements. I say this concerning members of the same order.
That is, the orders of the holy powers, the orders of souls, and the orders of demons.
The first are hidden from the middle ones, and these from the third, in nature, in their places, and in their movements.
Within each of these orders, however, they are hidden from their companions with respect to knowledge,
whether they see or do not see. But from those below them, they are hidden even in their very nature.
For the faculty of sight in incorporeal beings does not operate outside them as it does in bodily beings.
Rather, their seeing one another is said to occur within their movements—that is, in the superiority and density of their movements.
Therefore, if they are equal in this respect, they see one another even when they are far apart.
This is not through imagination, but through true sight, certain by nature.
Only the Cause of all is exalted above these distinctions, for he alone is to be worshiped.
Demons, however, although they are thoroughly unclean, are not deprived of seeing the members of their own orders.
They do not see these two ranks above them, because spiritual sight is the brightness of the inner movements.
These themselves are their mirror and their eyes. Whenever the inner movements grow dark, they do not see the orders above them.
But they see one another because, in comparison with these, they are denser than the order of spiritual natures. Such is the case with demons.
As for souls, as long as they are impure and darkened, they cannot see even the members of their own order.
Instead, they are deprived of seeing one another, and even of seeing themselves.
But if they are purified and return to the original order in which they were created, they clearly discern all three of these orders.
That is, those below them, those above them, and one another.
And it is not only when all these orders change into bodily forms
that souls see them, whether angels, demons, or another soul [?].
Rather, they see them in their very nature, while they remain in their spiritual order, whether an angel, a demon, or one soul seeing another.
But if you say that this is impossible—that a demon or an angel cannot be seen in their spiritual nature unless they change their appearance—then it is not the soul
that sees, but the body. And in that case, what need is there for purity? Look, even to those who are not pure,
demons sometimes appear, and angels likewise.
But when they see them, they see with the bodily eye, for which purity is not required.
The purified soul, however, does not see them in this way. Rather, it sees them in their spiritual nature, with the eye belonging to its own nature.
That is, with the understanding mind. And do not be surprised that souls also see one another even while they are in the body.
Here is clear proof that you will accept because its witness is trustworthy.
The blessed Athanasius, the confessor and catholicos, bears witness in the book he wrote about the life of Saint Anthony.
He says that once, while Saint Anthony was praying, he saw someone's soul ascending in great glory.
And he called blessed the man who had been deemed worthy of all this grace.
It was the blessed Ammon of Nitria.
He says that the mountain where the blessed Anthony lived was a journey [?] of thirteen days from the region of Nitria.
Here, then, the proof of all three things we mentioned has been established.
That is, spiritual natures see one another even when they are far apart, and neither distance nor the positioning of physical bodies obstructs their sight.
And souls see one another when they have been purified, and when they see, they do not see in a bodily way.
But in a spiritual nature. For it is clear that bodily sight can see what is before it.
But whenever it moves far away, it calls for another kind of sight.
Those heavenly orders are countless in the number of their beings.
Distinctions and ranks are also named among them.
Some of them are called Principalities, Authorities, Powers, and Dominions.
Perhaps, however, those honored with authority and leadership
are fewer in number than the subordinates appointed to obey their commands, says Diodorus the rhetorician, the great teacher.
In power and understanding, he says, they are great yet limited, according to the greatness of their ranks,
being arranged in degrees and ascending from rank to rank, until they reach that one who is older, mightier, and more glorious than all,
and who is the head and foundation of all created beings. I say the head,
not the Creator, but the foremost [?] of the wonders of God's works.
Angels and archangels fall far short of comprehending the wisdom of God, our Creator and theirs.
They fall short by as much as those below them fall short of them—and infinitely more.
By falling short, I mean their relative superiority and inferiority,
not in place, but in power and understanding. That is to say, they are higher and lower in natural power and understanding.
For knowledge of greater and lesser things accompanies them according to the measure they possess.
Divine teaching, then, has named all the heavenly beings with nine spiritual names.
It has divided them into three orders, each threefold.
The first of these consists of the exalted, lofty, and holy Thrones, and the many-eyed Cherubim,
and the many-winged Seraphim. Then comes the order of three ranks: Dominions, Powers, and Authorities.
The third consists of Principalities, Archangels, and Angels. Their Hebrew names are also interpreted:
Seraphim: those who give heat and those who burn. Cherubim: abundance of knowledge and outpouring of wisdom.
And Thrones: the reception and descent of God. This first order was called knowledgeable,
not as those who see spiritually through composite sensory images,
or understand the divine Being from the writings of the Spirit.
But as those filled with light that surpasses all immaterial knowledge;
and they are satisfied, as far as they are permitted, by the essential contemplation of the threefold rays of the Beauty that creates all beauty;
and are deemed worthy of communion with Jesus—not through sacred images bearing a form, which symbolically portray the divine likeness,
but as those who are truly close to him, they receive his imprint through a direct reception of the knowledge of his divine lights.
And they are filled with essential knowledge from the Godhead, as among the angels and the foremost intelligences of the Godhead.
The names of the higher orders, explained differently and more clearly.
Thrones: the honored ones. Dominions: those who rule over kingdoms. Principalities: those who govern the air.
Authorities: those who rule over nations and over individual human beings. Powers: those whose appearance is fearsome,
that is, mighty in strength. Seraphim: those who sanctify. Cherubim: those who carry. Watchers: those who guard.
Angels: those who are sent. On the first day, eight created natures came into being:
seven in silence and one through speech, namely light. On the second day, the firmament.
On the third day, the gathering of the waters and the sprouting of plants. On the fourth day, the distribution of the heavenly lights.
On the fifth day, birds, creeping creatures, and fish. On the sixth day, animals and humankind.
The shape of the whole world, it is said, has length and breadth. Its head is the east, and its end is the west.
Its right side is the north, and its left side is the south. The earth is shaped like a bed.
The upper heavens are like a vault, and the second heaven is like a wheel fitted to the upper one.
The edges of heaven and earth are joined together, and the Ocean surrounds them like a belt.
On this side of it are high mountains that rise as far as heaven.
The sun makes its journey behind those mountains throughout the night. The Great Sea is on this side of them.
It occupies one quarter of the dry land, and one quarter is dry land.
Against those who say, “If God is good, why were these things made by him?” 26.
Sin, Gehenna, and death have no existence at all with God, for these are occurrences, not independently existing beings.
Sin is the fruit of the will. There was a time when it did not exist,
and there will be a time when it will not exist. Gehenna is the fruit of sin, and it takes its beginning at some particular time,
though its end is unknown. Death, however, is an arrangement made by the Creator in his wisdom.
This which fills [?] has power over nature only for a time, and in any case comes to an end.
Satan: a name indicating the will’s turning away from the truth, not its nature.
But if, my brother, you find some of these things elsewhere too,
do not regard us as showing off because we express ourselves through the words of others.
Rather, regard us as humble people who draw nourishment from the milk of our early fathers. We have gathered these things and set them before us for contemplation,
as a goal set before us: to enrich the mind with provisions on which it may feed and be nourished.
For we have not forgotten that we have not risen above the rank of learners as long as we still dwell in the flesh.
Discernment is the capacity of natural thoughts to move.
Whenever these thoughts follow nature’s course in their movements, they encounter the variety of the elements and worlds. But when
they follow the latter way [?], they find that these created things have another use.
For although created natures have a twofold meaning in their use, they understand them in terms of only half their use,
namely, the order of inanimate things. When you encounter delight in the verses of the service,
then the mind becomes eager to remain continually in that very delight.
But if you wish to fulfill its request, hasten to discover the cause.
If you grasp this keenly, like a discerning person who is not blind, it will not be difficult for you to enjoy that delight continually, without disturbance.
And what, then, is the agent that is also called the cause? For iron, it is the file. It adds nothing to the iron
to bring it to brightness and radiance, for this belongs to its very substance.
What does it do, then? It removes from it the rust that has formed on it through disuse.
The very same consideration applies to the nature of the mind. Bring it to the file,
and then you will discover how it shines at the time of the service, rivaling the radiance of the stars.
For activity cannot advance ahead of it. It is indeed sluggish, though not inactive.
Why did I say “in psalmody,” and not “in prayer of the heart and in reading”?
The mind is held there only with difficulty. It is not so with these other practices, for a little care is enough for them.
These practices can also help with that one. Without them, however, fruitless is found
the care devoted to it. And these practices themselves, in turn, when the provisions already available run out and no further supply comes to them from anywhere [?].
Hunger knows how to contrive food, but it will not be persuaded to stop eating.
For bread gathered through his own sweat is sweet to the laborer.
For until he first sweats, he is not satisfied with the bread of truth. The working body sweats and nourishes the rational mind.
And this happens when the mind is deprived of the nourishment that comes from habit rather than nature.
Spiritual virtue is the daughter of voluntary virtue, and it compels the will.
For freedom is a natural faculty of the rational mind, not a state of bondage.
But whichever direction it inclines toward and persists in, it gives birth to another power that does not belong to nature.
Once this power is born, freedom itself is led captive and subjected to compulsion.
To speak plainly, it is imprisoned and has no authority over itself. Previously, the compulsion was voluntary.
Now, however, compulsion enslaves the will. And I say that this can be observed in both directions.
Whether a person subjects himself to the right or gives room to the left.
But a mind that knows how to look closely can see the compulsion belonging to each of these stages:
How, when that power which does not belong to nature is born from voluntary submission, it subdues freedom.
I am not speaking of the power that comes from habit, which is exceedingly difficult. This is
what they call the pursuer. In any case, habit is subject to the will, even though breaking away from it is a laborious undertaking.
We know of two powers besides this one. One of them enslaves the will.
The other overpowers even nature itself. It also has the authority to change nature.
That this influence has authority over nature is known to those who have experienced it.
To the changes of hearts and the differing thoughts that commonly arise from them—
free and unfree, life and death—the diversity of contemplations contributes greatly:
Those that dawn in human minds concerning divine judgments.
Through this diversity placed in its midst, the world has been preserved for thousands of years.
This diversity contributes greatly to the variety of ways of life along the path of mortality.
And most importantly, to the contemplation of the judgments that give rise to opinions about God.
Many hearts, once confidence has entered them, are like someone who has taken a deadly poison.
Even true and faithful children have five parts of fear mixed into the ten parts of love they possess.
A changeable nature cannot receive the fullness of divine truth here, or know the whole divine will
that he has toward rational beings—not even in someone like Paul and others like him—until changeability is removed from
the midst, so that nature will not go astray through awareness of this.
What are uniformity and lack of uniformity? Lack of uniformity in contemplation, which proceeds differently and unevenly from a single soul,
is the incomprehensibility of God's eternal purpose. Uniformity, however, is the revelation of truth.
And if a changeable nature receives certain truth here, it dies from the onslaughts of changeability.
The saying, “Oh, the depth of the riches!” and “His judgments are unsearchable,”
and “Who has known the mind of the Lord?” and so on, which flash upon the mind from time to time in wonder and with sighs,
and which some have called “the dark cloud,” arise from this lack of uniformity in contemplation and this variation in perceptions,
concerning the unfathomable investigation of divine judgments.
But when nature reaches its perfection in the unchanging world,
nature no longer fears knowing God's truth, lest it turn aside to the left because of confidence.
Confidence gives birth to contempt and to recklessness of mind.
Fear, on the other hand, usually restrains changeability, keeping it in check.
You can find this in yourself through contemplation of the differences between judgments and between worlds,
the inequality of ways of life, and the different recompenses administered to them even here,
and the justice that shows itself from time to time and is held in check by patience, and through contemplation of the righteous and sinners,
and the contrast between the dissimilar events providentially allotted to these opposite kinds of people.
When the mind considers these things, trembling settles upon the whole soul.
From this there arises within it an examination of thoughts, words, and deeds, and of the strict limits laid down by divine justice.
But when the mind withdraws from these things and rises toward the divine Being alone,
by contemplating these things—that this nature is good and possesses eternal knowledge, which precedes the coming into being of everything,
and the rest of its attributes—fear is immediately cast out, and the mind is supported by confidence.
But when the mind descends again from there and ranges over the worlds and their distinctions, this confidence immediately flees and gives way to fear.
For providence, too, is unwilling to let the mind remain continually in that same contemplation of truth.
Therefore, from time to time it removes from the heart that strength of confidence which arose from certain contemplation,
and allows it to be tossed about again by uncertainties of various kinds,
so that it will not cease continually examining the soundness of its thoughts and actions, and will acquire vigilance,
because it does not know how it will encounter God’s judgment. To him be glory forever and ever. Amen.
On the different ways in which human nature receives a vision of incorporeal beings. 27.
Now all natures that are not joined to bodies and are subtler than bodies—that is, intelligent beings—
can be perceived by human nature in three ways:
through dense forms without substance, through subtle forms without [?], and through contemplation of truth, which is the vision of essence [?].
The senses have authority over one, and the ordinary vision of the soul over another,
and the natural power of the mind over the third. Again, the will and the mind have authority over one of them,
and over another, the will, the light of the soul, and the one who strengthens it.
The will is the initial cause, and these are the offspring of freedom,
even though freedom and will become still when they are being used, for as long as the working has a place and remains there.
Over one, the revealer alone has authority, even without the recipients’ will and true knowledge.
For the senses receive everything that happens, even without the will.
The holy powers employ these three ways in their dealings with us, for our instruction and the discovery of our life.
But the unclean powers have the ability to employ two of these
and to use them when they approach us, for destruction rather than benefit.
They cannot approach the third way to use it, so as to be able to lead us astray through this as well.
For the children of darkness cannot approach the light.
For, it is said, demons do not have the power to stir up natural insights in the mind.
But the holy angels possess this ability: to stir them up and illuminate them.
Those others, however, have power and authority over false insights, the offspring of darkness.
The recipient receives light from the luminous ones, and darkness from the dark ones.
And why is this given to those but not to these? Each one of these teachers:
Whatever understanding each one presents and teaches, he first sees, learns, and tastes it himself, and then he can convey it to his pupils.
These first teachers of ours convey to us the very truth of things, from their sound knowledge of them:
What they themselves first discover through the keen perception of a nimble and pure mind.
Demons too possess keenness, but not illumination as well. Keenness is one thing, and illumination another.
The first, without the second, reveals the truth; that is, its own likeness.
For light reveals every precise detail that is sought, and it increases and decreases in proportion to one's conduct.
It is from their own knowledge that the holy angels pour into us concerning the stirrings of things:
What they themselves first taste and perceive, and then convey to us.
These second teachers too, in proportion to their knowledge, arouse stirrings in us concerning things.
As for what they themselves are not permitted to do, [?] arousing correct thoughts in us about such things is necessary.
Therefore, as I said, let this be certain for you: not even if we are capable of receiving it
Can they teach us contemplation of the truth, even though they themselves were formerly engaged in it.
Furthermore, each individual from either group, according to the way of life that he follows,
Teaches and urges us pupils too to live accordingly, whether they are holy angels or those on the opposing side.
For my part, I am also certain of this: our mind, even without the mediation of the holy angels,
Is moved toward goodness of its own accord, even without instruction.
But to receive knowledge of evil things without the mediation of demons or the senses,
Or to be moved toward them of its own accord, is beyond our mind's ability. Goodness is planted in our nature.
Evil, however, is not. Everything that is foreign, and knowledge of which enters from outside, requires an intermediary.
But toward what is planted within, nature stirs even without instruction, though only dimly.
Yet even though this is so, and our nature moves toward goodness of its own accord,
It cannot develop this goodness or become enlightened in it without the guidance of the holy angels.
We have them as teachers, just as they too have one another: those of lower rank
Have as their teachers those who are subtler and more luminous than they are.
And so from one to another, up to that one who has the Holy Trinity as his teacher.
And even he spoke confidently, not on his own authority, but having Jesus the mediator as his teacher.
He receives through his hand and passes it on to those below him. I myself also hold this view:
Although our mind does not naturally possess the power to engage in divine contemplation,
and we share this deficiency equally with all the heavenly beings,
for us and for them alike, without study or reflection about it, this contemplation is stirred within us by grace alone,
as something naturally foreign to the human and angelic mind.
For contemplation of the Godhead is not counted among other kinds of contemplation,
since we possess contemplation of these other things through sharing in the twofold nature of created beings.
For a part of everything is within us, but not of the nature of the divine Being; therefore neither is contemplation of it.
And since this is something beyond nature for all rational beings, both the first and the intermediate,
and the movement toward this contemplation in all heavenly and earthly minds comes from grace,
it is not a natural attainment like the others, however much the mind may be enlightened and purified.
I, however, hold this view, which is also true:
As for us human beings, concerning the revelations and insights that lead us until we attain this contemplation of Being,
which is the mystery of sure revelation, without their mediation we are not
led there in our minds. Our mind does not possess this power, as do those lofty and exalted beings,
who receive all revelations and contemplations from the divine Being itself without an intermediary.
Yet even they receive through its image, and not from it unveiled; our mind, too, does so in this way.
For not even the other ranks, apart from that one, from Jesus himself, who holds the [?] of the kingdom,
can receive revelations and contemplation on their own and for themselves without intermediaries—that is, other, higher ranks.
Rather, they receive through transmission from one another concerning all the divine arrangements and the insights about them.
I am not speaking of the divine Being. It passes from the first to the second, and so on, until the mystery has passed through all the ranks.
But many mysteries remain within that one first rank and do not pass out to the other ranks,
since, apart from that one, they are incapable of receiving the greatness of the mystery.
Some of the mysteries, after passing out of that first order, are revealed only to the second.
There the mystery is kept in silence, while these other orders remain unaware of it.
Others are revealed to the third and fourth. There are also higher and lower degrees in the revelation
that comes to each of the holy angels. One is rich in revelations,
and the mysteries revealed to him are of a high order, and he receives greater light.
Another is lower than he, and the movements of his mind are too weak for these mysteries.
Thus there are greater and lesser degrees, higher and lower degrees, among the spiritual orders in their reception of revelations.
In every case, however, the sole exception is that ruling order which is first among all the ranks.
The rest receive from their companions contemplation and indications concerning every aspect of God's providential activity.
If this is so with them, how much more are we unable to receive such mysteries apart from them and without an intermediary.
Rather, it is through them that an awareness of the revelation of any mystery comes into the minds of the saints.
And just as, when God permits it, a mystery is revealed to one order by the order above it, all the way down to the last,
so too, whenever the divine command permits it, the mystery is conveyed even to human nature, among those who are worthy.
In every case, it is through them that the saints receive the light of contemplation,
even concerning the glorious Being himself—a mystery that not even they learn from one another.
They are ministering spirits, sent to those who are to inherit life,
to give them awareness of the true insights in which they are versed. But in the world to come,
this order of transmission will cease. For then no one will receive from his companion
the revelation of God's glory for the delight of his soul. Rather, it will be given to each person directly from God himself:
whatever he is found worthy of receiving from the Lord of all, according to the measure of his virtue. He will not receive the gift through his companion, as he does here.
For there no one learns or teaches, and no one needs to receive from his companion what he lacks.
For there is one Giver, who is revealed there without an intermediary to all who receive.
Those who receive all spiritual delights receive them from him himself.
For they do not perceive him through concepts of particular things, but through his own revelation itself, without their minds moving outward away from him.
There the order of learners and teachers comes to an end, and the intense love of all is directed toward the One.
But I say that even those who are tormented in Gehenna are tortured by the scourges of love.
The scourges that come from love are harsher and more bitter—
that is, those suffered by people who have realized that they sinned against love—than the torments that come from fear.
The sorrow that pierces the heart because of sinning against love is sharper than any torment there is.
It is wrong for anyone to think that sinners in Gehenna are deprived of love for the Creator.
For love is born of the knowledge of truth, which, as is acknowledged, is given to everyone.
Love acts through its power in two ways: it torments those who have sinned, just as happens here too
between friends in their relations with one another. But love delights those who have fulfilled its obligations.
It is the same in Gehenna. I say that remorse arising from love is the severity of its torment.
But for those in heaven, the delight found in this love intoxicates their souls.
Someone was asked, “When can a person be confident that he has been granted forgiveness of his sins?”
He answered, “When he senses within himself that he hates them completely, with all his heart, and his outward conduct is the opposite of his former conduct.”
A person like this has confidence before God concerning the forgiveness of his sins,
through the testimony of conscience that he possesses within himself, as the apostle said. A heart free from reproach bears witness on its own behalf.
28. A figurative illustration concerning the contemplation of the Sabbath and Sunday.
Sunday is a symbol of the knowledge of truth, which cannot be received in flesh and blood, and of rising above conjectures.
In this world, however, there is no eighth day, nor indeed is there a true Sabbath.
God’s resting on the seventh day is a symbol of our nature’s stillness after the course of this life.
For the grave too is material; it belongs to this world. The six days are completed in the labor of life,
and the seventh is fulfilled in the grave, and the eighth in coming out of it.
For just as those who are worthy receive the mysteries of Sunday here in a figurative way,
and do not receive the day itself in their bodily existence, so too the mysteries of the Sabbath are received, as an illustration,
by the diligent here, but not the true Sabbath itself, which is complete release from afflictions.
God has given us a symbolic taste of everything, but he has not ordained that we should experience the realities themselves here in their full actuality.
For the true Sabbath, not the figurative one, takes place in the grave: complete rest from the weariness caused by the passions.
And there the whole person rests from the labor of opposing them, body and soul together.
In six days God ordered the existence of this world and established the elements.
He gave them an existence of ceaseless movement in service, not to stop their course before they are dissolved.
From the power of these—that is, the parent elements—he formed our own body.
He gave neither them a rest from their movements nor our body, their offspring, a rest from labor.
He set the boundary for the rest of these elements within us at the point when they rejoin their original kindred, which is release from life.
He also said this to Adam: “By the sweat of your face you shall eat bread.”
Until when? “Until,” he says, “you return to the earth from which you were taken. You shall work the earth, and it shall produce thorns and thistles for you.”
This is a symbol of the world: this world is a world of labor for as long as one lives.
But from that night when he sweated, our Lord changed the sweat of labor on the earth that produces thorns and thistles
into sweat in prayer as well, and into our sweating in the work of righteousness. Five
thousand years he left him to toil at that, because the way into the sanctuary had not yet been revealed, as the Apostle says.
But he came in his grace at the end of days and commanded our free will to exchange its sweat for another sweat.
Certainly, he did not command it to cease working; he showed it an exchange, because he had compassion on us on account of our long toil on the earth.
But if we stop sweating at this work, we must necessarily reap thorns.
For ceasing from this is cultivating the material earth, which produces thorns according to its nature.
In truth, the thorns are the passions that spring up for us from the seed within the body.
As long as we bear Adam’s image, we must necessarily bear his passions as well.
The earth cannot stop producing growth, for it produces according to its nature.
Our earth too shares its nature, according to God’s testimony concerning us: “The earth,” he says, “from which you were taken.”
That earth produces thorns; this rational earth produces passions.
But if our Lord became a symbolic pattern for us in everything, in all the distinct aspects of his saving work:
For he did not rest from labor or from suffering until the ninth hour on Friday.
This is the [?] of our whole life, a symbol of labor. He did not enter the Sabbath except in the grave.
Where are those who say that there is a Sabbath in this world—a rest from the passions? As for Sunday, it is too great a thing to speak of.
Our Sabbath is the day of the grave. There our nature truly rests. Therefore, every day
we must uproot the thorns from it, as long as this earth remains.
Continual cultivation reduces the undergrowth, but even so the ground is not completely clean.
If we neglect this for even a little while, the undergrowth springs up and covers its surface.
It saps your seed and makes your earlier labor as though it had never been.
Therefore, it needs clearing every day. A break from this work causes those weeds to multiply.
On the different beneficial forms of wise providence for the training of those under its guidance. 29.
All wisdom comes from the Lord, as it is said.
Through our own affairs we are trained to understand the Lord’s dealings with us.
A true father deals with his children in different ways. He guards against uniformity
in always presenting the same expression, for the benefit of his children.
Instead, for their training, he conceals his love. Outwardly he shows what is not there, while hiding what is.
From the changes in his father’s dealings with him, a wise son recognizes his father’s care for him, together with his discerning love.
To sound understanding, the activity of true love appears twofold: in things that bring joy, but also in things that bring pain.
That is, he is always ready to give his beloved relief. Yet he also causes pain at
times, because he loves greatly. He suffers with him even while causing him pain.
Yet he restrains even his natural compassion when it is stirred, for fear of the harm that would follow.
Love compels him to share in suffering; knowledge, in turn, gives him strength to resist even these feelings.
As free choice varies, so too do the forms of wise love vary
toward those who receive this care. Let us not ask a wise friend for foolish love.
Someone who kills his son by feeding him honey is no different from someone who kills him with a knife.
For it does not befit his wisdom to feed his beloved with just one kind of food, both in times of health and in sickness.
I am speaking here of the changes the will undergoes in choosing its impulses, not of bodily changes.
And if we know how to manage these occasions when we care for someone we love,
especially when he is under our authority, should we not allow God to fulfill the rightful demands of his discerning love for us?
Even if they are like the changes we know how to give to those who love us? Still, it is hard to endure.
I know that too. Nevertheless, it is beneficial. Your instability made this necessary for you.
Even if not as repayment for what has already happened, then certainly out of fear of what is to come.
Distressing events serve inward training as beneficial medicines serve bodily imbalance.
Whatever among created beings is not composite has no struggle in its way of life, whether you speak of bodily beings or
bodiless beings. Toil tends to arise from imbalance, and imbalance in composite beings is due to the fundamental duality of their constitution.
Although those who are not composite but simple are, and are called, capable of inclining, their inclination is entirely toward the right.
Yet this involves no toil, since they have no experience of the other kind. They are indeed susceptible to what is good.
For their inclination is held in check by intense love. Where there is love, there is neither struggle nor fear.
And this is so even though they are masters of their own will, which is said to allow room for inclination as well.
For this reason they are all the more worthy of praise. Good and evil deeds are the offspring of freedom.
Where freedom is lacking, even the performance of such deeds is irrelevant to recompense. For nature receives no recompense.
A reward is assigned for combat, and there can be no talk of victory without a struggle.
When opposition is removed, freedom too ceases along with it.
Then nature continues without struggle. A time has been reserved for the cessation of freedom; from then on, rationality becomes bound,
in human beings and angels alike. Rationality is not a capacity for movement that can be perceived by the senses.
For in its capacity for knowledge, rationality possesses two properties, that is, two powers:
the power of speaking and the power of knowing. The first comes to a complete end.
But through the second, nature is perfected—that is, through the power of knowing. Yet this too is bound then. It is not compulsory
bondage, but rather bondage through delight, a pleasant constraint. Sometimes, even now, this occurs mysteriously in a few.
Yet it involves change. Among the first rational beings, however, it is without change as far as possible, although they are not perfect.
What does it mean that they are without change and yet not perfect? For there are mysteries that cannot be received before the appointed time.
They are not perfect for this reason; it is not through [?] that they possess their present state.
This is entirely absent among them. Rather, there is constancy and no change. And if there is change, it is toward things that are more excellent.
Thus their change is a change for the better. Ours, however, is a cessation, because of the weakness of the flesh.
On the power of sin and its evil activity: what sustains it and what brings it to an end. 30.
Until a person sincerely hates the cause of sin from the heart, he is not freed from the pleasure it produces in the heart.
This is the fierceness of the struggle that confronts a person to the point of bloodshed:
in it his free will is tested in the singleness of its love for the virtues.
This is the force called provocations, whose very scent makes the weak soul recoil,
because of the fierce incitement contained in it. This is the mighty power of sin, by which it disturbs
the serenity of the chaste and forces upon the movements of the pure things they have never experienced or known.
Here let us show our endurance, my beloved. This is the time of martyrdom that is not put to shame:
through it, it is said, the order of solitaries wins glory at all times.
When this battle strikes, the mind even of those who are well established is disturbed and confused, unless it is extremely watchful.
Our Lord, almighty, source of every help, support, at these moments that are times of martyrdom,
the souls that have joyfully betrothed themselves to you, the heavenly bridegroom,
and have given you a promise of holiness, with complete serenity in their inward movements and not deceitfully.
Give them that power which subdues rebellious strongholds and every lofty thing raised against holiness,
so that they may not be turned aside from the goal set before them by the unbearable pressure of the time when the struggle to the point of bloodshed is being fought.
This difficult battle does not occur at all times in the struggle for chastity.
Perhaps abandonment occurs as a test. Woe to the weak person who is tested in this exceptional battle!
It has great power; it gains strength from habit
in those who have given themselves over completely to defeat, even once, by yielding to it in thought.
Beware of idleness, my beloved: spiritual death is hidden within it.
Without it, a solitary cannot fall into the hands of his captors.
It is not for the psalms that God will judge us on that day,
or for neglecting the appointed times of prayer whenever that happens. Rather, abandoning them provides an entrance for demons.
Once they have found room, entered, and taken possession of our inner chambers, they tyrannically bring about in us
those things which, under divine sentences, subject those who do them to severe punishment for them.
We become enslaved through neglecting small things, which the wise take pains to attend to for Christ’s sake.
As it is said: Whoever does not subject his will to God becomes subject to his adversary.
Let us therefore regard as walls against our captors these practices that seem insignificant, whose fulfillment takes place within the cell.
These were wisely established by those who hold the awesome offices of the Church, through the spirit of revelation, to safeguard our lives.
Neglecting these practices is considered a small matter by the unwise.
But they do not consider the transgressions that arise from this neglect.
The beginning and middle of their path is undisciplined freedom, which is the mother of disorders. To submit to constraint
by taking care over small things is better than giving sin room through freedom from them.
This is freedom at the wrong time, whose end is harsh slavery.
As long as your senses remain alive to encounters with whatever happens, consider your soul already dead.
For the burning of sin in all its forms will never cease in your members, nor will peace be able to settle in your soul.
If there is anyone among the solitaries who claims that he can guard his heart while exposed to these things, this man
does not want to know when he is being struck. A person who deceives his neighbor is liable to a curse, according to the law.
But someone who deceives himself—what punishments does he not deserve? Though he knows,
he makes himself unaware that he knows, because his conscience then demands that he remove the cause.
This is what seems difficult to him, and because of it, although he knows, he wants to be someone who does not know.
Oh, how sweet is the cause of the passions! Sometimes a person cuts off the passions themselves and finds relief in driving them away.
Often he rejoices when they cease, but he cannot uproot their cause.
For this reason, even against our will, we are tempted. We are distressed by the passions,
yet we love having their causes remain with us. We do not want sins,
yet we gladly welcome the things that bring them about. For this reason, the latter inevitably become the cause of the former.
It is said that whoever desires the causes of the passions is enslaved to the passions, even against his will.
Whoever hates his sins stops committing them, and whoever confesses his offenses receives forgiveness.
There is no stopping habitual sins without acquiring hatred for them, and no receiving forgiveness without confessing one’s offenses.
This is followed by genuine humility, and that by remorse arising from shame in the heart.
Until we come to share in hatred of blameworthy things, it is impossible to perceive the foulness of practicing them, or
their stench, as long as we carry them within ourselves. Until you cast the hateful thing away from you,
you will not even know what shame you are wrapped in, or the disgrace that comes from it.
When you see your own burden in others, then you will recognize the ugliness that envelops you.
Distance yourself from evil, and you will recognize its foulness. Unless you distance yourself, you will not recognize it.
For you embrace its foulness like a sweet fragrance, and the nakedness of your exposure like a robe of glory.
Blessed is the one who has withdrawn from darkness and seen himself. Within darkness, sight cannot function or distinguish things.
Blessed is the one whom the dizziness of his wine has left, and who has seen in others what the degradation of his drunkenness is like. Then he understands his own shame.
But as long as he himself carries the drunkenness of sins within him, everything he does is beautiful in his own eyes.
When nature departs from its proper order, it is the same whether it is drunk with wine or with lusts.
Both lead away from what is right. Both stir up the same heat in the body that receives them.
Their kinds differ, but the resulting condition is the same, and the madness is the same.
For the kinds that cause it are not alike, but there is no difference in those who receive them.
Every comfort, then, has hardship appointed after it, and every hardship, comfort.
But if everything in this world is subject to change, it undergoes its change into its opposite,
either here or there, or at the time of a person's departure. This applies especially to the comfort
that comes from recklessness, or to the hardship opposed to it that is endured in holiness.
God employs this in a measured way, so that a person tastes that torment either along the way or at its end, and then it passes.
And because of the abundance of God's mercy, this counts as repayment,
while that counts as a pledge, since the interest on good does not consume its principal.
But with evil, it does. As it is said, whoever is disciplined here eats into his punishment in Gehenna.
Beware of freedom that comes before submission. Beware of consolation that comes before battles.
Beware of knowledge that comes before encounters with trials.
And above all, beware of love that comes before the completion of repentance.
If we are all sinners, and no one is beyond temptation by sins, no virtue comes before repentance.
Remember that every pleasure has distress and bitterness as its counterpart.
Be wary even of joy, for a change without a cause is not bound up with it.
For everything whose direction comes from above, if you wish to know, you will find a reason for its changes.
Fear whatever seems to maintain an unchanging condition. It is said to lie outside the well-trodden path.
He who knows how to steer the world's ship wisely has joined change to everything in it. Anything exempt from this is a marvel.
Rest for the limbs is accompanied by wandering thoughts; excessive toil, however, by despondency.
Despondency, in turn, is accompanied by distraction. One distraction differs from another. The former is accompanied by a struggle with impurity
while the latter is accompanied by departure from the cell and a change of places.
But measured labors, when joined with perseverance, have no equal.
Too little of them produces excessive desire; too much of them gives room for confusion.
Endure the folly of nature that prevails in your body, brother, because you are destined to enter that wisdom whose crown of supremacy never passes away.
Do not be troubled by the turmoil of the body inherited from Adam, which is destined to enter that delight
the knowledge of which is beyond the minds of fleshly human beings here, when it puts on that heavenly image
who is the King of Peace. Do not be shaken by the turbulent changes of nature.
For the effort involved in [?] them lasts for a time, just as does the pleasure of welcoming them.
They are dogs accustomed to visiting the butcher. At the mere sound of your voice they run away.
But if you throw yourself into dealing with them, you will turn them into mighty lions.
Despise a small pleasure, so that you are not imprisoned by the violence of its heat.
A little endurance in the face of small matters
checks the danger of the arrival of great, very great matters.
There is no overcoming great evils without a small victory over lesser ones.
Remember, brother, that condition in which you are destined to be,
in which there will no longer be the vital forces that throb with heat, through which mortal life is worn down.
Nor will there any longer be the boiling of the bodily constitution, which, through the enticement of its pleasure, agitates immature nature.
Endure the toil of the struggle that has brought you to the test.
in it, as one who is about to receive a crown and pass on. For in a little while you will rest from this world.
Remember that rest without end, that life without deception, that fully mature stature,
that way of life without lapses, that captivity under the constraint of divine love, which rules over nature.
In which struggle there is greater toil—or rather, danger of falling. 31.
It is not possible to overcome the evil thoughts that accompany the stirrings in the body,
or to gain mastery over them—some have called them a double weapon directed against us—
nor can they be quieted while we are filled with bread, water, and sleep, and remain close to things that excite the senses.
It is better to lose one's life than to suffer shame in it.
When we attend to our duties, the activity of the flesh subsides in our limbs.
It is not possible both to concern ourselves with things perceived by the senses and to set our own passions right.
For without diligent [?] supplications and constant prostrations, it is not possible to draw mercy toward us.
It is necessary to practice these things together.
Without bearing the burden of small things, it is not possible to escape great evils.
On the purpose of guarding the heart, and on subtle contemplation within its narrow chamber. 32.
Do not let the power contained in spiritual songs escape your notice, when they are used with understanding.
For this power carries thought far away from the world. It also steals distraction away from the mind, even though it seems suitable for children.
For the mind receives help for a little while. The stirring of the spirit is stronger against the passions than the constraint of knowledge.
Whenever you are alone, guard your heart by these means, if you have not yet acquired strength
to guard yourself through contemplation, which is engagement with discerning knowledge; instead, also maintain constant remembrance of departure from the body,
and remembrance of the things awaited in hope, accompanied by righteous practices that produce delight:
keeping far away from things that excite you, and the small observances within the cell.
If you find your vessel moving forward freely after much discipline, give it room.
But if you see it behaving foolishly, put it under the yoke of rules. For here it is easily set right.
