As you travel with understanding through these changes and others like them,
in the treasure-laden ship of the cell, a great festival filled with the trade of the diligent,
Then carefully examine the [?] fruits that arise for you from changes perceptible to the senses.
Consider how the afflictions of the cross precede every delight of the spirit.
But the delight of sin is born from bodily ease.
And consider why spiritual contemplation, which heals the mind, is found in the harbor of chastity, while spiritual love has this contemplation as its cause.
The second does not exist without the cause that precedes it, nor does the third virtue exist without the one before it.
You can [?] of the mind, which sprout in the womb of chastity.
Through them it rises to divine love, through which it boldly ventures toward the dark cloud of [?].
This understanding gives a person great strength: vigilance to bring into his affairs, together with encouragement to persevere.
Let a way of life without eyes be abandoned, for it easily leads to discouragement through distraction.
Pray to our Lord to give eyes to your way of life. From this, joy begins to spring up for you.
Then afflictions become as sweet to you as a cake, and from then on you will find your enclosure to be a wedding hall.
It is impossible to overcome the passions without outward virtues, or the distraction of busy activity without engagement in spiritual knowledge.
Our mind is a flighty thing, and unless it is willingly bound by discernment, it does not stop wandering.
And this undertaking is not possible without fulfilling the earlier requirements.
For there is no peace without victory over enemies. And if peace does not reign, [?] to find
what lies beyond peace. The passions are a fence around the hidden virtues.
Unless these passions first fall through the outward virtues, it is impossible to see what lies inside them. For it is impossible to stand
outside the wall and speak about what is inside. It is impossible to see the sun through a dark cloud,
or the soul’s natural virtues amid the turmoil of persistent passions.
Pray to God to grant you awareness of the stirrings of the Spirit.
If these come into your soul, the world withdraws from you, and you from it.
These cannot be perceived without stillness, solitude, and engagement in carefully chosen reading.
Do not seek those things without these practices. But if you seek them without these, after a little while they change and become bodily.
Let whoever understands understand. That wise Lord willed that this bread should be eaten with sweat.
Not out of malice, but so that we would not suffer indigestion and die.
But with every virtue that is the mother of another, its premature discovery
is a viper to the souls that discover it, unless they cast it off little by little.
On the working of divine love. 33.
Since we have outlined above the impulses of the Spirit, the occasion now invites us to explain them.
There is a certain luminous power that springs up in the heart from love.
At first, without any sensory causes, it stirs the temperament [?], without any particular contemplation, or any concept or thought producing it.
For this reason, because the mind is still clouded, it seems to those who are untrained to be without causes of this kind—
so it seems to them. But to the mature, its cause too is subsequently revealed.
With the disclosure of the cause, this sweetness, that is, flies through the heart still more powerfully.
The recipient sends a portion of it coursing through the body, and transmits another portion to the powers of the soul.
For the heart is placed midway between the senses of the soul and those of the body, serving the former as an instrument and belonging naturally to the latter.
It is the recipient, and stirs in both directions a taste of its working.
Because of it, he is also compelled to seek relief from the world, and to withdraw from the things of the world.
The cause presses us to investigate. Love is something hot by nature.
Whenever it falls upon someone without measure, it makes that soul like one driven mad.
For this reason, the heart that has felt it cannot contain it and endure without some unusual change becoming visible in it.
These are its perceptible signs, which it displays in his face: immediately his face grows red and joyful, and his body becomes hot.
Fear and bashfulness are driven away from him. He becomes like someone who has cast restraint aside. The power of composure flees from him.
Impetuosity and bewilderment take hold of him. From that moment, his life is as nothing in his eyes compared with his beloved.
For this reason, even death, which is terrifying above all things, becomes to him a matter of relief.
Yet amid all these things, his mind’s gaze is not diverted from its absorbed wonder at him.
He is far away in place, yet speaks to him as though he were nearby.
Though he is hidden from sight, he marvels at his known hiddenness. The sight of his nature eludes
the senses. Yet through his deeds he is set ablaze, as though at the sight of him.
He dwells alone, yet his thought converses as though with someone else, and is held spellbound.
With this passion the martyrs became intoxicated; through it the apostles traveled around the whole earth like madmen.
The holy ones were mistreated and accepted mockery; they became wanderers in the wilderness. Though orderly, they became disorderly.
Though wise, they willingly became fools. Though dignified, they deliberately made themselves contemptible.
They were free from passions, though they had flesh that was constantly demanding, yet quiet without compulsion.
May we be found worthy to attain this madness even here, through the mercies of our worshipful God, who took a mediator from our race,
and through him gave us these things—he who was tested like us in everything that belongs to us, except sin.
Because of the natural oneness of his flesh with ours, and beyond this, without confusion,
in a union that preserves the properties of the natures, he granted him the seat at the right hand.
Through him, to him be glory, dominion, and worship, now and in the life without end, forever and ever. Amen.
Before you enter the city of humility, if you see yourself resting from the turmoil of the passions, do not trust yourself.
An ambush is being prepared for you. After that rest, expect great disturbance from them.
As you pass through all the dwelling places of the virtues, you will not find rest from your troubles or relief
from your pursuers until your journey reaches the dwelling place of humility.
On the natural offspring of the virtues, and other matters. 34.
Ascetic discipline is the mother of holiness, from which is born the taste of the first perception of God's mysteries,
which they call the first degree of spiritual knowledge.
Let no one deceive himself and conjure up fantasies. For an impure soul does not ascend to the pure kingdom,
whether you mean this [?] one or the real one; nor does it mingle with the holy spirits.
Rather, when the elements have mingled with their own kind,
at the dissolution of the natural union, the wretched soul is kept for the great judgment to come.
Polish the beauty of your chastity, my brother, through tears, fasting, and sitting alone with yourself.
When, therefore, the straight course of the natural sphere is completed and it has reached the great light,
which sustains the spheres of the stars with their many individual distinctions,
as Paul illustrates concerning the resurrection to come, and it has mingled with its rays—not by nature, I say—
then the chariot of the will will be bound by the reins of unknowing.
And both copiously flowing springs will cease to flow from their source. Then the priests too will come out of the sanctuary, from
before the cloud of the Lord’s glory, at that time when Solomon becomes king over Israel.
This peace, which is born of humility, will build a house for the Lord and equip it with all the sacred vessels.
A little suffering endured for God’s sake is more precious to God than great service performed without suffering.
For voluntary suffering tests the love that rests within it. Service performed at ease, however, comes from a satisfied conscience.
For this reason, the saints were tested through sufferings for the love of Christ, and not through service performed at ease.
Service without toil is the righteousness of worldly people, who are justified through their possessions but do not grow in virtue in their own persons.
But you, valiant one, taste Christ’s suffering in your own person, so that you may also be found worthy to taste his glory.
For it says, “If we suffer with him, we will also be glorified with him.” The mind is not glorified with Jesus unless the body suffers for Jesus.
At the same time, it tramples glory underfoot and receives glory.
A person is glorified in body together with soul. The body’s glory is humble submission to God.
The mind’s glory is true contemplation of God. Right submission takes two forms:
toil and humiliation, so that when the body suffers, the heart also suffers with it.
Unless you know God, love for him cannot be stirred within you.
You cannot love God unless you have seen God. You have seen God when you have known him. There is no precedence
of seeing him over knowing him. Make me worthy to know you, my Lord, so that I may also love you.
Not through that knowledge which comes, with mental exertion, from training in learning.
Rather, make me worthy of that knowledge through which, as the mind gazes upon you, it becomes a glorifier of your nature,
in that gaze which steals awareness of the world away from the mind. Make me worthy to rise above deliberate gazes that produce thoughts,
and to gaze upon you under the constraint of the bonds of the cross, in that second part of the mind’s crucifixion,
in which its freedom ceases to exercise its movements through the wondrous, supernatural gaze upon you.
Place within me the burning heat of your love, so that I may leave the world and follow you.
Stir within me an understanding of your humility, in which you lived in the world through the covering you put on from our bodily members,
so that through the wondrous and unforgettable remembrance of it, I may gladly accept the humbling of my own nature.
There are two parts to the ascent, the ascent to the cross. One is the crucifixion of the body.
Both lead upward to contemplation. But the first belongs to freedom, and the second to active practice.
The mind is not brought into submission unless the body is brought into submission. The mind’s kingship is the body’s crucifixion.
The mind is not brought into submission to God unless free will is brought into submission to reason.
It is difficult to entrust something exalted to someone immature. “Woe to you, city,” it says, “whose king is a child!”
Whoever has brought himself into submission is close to having everything brought into submission to him. Whoever knows himself is given knowledge of everything
to him. To [?] yourself is the fulfillment of the knowledge of everything.
Just as everything is contained within yourself, knowledge of everything is contained within knowledge of yourself.
And within the subjection of yourself is the subjection [?] of everything. When humility comes to rule your conduct,
your own self will become subject to you, and everything along with it, because the peace that comes from God will be born in your heart.
As long as you remain outside this state, you are constantly pursued not only by the passions but also by misfortunes.
Truly, Lord, unless we humble ourselves, you do not cease to humble us.
True humility is the offspring of knowledge, and sound knowledge is the offspring of trials.
A discourse in questions and answers concerning upright conduct and every kind of virtue.
Especially suitable for those who have renounced the world and those who live in the wilderness,
and for recluses and those who, through continual voluntary death, await the crown of righteousness. 35.
The student says: What bonds restrain the mind from running toward evil things? The teacher says:
The constant pursuit of wisdom and an eager appetite for life-giving instruction.
For there are no bonds stronger than these for restraining the mind’s disorderliness.
The student says: How far does the pursuit of wisdom extend in its inquiries,
and where does the course of learning end? The teacher says: The path of wisdom’s journey runs so far beyond any boundary
that even the holy angels fall short of this fulfillment. Indeed, there is no end to wisdom’s journey.
It rises so high that it unites with God the person who follows it.
This itself is a sign of its boundlessness. “There is no end to its insights,” it says. Wisdom is God.
The student: What is the principal and first path that leads to wisdom? The teacher:
That a person should seek God with all his strength and devote himself wholeheartedly and eagerly to seeking him:
so that he does not refuse even to strip off his own life and cast it away for love of him.
Student: Who deserves to be called a person of understanding? Teacher:
Someone who has truly understood that this life of his has a limit; he can also put a limit to his sins.
What knowledge or understanding is greater than this:
that someone should have the wisdom to leave this life unharmed, without his bodily members being stained by the stench of desires or his soul by the filth of their sweetness?
But if someone becomes subtle in his thoughts, entering into the mysteries of all created natures and abounding, so to speak, in the understanding of everything knowable,
while his soul is stained with the filth of sin, and he has no hope, based on the testimony of his own soul,
of safely reaching that harbor of confidence, there is no one in creation more foolish than he is. For so far,
his labors have brought him only to the hope of this world, in their constant rush toward it.
Student: Who is truly strong? Teacher:
Someone who, amid the afflictions that last for a time, in which the glory of his victory is hidden, has not longed for ease,
in which a shameful life is hidden, and which continually gives those who find it a cup of sighs to drink.
Student: Does someone harm his progress toward God if he draws back from hardship? Teacher:
There is no way for anyone to draw near to Christ without afflictions, nor can his righteousness be preserved unchanged without them.
Righteousness already acquired, from which the hardships that both nurture and preserve it have ceased,
is like a treasure suddenly found without guards;
like a fighter stripped of his weapons while an army of enemies surrounds him;
like a ship left in the middle of the sea without its equipment;
and like a garden laden with fruit whose source of irrigation has run dry. Student: Who is enlightened in his thoughts? Teacher:
Someone who has managed to perceive the bitterness hidden within the sweetness of the world and keeps his mouth away from its cup so that he will not drink it.
He diligently pursues the salvation of his life and does not stop running until the day of his departure from the world.
He closes the gates of his senses so that love of the world will not enter and settle within him and rob him of his hidden treasures.
Student: This is the world; and how can we recognize it, and by what
can it harm those who love it? Teacher: The world is a prostitute that, through desire for its beauty, draws those who gaze at it into loving it.
Anyone who has become even slightly entangled in love for it cannot escape from its hands.
Until it even strips him of his life, and, naked of everything, he departs from his house through death.
A person becomes aware of it when he strives to come out of its darkness.
Then he can see the many cords of its traps.
As long as he remains enclosed within it, he cannot see its snares.
For look: not only its disciples, its children, and the prisoners within its rebellion,
but also those who have renounced possessions, ascetics, and those who once broke its bonds and rose above it—
now it has begun to capture them little by little for its service, and makes them something to trample beneath its feet.
Student: Since you have convinced me that the world is indeed the strangler of its inhabitants,
and that the craft by which it binds them is so difficult to comprehend,
this is what I first want to learn: What is the initial impulse through which the mind begins to question the world,
when its bonds are so strong and the forms of its snares are hidden? Teacher:
When a thought of love for his soul is stirred within him, this stirring of thought begins to make the world hateful in his eyes
and casts doubt about it into him. Student: Where did this stirring within him come from,
so that what he had always praised, and what had constantly seemed beautiful to him,
should suddenly seem unbeautiful to him, and he should regret his life and his former understanding,
like someone whose thinking about the world had been misguided? Teacher:
First, nature itself places a discerning impulse within him, silently pointing out to him
the instability of the world's existence and the end that will come to its course,
and the impermanence of those who enter it. He sees that this world is set before those who enter it as a passageway,
and he considers the many generations before him, whose number he cannot fathom,
who entered it as a lodging place and departed from it like travelers on the way of all the earth, never to return.
Some of them were kings, and some rulers; some were wise, and some held in honor,
men of power. Some abounded in wealth, and some owned possessions.
Now nothing remains after them: neither the order of their ranks nor the crowns of their authority,
neither their fearsome thrones, nor the luxuries of their grandeur, nor the praise of those who honored them;
Neither the affection of their loved ones, nor their bodies pampered with good things, nor the splendid beauty of their elegance,
nor the lofty bearing of their pride, nor their learned intelligence, nor their minds rich in thoughts, nor the abundant streams of the Gihon
of teaching that used to pour from their mouths and captivate their listeners’ hearts with its eloquence.
And look: they have been sleeping in Sheol for many years, as though for a single night.
And it is not known how much longer they have to remain in this long sleep,
or when the morning of resurrection will dawn for them and awaken them from their slumber.
And he reflects, “Could they perhaps be left like this?” It is a great sorrow.
And look how many generations are confined beneath this earth, unknown.
“I too am passing away like one of them. Cursed are riches and comforts!”
And at this thought, great bewilderment falls upon his heart, and his mind fills with sorrow.
And under the weight of sorrow he sheds tears in deep grief.
From then on he despises the world and weeps over his life. He mourns for himself with varied and bitter lamentations.
And with sighs he says to himself, “Where are you, my wretched soul?
And where will you be found after my death?” Perhaps this thought also assails him: “If only I had not come into existence or emerged from the womb!”
And with lamentations like these he pours out copious tears from the anguish of his heart and drenches his clothing with his tears.
From then on, this world appears to him like a prison.
And its former sweetness is more bitter than anything bitter.
And love of life in it and its enticing beauties are like an image of Sheol [?].
Then he turns his mind to Scripture, which stirs in him faith in the resurrection and in the end that will come
to all the affairs of this world, and in the promises recorded in it for those who lived well in the world,
and in the divine sentences of judgment threatened against those who transgress the law
and those who, during the brief span of their lives, loved the broad road of sin.
And from this, like someone encountering a light, he casts off the burden of grief.
And great joy is stirred within him, like someone who has found a noble and certain hope.
Nature cannot produce these things and things like them through its own impulses.
Through faith alone, [?] from the written signs.
A person cannot acquire knowledge about everything from nature and from the activity of the discernment within him.
But God's acts of providence, both those that have passed and those yet to come, we can learn about from the Scriptures,
or from revelation by the Spirit. Then, through the rays of faith and Scripture,
the mind's eye is illuminated, natural discernment shines out, and a person is awakened to care for his soul.
From then on he considers ways to remove his life from the world,

so that, before leaving the body, he can prepare provisions for himself that will help him there.
Student.

And how can a person leave the world completely?
Teacher. Through the longing stirred by remembering the good things to come,
which divine Scripture sows in his heart through the sweetness of its hope-inspiring words.
For as long as no desire for something better enters in to displace the things considered splendid and pleasant, to which

a person clings, the mind cannot despise its former love.
Student.
But human nature is weak and cannot suddenly abandon its former habits all at once and embrace a life of hardship.
Teacher. Unless a person, with great wisdom, compares in his mind the greatness of the life to come
with the insignificance and brevity of life in this short time,
he cannot take courage to face hardships and begin his journey along the road to the new world.
Calculate in your mind the number of years in the place where we are, and raise it as high as you can.
Compare it with the days of the world to come, and see whether what you give amounts to anything beside what you are going to receive.
Consider what you are leaving behind and what you are receiving in exchange, and whether the exchange you are making is worthwhile.
For this reason, marveling at the greatness of that world and the endlessness of the life within it,
and at the shortness of life here, the wise man says: “The number of a person's days, if he lives a very long life,
is a hundred years. It is like filling a waterskin from the sea, or taking a grain from the sand.

But a thousand years of this world are not like a single day in the world of radiant light.”
Student.
And what should we do with the body, since, when sufferings surround it, the will also grows weak along with it, losing its desire for good things

and its former determination?
Teacher. This happens most often
to those who have gone after God with only half their being, while their other half has remained entangled in the world.
That is, their hearts are not yet free of the things of this world, but they are divided within themselves, looking sometimes behind them and sometimes ahead.
And I think that the wise man admonishes those who approach God's way with this divided mind, saying:
"Do not approach it with two minds, but approach it like a sower [?] and like a reaper."
Our Lord too, when he saw that among those who wanted to make this complete departure there were some like this:
their will was ready, but their thoughts were still being pulled backward because of their fear of afflictions,
because of the love of the body, which they had not yet cast away [?] from themselves—while freeing them from their weakness of mind,
he spoke decisively to them: "Whoever wants to come after me must first deny himself."
What is the denial he mentions here? It is the denial of the body.
Like someone about to go up onto the cross, he should take the thought of death into his mind beforehand, and then set out,
like someone who does not think that he still has any share in this life.
This is what is meant by, "Let him take up his cross and come after me." He calls a will prepared for every affliction a cross.
And to explain why this is so, he says: "Whoever wants to keep himself alive in this world
deprives his soul of true life. And whoever loses himself for my sake
here will find himself there." That is, whoever sets his steps on the way of crucifixion,
yet still takes care to concern himself with this bodily life,
deprives his soul of that hope for whose sake he set out to suffer.
For this very concern does not allow him to approach afflictions.
Instead, by constantly remaining with him, it draws him away little by little and takes him out of the struggle for the blessed life,
as that thought grows within him, until he is [?] by it.
But whoever accepts in his mind the loss of his own self in order to attain love for me is kept unharmed for eternal life.
This is what is meant by, "Whoever loses his life for my sake will find it."
That is, as far as it depends on you, prepare yourself beforehand for the complete loss of life.
And if the loss of this life overtakes you while you have this resolve, I will give you eternal life, as promised [?].
And if you remain in this life, I will demonstrate my promise in you through deeds, beginning here, to confirm the good things to come.
For it is then that you find that immortal life: when you hold this life in contempt.
When you enter the struggle with this preparation, then everything very painful and difficult becomes insignificant in your eyes.
But when the will is prepared in this way, a person does not even feel anxiety about his life when he is confronted
by the danger of death. In short, unless a person hates his life here out of love for the life to come,
he cannot endure afflictions. Student: How can a person break off his former habits
and accustom himself to a life of [?]? Teacher:
The body will not agree to live with little as long as it is surrounded by occasions for luxury and laxity.
The very sight of possessions and splendors, and their availability, kindle within it a greater blaze of desire for them.
Our Savior, too, rightly commands those who follow him first to give up their possessions and leave the world.
He first removes from them the occasions for laxity, and then commands them to approach the work.
Our Lord himself, too, when he stood firm in battle against the devil, fought against him in a dry and desolate wilderness.
Paul also commands those who carry Christ’s cross to go outside the city.
He says, “Let us go with him outside the city, bearing his disgrace, for he himself also suffered outside the city.”
By separating himself from the world and what belongs to it, a person easily forgets his former habits as well, and does not suffer long in doing so.
Proximity to possessions, however, readily weakens the mind’s resolve.
Indeed, it is fitting and very helpful in the struggle for a person’s way of life to be ordered in complete deprivation and need,
devoid of everything that entices him to take his ease. When, in this way,
the occasions that invite laxity are kept far from a person, he is not tormented by a double battle, from within and from without.
See how much less of a struggle it is for someone to desire things from a distance
than when the things themselves are nearby and, through the sight of them, provoke his thoughts.
Here we see that there is a double struggle. For when a person lives in want,
and what he uses is of little value, he does not look at it with desire even when he needs it.
He satisfies his body with a little, while even this is despised and scorned by him.
He does not approach it because of its attractiveness or pleasantness, but only to sustain his nature.
These means readily lead a person to ascetic discipline, without wearisome struggles and battles with thoughts.
A person ought, in the case of things with which it takes a struggle to avoid becoming entangled,
that he should be on his guard even against seeing them and keep away from their company. I say this not only about things concerning the stomach,
but also about all those things through which a solitary’s freedom is put to the test,
and from which he has entered into a covenant with God to separate himself.
That is, I also mean looking at a woman’s face and looking at displays of grandeur,
as well as proud people and their luxuries, adornments and those who wear them, and the whole manner of worldly living,
and speaking and hearing about these things. For the passions gain great strength from the proximity
of such things, weakening those engaged in the struggle and bringing about a change in their minds.
If the sight of good things stirs the mind with zeal to turn toward practicing them,
it is clear that the sight of their opposites also has the power to take the mind captive and draw it toward them.
Even if nothing further happens, and it merely throws a mind that was at rest into a struggle, this too is a great loss:
that someone should willingly be driven from peace into turmoil. Now, if that hardworking elder, one of the saints,
considered the sight of a male who resembled women harmful to the mind and damaging in the struggle,
when he once [?] came to one of the monasteries, who would be careless about other things,
when that blessed man would not even agree to enter it and pray? That wise elder reasoned discerningly:
“Even if the thought merely comes into my heart tonight, wherever I spend the night, that there is something like that here,
it is a great loss.” For this reason he did not enter. “I am not afraid, my sons,” he said.
“But why should I take on a needless battle?” That is, why should even memories of such things take the place of the purity of my practice?
For all those things that belong to this body, against which a person must struggle to guard himself—
the farther they are from him, the less struggle he has because of them.
Likewise, when they are near, however much he is guided toward good things by fear, their proximity excites him to make use of them.
We see many roots buried and sunk beneath the earth,
which in summertime, because of the strength of the sun and the intensity of the heat, are not even known to exist.
When drops of water reach them, along with the cooling influence of the air,
each one immediately begins to show its shoots from wherever it is buried. So you too should not suppose
that through the intense heat of ascetic discipline and the rays of the grace of stillness you are entirely at rest from the passions.
But if you come into contact with these things, then you see how each of them comes back to life,
and raises its head from its place—that is, if they catch even a faint scent of rest [?].
I have said these things to show that no one should feel secure until he dies and departs from this life,
and how much fleeing and keeping one's distance help us in our struggle.
We ought to fear encountering those things whose very memory secretly makes us ashamed.
Let us not trample on our conscience or scorn what reminds us. For let us test our body in a desolate and unproductive land,
training it in endurance. There is also another reason, greater than all the others:
as long as a person is not near the thing that causes his struggle, he is free from danger, even if he is worn down in his mind.
[?] When he is overcome by a thought, he is also drawn into putting it into practice because it is close at hand.
The student: When someone has cast off everything that hinders him and entered the arena,
what is the beginning of his struggle against sin, and where should he begin the battle? The teacher: This is known to everyone:
the labor of fasting comes before every struggle against sin and its desires,
especially for someone who fights against sin within himself. And the sign of hatred for sin and its desires
is seen in this among those who enter this invisible struggle: they begin with fasting,
and afterward, standing in prayer at night. Whoever loves the practice of fasting throughout his life
is a lover of chastity. For just as at the head of all the world's good things
and before all its shameful things come a satisfied stomach and the languor of sleep that incites one to an impure bed,
so fasting is the foundation of the beginning of God's holy way and of all the virtues,
together with radiant wakefulness in God's service, keeping the body [?] upright all night in opposition to the sweetness of sleep.
For fasting strengthens all the virtues. It is the beginning of the struggle, the crown of ascetics,
the beauty of virginity and holiness, the adornment of chastity, the beginning of the Christian way,
the parent of prayer, the fountain of gentleness, and the teacher of stillness. It precedes all good things.
For just as the enjoyment of light accompanies healthy eyes,
so the desire for prayer accompanies fasting practiced with discernment. For as soon as someone begins
to fast, his mind immediately begins to long for communion with God.
A fasting body cannot endure sleeping on its bed all night.
For fasting naturally encourages watchfulness toward God, not only by day but also by night.
For the empty body of someone who fasts does not grow very weary in its struggle with sleep.
And although his senses are weak, his mind is awake toward God in supplication.
For it is better to cease working because of the weakness caused by fasting than because of the heaviness caused by food.
But there is little need for us to recount the beauties of fasting.
Many of the teachers and fathers have spoken about the victories of fasting and the great beauties that shine forth from it.
And all the Scriptures make known the greatness of fasting and the victories it has achieved in every generation,
and the great help it provides, and the exalted glory of those who fast.
Everyone also knows from experience that it is the source of all good things.
As long as the seals of fasting are placed upon a person's mouth, his mind meditates on contrition of soul.
His heart stirs up prayers, and sorrow rests upon his face.
Ugly impulses are far from him. Cheerfulness is not seen at all upon his brow.
For it is an enemy of desires and idle thoughts [?].
No one who fasts with discernment has ever been seen enslaved by an ugly desire.
For it is the foundation of every virtue, and whoever despises it shakes all the virtues. For
the first commandment laid upon our nature in the beginning warned it about tasting food,
and through this the ancestor of our race fell. Therefore, at the very point where the first ruin occurred,
the athletes of the fear of God begin rebuilding, when they begin to observe his laws.
Our Savior too, when he was revealed to the world at the Jordan, began [?] with this.
“After he was baptized,” it says, “the Spirit led him out into the wilderness, and he fasted forty days and forty nights.”
And all who follow in his footsteps lay the beginning of their struggle upon this foundation.
It is a weapon forged by God. Who can despise it and remain free from blame? If the Lawgiver fasted,
who among those who observe the law has no need of it? Now, until that time the human race had not known victory,
nor had Satan ever experienced defeat at the hands of our nature; but through this weapon he was brought low by it from the outset.
And he was the firstborn of victory, to place the first crown on the head of our nature.
Whenever this weapon is seen on a person, terror immediately falls upon the thoughts of Satan, that leader of rebellion.
And immediately his mind is shaken by the memory of his condemnation in the wilderness and the first defeat that began there.
His strength is broken at the sight of the weapon that our commander placed in our hands.
As soon as he sees this weapon on a person, he immediately recognizes that the person is prepared for the contest.
What weapon is stronger than this and gives courage to the heart in the battle with evil spirits, as does
hunger for Christ’s sake? For the more a person is worn down and weakened in his body,
when Satan’s ranks surround him, the more firmly his heart rests in confidence.
Whoever constantly wears this weapon is always ablaze with zeal, as though with fire.
Constant fasting is a sign of zeal and shows fervor in battle.
Elijah, too, that zealous man, took this hardship upon himself when he burned with zeal for the divine law.
For forty days he kept his mouth from food during his long journey through the wilderness.
For it reminds whoever possesses it of the commandments of the Spirit.
For it is the mediator between the old law and this grace that we have received in our Lord Jesus.
Why should I dwell any further on its glories, which are known to everyone? Whoever despises this
is also weak and feeble in pursuing the other victories, because he does not wear the weapon
with which the divine athletes won their victories. From the very beginning, he shows a sign of cowardice in himself,
and he himself gives his opponent a means of defeating him, entering the contest unarmed.
It is clear that he will leave it without victory, because he has cast away the strength that stirs divine zeal within him,
and he enters the struggle coldly, not fervently.
For his limbs are not clothed in the flame of hunger—that is, of fasting—
through which the mind remains unshaken when confronted with every hardship and distress.
For it is also said of many of the holy martyrs
that, if they happened to learn beforehand of the day on which they were to receive the crown, through a revelation of the Spirit
or through one of their friends, they would taste nothing that night and would take no food.
Instead, from evening until morning they stood keeping vigil in prayer,
praising God with songs, praises, teaching hymns, and spiritual melodies.
They rejoiced and were glad as they awaited the hour, like people invited to enter a wedding feast.
They hoped to face the sword while fasting and to receive the crown of confessing the faith.
Let us too, my brothers, remain constantly in this state of readiness, for we are summoned to an unseen martyrdom,
so that we may receive the crown of holiness, lest through one of our bodily members a sign of [?] be given to our enemies.
Rather, let us put on the whole armor of God over our outward senses and our inward impulses,
so that we may earnestly receive this crown, enter his glory with the holy martyrs, and leave our enemies astonished.
For no one receives a crown without toil, as the great teacher Diodore said:
“It is clearly very shameful if merchants cannot secure wealth without toil and the storm of danger—
meager wealth—yet a righteous person expects the reward of a crown without hardship and without toil for righteousness.”
Student: Look, there are many who undertake these labors,
yet experience neither calm freedom from passions nor peace from thoughts. Teacher:
My brother, the hidden passions in the soul are not calmed merely by bodily labors performed in solitude.
Nor do these restrain the thoughts that are constantly stirred up by the senses.
These labors protect a person from desires, so that he is not overcome by them,
and from demons, so that they do not harm him in any way. But they do not also give peace and calm to the soul.
These labors give freedom from passions, put to death the earthly bodily members, and bring rest from thoughts only
when they are joined to stillness, when the outward senses themselves are also given rest from disturbance,
and time is devoted continually to the practice of wisdom. That is, until a person withdraws from encounters with other people,
keeps his bodily members from dissipation in many things, and gathers himself inward, he does not even become aware of his passions.
For stillness, as the blessed Basil, the shining lamp of the whole world, said,
“is the beginning of the soul’s purification.” For when the outward bodily members become quiet, away from external turmoil,
then the mind returns from distraction inward to its own place, and the heart is stirred to examine the soul’s inward movements.
And if a person perseveres well in this, through his discipline he reaches purity of soul. Student:
And can the soul not be purified through outward activity, if it makes a determined effort? Teacher: A tree that drinks every day—when
will its root dry up? And a vessel that receives an addition every day—when will its contents diminish? If purity is nothing other
than forgetting ways of life that lack freedom and finding peace from their memory,
yet this person renews their memory in his soul every day through his senses, whether by actually doing these things himself or through others,
that is, his knowledge of evil things, when will he be purified of them? Or when will he be free from the struggle with these outward things [?],
so that he can see and quiet those within? When the heart is defiled every day,
when will it be cleansed of its filth? Perhaps he cannot even resist the actual deed, let alone cleanse its root.
For he stands in the middle of the camp, and every day reports of battles pour into his ears.
How does he dare proclaim peace to his soul? But if he withdraws from these things, then he can gradually quiet those within.
Until a river is dammed upstream, its waters will not dry up downstream.
But when someone enters stillness, then the soul can distinguish the passions and examine the wisdom within it.
Then the inner person awakens to spiritual work, and day by day becomes aware of the hidden wisdom awakening in his soul.
Student: What are the sure indications and immediate signs
when, through a person's toil, the hidden fruits in the soul begin to appear? Teacher:
When he is deemed worthy of the gift of tears that flow abundantly and without being forced. Tears are set as a kind of boundary
for the mind, between the bodily and the spiritual, and between being subject to passions and purity.
For until he receives this gift, the toil of his work is still in the outer person.
And he has not become aware, even in the slightest, of the hidden work of the spiritual person.
But when he begins to leave behind the bodily life of this world
and crosses that boundary into what lies within this visible nature, he immediately attains this grace of tears.
These tears begin in the very first chamber of that hidden way of life, and they lead him all the way to the perfect love of God.
As he advances toward that, he becomes so rich in these tears that he drinks them with his food and drink, because they are so constant and abundant.
This is the sure indication that the mind has departed from this world and has become aware of that spiritual world.
The more he draws near to this world in his mind, the more these tears diminish.
And when his mind is entirely occupied with the things here, his tears also cease entirely.
And this is the sign of its hiddenness in the passions: some tears burn, and others anoint.
All tears that fall from repentance and from the heart’s distress over sins dry out the body and burn it.
Often a person even feels damage to the brain as they flow.
A person necessarily encounters this kind of tears first, and through them there is opened
for him a door to the second kind, which is far superior to this one and is a sign that mercy has been received.
What kind is this? Those that pour out from understanding anoint the body. They flow of their own accord, without any forcing.
They also nourish the body, and the appearance of the face changes.
For it is said, “A joyful heart makes the body beautiful.” They pour over the whole face while the mind is still.
The body receives something like nourishment from them, and gladness is imprinted on the face.

Let whoever has experienced these two different kinds understand.
Student.

What is the resurrection of the soul spoken of in the words, “If you have risen with Christ”?
Teacher.
It is what the apostle says elsewhere: “God, who said, ‘Let light shine out of darkness,’
will himself shine in your hearts.” He calls the departure from the old state “resurrection”—
that state which, like Sheol, is shut before a person’s face, preventing the light of the gospel from shining on him mystically,
the gospel which breathes life through the hope of the resurrection, through which the dawning light of divine wisdom shines in the heart.
The person is henceforth a new human being, with nothing in him belonging to the things of this world.
As it is said, “I will give them a new heart and a new spirit.”
Then Christ is truly formed in them through the spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him.

Student.
What, in brief, is the effective power of the practice of stillness?
Teacher.

It puts the outward senses to death and brings the inward movements to life. Outward activity, however, does the opposite.
Student.
What is the reason that some people experience visions and revelations, while others, though they labor harder than these,

do not experience such things?
Teacher.
There are many reasons for revelations and visions, not just one.
The first reason for revelations and visions is to demonstrate God’s compassion:
they are provided by him for the help [?] of human beings. Some also occur as part of his providential ordering.
This is general. The others, however, occur to strengthen and encourage the weak,
and to comfort them and teach them about God's plan, as with those who appeared beside the tomb,
and those who appeared to the apostles at the time of the ascension, when they were distressed, astonished, and filled with uncertainty
at our Lord's departure from them. Immediately two angels appeared beside them, standing in white clothing.
And likewise in prison and in various places, when they fell into human hands.
They also appear to individuals, as to the other saints who came after them, even down to the present day.
Such events are arranged, for the most part, for these three kinds of people:
either those who are exceptionally simple and innocent, or holy and perfected people,
or those who, in burning zeal and with all hope cut off, leave the world and abandon it
completely, and withdraw far from every human settlement,
and go out after God stripped of everything, without hope or help from anything visible.
Fear arising from their isolation comes upon them, or the danger of death surrounds them,
whether from hunger, illness, or one of those other afflictions, and they are close to despair.
As for the fact that some people receive comforts like these, while others who surpass them in their labors
experience nothing of the kind, the first reason is purity and impurity—
of conscience, I mean. The second reason, which is certainly true, is this:
as long as someone has comfort from other people, or from any of these visible things,
comforts like these do not come to him, except as a matter of providence. This is the general rule.
Our discussion, however, concerns solitaries. A witness to this is one of the saints who had lost hope about this.
A voice came to him, saying, “The comfort and company of other people are enough for you.”
Another likewise pleaded with God. While he was living a solitary life and following the practices of solitude,
he constantly enjoyed the comforts that come from grace,
and divine care continually revealed itself to him in a clearly perceptible way.
But when he came near the inhabited world, he sought these same things as usual and did not find them.
He implored God to make known to him the truth of the matter, saying, “My Lord, is it perhaps because of the episcopate that you have withdrawn?”
grace from me. And he was told, “No. But at that time it was a desert.”
There were no people, and God was taking care of you.
But now the world is inhabited, and people take care of you.

That is to say, a person cannot share in spiritual consolation together with visible consolation.
Student.

Are vision and revelation one and the same, or do they differ in their workings just as they differ in name?
Teacher.
There is a distinction between vision and revelation. Although the term “revelation” applies to both,
since something hidden is being revealed—something that was previously hidden and has now come to light in one of these ways—
nevertheless, not everything that is a revelation is also a vision. Everything that is a vision is also called a revelation,
because something hidden is being revealed. But not everything that comes to light and becomes known takes place in a vision.
The term “revelation” is generally applied to things that become known and are tasted in the mind.
Vision, however, always takes place through images, as in the experiences of people of old:
as in some kind of trance [?], during sleep [?] or wakefulness [?], sometimes distinctly and sometimes indistinctly.
The person to whom the vision comes often does not know whether he is seeing it while awake or asleep.
Even after coming to himself, he does not know whether the event actually took place or was like a dream.
Sometimes a voice offering help is heard, and sometimes there is a symbol
of some kind. Sometimes it happens clearly and face to face, with seeing, speaking, questions, and conversation.
These are holy powers who appear to those who are worthy.
It is clear that things like these happen in the desert, in desolate country, in isolated places, and in withdrawal [?] from the world,
where a person also has an urgent need for them, since he has no help from anywhere else.
But revelations of things perceived through understanding are received through purity,

and only by people who possess knowledge and are perfect.
Student.

If someone reaches purity of heart, what is its sign? When will he himself know whether his heart has attained purity?
Teacher.
When he sees all people as good, and no one appears to him unclean or defiled,
he truly stands in purity. Otherwise, how can he fulfill the apostle’s saying,
that even when a person possesses every virtue, he should sincerely and from the heart consider everyone better than himself?
Unless he reaches the state spoken of: “His eyes are pure; he does not see evil.”
Student: What is purity, and how far does its boundary extend? Teacher:
Purity is understood to be the forgetting of the forms of knowledge that are outside nature,
which nature acquired in the world. Its boundary is that this nature should be entirely freed from them,
so that it comes to nature’s original simplicity and innocence, like a little child, apart from minor things
alone. Student: Can a person attain this state? Teacher: Yes.
Indeed, one of the elders reached this point, so that he would even continually ask his disciple whether he had eaten bread or not.
And one of the saints, a certain very old man in former times, became so thoroughly purified and simple,
and attained such innocence and serenity, that he was almost like an infant in his forgetfulness of the things of this world.
Perhaps many will not believe what we are saying, for it is truly a marvel.
Even at the time of the mysteries, he did not know how to observe the restraint required to receive the mysteries, or whether he had observed it or not,
so that his disciples would watch over him in his cell and bring him to Holy Communion,
as though he were a little child. That blessed man had become so thoroughly serene and simple.
Yet although he was like this concerning the things of this world, in his soul he was perfect toward God. Student:
What meditation and occupation should a person have in his seclusion and stillness,
so that his mind is not occupied with distracting thoughts? Teacher:
You are asking what meditation someone who is dead to the world should have in his cell? Does a person who is diligent and whose soul is watchful
need to ask what work he should have when he is alone?
What is a solitary’s meditation in his cell except weeping? Does he have enough of weeping that he can turn to another thought? What meditation is better than this?
His very dwelling, solitary and isolated like a tomb, silent amid all the world’s delights, teaches him
that his work consists in weeping. Even the title by which he is known urges him toward this.
For he is called a mourner, that is, one whose heart is bitter. For all the righteous departed from this world in weeping.
If the saints wept, and their mouths were always filled with their tears,
and they departed from this world in this way, who should not weep? A solitary’s consolation is born of weeping.
But if those who were [?] shed tears here, what of the one who is full of wounds?
How can the master of a household bear to stop weeping when his loved one lies wounded before him [?]?
Does he need instruction about what thought will stir him to weep? Your soul lies before you, wounded by sins,
and it is worth more to you than the whole world. But if we enter into stillness, we can also persevere in weeping.
Therefore let us ask our Lord with earnest intent [?] to grant us this.
If we receive this gift, which surpasses all others, through weeping itself we enter into purity.
Once we have entered there, it is no longer taken from us, until the day of our departure from the world.
Blessed, then, are the pure in heart, for there is no time when they do not delight in this sweetness of tears.
Through it they continually see our Lord. With tears in their eyes, they are deemed worthy to behold his revelation
at the height of prayer. For they have no prayer without tears. This is what our Lord said:
"Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted." It is through mourning, that is, that a person comes to purity of soul.
Therefore, when our Life-giver said, "Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted," he did not explain what kind of comfort.
When the solitary is deemed worthy, through mourning, to pass through this region of the passions
and reach that plain of purity of soul, where he encounters the comfort that never leaves those who have found it here,
then he understands that our Lord invited those who mourn to this comfort, which is received through purity at the completion of mourning.
For no one weeps continually while the passions remain close to his heart, because weeping lies beyond subjection to the passions.
And if, for someone who mourns and weeps for a time, tears can wipe the memory of the passions from the mind,
what shall we say of someone who has made this his regular practice night and day? Who knows the help that comes from weeping,
except those who have devoted themselves to it? All the saints long for this entrance.
Through weeping the door is opened before them, so that they may enter that region of comforts,

where the traces of God's love are marked out through revelations.
The student.
But since a person cannot sustain this constancy because of the weakness of bodily nature,
he ought also to have something else after this, something suitable for occupying his mind, so that

the passions do not attack him through the idleness of his understanding.
The teacher.
The passions cannot attack the soul and disturb the solitary whose heart is cut off from the world in a solitary dwelling,
amid all that stillness of the wilderness, sheltered from all the noises and sounds of the world's turmoil, unless he neglects his duties.
Especially when he engages with the Scriptures and the helpful thoughts with which he occupies himself:
through the excellence of contemplating their meanings, trivial thoughts are driven from his company,
so that his mind cannot break away from them and turn its attention toward the world as a whole,
because of the great delight of that meditation through which the mind is lifted up as though intoxicated in the vast solitude of the wilderness.
He forgets himself and becomes oblivious to his own nature. He becomes like someone who has lost his senses and does not remember the world at all.
And still more so when he reflects and considers in his mind the greatness of God, the glory of his nature,
the wonder of his works, and also the insignificance of his own person, and how high he has been raised:
on whom he may meditate, and what thoughts he may dare to take into his soul for his delight,
so that he may always be intoxicated by the wonder of his inner stirrings, as in that way of life after the resurrection.
For stillness greatly assists this, since the mind has room to dwell within itself in the peace that stillness provides it.
At the same time, it is stirred from here through recollection, in keeping with the aim of its way of life,
and takes into its thought the glories of the world to come, the hope reserved for the righteous,
those lives stirred by the Spirit and awake in God
in their entirety—that new way of life, without remembrance or stirring concerning the things here.
When he has become intoxicated with these things, he again moves from there in his contemplation toward the things of this world, in which he still lives,
saying reflectively, “Oh, the depth of the riches [?], wisdom, knowledge, and unfathomable understanding of God!
No one can probe his judgments, and his ways cannot be traced! Although he had prepared another world so wonderful,
into which he would bring all rational beings and preserve them without change in life without end,
what, then, is the reason he made this one first, expanding and enriching it with such a great abundance of created natures,
and placing many sufferings in it? He placed us first in this world and fixed in our nature a great love for its life,
yet he removes us from it little by little through death and keeps us for no short time without sensation, like stones and pieces of wood.
He destroys our forms, pours out our bodily composition, and mingles it with the earth.
He allows our structure to be dismantled and collapse until it loses every semblance of an organized body.
Then, at the time appointed by his wisdom, whenever he wills,
he raises us in another form that he knows and brings us into that other constitution.”
And not only for us, but also for the holy angels, who have no need to make use of this world. Because of the wonderful character
of their nature, though they stand only a little short of perfection, they all await our rising to life and the resurrection of our corruptible bodies.
They await the time when the human race will rise from the dust, stir, and pass from corruption into renewal.
For our sake they are kept from entering, so that the gate of that new world which they await may be opened to all at once.
For the angelic creation itself groans with us because of the burden of the body in which it sees us living,
and hopes and waits for the revelation of the children of God,
so that it too may be freed from slavery to corruption into the glorious freedom of the children of God.
First he tears down this world in its entire structure and dissolves it into nothing, just as he does the original structure of our body.
Then he rises in his mind beyond the beginning of the world's existence, to when there was no creation and nothing existed:
no heaven, no earth, no angels, and none of the things that came into being.
And he considers how God suddenly brought them all into being, when merely willing it was enough for him.
And everything stood before him complete. Then he descends in his thought, passing over all God's creatures,
and contemplates his lofty and astonishing works, and the wisdom of his creative power within them;
his providence, which instructs every mind; the wonderful and all-capable power of his workmanship;
the creation that he brought into being from nothing, with its countless different varieties;
and how he is going to dissolve this creation once again, removing it from this wonderful order,
from this adornment of natural things, from this orderly course of creatures:
the times and seasons, the harmony of night and day, the beneficial changes of the year, the earth's adornment,
the varied kinds of things that come from it, the finely constructed buildings of cities, and the splendid citadels within them;
the ceaseless activity of human beings, a nature that toils and wears itself out
from the time it enters this world until it leaves it; and how this astonishing order suddenly comes to an end,
and another world comes, in which no memory whatsoever of this first creation enters anyone's mind.
There will be another way of life, other thoughts, and another meditation. And again:
human nature will not remember this world or its former way of life in it.
For the gaze of their minds will be held fast by the vision of that new order.
And he can no longer turn his thoughts back to the generations of flesh and blood.
For at the very moment when this one dissolves, that one begins.
O mother, suddenly forgotten by the children whom she bore, nourished, and taught!
In the blink of an eye they are carried off to another bosom and become true children of that barren woman who has never given birth.
“Rejoice,” it says, “you barren woman who does not give birth, in the children whom the earth has borne for you.”
And in his amazement he reflects: “Will this one really rise again after this?
And when will that beginning take place? How long will these bodies sleep in this way,
with bodily substance and dust mingled together? How will that way of life be? In what form will this nature rise,
and in what manner will it come to a second creation?” Amid these thoughts and others like them, stillness falls upon him, and all
awareness of his bodily existence is stolen away. He remains silent for a long time, marveling at God's incomprehensible deeds.
At that moment he rises, kneels, and offers thanksgiving with many tears to God, who is wise in his works,
whose deeds cannot be comprehended, nor the hidden purposes of his glorious mind in what he has done and what he is yet to do.
What heart of stone would not become as though lifeless at these stirrings, with silence and astonishment falling upon it,
and be drawn away from every activity of the senses and every inner movement? Blessed is the person who has been found worthy of these things!
Blessed is the person whose meditation this has become, night and day! Blessed is the person who has occupied himself with these things throughout his life!
This reflection is fitting for everyone, and especially for anyone who lives in stillness.
He ought to persevere in meditating on these things at all times.
A person must take these images into his mind, and when he has finished praying,
he should reflect and meditate on them. With these subjects occupying him and with this meditation,
there will be no room within his mind for an alien thought to distract him from the constant remembrance of God.
And if, at first, because of his distraction, he does not feel the helping power that comes from these things, he should not lose heart.
When a farmer casts seed into his field, he does not immediately see the shoot at the very moment he sows the seed.
Sowing is accompanied by discouragement and anguish.
But the laborer finds delight when he eats his bread, and his sweat is all the sweeter to him. This meditation, however, amid
safeguarded stillness, pours boundless sweetness into the heart.
And it readily draws the mind toward inexpressible wonder.
Blessed is the person before whom this spring has opened, and who drinks from it at every hour of night and day!
Student: What encompasses all the labors of this way of life, so that when someone reaches it,
he knows that he has reached the goal of this way of life [?]? Teacher: When he is found worthy of unceasing prayer.
When he reaches this, he has arrived at the goal of all the virtues, for from then on he has become a dwelling place of the Spirit.
Unless someone has truly received the gift [?] of the Paraclete, it is not possible for him to achieve this constancy in prayer with ease.
For when the Spirit dwells in a person, the Spirit does not cease from prayer: the Spirit himself prays continually.
Then, whether he is asleep or awake, prayer does not cease within his soul.
Rather, whether he eats or drinks, whether he sleeps or attends to some task, and even when he is sunk in sleep,
the fragrances of prayer spread within his heart without effort. Then his prayer is no longer confined to set limits,
but continues at all times. Even when he is outwardly silent, prayer itself is being offered in his hidden depths.
“The silence of the pure is prayer,” says someone clothed in Christ [?], “because their thoughts are divine stirrings.”
“The flutterings of a pure mind are quiet voices with which they secretly sing to the Hidden One.”
Student: What is spiritual prayer, and how can someone be found worthy of it? Teacher:
It consists of stirrings of the soul that share in the activity of the Holy Spirit through complete purity.
Only one person in ten thousand is found worthy of this. It is a mystery of the life of the world to come.
For human nature is raised above every stirring of remembrance of the things of this world and rests from them.
The soul is not actually praying; rather, it is perceiving the spiritual realities of that world,
something beyond human thought. Understanding of those realities is stirred within the person by the power of the Spirit.
It is a vision of the mind, not the movement and petition of prayer, though it takes its beginning from prayer.
For people like these have already reached the height of purity.
There is no time when their inward stirrings are not awake in prayer, as I said above.
Whenever the Spirit looks upon them, he finds them at prayer.
From prayer he leads them through contemplation, which is interpreted as spiritual vision.
It is not that they need prolonged prayer or a prescribed sequence of lengthy worship.
For them, the mere remembrance of God is enough, and immediately they are carried away by love as though into captivity.
Yet they do not entirely neglect standing during prayer, giving prayer its due honor
by standing on their feet at appointed times, apart from their continual prayer.
For we see that Saint Anthony, while standing on his feet at the prayer of the ninth
hour, felt his mind being lifted up. And another of the saints,
while standing in prayer with his hands outstretched, remained in a state of wonder for four days.
There are also many others whom anyone who wishes can find in the accounts of their lives,
who were found in the prescribed posture of prayer when they received such a gift.
A person is deemed worthy of this when he strips away sin, outwardly and inwardly,
by keeping our Lord’s commandments, which are laid down to oppose it.
If someone practices these in their proper order, he is necessarily compelled to go beyond all human activities as well.
That is, to strip off the body and be outside it, so to speak—not outside its nature, but outside its use.
No one has practiced these according to the [?] of the one who prescribed them, and yet had sin persist in remaining with him.
For this reason, our Lord also promised in the Gospel to make the person who keeps them his dwelling. Student.
And what is the culmination of all the fruits of the Spirit? Teacher. When a person is deemed worthy of the perfect love of God.
Student. And how can someone who has reached this be recognized? Teacher.
Whenever the remembrance of God is stirred in his mind, his heart immediately burns with love for him.
And his eyes pour down tears abundantly. For love naturally brings forth tears at the remembrance of the beloved.
Someone in this condition never has a time free from tears,
because he never lacks material for the remembrance of tears. Because he never lacks material for the remembrance
of God, so that even in sleep he speaks with him.
Love naturally does these things. And this is a human being’s perfection in this life. Student.
When, after much labor and hardship and the victories he has diligently achieved, someone is assailed by the thought of pride,
which draws its material from the beauty of his virtue and brings to mind the many labors he has endured,
how can he restrain his thoughts and make himself watchful so that he does not yield to it? Teacher.
When he knows that he falls away from God like a dry leaf falling from a tree, then he knows his own strength:
whether he acquired these virtues by his own strength and endured all these struggles for their sake.
If the Lord withdraws his help from him and sends him alone into battle with Satan,
without that power which accompanies the victorious in their struggles coming down with him as usual,
then his strength is revealed—or rather, his weakness.
For there is [?] God's providence over a person, which always guards and strengthens him.
Through it people of every rank are victorious, whether in the struggle for chastity,
or in the suffering of martyrdom, or in all the other hardships they endure for the sake of these divine things.
This is clearly known, and there is no doubt about it.
For how can human nature overcome all the force of the unceasing impulses lodged in its limbs,
which buffet it, and withstand them? And how is it that others, although they love and long for purity,
cannot achieve this, even though they struggle intensely,
but are defeated by nature every day, battered, mourning, and weeping over themselves,
while you easily bear the hardships of nature, harsh as they are, without being greatly distressed? Or how could another person,
in flesh subject to suffering, encounter cutting with iron blades and combs over all his limbs,
and every kind of torture, without being overcome by the pain—someone who cannot endure even a little thorn piercing his fingernail—
and endure all this variety of tortures without suffering as nature ordinarily does,
unless he had another power, beyond that of nature, coming from elsewhere,
which holds the pain back from him and dulls the force of the tortures?
For nothing prevents us from setting down a story here as well, whose subject is truly a marvel to those who hear it.
Since we have brought up the subject of God's providence toward humanity,
which makes a person victorious in every struggle for virtue, we should not pass over this story.
Socrates the historian, in the account of church history that he wrote,
when recounting the Roman emperors and reaching the emperor Julian,
briefly describes the evils that the members of the Church suffered and proceeds a little further in his account:
He related one of the stories of what happened in Antioch
the city. Now a certain youth named Theodore, he said,
who had been brought by the pagans before Sallustius, who had been put in charge of this matter, was handed over by him to suffering and torture.
He ordered his whole body to be scraped, and then stopped torturing him, supposing that he would no longer live.
But God was that blessed man's deliverer, for he lived a long time after that confession of faith.
Rufinus, who wrote the Ecclesiastical History in Latin, said of this Theodore
that a long time afterward he had conversed with this blessed Theodore.
He asked him whether he had felt great pain while he was being beaten.
He reportedly answered him that he had felt only a very little of the suffering.
For a young man had stood beside him and wiped away the sweat of his struggle,
strengthening his soul and giving him relief during the struggle of his tortures.
Oh, the mercy of God! How near his grace is
to those who enter the struggle for his sake, to endure suffering gladly on his behalf!
Do not deny God's grace toward you, O human being.
But if it is therefore clear that you are not the victor, but are like an instrument,
and that it is the Lord who wins the victory on your behalf, while you receive the title of victor as a free gift,
what prevents you from always asking him for that same strength,
so that you may always receive those same victories while acknowledging this? Have you not
heard, O man, from the beginning and from ancient times,
how many athletes have fallen from the height of their victories because they denied this? On the subject.
Although God's gifts to the human race are many and varied,
there are differences among them according to their recipients, and there are lesser and greater gifts.
Although they are all wonderful and glorious, one surpasses another in glory and honor.
And one rank is higher than another, according to the word of Scripture.
This too—that someone should be set apart for doing good and for upright conduct—is one of Christ's foremost gifts.
For many forget this grace: that they were considered worthy for God to make a distinction between them and the rest of humanity,
and for them to become recipients of his gifts—all this to the point that they are even chosen for the Lord’s service.
Instead of keeping thanksgiving continually on their lips for this, they have turned toward arrogance
and become proud in their thinking, not behaving as recipients of grace
in having been considered worthy to serve God through pure conduct and spiritual labors.
Rather, they think of themselves as though they were bestowing a favor on God himself by this,
in return for having been chosen from the rest of humanity to belong to his household and to know his mysteries.
They do not even tremble with their whole souls when they entertain these thoughts,
although they have seen what happened to their companions who thought these things: how there was taken away from them
suddenly that power which had been entrusted with their protection, and in the blink of an eye they were cast down from the great honor they had possessed.
They suddenly turned toward recklessness and reverted to the shameful behavior of irrational animals.
Because they failed to recognize the strength of their own souls and to remember continually the one who had deemed them worthy of all this greatness—to serve him
and to share in the honor of his kingdom, making them companions of spiritual beings
and bringing them close to the way of life of the angels—he dismissed them from their service.
Through the sudden changes in their conduct, he showed them
that it was not within their own power to persevere in upright conduct amid all that pressure from nature, demons, and all the other opposing forces.
Rather, it was the [?] of the gift that came from him.
For what the rest of humanity could not even bear to hear about because of its difficulty, they endured for a long time without growing faint,
because that power which accompanied them was sufficient to help them in everything and to protect them in everything.
Therefore, when they forgot this, the saying was fulfilled in them: “Because they did not see fit to acknowledge God”—
that is, their Lord, who brought dust near to the service of spiritual beings—“God handed them over to a worthless mind.”

And they received in their own persons the recompense their error deserved.
Student.
Is there anyone who ventures, so to speak, to leave human habitation all at once and suddenly goes out like Adam into a wilderness
that is uninhabited, into a terrifying wasteland, out of noble zeal, and because of this immediately dies of hunger—

that is, also from the lack of shelter and the other necessities?
Teacher.
For he who prepared a dwelling for the animals before creating them, and provides for their needs, does not neglect those who fear him.
Especially those who followed him in simplicity and without preparation. Whoever surrenders his will to God in everything
never considers remaining in filthy conduct because of the body's sufferings and its fear,
or enduring a degraded life because he shrinks from afflictions.
Instead, he considers this preferable and pleasant: that, estranged from the whole world through purity of conduct,
he should wander among hills and mountains and roam where wild animals live, rather than live at ease in a body full of filth,
subjecting himself to continual death arising from the holiness of pure conduct toward God.
To him be glory and honor. May he preserve us in his holiness and sanctify us by his Spirit for the honor of his name,
so that we may praise him purely all the days of our lives. Amen.
For one of the saints said, “The body becomes sin's [?].”
For the Spirit of God presses it in this way to die. It is well known that unless it dies, it does not overcome sin.
“But whoever wishes our Lord to dwell in him,” he says, “disciplines his body and serves our Lord with those fruits of the Spirit that are written about in the Apostle,
and guards himself against those works of the flesh that Paul described.” But the body in which sin is mingled
finds its rest in the works of the flesh, while the Spirit of God finds her rest in her fruits.
For, he says, when the body is weakened by fasting and humiliations, the soul is strong—the soul [?] in spirit, in prayer.
The body is accustomed, when it is severely pressed by the hardships of solitude and deprivation,
and its life is close to being lost, to plead with you: “Ease up on me a little, so that I may be disciplined in moderation.
Now I am setting myself right, since I have experienced such sufferings.”
And when you have relieved it a little of its hardship and supported it with a little rest because you pitied it,
and it has recovered a little, then it whispers gently to you, little by little, that we should also leave the wilderness.
Its persuasions are very powerful: “From now on,” it says, “we can conduct ourselves well even near inhabited places.
For we have been tested in many things, and we can follow these same practices there.
Just put me to the test,” it says, “and if I do not act as you wish, we can come back again. Look, the desert is before us.”
Do not believe it, even if it pleads earnestly and makes promises, because it does not carry them out.
For once you have given it the little that it asked for, it pushes you into greater things from which you will no longer escape.
Whenever you lose heart under afflictions because you have had enough of them, say to yourself: “You are longing for that impurity and a life stained with sin.”
And if he tells you that it is a great sin, since you are killing yourself,
tell him: “I am killing myself because I cannot live purely.
I will die here and never again see the dreadful death of my soul that comes from God. It is better for me
to die here for the sake of purity than to live an evil life in the world. I have chosen this death [?] for my sins.
I am killing myself because I have sinned against God, and I will not anger him again.
What use to me is a life far from God? I endure these hardships,
and because of them I will not become a stranger to that heavenly hope. Why was I created in the world,
if I entered it and leave it to no purpose? And what benefit does God gain from my life in the world,
if I live wickedly in it? On the contrary, I am only provoking him to anger!”
On the different ways Satan wages war against those who travel the narrow path above the world. 36.
Our enemy Satan also has other practices:
he cunningly arranges his battle lines against those who enter this contest.
From examining their dispositions, and according to each person's purpose, he changes the manner of his struggle.
With those whom he sees to have a slack will and weak thoughts,
he fights fiercely from the very beginning, stirring up powerful and terrifying trials against them,
so that he may overwhelm them with the forms of his wickedness at the very beginning of the path.
In this way, by instilling terror in them from the very first contest,
he makes this path seem difficult for them to travel. They say: “Since its beginning is so difficult and harsh, who can endure
to its end and face all the contests arrayed along the way?”
They no longer dare to stand before him or turn their attention to anything else, because of the force of their anxiety about these things he does.
And when he presses his assault against them a little, they take to flight.
Indeed, God himself allows him to gain power over them, giving them no help,
