because they enter the Lord's contest halfheartedly and with hesitation.
For it says: “Cursed is everyone who does the Lord's work carelessly and keeps his hand from blood.”
And again: “His help is near to those who fear him.” And he commands them not to face the adversary halfheartedly and fearfully.
“Begin,” he says, “to destroy him, and engage him in battle.
And I will begin to put fear and dread of you upon all the peoples under heaven.”
Unless you willingly die a death perceptible to the senses for the love of God,
you will unwillingly die a death perceived by the mind, which comes from God.
Do not shrink from willingly accepting what is your allotted share through suffering that lasts for a time, and from entering into the glory of God.
But if you die bodily in the Lord’s contest, the Lord himself will crown you.
And he will bestow on your victorious bones the honor of the martyrs. Therefore, as I said above,
when people have not prepared themselves from the beginning, taken courage, and given themselves over to death, they consequently prove weak in all their battles.
This is especially so when God also leaves them to be pursued, because
they try to carry out the Lord’s work as though in mockery and as an experiment.
For Satan himself has known them from the beginning and has examined their thoughts to discover what they are like.
That is, they are fearful and love their own lives, or rather, they are protective of their bodies; and he pursues them like a whirlwind.
For he does not see with them that awe-inspiring power that he usually sees with the victorious.
For in proportion to a person’s willingness toward God and love of hardships endured for his sake,
God brings his help near to that person and shows his providential care for him.
For Satan cannot approach anyone or bring a trial upon him unless that heavenly command has left him unprotected,
or unless he has willingly grown slack and given himself over to ugly, wandering thoughts, or has become arrogant, or has fallen into doubt.
But Satan does not ask to test people like these as he does mature and great people.
For he knows that they are not even handed over to him. For God knows that they cannot cope, unless they are handed over to him.
For God knows that they cannot cope, except through one of these causes that I mentioned,
when the power of God’s providential care withdraws from them. This is one form of the adversary’s warfare.
But those whose resolve he sees to be courageous, and in whose eyes death counts as nothing,
who have gone out with fierce zeal, surrendering themselves to every trial and to death, and have trampled on life, the world, the body, and its temptations—
these he generally does not immediately confront or reveal himself to. Instead, he holds himself back.
And he gives them room. He does not confront them in that first onrush or draw up his battle line against them.
For he knows that the beginning of a battle is usually fierce, and the contestant is full of zeal.
Zealous fighters are not easily defeated. He does not do this because he is afraid of them,
but because of that divine power which sets them ablaze through the resources they carry,
until they themselves, of their own will, gradually cast it away as they grow self-confident.
Instead, he leaves them alone for a considerable time, until their zeal grows dull and the readiness of the weapons they have prepared, with which they armed their minds, falls into disarray:
the various divine sayings and the helpful, strengthening recollections. Meanwhile, he watches for a time of carelessness.
Once their initial thoughts have lost a little of their vigor, how often they themselves discover occasions for condemnation within themselves,
through enticements that spring from their own minds. They themselves dig a pit for themselves,
through the distraction of thoughts born in their minds from listlessness, through which coldness has come to rule over them.
It is not of his own free will that Satan does this, delaying the time of combat.
It is neither because he pities them nor because he fears them: they count as nothing in his eyes.
But I think that a certain power surrounds those who are ablaze with fervor toward God
and have set out in childlike simplicity, without a thought, trusting in him through faith, not knowing against
whom they must fight. For this reason he restrains his evil impulse toward them, so that it does not approach them.
For his impulse is bridled by that guardian whom he constantly sees beside them.
If, however, they do not cast away the means of receiving help—supplication, toil, and humility—
their helper never withdraws from them. But love of comfort is a cause of abandonment.
If they persevere diligently in these things, they are never stripped of help.
The enemy is not allowed to approach them. And if they are abandoned from time to time, it is for training,
while that holy power holds them firmly, and they are not afraid of those who tempt them.
For their mind takes courage and scorns them because of that power.
It trains them like someone teaching a small child to swim. When he begins to sink, the teacher lifts him up.
For the child floats above his teacher’s hands. And whenever the child begins to lose heart, afraid that he will sink,
the one holding him in his hands calls to him, “Do not be afraid; I am holding you.”
And again, like a mother teaching her little son to walk, who sets him at a distance from herself and calls him,
when the child begins to come toward his mother on those little, unsteady feet of his,
they tremble because of their weakness. And when the child begins to fall, his mother runs and takes him up in her arms.
In this way God's grace carries and trains human beings:
those who sincerely and simply entrust themselves into the hands of the one who created them,
leave this world with all their heart and follow him.
But you, a human being who has set out to follow God, throughout the whole time of your struggle,
keep constantly remembering the beginning, and that first zeal with which you entered the race,
and that burning resolve with which you left your former way of life and enlisted in the ranks for battle.
Examine yourself every day, to see whether your soul's fervor has cooled from that zeal with which you once burned.
See whether you lack any of the armor with which you were equipped at the beginning of your struggle.
Continually raise your voice within the camp, and encourage the thoughts within you that belong to the right side.
And show those on the opposing side that you are alert.
And if, at the beginning, you see the tempter stirring up a violent assault, do not lose heart. Perhaps this is what will help you.
Your Savior does not allow anything to happen to you without a purpose, but only after considering it and arranging it for your benefit.
Do not show weakness at the very beginning, lest, by showing weakness here,
you become unable to [?] before the other things that follow: hunger, sickness, terrifying visions, and the rest.
Do not turn the purpose of the one who appoints your struggle, which is directed toward helping you, over to the opposing side, lest
your enemy find you just as he hopes. Instead, call upon God without ceasing,
and weep before his grace. Beg and plead insistently until he sends you a helper.
But if you once see that Savior beside you—these are the two kinds of combat discussed up to this point.
Another purpose of Satan's combat against the resolute. So when, after all these things,
Satan stands in battle against someone and cannot match his strength in the struggle—or rather, the strength of the helper who helps him,
because of whom the man rises above him, while this helper continually helps and strengthens him,
so that one who is solid flesh and body may defeat an incorporeal spirit.
When Satan saw all this help that the man had received from God,
and that his outward senses were not overcome by sights and sounds, nor his thoughts weakened by enticements and seductions,
and perhaps he even scorned the blows they inflicted, he now wanted to find a way to separate him from the angel who helped him.
Rather, he wanted to blind the mind of the man receiving help, so that he would be left without assistance.
He stirred up presumptuous thoughts in him: that it was the strength
of his own mind that accounted for all this steadfastness and the glorious wealth he possessed in his soul.
As for his protection from all these hideous, unspeakable, bloodthirsty adversaries, sometimes
he attributed it to chance, and sometimes to their weakness.
I pass over other things too, the mere remembrance of which makes the soul shudder as though at blasphemy.
Sometimes he also introduces falsehoods in the guise of revelations from God.
Through sleep he reveals things to him, and again, when he is awake, he appears to him as an angel of light.
All this is so that, if possible, he might yield to them even a little and thus fall into their hands.
But if that wise man keeps careful control of his thoughts, especially with God helping him,
and fixes his heart’s gaze on heaven so as not to attend to their whisperings, the enemy devises yet another stratagem:
another turn in the battle. This one alone is now left to him, since it also has an affinity with human nature.
That is why he has all the greater expectation of making the man stumble.
What is this? He contrives by every means to bring him into contact with those things
through which he has so often defeated him because of his nature.
For the mind engaged in the struggle is blinded by the sight and proximity of these things,
and is easily defeated in the contest when it encounters them,
especially when they are set before its eyes. The cunning one has acquired a thorough knowledge of this art
through his experience with many steadfast contestants whom he brought down by it. For this reason, this too
he cunningly arranges. And if he cannot bring it about in actual circumstances because of the strictness of the man’s solitude
and because his dwelling place is far from occasions of temptation, he strives to conjure these things up before him, even through hallucinations.
He shows him unreal images in the guise of reality, so that he may become engrossed in looking at them and be stirred up.
and entertain shameful thoughts about them in his mind, and become guilty, and drive away from himself the one who helps him.
For he knows that his victory and his condemnation, his treasure and his help, and everything belonging to the solitary depend on thought.
And that it takes only a slight gesture for the mind to be moved from its place,
and to fall to the ground from that lofty height of life, and to show its consent by a momentary gesture.
Thus he showed many of the saints images of a beautiful woman.
As for those whose dwellings were near an inhabited place, a parasang or two away, or as far as a day's journey,
he contrived to bring an actual woman to them.
But to those for whom he could not do this because their dwellings were far away, he showed images of a woman's beauty.
Sometimes he appears to them with adornment, splendid clothes, and a wanton appearance, and sometimes even in the guise of a [?] woman.
Through these things and others like them, he overcame some of them: some in the actual deed,
while others were made fools of through apparitions because of the weakness of their thoughts, and descended into the depths of despair.
They turned toward the world and cast themselves away from heavenly hope. But others, who were steadfast
and enlightened by grace, overcame him and his enticements.
They trampled on bodily pleasures and were found approved in their love for God.
And many times, apparitions of gold and precious objects too,
as though they were treasures buried somewhere, he conjures up before them. Sometimes he even shows them these things in reality.
Thus, through one of these different means, he may perhaps be able to hinder one of them and make him stop running,
as he becomes entangled in one of these snares laid to catch him. Do not bring me, Lord, into these trials.
For even the strong and the chosen scarcely pass through this gate victorious.
The tempter is permitted to bring all these things against the saints as temptations, so that their love for God may be tested through them:
whether it is because these things are removed and far away and unavailable that they love God and remain in his love,
or whether they truly love God himself, and even when these things are present and available,
they struggle and despise them for his sake, and are not overcome and do not exchange their love for him for the things that entice them.
It is not so that they may become known to God himself through these things, but to the devil, who is very eager
to learn these things, if indeed he could. Thus he also spoke about Job and made a request concerning him to God:
“Does Job fear God for nothing?” he says. Then there is a slight withdrawal of care,
and the tempter approaches with authority, in proportion to their measure. Then
the wicked one gloats, as he desires to do in these circumstances. Through these things, those who are steadfast in God's love are tested: they despise all these things,
and these things count as nothing in their eyes compared with the love of God, while they remain humble
and attribute the victory to him who strengthens everyone and is the cause of their victory. They entrust the struggle into his hands:
“You are the mighty one, and the struggle is yours. Fight and win it for us, Lord.”
Then through these things they are tested like gold in a furnace.
But those who are counterfeit are exposed there by these tests and thrown out like refuse,
as they surrender to their adversary and leave the struggle defeated because of the weakness of their resolve,
or else because of their pride, since they were not worthy of that mighty power which is always with the holy ones to help them.
For the power of our helper does not fail. He is strong in everything, capable of everything, and always victorious in the bodies of those who resemble him,
whenever he goes down into battle with them. But it is clear that those who are defeated are defeated without him.
These are the ones who, by their own choice, are stripped of him because of their wrongdoing, being unworthy of that power which helps the victorious.
At those very times of battle, they also perceive that they are empty of their accustomed strength,
which they used to see within themselves in every fierce and difficult battle.
How do they perceive this? They see within themselves that their defeat is pleasing to them, and that the hardships of the struggle are difficult for them
to endure—those hardships through which they had always attained their victory in purity.
And that stirring of zeal which vigorously rouses their nature at times like these,
which used to grow fierce with fiery ardor, they cannot find within themselves. But those who are weak from their very foundation
are terrified not only by these struggles and others like them, but even by the sound of the leaves on the trees.
Under a little distress from hunger or a slight illness, they are defeated, deny their faith, and turn back.
But those who are steadfast and tested do not even eat their fill of herbs and greens.
Rather, even when they subsist on roots and dry grasses,
they will not, even then, be persuaded to open their mouths for food before the appointed time.
But even when they lie on the ground, their bodies weakened and their eyes dimmed by the severity of their bodily exhaustion,
And their soul is at their lips because of suffering; even so, they do not yield to defeat,
abandoning their firm resolve. For they delight in suffering for the sake of love,
in hardships for the sake of virtue, more than in this temporary life and all its comforts.
And when afflictions meet them, they rejoice, knowing that these are what bring them to perfection.
Not only do they remain unwavering in their love for Christ despite the bodily torments that come upon them, but even the loss
of life they gladly accept for his sake, and they do not part from him.
Concerning the things whose precise usefulness I learned through discerning knowledge. 37.
For after I had often been tested by things on the right and on the left,
and had tested myself many times in both kinds of change,
and had received countless blows from the adversary and been granted great help in secret,
and had gained experience of myself over many long years, I learned this through experience:
that the foundations of all good things, the soul’s return from captivity to its enemies,
and the road to life and light are these two things: staying in one place and continual fasting.
That is, a person should wisely establish a fitting rule for his stomach, while remaining steadfastly and continually in his place.
From this comes control of the senses. From this comes alertness of mind.
From this comes the calming of the animal passions that bark within the body. From this comes tranquility of thoughts.
From this come enlightened movements of the mind. From this comes eagerness for virtuous deeds.
From this come lofty and subtle insights. From this come unceasing, immeasurable tears.
From this comes radiant chastity, entirely removed from the temptations of images in the mind.
From this comes a swift and keen perception of distant things. From this comes
a deep understanding that plunges into and grasps the hidden things of every depth:
the power of sayings [?], the hidden movements within the soul, and the distinctions between spirits and between the holy powers,
and true visions and false images. From this comes fear of the roads and paths in the sea of the mind, which puts an end to negligence,
and the blaze of zeal that tramples every danger and strides over every fear, and the fervor that despises every desire
and drives from the mind and makes it forget the memory of all passing things, together with still other things, and others besides.
And in short: the liberation of the true human being, the renewal of the soul, and resurrection with Christ in the kingdom begin here.
Whoever neglects these two things should know that he is not depriving himself of these alone,
but is shaking the foundation of all the virtues by treating these two virtues with contempt.
And just as these principal practices of all divine things are the beginning of all these things in the soul,
and the gate and path to Christ for whoever holds to them and perseveres in them, so also departure and a leap away from them,
toward the two things opposed to them—I mean bodily distraction and an unrestrained belly—
make room in his soul for the beginning of everything opposed to what has been mentioned.
The beginning of the first of these is that he first releases his restrained senses from the bonds of restraint.
And what follows from these things? From this come shameful encounters beyond expectation, the imminent danger of
falls, turmoil, and mighty waves stirred up by the gaze of the eyes.
Fierce flames that seize the body; swift slips in the mind;
uncontrollable thoughts that rush toward a fall; a cooling of love for his spiritual work;
the gradual forgetting of the insights of stillness; complete abandonment of the rules governing his way of life;
the revival of former things that had been forgotten, and learning about other, new things that he had not known.
These come from the varied and constant things he hears and the many kinds of sights that, without his choosing,
confront him through his constant traveling from region to region and from place to place.
Thus those passions that, by God's grace, had long been asleep in the soul,
through the forgetting of memories that had vanished from the mind, begin to awaken into activity again.
And they begin to force the soul into deeds, along with other things that I cannot recount in full.
These things, then, are unleashed upon him through the first of those faults, for him to endure miserably.
And what happens through the other? That is, when he begins to behave like pigs.
And what is the behavior of pigs? To set no limit for the belly,
to fill it at all times, and to have no appointed time for eating, as rational beings do.
And what follows? From this come deep and heavy sleep, great heaviness of the body, along with slackening
of the shoulders; a compulsion to refrain from the services; sluggishness in performing the bows during them.
Disdain for the customary prostrations; dullness and coldness of mind.
A dull mind that cannot discern; confusion and great darkness of thought.
Thick fog and darkness spread over the whole soul.
Great despondency in every work of God, and also in reading,
because he does not taste the sweetness of the words’ meaning. Frequent neglect of necessary duties.
An uncontrollable mind that roams distractedly throughout the whole world; great heat gathering in the limbs.
Restless fantasies throughout the night, through filthy images and shameful figures that inflame desire,
which seize the soul and shamefully accomplish their will in it.
His bedding and his whole body are soiled by an abundance of shameful discharge, which flows from him as from a spring.
And these things happen not only at night but also during the day: the body discharges continually and defiles the mind.
And through these very acts, as it were, he has already renounced chastity.
And the sweetness of the sensations of arousal that work throughout his whole body, with an unbearable heat that never subsides.
Enticing thoughts bearing the beauty of faces, which readily appear before him at all times and arouse him;
and the mind, wearied by engaging with them, unhesitatingly surrenders to them with longing and brooding, because its discernment has been blinded.
And this is what one of the great teachers among the philosophers said: whoever feeds his body lavishly
places his soul beneath a precipice. Even if he sometimes remembers himself and wishes to compel himself,
he cannot restrain himself because of the heated impulses in the body,
which, through the force of their stimulation, forcibly take the soul captive to their will.
As Mar Diodorus of Tarsus, polished in eloquence and lofty in understanding, said:
“Feeding the body luxuriously and delicately gives the soul an acute sensation of passion;
death becomes sweet to it, and it incurs the fearful judgment of God.
But the soul that constantly reflects with concern on its duties is at peace within itself, and its thoughts are clear,
while it remains free from regret. Concern for virtue is the charioteer of the passions,
the guardian of virtue, and unfailing nurture,
joy without anxiety, a good life, and a harbor without danger.”
For bodily diversions strengthen the passions and make them more powerful against the soul.
And he says, “They uproot it, as though from its very roots.”
And despite all these things, he still inflames his belly through gluttony and irregular mealtimes.
He is unwilling to master his soul through the slight pains of hunger, though he himself forcibly drives it into the onslaught of the passions.
These are the shameful fruits that come from the belly, and these are the fruits that come from a lack of
endurance in remaining quietly in one place.
Therefore our adversary, who is always at our side, knows these times:
that at these two times our nature is disturbed more than usual, and the passions sting it.
The mind is greatly confused—that is, by what the eyes look at and by satisfying the belly.
He too makes an effort to add to what nature produces.
At these times he casts all kinds of thoughts into the mind, so that, if possible, passion may overpower nature
through an even fiercer blaze and plunge a person into a fall. For this reason,
just as our adversary knows these times, we too ought to recognize them, as well as our weakness
and the strength of our nature, which is insufficient to withstand the onslaughts of the impulses stirred up at these times,
and the subtle thoughts that he scatters like dust before our eyes, so that we cannot see ourselves or stand firm against what befalls us.
Through the trials that we have so often suffered miserably at his hands, we should henceforth learn wisdom.
We must not let ourselves relax into doing whatever pleases our desire for comfort and give in to hunger, even if we are greatly distressed.
Nor should we leave the place of our stillness and join others where such mishaps can easily occur,
inventing excuses and devising ways to go out of the wilderness.
These are plainly Satan’s tricks. But if you persevere in the wilderness, you are not tempted.
For in the wilderness you see no woman, nor
anything that undermines your way of life, nor do you hear improper talk.
What have you to do with the roads to Egypt, going to drink water from the Gihon? Understand what I am saying.
Give your adversary proof of yourself through your endurance in small things, so that he does not demand great things of you.
Always keep the rules concerning these [?], so that through the struggle over them you may keep offering him bait.
so that he will not be able to use them to hide great traps for you.
But someone who cannot be persuaded to go even five steps beyond the door of his enclosure:
how can he persuade him to leave the wilderness or attend a gathering in the village?
And someone who cannot even be induced to look out through the window of his confinement:
how can he persuade him to go outside it? Someone who cannot be persuaded to eat even late in the evening, even when he is trembling with [?]:
how can he entice his thoughts into breaking his fast before the appointed time? And someone who is ashamed to eat his fill even of humble foods:
how can he invite him to lavish ones? And someone who cannot be persuaded even to gaze at his own body:
how can they entice him toward the beauty of others? A person is first overcome by small things when he treats them carelessly;
and then he provides an opening for being driven toward greater things.
And someone who is not the least concerned about continuing in this temporary life:
how can he frighten him with afflictions that lead to the death he loves? Such is the battle fought with discernment: the wise do not allow
their enemy to summon them to great contests.
Instead, the endurance they show in small things protects them from falling under great assaults.
First he gives up prayer—that is, perseverance in supplication within the mind;
and then he persuades him to neglect bodily prayer too, and the appointed times prescribed for it.
First the mind grows lax, so that he breaks his fast before the appointed time with small, insignificant things and just a little food.
And after falling away from endurance, he slips into eating greedily.
First he is overcome—or rather, it seems a small thing in his eyes—to look at his naked body,
or to gaze at the beauty of one or another of his limbs when it is uncovered by clothing, or else carelessly to relax his senses
when he goes out to attend to his bodily needs, or confidently and boldly to put his hand inside his clothes and feel his body.
Then one thing after another flashes upon him. Once he has first relaxed his mental vigilance
and shown negligence in one of these things, then the door to greater things is opened against him.
Our thoughts, to use an illustration, are like water.
As long as they are confined on every side, they flow in an orderly course.
But if they find even the smallest outlet, they flow out through it, making breaches and causing great destruction.
For that cunning one stands [?] our appointed time, waiting as he sits day and night before our very noses and looks
at us, to see where an opening against us might be made for him through one of our senses, or through neglect of one of these things I have listed.
And immediately he launches his own attacks against us. Sometimes it is also our own nature,
for it too loves ease, loves foul conversation, loves idle amusement, loves diversion, and loves laxity.
It is a fountain of passions and a sea of turmoil. At other times, however, it is our enemy.
Let us therefore exchange great labors and occasions of dangerous distress
for the small efforts we make over these little things that amount to nothing,
which, if neglected, can give rise to great struggles, troubles difficult to remedy, entangling battles, and great wounds.
Who would not sleep peacefully at so small a cost? O wisdom, how wonderful you are!
How far in advance you foresee everything! Blessed is everyone who has found you,
for he has been freed from the drowsiness of youth, which purchases great troubles through a little negligence.
A certain wise man spoke well when, on one occasion while stretching, he suddenly stirred and straightened up.
He immediately sat upright, although the matter itself was not worth being afraid of.
Someone laughed at him for this, as though he were weak-minded. He answered him, saying:
“It was not that which frightened me; it is temptation that I fear. How often negligence in little things
leads to danger in great things! That is why, when I stirred, I immediately straightened up and sat upright:
I showed that I was watchful, and that I do not treat even something unworthy of fear with indifference.”
For this is philosophy: through the little things that a person does watchfully, he gains great peace for himself.
He must not sleep until the calamity comes and overtakes him, but must take hold of its causes ahead of time,
and, through something that costs a little trouble, secure beforehand what is great.
For fools value a little comfort close at hand more than a kingdom far away.
It is better to endure torments diligently than to lounge on a bed of comforts in a kingdom under the reproach of baseness.
For the wise prefer death to being reproached for failing to watch over their affairs.
“Be watchful over your life,” says the philosopher, “for the sleep of the mind is akin to real death.”
Basil, the philosopher of the house of God, says: “Do not trust someone who is negligent in his small affairs to be diligent in his great ones.”
Do not shrink from dying for the very things for which you wish to live.
Brief chapters on discerning the movements [?] of the mind. 38.
Faintheartedness is a sign of despondency. Negligence is the mother of both.
A fearful person shows that he suffers from two illnesses:
love of the body and lack of faith. Love of the body is a sign of unbelief.
Anyone who holds the body in contempt shows that he trusts in God and awaits the things to come.
If anyone has drawn near to God without afflictions, you too should imitate him.
Courage of heart and a person's disregard for every danger arise from one of two causes:
either hardness of heart or great faith in God.
Pride accompanies the former, but humility of heart accompanies the latter.
No one can acquire trust in God unless he has first fulfilled God's will to some extent.
Trust in God and courage of heart are born from the testimony of conscience.
It is said, “From the truthful testimony of our mind we have confidence toward God.”
The mind's testimony comes from a person's not condemning himself for neglecting his duty, insofar as he was able to fulfill it.
If our heart does not condemn us, our faces are unveiled before God.
This openness before God comes from upright conduct and a good disposition.
It is hard to serve the body as a slave. But anyone who has experienced even a little of the abundance of his hope does not
consent any longer to toil under the compulsion of this harsh master.
A person's perseverance in the aforementioned silence and the observance and observance of stillness [?] comes from one of three causes:
either for the sake of human praise, or because of fervent zeal for virtue,
or because he has some divine communion within him that draws his mind toward it.
Anyone who lacks these last two necessarily suffers from the first.
Virtue does not consist in the many different kinds of outward bodily acts,
but in a heart wise in its hope, which joins a right intention to its deeds.
For often, when outward actions do not assist the work, the mind is able to do so, and it advances in virtue without them.
But the body, without the wisdom of the heart, cannot benefit even when it labors.
Yet a man of God cannot hold back, whenever there is an opportunity to do good,
from showing his love also in outward actions, through the labor of carrying them out.
The first way always succeeds. The second, however, sometimes succeeds and sometimes does not.
Do not think it a small matter for the causes of the passions to be far removed and kept away from someone.
As for the arousal of the lower organs that occurs intensely without thoughts,
or the shameful lust that leaps hotly down from the wall and leads the soul
into frenzy against its will, be certain beyond doubt that it springs up in the body from a full stomach.
Consider keeping away from the sight of women a strong weapon in this struggle.
What nature accomplishes by its own power, not even the enemy can accomplish.
Do not suppose that nature ever forgets, until death, what God has sown and buried in its roots
for the continuation of our nature and for our testing in the struggle. So it is with every desire:
distance from its objects puts it to sleep in the body's members and consigns its memory to disappearance and oblivion.
Thoughts of distant things are one kind:
they make a simple passage through the mind, with a faint, cold stirring that arises of itself.
Those arising from a living object are another kind: it stamps the mind with an unforgettable image and excites the passion from close at hand,
feeding it as oil feeds the flame of a lamp that had already begun to flicker and was close to going out,
and churning up the sea of the body with its turbulent movements against the ship of the mind.
The arousal that comes from nature alone, of itself and for itself,
which God the Creator has implanted in us for the increase of the bodily world, without any addition from outside,
cannot disturb the will's serenity or unsettle it so that it departs from chastity.
For God does not give nature the power to overcome a virtuous will directed toward him.
But whenever someone is overcome by anger or desire,
it is not what is implanted in nature that forces him to go beyond nature's bounds and outside what is proper,
but the addition we make to that natural impulse through causes introduced by our own will.
God made everything he made well and in due measure.
And as long as the measure of the natural impulses is properly maintained in us,
they do not force us to be swept away, as by a torrent, outside the path of God's law.
Rather, the body merely stirs with peaceful impulses in its movements.
In this way, we are only aware that the passion is present,
but it does not debase or disrupt the course of chastity and trouble it, or turn peace into anger.
But if at any time we become greedy for things perceived by the senses—things that also habitually give unnatural anger its impetus—
or persist in excessive eating and drinking, or in looking at a woman close at hand,
or in stories about her, through which the fire of desire is habitually kindled in the body,
by this we exert force upon the peacefulness of nature, driving it toward a bestial state,
either through the abundance of humors in the veins or through various sights of things.
There is also what comes from abandonment because of conceit. This, however, is not the same as that.
We call these the struggles of free will, which follows the course of our common nature.
Let us recognize the struggle that comes from abandonment because of conceit:
when we have spent a long time in labors and vigilance, and apart from
these causes, an onslaught of desire beyond our strength is stirred up against us.
The other struggles arise in us from our laxity. Whenever nature receives an excess through the senses or through the belly,
it no longer consents to keep the original measure of its constitution.
But anyone who despises afflictions and deprivation is compelled, against his will, to love sins.
For without these we cannot keep away from the enticements in our thoughts. The more those increase, the more these diminish.
For afflictions drive away the pleasure of the passions, while comforts nurture them and bring them on.
It has therefore become clearly known that God and his angels rejoice in afflictions,
but Satan and his servants rejoice in comforts. For if God's commandments are fulfilled through bodily hardships,
and we despise these, then we are exposed as despising the very one who gave the commandments,
so that through the passions, which are the offspring of comforts, we abolish what gives rise to virtue.
That is, hardship. To the same extent that we bring comforts near us, we make room for the passions.
For when the body is under hardship, thoughts cannot wander among useless things.
But whenever someone bears hardships joyfully, he also has greater strength to restrain his thoughts.
For even the thoughts themselves do not grow weary amid labors.
Therefore, whenever someone disciplines himself with afflictions in remembrance of his former evil deeds,
then God also devises ways to give him rest, rejoicing
to see that he has already pronounced judgment on himself for straying from his way, which is a sign of repentance.
And the more he subjects himself to hardship, the more honor he receives from God.
Every joy that does not arise from virtue immediately stirs impulses of desire in the person who experiences it.
Understand this as referring to every passionate desire, not merely to natural desire.
Further helpful counsels of love. 39.
Hardships endured for the sake of what is good are as lovable as the good itself.
No one can achieve complete renunciation unless he has resolved in his mind to bear afflictions gladly.
And no one can bear afflictions unless he believes that there is something better than bodily comforts
that he will receive in exchange for his afflictions. Everyone who prepares himself for renunciation—
first a love of afflictions is stirred within him, and then the thought arises in him of renouncing the things of this world.
And everyone who approaches afflictions is first strengthened in faith, and then approaches the afflictions.
Someone who has renounced material things but has not renounced the sensory experiences of seeing and hearing
has prepared double afflictions for himself and is afflicted twice over.
Or rather, although he has abstained from using those things, he enjoys them through his senses and suffers from the very same passions connected with them
in which he formerly indulged through his actions. For the memory of his habitual involvement with them is not erased from his mind.
But if imaginary images arising in the mind afflict a person even in the absence of the things themselves,
what shall we say about their actual presence nearby? Solitude, then, is good and very helpful:
it powerfully silences thoughts and vigorously calls for training in endurance.
It also teaches a person great perseverance through the training imparted by the pressure of afflictions, which are necessarily present in it.
Do not seek advice from someone who does not share your aim in his way of life, even if he is very wise.
An uneducated person who has experienced things is more trustworthy than a wise person who speaks from examination without experience of them.
What is experience? Experience? Experience is not this: that someone enters into things and comes into contact with them,
without gaining knowledge of them through profit and loss and spending time with them.
How often the outward appearance of things suggests loss, while within them
there is a trade full of profit. In the same way, the opposite of this is also to be understood.
There are also many who suffer loss from profitable things.
Nor is the testimony of their knowledge reliable,
but rather that of someone who knows how to examine things with patient discernment.
For this reason, not everyone can be trusted to give advice, but only someone who has first conducted himself well,
has experiential knowledge in every matter, does not love himself, and does not shrink from blame. For whenever
you find the path of your journey peaceful and without change, be afraid.
You are indeed moving away from the divine paths, worn by the weary footsteps of the saints.
For as you advance along the road to the city of the kingdom and approach its vicinity,
let this be your sign: severe trials meet you. And the closer you come, the more you will enter into trials.
Thus, whenever your soul senses difficult changes along its path, know at those times
that your soul has secretly undergone a change of rank [?], and that its gift has increased beyond the level at which it previously stood.
In proportion to the greatness of the gifts, God brings the soul into severe trials.
But if there is a soul that is weak and cannot endure a very severe trial, and God deals gently with it,
understand wisely that just as it cannot bear a great trial, neither can it bear a great gift.
Just as the greatness of the trial has been withheld from it, so too the greatness of the gift has been withheld from it.
God never gives a great gift and a small trial.
Trials, then, are ordered in proportion to the gifts. Therefore, from the hardships that have been allotted to you,
you can perceive the degree of greatness your soul has received [?]. Consolation is in proportion to suffering.
What, then? A trial, and then a gift? Or a gift, and after it a trial?
For trial does not come unless the soul has secretly received an increase beyond its former measure and has received
the Spirit of adoption. We have evidence of this from the trial of our Lord,
and likewise from that of the apostles. For they were not allowed to enter into testing until they had received the Paraclete.
Those who share in good things ought also to endure trials.
Along with the good thing come its afflictions. Thus it pleased the all-wise [?] God.
Yet even so, the experience of trial comes before the experience of the gift, so that free will may be tested.
Grace has never come to a person before the taste of trial. In its presence, indeed, it comes first; but in being felt, it comes later.
Therefore, at these times you ought to have within you two opposing, dissimilar things.
What are they? Joy and fear. Joy, because on the path marked out for the holy ones [?],
or rather for the Giver of life to all, you are found walking, as the signs of your trials show.
Fear, however, lest it is because of pride that you are being tested by these things.
But the humble are made wise by grace, so that they recognize the distinctions between these things.
That is, between trials arising from the fruits of pride and blows received from love.
For the trials that come for the training of one's conduct differ from those that come through abandonment,
to strike down the heart's arrogance. Now the trials that come under the rod of fatherly discipline for the training of the soul,
through which it is exercised and tested and becomes victorious,
are these: weariness, heaviness of the body, slackness of the limbs, despondency,
confusion of mind, bodily pains [?], despair lasting for a time, darkening of thoughts,
lack of human help, lack of bodily necessities, and the rest.
Through these a person acquires a solitary soul, humility, and a deadened heart.
Through these he is tested in his loving devotion to the Creator.
The Guide apportions the benefit of these to the recipient according to his strength.
In these things, consolation and distress, light and darkness, battles and help are mingled.
In short, he brings distress and relief, which is a sign of helpful discipline.
But the trials that come through abandonment:
For those who, in the face of the kindness of our benefactor, dare to exalt themselves in their thinking,
and arrogantly show ingratitude for his blessings, these are the trials: open attacks by demons,
which exceed the limits of the soul’s strength, when they are deprived of the power within them that gives wisdom;
an intense awareness of impulses toward sexual immorality, to which they are abandoned so that their arrogance may be brought down;
readiness to become angry; stubbornness of will; a love of winning arguments; irritability; a contemptuous heart;
complete confusion of mind; blasphemy against him whose glory is blessed; foolish thoughts full of laughter—
or rather, weeping; contempt from other people; dishonor in place of dignity;
mockery by demons in many forms, both secretly and openly;
a love of mingling with others and engaging in worldly affairs; frequent outbursts of foolish words; novel inventions
of one’s own, along with false prophecies and many promises beyond one’s strength.
And in bodily matters too: continual difficult and obstructive misfortunes that are not easily resolved;
constant encounters with wicked and godless people; falling into the hands of evil people;
continual agitation of the heart through sudden, groundless fear;
and sometimes a violent fall from cliffs, high places, and the like, so that the body itself is broken;
the heart’s loss of support from reliance on divine providence and from the confidence of its faith.
In short, everything impossible and beyond his strength is hurled upon him and those around him.
All these things that I have listed belong to the category of trials arising from pride.
Their onset becomes evident in a person as soon as he begins to be wise in his own eyes.
He is led into all these evils in proportion to his acceptance of this thought.
Thus, by discerning your trials, you come to understand the subtle paths of your mind.
But if you see some of these things mixed with those others, know that, in proportion to the amount of these things,
conceit is also hidden there. Now listen to another point as well.
All difficulties and afflictions that are not accompanied by patience bring twice the torment.
A person’s patience drives away his troubles, but faintheartedness is the mother of torments.
Patience is the mother of consolations.
A certain strength is born from openness of heart. It is difficult for a person to find this within himself in his afflictions,
apart from the gift of God, which is obtained through petition in prayer and the shedding of tears.
But when God wishes a person to suffer greater affliction, he leaves him in the grip of faintheartedness.
This produces in him the powerful force of despair, through which he experiences a choking of the soul:
these things are a foretaste of hell. From this, a spirit of turmoil is stirred up against him,
from which spring countless trials: confusion, anger, blasphemy, faultfinding,
unsettled thoughts, moving from place to place, and other things like these.
But if you ask, “Who is the cause of all these things?” I tell you: you are.
For you have not taken care to investigate what brings about their healing. There is one remedy for all these things,
through which a person immediately finds comfort within himself. What is it? Humility of heart.
Without this, a person cannot break down the barrier of these evils. Rather, he finds that they grow stronger against him.
Do not be angry with me for telling you the truth: you have never sought this within yourself.
But if you wish, pursue it, and you will see how it brings release from your evils.
In proportion to your humility, endurance in your troubles is given to you.
And in proportion to your endurance, their weight upon your soul grows lighter, and you will be comforted
in its afflictions. In proportion to its comfort, your love for God increases. And in proportion to your love, your joy in the Spirit increases.
When our merciful Father wishes to give relief in their trials to those who are his true children,
he does not take the trials away from them, but grants them endurance in their trials.
Through this they receive all these good things, for the perfection of their souls.
May Christ, in his grace, make us also worthy to endure hardships for love of him, with heartfelt thanksgiving. Amen.
Explanation of the orders of conduct: what the power of the practice of each of them is. 140.
Bodily discipline in stillness purifies the body of the material elements within it.
The discipline of the mind purifies the soul and clears it of coarse impulses concerning perishable things,
so that, instead of being occupied with them passionately, these impulses are directed toward contemplation of them.
This brings the soul close to the nakedness of the intellect, which they call immaterial contemplations. This is spiritual conduct.
This, however, as it raises the mind above earthly things, brings it near to the first contemplation of the spirit.
It places the mind before God in a vision of inexpressible glory, and the mind delights inwardly in the hope of things to come.
What each of these is and how it works. Bodily conduct directed toward God is the name given to bodily labors undertaken for the purification
of the body through the practice of virtue in its own outward actions, through which it is cleansed of the impurity of the flesh.
The practice of the mind consists in nighttime labor, carried out without rest in meditation on that great judgment to come,
and in the continual prayer of the heart, and in meditation on God's governance and care in this world,
both in particular instances and in general, together with guarding the boundaries of the inward passions,
so that none of them enters the hidden, spiritual place. This is the labor of the heart that they call the practice of the mind.
Through this labor of discipline, which is called the work of the soul, the heart becomes refined
and is separated from participation in the corruption of the passions that are contrary to nature.
From this very point it begins to be continually stirred to an understanding of things perceived by the senses,
which were created to meet the body's need for nourishment and, through their service, give strength to the four elements in the body.
Spiritual practice is work without the senses.
This is what is written by the fathers: When the minds of those who are detached have received contemplation of their own being,
then the density of the body too will be removed from between them, and henceforth the vision will be spiritual.
By “contemplation of their own being,” he means the original created state of their nature.
For from this point onward it will be moved [?] toward what is called the knowledge of unity,
which, to explain it plainly, is wonder at God.
This is the order of that great way of life to come, which is given in the freedom of life without mortality, in that manner of living
after the resurrection. For from that point onward human nature is no longer interrupted
in its continual wonder at God, to be diverted toward anything in creation.
If there were anything else to distract it, it would attend sometimes to him and sometimes to those things.
But if the beauty of everything that exists in that future order is inferior to his beauties,
how can the mind, in its vision, go outside this? What, then? Mortality compels it,
or else the weight of the flesh, or else the memory of its relatives, or else the needs of nature, or else the adversities that arise.
or distraction through ignorance, or the imperfection of nature, or distraction among the elements,
or interaction with one another, or discouragement that wears us down, or the weariness of the flesh.
But even in this world, where all these things exist, whenever the veil of the passions is sometimes rolled away from before the eyes of the mind,
and it gazes intently at that glory, the understanding is immediately carried away in wonder.
And if God had not set a limit in this life to such things,
determining how long one may remain in them, a person, if allowed, would never come out of there for his entire life.
How, then, there, where none of these things exists, where life is without limit, and amid these very realities in person,
when we are henceforth within the courts of the kingdom—if our conduct is worthy—will the mind still have a way out,
to withdraw from the vision of God's wonder and dwell on something else? Woe to us, who do not know
ourselves or the way of life to which we are called! Yet this life of weakness and this animal condition,
and the world with its afflictions, its evils, and its comforts, we consider to be something of value.
Christ, who alone are mighty [?], blessed is the person whose helper you are, and in whose heart are your paths of ascent.
You, my Lord, turn our faces away from the world through longing for you,
so that we may see it as it is and no longer take shadows for realities.
Place zeal in our minds, my Lord, before death, so that at the time of our departure
we may know the purpose of our entrance into this world and our departure from it; so that, having completed the task to which we were called,
in keeping with your purpose in first placing us in this life, we may await, with a mind full of confidence,
the reception of the great things which, according to the promises of the Scriptures, are prepared in the second creation for those who love you,
the remembrance of which is preserved among us through faith in the mystery.
Purity of the body is freedom from defilement.
Purity of the soul is freedom from the hidden passions that establish themselves in one's thoughts.
Purity of the intellect is its being purified through revelations from impulses concerning everything that falls under sense perception in its material aspect.
Even little children are pure in body, and their souls are free from passions.
Yet no one calls them pure in intellect. Purity of intellect is the perfection attained through the practice
of heavenly contemplation, in which it is stirred, independently of the senses, toward the spiritual powers of those worlds above.
Wonderful and beyond counting, distinct in their activities yet united in their invisible service;
who, stirred by divine revelations, abound in their continual changes.
A letter he wrote to one of the brothers who loves stillness.
On how Satan contrives to prevent the diligent from persevering in stillness,
under the guise of love for one's neighbor and for visitors; and on how everything ought to be despised in one's eyes
for the sake of the knowledge of God that is found in stillness, as the example of our early fathers has shown. 41.
Since I know that you love stillness, and that Satan hinders you in many ways under the guise of virtue,
because he knows the aim of your mind and wants to distract you from this all-embracing and many-sided virtue,
O virtuous brother, I have taken care, as one bodily member cares for its fellow, to help your good intention with a word of [?].
I have acquired this from people wise in their way of life, from the books of his fathers, and from experience.
For unless a person disregards both honor and dishonor and endures reproach, insult, and losses for the sake of stillness,
even to the point of death, and becomes a laughingstock and is considered mad and foolish by those who see him, he will not attain the benefits
of stillness. For if a person once opens the door to pretexts,
Satan will not stop bringing people to him on one pretext after another, with constant, countless encounters.
Therefore, my brother, if you love the strict practice of life in stillness,
in which there is no distraction, restless movement, or interruption, just as the early fathers distinguished themselves in it,
you can fulfill this praiseworthy desire in this way: by imitating your fathers
and carrying in your mind, as though imprinted there, the memory of their stories.
Those among them who cherished perfect stillness were not concerned to fulfill love for their neighbor
by relaxing their own discipline, nor were they ashamed before people considered important when they fled from encounters with them.
Although they conducted themselves this way, knowledgeable and wise people did not consider them despisers of their brothers,
nor contemptuous, scornful, or lacking in discernment, as some of them have been called,
as though to discourage those who value solitude and withdrawal more than meeting their neighbor.
“A person,” it is said, “who has learned through experience the sweetness of solitude in his cell
does not flee from meeting his neighbor because he despises him, but because of the fruit he gathers from stillness.”
How did they flee? Abba Arsenius, it is said, would not agree to meet anyone.
But Abba Theodore, even if he met someone, was like a sharp sword in his encounter.
That is, he would not even greet anyone whenever he happened to be found outside
his cell. Saint Arsenius, however, would not even greet someone who came to greet him.
Once, it is said, one of the fathers went to see Abba Arsenius. The old man opened the door, thinking
that it was his attendant. But when he saw who it was, he threw himself face down.
And although the visitor pleaded earnestly with him, saying, “Get up, Abba, so that I may at least greet you here at the door and leave,”
the holy man insisted, saying, “I will not get up until you leave.”
And he did not get up until the visitor left him and went away. That blessed man used to do this
so that, if he gave them an opening once, they would not come again another time.
“One of the fathers,” it says. Notice the wording of the account, so that you do not say that perhaps he despised him because of his low standing.
Rather, he tells him, “One of the fathers.” We have a very striking demonstration from another direction,
so that you do not say that he despised one person but showed favoritism toward another because of his rank and conversed with him.
Rather, he maintained the same impartiality in fleeing encounters with people of every rank.
In his eyes it was all the same to disregard encounters with the great as with the small for the sake of solitude,
and to bear reproach from everyone because of his esteem for solitude and silence.
For we know that once, when the blessed Theophilus, archbishop of Alexandria, went to him,
taking the governor of the region along with him, to honor the holy man and out of a longing to see him,
as he sat with them, he did not oblige them with even a little word to honor them, although they were very eager
to hear him speak. When the archbishop pleaded with him about this, the old man, it is said, remained silent for a little while.
Then he answered them, saying, “If I tell you something, will you keep it?” And they promised him.
The old man said to them, “Wherever you hear that Arsenius is, do not go near that place.”
Have you seen how remarkable the old man was? Have you seen his disregard for human honor? This is the man who knew how to gather the fruits of solitude,
since that blessed man took no account of the fact that the man was the catholicos and head of the whole church.
For this was his resolve: “I have once and for all [?] to the world.
What benefit can a dead man bring to the living? He received a loving rebuke about this from the blessed Macarius, who said to him:
“Why do you flee from us?” And the holy elder gave a wonderful, Spirit-inspired answer worthy of praise:
“God knows that I love you, but I cannot be with God and with people.”
On another occasion, the archbishop sent him a message about this.
The elder sent him a reply, saying, “If you come, I will open the door to you.
But if I open it to you, I will open it to everyone. And if I open it to everyone, I will no longer remain here.”
He learned this wonderful teaching not from anyone else, but from a divine voice:
“Arsenius, flee from people, and you will live.” Let none of those who are idle and love conversation
dare to undo this with the twists of their words, or speak against it as though
the pursuit of solitude were a human invention. For look: it is a teaching from heaven.
And so that he would not suppose that this had been said to him about fleeing and departing from the world,
and not about fleeing equally from the brothers as well, after he had left the world
and was now living in a monastery, he prayed again to our Lord about how he could live well.
“Lord,” he said, “guide me to life,” expecting that now he would hear something different.
But the Lord’s voice again made him hear the very same words a second time, adding by way of explanation:
“Flee, keep silent, and remain in solitude. Even though seeing the brothers and conversing with them is very beneficial,
conversing with them does not benefit you as much as fleeing from them.”
When the blessed Arsenius received these things through divine revelation—that while he was still in the world, he was commanded to flee,
and that even when he was among the brothers, the very same thing was said to him—he then became certain and understood
that fleeing only from worldly people is not enough to attain an upright life, but that one must flee equally from everyone.
Is there anyone who has anything to say against the divine voice? Abba Antony, too, was told in a revelation:
“If you wish to live in solitude, go not merely to the Thebaid, but to the inner desert.”
Now if God thus commands us to flee from everyone, and so loves solitude and his friends’ perseverance in it,
who will make excuses to persist in conversation and close association with people? But if
watchfulness benefits Antony and Arsenius, and fleeing helps them,
How much more so for the weak? And if, in the case of those whose words and the benefit of seeing them were needed by the whole world,
God honors their remaining in solitude more than the benefit of all humanity,
how much more so for someone who cannot even guard himself properly? We know of another of the saints,
whose brother by birth was sick, while he had shut himself away in another cell.
Throughout his brother’s illness he resisted his affection and did not go out to see him. Then, when the time came for his brother to depart from the world,
his brother sent him this message: “Come at least now, so that I may see you before I leave the world, even if you come at night. Let me bid you farewell and find relief.”
But that blessed man would not be persuaded, even at this time, when natural affections usually stir people up
to overcome the boundaries they have voluntarily set. He said, “If I go out, my heart will not be pure before God,
because I have refused to visit my brothers in the Spirit, yet would honor natural kinship more than Christ.”
His brother died, and he did not see him. Therefore let no one make laxity of thought an excuse,
one supposedly beyond reproach and not subject to being set aside, or a dispensation from above for abandoning solitude.
If the saints overcome natural affection, powerful as it is, and Christ loves it when solitude is honored, even though he is slighted in his children,
what other pressing need is there that will not yield to being disregarded when it arises? That commandment, “Love the Lord your God with
all your soul and all your heart, and more than the whole world and nature and everything belonging to it,” is fulfilled in this way: by your remaining here.
The commandment concerning love of one’s neighbor is also contained within it.
Do you want to acquire within yourself love of your neighbor according to the commandments of the Gospel? Keep your distance from him.
Then the flame of love for him will burn within you, and you will long to see him as you would long to see an angel of light.
Do you also want your loved ones to long for you? See their faces only after many days.
Truly, experience is the teacher of everything. Stay well.
A letter that he sent to his brother by birth and in the Spirit,
who had urged him in writing to go and visit him in an inhabited place, expressing his longing to see him. 42.
We are not as strong as you suppose, blessed one.
But perhaps you are aware of my weakness, yet take my destruction lightly.
That is why you constantly demand this of me, elevating natural affection above the understanding that burns within you as it usually does.
It is not worth the concern it entails and seems to you to deserve, if it is to receive attention from us. [?]
Do not ask me, my brother, for what brings comfort to the body and mind; instead, devise a way for my soul to be saved.
Only a little time remains, and we will pass from this world. How many people will I encounter when I go there,
and how many kinds of people and places, before I return again to my own place?
And what occasions for thoughts does my soul receive through encounters with them,
so that it is disturbed by the passions awakened within it? It finds little relief from them. These things are not hidden from you.
You know, then, that the sight of worldly people wounds the solitary—not only the sight of women, but also of men.
And see how many changes take place in the mind of someone who has remained alone in stillness for a long time,
whenever he suddenly encounters these things again and hears and sees something outside his usual experience.
But if encounters with members of his own monastic order wound someone who is engaged in the contest
and is still fighting his enemy, whenever they do not share his purpose,
into what pit, then, must we fall to escape our enemy’s guile? This applies especially to those who, through experience of many things,
have already acquired knowledge. For this reason, do not persuade me to do this without necessity.
Let our hearts not be led astray by those who say, “Hearing and seeing do us no harm at all,
and we are the same in our thoughts in the wilderness and in inhabited places, in our cell and outside it, because we are at rest from disturbance,
undergoing no harmful change and feeling no agitation of the passions when we encounter people and things.”
Those who say these things do not even know when they are being wounded.
For we have not yet attained this health of soul. We have festering sores.
If they are left without treatment even for one day and are uncovered from beneath the plaster and bandages, they will swarm with worms.
43. Profitable discourses filled with the wisdom of the Spirit.
Faith is the gateway to the mysteries. What the eyes of the body are to things perceived by the senses,
faith is to the eyes of the mind in relation to hidden treasures.
We possess two eyes of the soul, as the fathers say, just as we have two eyes of the body.
But each does not serve the same purpose in seeing.
With one of them we see God’s hidden glory, concealed in the natural world, and his power and wisdom,
and his eternal purpose for us, which we perceive through the excellence of his providential care for us.
And in it itself we also see the spiritual ranks, our companions. And in it alone we see the glory of his holy nature.
Whenever our Lord wishes to bring us into spiritual mysteries, he opens the sea of faith within our minds.
As grace upon grace, repentance has been given to human beings.
Repentance is a second birth from God.
What we received as a pledge in baptism, we receive as a gift through repentance.
Repentance is the door of mercy, open to all who seek it.
Through this door we enter into divine mercy. Apart from this entrance, there is no way to find mercy.
For all have sinned, as Scripture says, and are freely justified by grace.
For repentance itself is a second grace. It is born in the heart from faith and fear.
Fear is a father's rod that guides us as far as spiritual Eden. And when
we reach that place, it leaves us and turns back. Eden is divine love.
In it is the paradise of all blessings, where blessed Paul was nourished with food beyond nature.
And after tasting from the tree of life there, he cried out and said, “The eye has not seen,
nor has the ear heard, nor has it entered the human heart, what God has prepared for those who love him.”
Adam was deprived of this tree through the devil's promise.
The tree of life is the love of God, from which Adam fell.
And joy no longer came to him; instead, he worked and struggled in a land of thorns.
Those deprived of divine love still eat the bread of sweat in their labor,
even if they practice righteousness—the bread that the ancestor of our race was commanded to eat when he fell away from that love.
Until we find love, we labor in a land of thorns.
Among thorns we sow and reap, even if what we sow is the seed of righteousness.
We are constantly pricked by them, and however righteous we become, we live by the sweat of our faces.
But when we find love, we eat heavenly bread and are nourished without toil or weariness.
The heavenly bread is the one who came down from heaven and gives life to the world. This is the food of angels.
Whoever has found love eats Christ at all times and becomes immortal from that moment onward.
“Whoever eats of this bread,” he says, “will never taste death.” Blessed is the one
who has eaten of the bread of love, which is Jesus. Whoever feeds on love feeds on Christ,
who is God over all. John bears witness to this when he says, “Love is God.”
Thus, whoever lives in love in this creation draws life from God.
Such a person draws here from that air of the resurrection. In this air the righteous delight at the resurrection.
Love is the kingdom in which our Lord mystically promised the apostles that they would eat in his kingdom.
“You will eat and drink,” he says, “at the table of my kingdom.”
What will they eat, if not love? Love is sufficient to nourish a person in place of food and drink.
This is the wine that gladdens the human heart. Blessed is whoever has drunk of this wine!
This is what the dissolute drank, and they became chaste; sinners drank, and they forgot the paths that lead to stumbling;
drunkards drank, and they became people who fast; the rich drank, and they longed for poverty;
the poor drank, and they became rich in hope; the sick drank, and they became strong;
and the uneducated drank, and they became wise. How no one passes over to love without fear.
That foul sea which lies between us and the spiritual paradise—we cross it in the ship of repentance,
which has fear for its oars. If the oars of fear do not guide this ship of repentance,
in which we cross the sea of this world toward God, we drown in the foul sea.
Repentance is the ship, fear is its pilot, and love is the divine harbor. Putting
us aboard the ship of repentance, fear carries us across the foul sea of the world
and brings us to the divine harbor, which is love, toward which all those worn out by the toil of repentance look.
When we reach love, we have reached God.
Our journey is finished, and we have crossed over to the island beyond the world, where the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are.
To him be glory and [?], and may he make us worthy of fearing him and loving him. Amen.
On how many degrees of knowledge there are, and the degrees established for faith. 44.
There is knowledge that precedes faith, and there is knowledge that is born of faith.
The knowledge that precedes faith is natural knowledge. The knowledge born of faith is spiritual knowledge.
What is natural knowledge? It is knowledge that distinguishes good from evil, and it is also called natural discernment.
God has placed in rational nature the ability to know good from evil naturally, without instruction.
Through instruction, however, it grows. There is no one in whom it is not present.
This is the natural power of knowledge belonging to the rational soul: discernment of good and evil is continually active within it.
Those who lack this are below the rank of rational beings.
But those in whom it flourishes stand in the proper condition of the soul’s nature,
since what God gave to the soul’s nature, to honor its rationality, remains uncorrupted within them.
The prophet rebukes those who have lost this knowledge that distinguishes good from evil, saying, “Man did not understand his own honor.”
The honor of rational nature is precisely this discernment that distinguishes good from evil.
And he rightly compared those who have lost it to an animal that possesses no discerning, rational soul.
Through this it is possible to find the way of God. This is the natural knowledge that precedes faith,
and it is the way to God. Through this knowledge, by which one distinguishes good from evil, one accepts faith,
as the power of nature itself bears witness that it is good for a person to believe in the one who brought all these things into being,
to affirm the word of his commandments, and to carry them out. From this act of believing, the fear of God is born.
When a person commits himself to practicing this fear of God and advances a little in its practice,
it gives birth to that spiritual knowledge which we said is born from faith.
It is not simply born from faith itself. From mere faith alone,
spiritual knowledge is not born. Rather, from faith the fear of God is born.
And when a person begins to practice the fear of God, spiritual knowledge is born from the practice of the fear of God,
according to the words of the blessed Interpreter: “For when a person acquires a will committed to the fear of God
and an upright mind, he readily receives the revelation of hidden things.” “The revelation of hidden things”
is what he calls spiritual knowledge. It is not that the fear of God itself gives birth to this knowledge.
It cannot produce something that it is not naturally appointed to produce.
Rather, that knowledge is given as a gift—a gift bestowed for the practice of the fear of God.
But when you examine the practice of the fear of God carefully, you find that it is repentance itself.
And the spiritual knowledge spoken of here is what we said: that what we received a pledge of in baptism,
we receive as a gift through repentance. The gift that we said we receive through repentance
is the knowledge of the Spirit, which is freely given through the practice of reverence for God.
Spiritual knowledge is the perception of hidden things.
But when someone perceives these invisible and far more excellent things,
from which the spiritual character of knowledge takes its name, another faith is born through this perception.
It does not oppose the first faith, but confirms what the person believed.
They call it the faith of seeing. Until then there was hearing; now there is seeing.
Seeing is more certain than hearing. All these things arise from that knowledge which distinguishes good from evil
and awakens naturally. This is the seed of virtue that has been spoken of.
But when we cover it over with our desire-loving will [?], we fall away from all these good things.
This knowledge is accompanied by the constant pricking of conscience, distress, and sorrow;
fear of God and natural self-denial; sorrow over past transgressions;
and diligence in doing what ought to be done; constant remembrance of death, troubling reflection on this passage, and concern for its provisions;
and earnest supplication to God that we may enter well through this gate, which is the passage for all human nature;
contempt for the world, and the noble struggle for virtue.
All these things are found in this natural knowledge. Let a person examine his conduct by these things.
When a person lives in these things, he walks along the path of nature.
But when he has risen above these things and reached love, he has risen above what belongs to nature, and struggle, fear, and toil have passed away from him.
In light of what has been said, let a person assess his own affairs: on which path is he walking? On the one below nature,
or in accordance with nature, or in those things above nature? From these distinctions, which have been clearly stated,
a person can easily understand the conduct of his entire life.
Whenever you are not living in the things belonging to nature that have been described here,
nor in those above nature, it is clear that you are dwelling below nature.
Counsels Full of Benefit. 45.
There is no good impulse that enters the heart except as a gift from above.
And there is no evil thought that approaches the soul except as a trial.
A person who has come to know his own weakness has come to understand humility.
The forerunner of God's blessings toward a person:
A heart continually stirred by gratitude.
The forerunner of trials coming upon the soul is an impulse to grumble that continually stirs in the heart.
God bears with all human weaknesses. But he will not bear with someone who continually grumbles without disciplining him.
A soul far removed from all the light of knowledge is found amid these impulses.
A mouth that continually gives thanks receives blessing from God. And grace dwells in a heart that remains continually grateful.
Humility runs ahead of grace, and presumption runs ahead of discipline.
Whoever becomes inwardly proud because of his knowledge is tried by blasphemy.
And whoever becomes proud because of the excellence of his spiritual work is scourged by sexual immorality.
And whoever exalts himself because of his wisdom becomes bewildered among hidden snares.
A person who carries resentful thoughts against his neighbor in his heart is far removed from all remembrance of God.
Whoever honors everyone in remembrance of God finds everyone a helper through God's hidden prompting.
Whoever sighs over the oppressed finds his Creator an advocate.
Whoever offers his arm to help his neighbor receives God's arm in return.
Whoever accuses his brother of his wrongdoings finds God his accuser.
Whoever corrects his brother in private heals his wrongdoing. Whoever accuses him before the assembly makes his wounds worse.
Whoever heals his brother privately shows the strength of his love. But whoever exposes him before his companions reveals the power of his envy.
One who rebukes pride in secret is a wise physician. But one who, in front of many,
offers healing is truly a mocker. The sign of compassion is forgiveness of every offense.
And the sign of an evil disposition is arguing with the offender.
Whoever administers discipline for healing disciplines with love.
But whoever seeks revenge in his demand for redress is devoid of love. God disciplines with love, not for revenge—far be it!
For he wants his image to be healed, and he does not hold on to anger against someone who resists correction for a time.
For he does not seek revenge for himself. This is the aim of love.
Love’s discipline is for correction; it does not have retribution as its aim.
The compassionate righteous person resembles God. He never disciplines anyone in order to exact payment for his wrongdoing,
but so that either that person may be corrected or others may be warned. Anything different from this is not discipline.
Through this, as in an image, the Spirit portrays the disposition that God has eternally.
Anyone who wishes to think of God as an avenger, while imagining that he is upholding justice, accuses him of lacking goodness.
Far be it from that fountain of love, that sea filled with goodness, that vindictiveness should be found in him.
The aim of his intention is the correction of human beings.
And were it not that the dignity of freedom would be stripped away, perhaps he would heal us without even using rebukes.
The scope of freedom, through our actions, grants the power of confidence to our rational nature.
For this too, bow down before the greatness of his goodness.
For he wishes to rejoice, not as though in something of his own, but in the merits of our deeds. For although everything is his,
he does not like to count it as his own, but to take delight in it as though it were ours.
