In proportion to a person’s goodness, he is enlightened concerning God; and in proportion to his ascent toward knowledge of him, he draws near to freedom of soul.
Anyone who excels in good deeds for the sake of a future reward is very easily subject to change.
Anyone whom the power of knowing him fills with wonder at the sight of the love God has—
even if his flesh is cut apart, his mind is not shaken, nor does he turn away from virtue.
Anyone whose mind is enlightened concerning the pangs God feels for us descends into the depths of humility, in both body and soul.
Before a person draws near to knowledge, he rises and falls in his conduct.
But once he draws near to knowledge, he continues to rise entirely upward; and however far he rises,
the ascent of knowledge does not end before that world of glory comes and he receives the fullness of its riches.
However perfect a person becomes in relation to God, he is still walking behind him.
But in the world of truth, he shows him his face, not his essence.
However much [?] are shaped by visions of him, they see only an enigmatic likeness of the vision, like an image shown in a mirror.
There, however, they see the revelation of the truth. A fire that takes hold of dry wood is hard to extinguish.
And the fervor for God that falls into a heart cut off from the world has a flame that cannot be extinguished.
And it is fiercer even than fire. When the strength of wine enters the veins, the mind forgets its exact knowledge of everything.
And when the remembrance of God takes root in the soul, it wipes the memory of visible things from the heart.
A mind that has found the wisdom of the Spirit is like someone who has found a ship ready for use in the middle of the sea.
When he boards it, it carries him across the sea of this world and brings him to the island of the world to come.
For the perception of things to come in this world is like a small island in the middle of the sea.
And whoever has drawn near to it is no longer battered by the waves of worldly concerns.
When a merchant has finished his trading, he then hurries to go home.
And as long as the time for his work still remains, a monk is distressed at the prospect of leaving the body.
But when he senses within himself that he has bought his merchandise and received his pledge, he longs for the world to come.
As long as a merchant is at sea, trembling rests upon his limbs, lest a wave rise up and sink the hope of his labor.
And as long as a monk is in the world, fear hangs over his work.
For a storm might rise against him, and the labor of his youth through old age might be lost.
The merchant looks toward dry land, and the monk toward the hour of his death.
A sailor watches a star when he sails in the middle of the sea. He steers his ship by its direction, so that it may show him the harbor.
And a monk looks to prayer, for it sets his course and shows toward which harbor his way of life should be directed.
The monk looks to prayer at all times, so that it may show him an island where he can moor his ship away from danger.
And there, at each stop, he can gather provisions and set his course
again for another island. Such is the journey of the solitary as long as he remains in this life.
He passes from island to island, and from knowledge to knowledge.
And just as he encounters different islands, he encounters different kinds of knowledge.
This continues until he comes up from the sea and his journey reaches that true city of his.
Its inhabitants no longer engage in trade there; instead, everyone rests from his labors.
Blessed is the one whose journey has not gone astray in the great sea!
Blessed is the one whose ship has not been wrecked and who has reached that harbor toward which he looks!
The diver plunges naked into the sea to find a pearl.
And the wise monk travels naked through the world to find the pearl—Jesus Christ himself.
And when he finds it, he acquires nothing else besides it. A pearl is kept safe in inner chambers.
And the solitary's delight is found in stillness. A virgin is violated in gatherings.
And the monk's mind is violated in conversations. A bird hastens from everywhere to its nest to produce young.
And the discerning monk hurries to his cell to produce within it the fruits of life.
Even when its whole body is being crushed, a snake takes care to protect its head.
And a wise solitary takes care amid every adversity to protect his faith, which is the head of his life.
A cloud covers the sun, and excessive talk covers the soul that has begun to shine in the contemplation of prayer.
That bird called the owl rejoices and delights, according to the saying of the wise, when it separates itself from
settled places and goes to live in a desolate region.
And the solitary's soul receives heavenly joy when it distances itself from other people
and goes to live in quiet places, waiting there for the time of its departure.
For it is said of that bird called the siren that whoever listens to its song
is completely captivated and follows it on its journey through the wilderness, until the sweetness of its melodies makes him forget his life, and he falls down dead.
The soul's experience is like this: whenever that heavenly sweetness enters it
through the melodies of God's words, by means of perception in the mind, it follows him completely,
until it forgets its bodily life and, because of its delight, abandons the body and is lifted up to him out of this life.
Life in this world is sweet to someone who lives bodily.
But it is not as sweet as separation from it is to someone who parts from it through an awareness of God.
Until a tree sheds its old leaves, it does not put out new shoots.
And until the solitary shakes from his heart the memories of his former ways, he does not put out new shoots through Jesus Christ.
The wind makes fruit grow plump, and the Spirit of God does the same for the fruits within the soul.
The oyster in which a pearl is formed receives its substance from the air, as the saying goes.
And until then, it is ordinary flesh. And the heart of the monk,
until it receives heavenly substance through spiritual insights, still has ordinary work to do, and there is in it
no consolation amid his sweat. The fruits of trees are sour and astringent to the taste,
and are not fit to eat until sweetness from the sun enters them.
And the first labors of repentance are very bitter and astringent, and they do not console the solitary,
until the sweetness of contemplation enters them, carrying the heart away from earthly things, so that it forgets itself.
A dog licking a file drinks its own blood, and does not know the harm it suffers because of the sweetness it finds in it.
And a solitary who stoops to drink worthless praise sucks away his own life,
and does not perceive the harm he suffers because of the momentary sweetness. Praise from worldly people is like a reef hidden in the sea,
which the sailor does not discover until the ship strikes it. It pierces the ship’s bottom, and the ship fills with water.
The fathers have said about it that through it all the passions return again into the soul,
those that had once been defeated and had left it.
A small cloud covers the sun’s disk, but the sun behind it is very bright.
And a little despondency covers the soul, but the joy that comes after it is still more radiant.
A musician playing a flute is not nourished by the sound of his melodies. And when he stops playing, his stomach is even hungrier.
And the sweetness of words without deeds does not satisfy. And when a person leaves them behind, he is all the more ashamed.
Just as it is impossible for someone to drink wine without its smell coming from his mouth, so it is impossible for someone to be granted spiritual
refreshment in his way of life without the change in his affairs becoming known to the wise.
A heart that has received heavenly seed is transformed in its speech, transformed in its thinking, transformed in its conduct, transformed in its senses.
And in everything belonging to it, it differs from the rest of ordinary humanity. It is like someone who was asleep and has awakened from sleep.
Do not approach the words of mystery in the Scriptures without prayer and a request for help from God,
saying, “Lord, grant me a perception of the power within them.”
Regard [?] prayer as the keys to the true meanings in Scripture.
Whenever you wish to draw near to God in your heart, first show him love through bodily deeds.
This is where the spiritual way of life begins. For the heart draws very near to God,
By renouncing all material needs at once and embracing hardships, our Lord too laid the foundation of perfection in this way.
Consider idleness to be the beginning of the soul's darkness. Conversation is darkness upon darkness.
The second is also the cause of the first. Even beneficial words produce darkness when they have no limit.
The soul grows lax through excessive conversation, even if it is a preparation for the fear of God and a means of drawing near.
Consider darkness of soul to be what stirs up agitation.
Darkness in the soul comes from disorderly conduct. Moderation and proper timing in one's conduct illuminate
the mind and restrain agitation. When the mind is confused by disorder, it becomes dark.
When it becomes dark, the soul is agitated. Peace comes from order.
From peace, light is born in the soul; and from peace comes a clear atmosphere in the mind.
To the extent that the heart draws near to wisdom, it receives joy in God.
You perceive within your soul the difference between the wisdom of the Spirit and the wisdom of the world.
With the former, silence reigns over your soul. With the latter, you become a fountain of distraction.
After finding the former, you are filled with great humility,
with serenity, and with peace that reigns over all your thoughts; and your limbs become calm and cease their restlessness and agitation.
After finding the latter, you acquire conceit in your thinking,
various indescribable thoughts, disturbance of mind, and senses that become restless and anxious.
Other Thoughts. 46.
Do not suppose that a person bound to bodily things can approach God with confidence in prayer.
A miserly soul is deprived of wisdom, but a compassionate soul is made wise by the Spirit.
As oil feeds the flame of a lamp, so compassion nourishes knowledge within the soul.
The key to divine gifts is given to the heart through [?] for one's neighbor. To the extent that the heart is freed
from bodily bonds, the door to knowledge is opened before it.
Understand that the soul's passage from one world to another takes place through receiving insights.
Love of one's neighbor is glorious and excellent, but only when concern for it does not distract us from the love of God.
Conversation with our spiritual brothers [?] is pleasant, but only when it is possible to preserve that love along with it.
For the one who is with our Lord, then, it is right to take on the burden of these things as far as duty requires.
That is, only so far that their demands do not cause him to fall away from hidden service and the aforementioned communion with God.
Disruption of the latter preserves the former. The mind cannot manage two occupations.
The sight of worldly people disturbs the soul that has once renounced their affairs for the sake of serving God.
For those, it is constant interaction; for these, even the outward sight.
Bodily labors are not hindered by encounters through the senses.
There is a kind of work in which even sounds, without anything being seen, disturb the quiet of one's heart.
Inward deadness cannot be maintained without the cessation of sensory activity.
Bodily discipline requires the vigilance of the senses; spiritual discipline requires the vigilance of the heart.
Just as the soul is by nature superior to the body, so the soul's work is superior to bodily discipline.
And just as the body comes into existence before the soul, so bodily acts of righteousness precede spiritual work.
Great is the power of a small practice when it is joined to persistence. A soft drop of water, because of
its persistence, has pierced even hard rocks.
When the spiritual person is about to rise to life within you, deadness to everything awakens within you.
And your soul seethes with a joy that has no equal among created things.
And your thoughts gather inward within you through the sweetness in your heart.
But when the world is about to rise to life within you, distraction of mind increases within you.
And your thinking becomes petty and unstable. By 'the world' I mean the passions that distraction conceives.
And when they are born and reach maturity, they become sin and kill the person.
Just as children are not born without a mother, so passions are not born without distraction of mind.
Nor does sin reach completion without engagement with the passions.
When endurance increases in our soul, it is a sign that the soul has secretly received the gift of consolation.
The power of endurance is strengthened by the stirrings of joy that wells up in the heart.
Life in God is the downfall of the senses. When the heart comes alive, the senses fall.
The revival of the senses is the death of the heart. When the senses revive, it is a sign that the heart is dead to God.
The conscience is not set right through virtues displayed among people.
Virtue that a person practices toward others cannot purify the soul.
It is indeed counted before God as deserving wages and a reward.
But the virtue that a person practices within himself accomplishes both: it is counted as deserving a reward, and it brings about purity.
Therefore, turn away from the first by adhering to the second. Without diligence in the latter, ceasing from
the former is an obvious falling away from God. The second, however, also takes the place of the first, even without practicing it.
Be dead while alive, so that you may be free when you die. Be dead to the world, so that you may be free from its laws.
For of those who have lived under them, not one has attained their fulfillment in this life.
The living dead man has been freed while still alive, and he lives when he dies.
Recognize concern for ornate speech as a sign of a heart barren of God.
A soul that has perceived the life above the body does not adorn itself for the world.
Without discovering these things, a person can hardly despise those things. But to do so completely is altogether impossible.
Anyone who forces himself stirs up a great struggle against himself. But once he has discovered these things, he can renounce those things without a struggle.
Comforts and idleness are the destruction of souls. They can harm them even more than demons can.
But where there is a soul dwelling in the light through the glorious labors of good deeds, demons can do nothing.
A darkened soul, however, itself becomes an accomplice to the demons within it in carrying out every kind of evil.
When a weak body is forced into excessive labors, it heaps darkness upon darkness in the soul.
It brings the soul still greater confusion and gloom. But a sturdy body, or one with a strong constitution,
if it gives itself over to idleness and relies on comforts, brings every kind of evil to completion in the soul that dwells in it.
Even if the soul is deeply intent on good, after a little while it strips the soul even of the thought that is intent on good. But when the soul becomes drunk
with joy in its [?], and with that delight in God, the body becomes insensible to afflictions, even if it is weak.
For it bears a double burden without growing weary. For it is as though it were being nourished,
and the body itself is sustained by the soul’s delight, even if it is weak, when the soul enters into that joy in the Spirit.
If you guard your tongue, my brother, a gift will be given to you by God: sensitivity of heart,
through which you may see your soul. Through this very thing you will enter into joy in the Spirit.
But if this overcomes you, be assured of what I say: your soul will never [?] from darkness.
If you have a pure heart, let your mouth also be pure.
As blessed John said: When you want to encourage someone to do good,
first provide him with bodily comfort, and cheer him with a word full of love.
Nothing so puts a person to shame and persuades him to turn from evil to good
as a kindness to his body and the honor he receives from another person.
There is also a second means of persuasion: a person's care for himself with a view to noble deeds.
Someone who has managed to gain possession of himself through prayer and watchfulness can easily [?] his companion toward life,
even without the labor of words and outward admonition.
But contempt and laxity harm not only those who embrace them, but also those who observe them.
For if someone, through care for himself, inspires his companions with zeal for good deeds
and puts the lax to shame by the sight of him, no words can adequately describe his blessedness,
how great it is! The silence of action is more powerful for correcting others
than earnest words contradicted by lax conduct.
When you correct yourself, your neighbor receives no less benefit.
The more a person admits no image other than God into himself, the closer he comes to confidence of heart in his prayer [?].
And the more he is pulled about by many things, the more he is stripped of help.
The soul that is free from the body's distractions will be peaceful in its movements.
Be free in body, so that you may be found worthy of freedom in spirit.
Accept a yoke in your freedom, so that you are not yoked in slavery to your enemies.
If you have once shown beforehand in yourself that image of the dissolution of temporal life,
then, by resting from its activities, be completely dead, as a demonstration of that cessation which is to come,
just as concern for everything is destined to cease in you through death.
Do not be distressed by bodily losses, for death is destined to take your body from you completely.
Do not fear death, for God is destined to raise you above it.
On the angelic stirrings that divine acts of providence awaken in us to nurture the soul in spiritual things. 47.
The first stirring that comes upon a person through divine mercy and draws the soul toward life concerns the passing away of this nature and falls
into the heart. This thought is naturally followed by contempt for the world.
From this, those beautiful stirrings that guide a person toward life begin within him.
The divine power that accompanies a person, wishing to reveal life within him, lays within him as a kind of foundation
this very stirring of which I have spoken. And if a person does not extinguish it through attachment to the things of this world and idle occupation,
but nurtures this stirring in his soul through continual inward recollection and attention to it,
it brings him close to something that the tongue cannot describe.
Satan greatly hates this thought and fights with all his strength to make a person forget it.
And if it were possible for him to give that person dominion over the whole earth,
so that through its distractions he might erase this thought from his mind, he would not hesitate.
For he knows that if this remembrance remains with a person, his mind will no longer remain in this land of error,
and his schemes will not come near him. This vision is clothed in fiery stirrings.
Anyone who has received it no longer fixes his attention on the world or remains occupied with the body.
Truly, my beloved, if God were to let this clear vision remain with people for a little while,
the course of the world would cease to continue. It is a bond that nature cannot withstand.
When this occupation is given to someone in his soul, it is a gift from God,
more powerful than all the individual workings
bestowed at this intermediate stage upon those who desire repentance with an upright heart.
It is bestowed with certainty upon someone whom God knows to be fit for a firm passage from the world to a life of virtue,
because of the good will he finds in him. It grows and remains with him through his dwelling alone with himself.
Let us seek this in prayer. For its sake, let us keep long vigils.
As for a gift beyond compare, let us keep watch with tears at our Lord’s door, so that he may bestow it upon us.
Then we will no longer wear ourselves out in the turmoil of this world. This is the beginning of the stirring of life,
which brings the whole perfection of righteousness to completion within a person. On the second working in a person.
Another effect that follows this: When a person advances well in his way of life,
and reaches the point of rising from the stage of repentance, and comes close to tasting the contemplation that comes from his spiritual work,
when the gift from above comes upon him, enabling him to taste the sweetness of spiritual knowledge, its beginning is here.
First, he becomes convinced of God's care for humanity and is enlightened about his love for creation—
the creation of rational beings—and his great care for those things that are for their sake.
For from here that sweetness of God begins within him, along with the flame of his love, which burns in the heart and burns up all the passions of body and soul.
He perceives this power in all the natures of creation and in everything he encounters. From time to time he becomes drunk with it,
as though with wine. His limbs grow limp, his mind comes to a halt, and his heart is carried away after God.
Thus he becomes, as I have said, like someone drunk with wine.
The stronger his inward senses become, the stronger this vision becomes.
And the more he attends to his way of life and to vigilance, and labors at reading and prayer, the more its power becomes settled and firmly established within him.
Truly, [?], at times he reaches the point where he does not remember that he himself is clothed in a body, and does not know that he is in the world.
This is the beginning of spiritual vision in a person, and this is the starting point of all revelations to the mind.
Through it the mind is nurtured and instructed in hidden things, and through it the mind advances by stages toward other things that are above human nature.
To put it briefly, through it there are conveyed to a person all the divine visions and revelations of the Spirit
that the saints receive in this world; and human nature can know the gift of revelations in this life.
This is the root of our awareness of our Maker. Blessed is the person who guards this good seed when it falls into his soul,
and nurtures it, and does not squander it on idle pursuits and distraction with passing things!
On the changes of light and darkness that the soul undergoes at all times, and the training it receives from the right and the left. 48.
Let us examine ourselves, my beloved, at the time of worship and prayer.
Do we have contemplation of the verses of psalmody and prayer? This comes from genuine stillness.
When we are in darkness, let us not become troubled, especially if we ourselves are not its cause.
For divine providence brings this about for reasons that he alone knows.
For our soul is suffocated and feels as though it is amid stormy waves. Whether a person turns to Scripture or to worship,
whatever he approaches, he receives darkness upon darkness and comes away. Often he is not even allowed to approach.
He does not believe at all that he will undergo another change and be at peace. This hour is full of despair and fear.
Hope in God and the consolation of faith vanish completely from the soul.
It is filled entirely with doubt and fear.
Those who have experienced the storm of this time know from experience the change that follows on its heels.
God certainly does not leave the soul in this state for a whole day.
Otherwise, it would perish, cut off from life and from all the hope of Christians.
But soon, even if this same darkness comes on repeatedly, changes toward life become visible in its midst.
But I advise you, whoever you are: if you do not have the strength to restrain yourself and fall on your face
in prayer, wrap your head in your cloak and lie down until the hour of darkness passes from you. But do not leave your cell.
Those who wish to follow a spiritual way of life are especially subject to this trial,
and long in their journey for the consolation that comes from faith.
For this reason, this dark hour troubles them more than anything else, through doubt in their minds.
Fierce blasphemy also accompanies it, and sometimes even doubt about the resurrection, and other things that we need not mention.
We have experienced all these things many times, and we have written them down for the consolation of many.
Those whose way of life consists only of bodily labors are entirely removed from this struggle.
The despondency familiar to everyone comes upon them, but its forms differ from these things and others like them.
The cure for this springs from stillness itself—that is, its consolation.
But through conversation he never receives the light of consolation.
He only finds relief for a time; afterward, however, it rises forcefully against him.
One does need an enlightened man experienced in these things, so that one may be stirred and encouraged by him from time to time, but not continually.
Blessed is the one who perseveres amid these things behind his door!
For a great and powerful calm comes after these things, as the Fathers say.
Yet this struggle does not pass away suddenly, nor does grace come in its fullness and dwell in the soul all at once,
but little by little: some of this and some of that. At times there is trial,
and at times consolation. Something of it remains, even until one's departure.
For complete deliverance, which we should not expect from him here, nor for complete consolation.
For this is how God has willed our lives here to be governed. These things apply to those who are traveling along the way.
On the gloomy darkness that comes in stillness to those who conduct their lives according to knowledge. 49.
In a time of darkness, kneeling helps more than anything else.
Even your inability to undertake this and persevere in it is an attack by Satan.
You must struggle against this, for Satan knows the help that comes from kneeling.
That is why he strives with all his strength to keep you from approaching it. Whenever you approach to fall on your face, he agitates you.
Even if you overcome him and kneel down, he pressures you not to remain in that position.
Even if our inward movements are cold and dark, let us remain kneeling.
Even if our hearts are downcast at these times, and we have no prayer at all and do not know what to say,
because neither words of petition nor supplication come to us,
even so, let us remain continually lying on our faces, even if we are silent.
Whenever we need some help from God and are deprived of it,
we deservedly do not receive it, because we do not approach God in prayer diligently and fervently, night and day,
crying out to him in pain. Instead, we wait for him to give it to us of his own accord.
He, for his part, devises an occasion for us to [?] him; for this reason he allows us to be afflicted.
By delaying our deliverance so that we linger at his door with our petitions, he is devising a means to help us.
But when occasions for help come upon us, we encounter them and hold back,
and give ourselves over to sluggishness, weariness, and despair, becoming colder than water.
In all the troubles and trials that come upon you, whether from within or from outside, the way of prayer lies before you.
Fall on your face, even for a whole night and day, pleading with God with anguish of heart.
And God, who is compassionate and good, will not delay in giving consolation and relief,
when he sees that you are pleading with him in heartfelt pain, unless what you ask is contrary to the way.
You must act this way throughout your life. You receive, and you lose.
Then you plead again in pain, and he gives to you. Then it leaves you again.
And now you encounter something and think, “This is the end of everything.”
But when you look for it again, an hour later it is gone. This is how this journey is arranged; do not lose heart.
When that thick darkness presses upon the soul, let us guard against despair.
Listen to me, my brother: like a woman in labor struggling against her birth pains, struggle not to leave your cell,
and like someone enduring torture. For above all else the enemy uses great cunning
to bring you out of your cell on the pretext that you cannot endure the struggle.
His whole effort to force you outside is prompted by the fear that, if you remain, you may come to kneel in prayer.
He greatly fears this act, more than anything else.
Again, short chapters containing various thoughts, which explain the harm caused by foolish zeal disguised as the fear of God,
and the benefit that comes from gentleness, together with other subjects. [?]
A zealous person never attains peace of mind, and whoever lacks peace also lacks joy.
For if peace of mind is called perfect health, and zeal is the opposite of peace,
then anyone stirred by zeal is sick with a serious illness.
O human being, while you think you are stirring up your zeal against the sickness of others,
you have driven health away from yourself. Be more concerned about your own healing.
But if you also wish to heal the sick, know that those who are sick need care more than rebuke.
Thus, while you give others no help, you defile yourself with a serious illness.
Zeal is not counted among the forms of wisdom
found in human beings, but among the soul’s illnesses: narrow-mindedness and great ignorance [?].
The beginning of divine wisdom is calmness, acquired through greatness of soul, and bearing with human weaknesses.
“You who are strong,” it says, “bear the burden of the sick,” and, “Restore the transgressor in a gentle spirit.”
The apostle counts peace and patience among the fruits of the Holy Spirit.
A heart filled with sorrow over its inability to undertake outward bodily labors is the culmination of all bodily labors.
Bodily labors without sorrow of mind are like a body without a soul.
Someone who is sorrowful in heart but unrestrained in his senses is like a sick person suffering bodily pain who leaves his mouth free to consume [?] harmful foods.
who is concerned in his heart but lax in his senses: like a man who has an only son and slaughters him little by little with his own hands.
Attentiveness of mind is a precious gift from God.
Whoever bears it together with its rightful duties is like someone carrying a holy object upon his limbs.
A person whose tongue rules him in everything, good and bad, is not worthy of this grace.
Repentance and social conversation: a jar full of holes. A gift and insults: a knife hidden in honey.
Chastity and companionship with a woman: like a lioness and a lamb in one house.
Toil and harshness before God: like someone slaughtering a son before his father.
Someone who is sick in his own soul and corrects his companions is like a man
whose eyes are blind and who shows others the way. Mercy and justice in one soul:
like someone worshiping God and idols in one house. Everywhere, mercy is the enemy of justice.
Justice is the uprightness of an evenly balanced scale, giving everyone what they deserve,
without inclining to either side to show favoritism in its repayment.
Mercy, however, is a feeling stirred by goodness, inclining compassionately toward everyone.
It does not repay someone who deserves evil, and it showers many times as much upon someone who deserves good.
If this belongs on the side of righteousness, then that belongs on the side of wickedness.
Just as [?] and fire cannot endure together in one house, so justice and mercy cannot endure together in one soul.
Just as a grain of sand does not weigh as much as a great weight of gold,
so the exercise of God's justice does not weigh as much on the scales as his mercy.
Like a handful of sand falling into the great sea, so are the sins of all humanity compared with God's disposition.
Just as a spring with abundant streams cannot be stopped up by a handful of dust,
so the Creator's mercy cannot be overcome by the wickedness of his creatures.
Like someone sowing in the sea and expecting to reap, so is someone who holds a grudge and prays.
Just as flames of fire cannot be restrained from rising upward,
so the prayers of a merciful person cannot be prevented from ascending to heaven. Like
a rush of water on sloping ground, so is the force of anger whenever it finds an opening in our mind.
Whoever acquires humility in his heart becomes dead to the world. Whoever is dead to the world is dead to the passions.
Whoever has died in his heart to his relatives finds that Satan is dead to him.
Whoever has found envy has also found the one who first discovered it.
There is humility that comes from fear of God, and there is humility that comes from love of God.
One person is humbled by fear of him, and another is humbled by joy in him.
The former is accompanied by modesty of the limbs, discipline of the senses, and a heart that is always contrite.
The latter, however, is accompanied by great outpouring and a heart that leaps up and cannot be restrained.
Love knows no concealment. Therefore it does not know how to give its limbs a formal and orderly bearing.
Love is by nature unable to conceal itself and forgetful of its own measure.
Blessed is whoever has found you, haven of every joy! The assembly of the humble is dear to God, like the assembly of the seraphim.
A chaste body is more precious to God than a pure sacrifice.
Both together prepare a dwelling for the Trinity in the soul.
Conduct yourself with decorum among your friends. When you do this, you will benefit both yourself and them.
For very often, under the guise of friendship, the soul casts off the reins of vigilance.
Be wary of conversation: it is not always beneficial.
In a gathering, value silence, for it checks many deceits. As for the stomach,
practice restraint, though not as much as with your gaze. The battle within is easier in every respect.
Do not believe, my brother, that inward thoughts can be disciplined without disciplining the body.
Fear habits more than enemies. Whoever feeds a habit is like someone who feeds a fire.
The strength of both depends on the fuel supplied to them.
If, when a habit makes a demand, its request is denied once, you will find it weaker the next time.
But if you fulfill its desire this time, you will find its demand upon you stronger the second time.
Keep this reminder with you in everything you do. The help that comes from vigilance is better than the help that comes from toil.
Do not befriend someone who loves laughter and idle chatter, for he will draw you into lax habits.
Do not smile at someone whose conduct is undisciplined. But beware of hating him.
If he wants to get up, give him your hand. Care for the one you have found until death.
If you are still sick, neither you nor medical treatment [?]. “Hold out the end of your staff to him,” it says, and so on.
Speak cautiously in the presence of someone who is boastful and sick with envy.
For while you are speaking, he interprets your words in his heart however he pleases.
Even from the good things in you, he takes material for causing others to stumble.
And in his mind your words are turned into material for sicknesses. When someone begins speaking about his brothers
in your presence, make your face look stern. When you do this, you show yourself to be watchful toward both God and him.
If you give something to a needy person, let a cheerful face, kind words, and encouragement for his distress come before your gift.
When you do this, the comfort your gift brings to his mind outweighs its benefit to his body.
On the day you open your mouth to speak against another person, consider yourself dead to God
and all your labors wasted, even if it seems that your thoughts are urging you to speak for correction and edification.
Why must someone tear down his own building to put his neighbor’s in order?
On the day you suffer for another person in any way, whether for good people or wicked people, in body or in mind,
consider yourself a martyr on that day, and someone who has been found worthy to suffer for confessing Christ.
Remember that Christ died for the wicked, as Scripture says, not for the good.
See how great a thing it is to suffer for evil people and to do good to sinners—even greater than doing so for the righteous.
The apostle mentions this as something worthy of wonder.
But if you can become righteous within your own soul, do not trouble yourself to seek another righteousness.
Let bodily chastity and purity of conscience precede all your actions.
Without them, every action is worthless before God.
Whatever deed you do without thought and without examination, know that your labor in it is wasted, even if it is
a good deed. For God assesses righteousness according to the benefit of discernment, not according to the labor of busy activity.
A righteous person without wisdom is a lamp in the sunlight. The prayer of someone who bears a grudge is seed on rock.
An ascetic without mercy is a tree without fruit. A rebuke prompted by envy is a poisoned arrow.
The praise of a deceitful person is a hidden trap. A foolish adviser is a blind watchman.
Sitting with fools breaks the heart; conversation with the wise is a sweet spring.
A wise counselor is a wall of confidence; a foolish friend is a storehouse of loss.
It is better to see a house of mourners than to see a wise person attached to a fool.
It is better to live with wild animals than to live with envious people.
It is better to dwell in a grave than to live with people whose conduct is vile.
Sit with vultures, not with greedy people. Keep company with a murderer, not with a quarrelsome person.
Converse with a pig, not with a glutton. A pig's trough is better than a glutton's mouth.
Sit among lions, not among the proud. Be persecuted, but do not persecute.
Be crucified, but do not crucify. Be wronged, but do not wrong others. Be oppressed, but do not oppress.
Be peaceful, not zealous. Hold to kindness, not justice.
Justice is not part of the Christian way of life, nor is any mention of it recorded in Christ's teaching.
Rejoice with those who rejoice, and weep with those who weep, for this is
a sign of purity. Be sick with the sick, mourn with sinners, and rejoice over those who repent.
Be a friend to everyone, but remain solitary in your mind. Share in everyone's suffering, but keep yourself physically apart from everyone.
Rebuke no one and reproach no one, not even those whose conduct is very wicked.
Spread your cloak over the sinner and cover him. If you cannot take his offenses upon yourself
and accept punishment in his place, at least make the effort not to expose him.
Do not quarrel over food. Do not hate for the sake of honor. Do not love passing judgment.
Know, my brother, that we stay behind closed doors for this reason: so that we may not know people's evil deeds,
and so that, seeing everyone as good, we may attain purity in our minds.
But if we too become people who rebuke and chastise, judge and demand an accounting, and investigate,
how does living in cities differ from dwelling in the wilderness? If you are not quiet in your heart, be quiet with your tongue.
If you cannot discipline your thoughts, discipline your senses.
If you are not solitary in your mind, be solitary in your body.
If you cannot keep vigil on your feet, keep vigil on your bed.
If you cannot manage prolonged fasts, at least fast until evening. And if you cannot manage a fast
until evening, at least keep yourself from eating your fill. If you are not holy in your heart, be holy in your body.
And if you do not mourn in your heart, at least clothe your face in mourning.
If you cannot act righteously, speak as a sinner. If you are not a peacemaker, do not be a troublemaker either.
If you cannot be diligent, be lowly in your thoughts. If you are not innocent, do not flare up against the guilty.
If you cannot shut the mouth of someone who speaks against his neighbor, at least guard yourself against becoming his accomplice.
Know that if fire goes out from you and burns others, you will be held accountable for the souls of everyone that fire touches.
And if you do not yourself set the fire, but agree with the person who does and take pleasure in his action, you share in his judgment.
If you love tranquility, you will be peaceful. And if you are found worthy of peace, you will rejoice at all times.
Seek understanding, not gold. Clothe yourself in humility, not fine linen. Acquire peace, not a kingdom.
No one has understanding without being humble. And whoever is not humble has no understanding either.
No one is humble without being peaceful. And whoever is not peaceful is not humble either. No one is peaceful without rejoicing.
Though people travel every path there is in this world, they cannot find peace until they draw near to hope in God.
The heart finds no peace from disturbances and stumbling blocks until it draws near to this.
This hope brings them peace and pours joy into their hearts. This is what was said by that mouth,
worthy of worship and full of holiness: “Come to me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest.”
“Draw near,” he says, “to hope in me, and leave your many paths behind, and you will find rest from toil and fear.”
Hope in God lifts up the heart. Fear of hell breaks it.
The light of the mind gives birth to faith, and faith gives birth to the consolation of hope.
And hope supports the heart. Faith is the revelation of insights.
When the mind grows dark, faith is hidden, and fear rules over us and cuts off our hope.
Faith that comes from instruction does not free a person from conjecture and doubts,
but rather the faith that dawns through insights and is called the revelation of truth.
As long as the mind understands God as God through the revelation of insights, fear does not approach the heart.
When we are left in darkness and lose this understanding so that we may be humbled,
Fear comes upon us to bring us to humility and repentance.
The Son of God endured the cross. Sinners, take courage in repentance!
If the outward appearance of repentance turned wrath away from the king, he will not now reject the sincerity of your minds.
If, even for someone whom he knew to be insincere, the outward appearance of humility turned wrath away from him,
how much more for you, who truly grieve over your transgressions!
Sorrow of mind is enough for him in place of the whole range of bodily labors, according to the words of the Interpreter.
A temple of grace is the person who is united
with God through continual meditation on him. What is meditation on him? Constant preoccupation with pleasing him, sorrow at all times,
and the constant toil of thought over those things that, because of the weakness of our nature, continually remain unfulfilled,
and continual sadness over them, which the mind bears with intense inward movements,
and offers before him in prayer, like a sacrifice, with humble remorse.
As far as possible, according to his strength, he holds concern for the body in contempt.
This is the person who carries within his soul the constant remembrance of God, as the blessed Bishop Basil said.
Prayer without distraction, he says, is prayer that produces constant meditation on God within the soul.
For this too, he says, is God's dwelling: through the constant remembrance with which we remember him, he dwells in us.
That is, through persistent meditation in the heart on preparing what pleases him.
Involuntary evil thoughts arise from the laxity that preceded them.
My brothers, people who wish to give the body a little rest merely to sustain it for God's service,
so that they may regain their strength and return again to their work.
During the few days of our rest, let us not abandon our vigilance completely
and surrender our whole soul to laxity, like people who are no longer expected to return to their work.
Those who are struck by arrows in a time of peace are those who, through willful lack of restraint, have stored up material within their souls.
And the filthy garment that they see themselves wearing in the holy place—that is, at the time
when God shines within their souls—is what they wove during the time of laxity.
These are the things that put us to shame at the time of pure prayer, when we wish to draw near.
These are the ones we made members of our household when we neglected our senses.
Watchfulness helps a person more than hard work does, and laxity harms him more than ease does.
For ease gives rise to inner battles. Even if they wear a person down, he has the power to end them.
As soon as he gives up ease and turns back to the realm of the world, they fall silent and flee from him.
What arises from laxity is not like this, even though slackness itself arises from comforts.
For as long as he is still within the realm of his freedom, he can once again bring his conduct back into conformity with his rules.
He is still within the realm of his freedom; but through laxity he has gone outside the realm of freedom.
Unless a person completely casts away all his watchfulness, he is not overcome by force,
so as to be compelled against his will to submit to things that give him no peace. And unless he completely abandons the boundary of his freedom,
events do not press upon him that bind him to a necessity he cannot resist.
Do not abandon the realm of freedom through any of your senses, O human being,
lest you be unable to enter it again. Ease harms only the young, but laxity harms even
the mature and the elderly. Those who, through ease, were led away by evil thoughts,
through watchfulness returned again and stood on the heights of good conduct.
For those who neglected watchfulness because they trusted in their hard work were carried captive from the heights of good conduct into a lax way of life.
Some were wounded in enemy territory and died in peacetime.
And some went out to trade for life and brought back plunder for themselves.
We should be distressed not when we stumble in something, but when we persist in it.
For stumbling sometimes happens even to the watchful, but remaining in those falls is utter death.
The sorrow we endure for the individual transgressions into which we are forcibly drawn
is counted for us as pure service by the grace that sustains our lives.
Anyone who sins in hope as he repeats his fall deals deceitfully with God.
The blow of punishment suddenly falls upon him unawares, and he does not reach the time he hoped for.
Everyone whose senses are unrestrained has an unrestrained heart. The work of the heart is a restraint upon the outward limbs.
If there is anyone who does this with discernment, like the fathers who came before us:
For it is known from the other things that can be seen in him:
that he is not bound to bodily advantages, does not love money, and is entirely free from anger.
But wherever these three are found in their opposite forms—love of bodily advantages, whether small or great,
readiness to anger, and being overcome by the belly—even if he studies the saints of old, know
that his outward laxity comes from an inward inability to endure, and not from a disregard for himself that arises from discernment.
Otherwise, why has he not acquired disregard for bodily things and gentleness? Disregard arising from discernment is accompanied by
voluntary freedom from attachment, disregard for life, and love for other people.
If he willingly endures losses for God's sake, he is pure within.
If he does not despise anyone because of that person's faults, he is truly free.
If he neither yearns for those who honor him nor is disturbed when he encounters those who do not greet him, he is truly dead to life here.
The watchfulness of discernment is better than practices of every kind undertaken at every level of human ability.
Do not hate the sinner. We are all guilty. If it is for God's sake that you are moved, weep for him.
Why do you hate him? Is it his sins that you hate? Pray for him,
so that you may become like Christ, who was not angry with sinners but prayed for them.
Have you not seen how he wept over Jerusalem? For we are deceived by Satan in many things.
Why should we hate someone who, like us, has been deceived by the one who deceives us? Why do you hate
the sinner, fellow human being? Is it because he is not righteous like you? And how are you righteous,
when you have no love? And if you have love, why do you not weep for him,
instead of persecuting him? It is through ignorance that people who are considered discerning become agitated over the deeds of sinners.
Be a herald of God's grace, since he provides for you even though you are unworthy.
And though you owe him much, his demand for repayment is not apparent in his dealings with you.
And for the little things in which you show willingness, he rewards you with great things.
Do not call God just any longer, for his justice is not apparent in his dealings with you.
Although David called him just and upright, his Son revealed to us that he is good and kind.
"He is kind," he says, "to the wicked and the ungrateful." How can you call God just,
When you come across that passage about the workers’ wages: “My friend, I am not wronging you.
I want to give this last man the same as you.
Or are you envious because I am good?” How can anyone call God just
when he comes across that story about the prodigal son? After he had squandered his possessions in debauchery,
merely because he showed repentance, his father ran and fell on his neck and gave him authority over all his possessions.
It is not someone else who says this about him, so that we might doubt his goodness. His own Son testifies to these things about him.
Where is God’s justice, seeing that while we were sinners,
Christ died for us? And if he is merciful here, we believe
that he does not undergo change. Far be it from us to entertain this wicked thought: that there is ever a time when God is not merciful.
God’s attributes do not change like those of mortals.
There is never a time when he lacks something and then acquires it, nor does what he possesses diminish or increase as it does with created beings.
Rather, whatever God possesses is with him eternally and without end,
as the blessed Interpreter also said in his commentary on Genesis.
Fear him because of his love, not because of the reputation for harshness attributed to him. Love him, because we owe him our love,
not only for what he will give, but also for what we have received. Even if he had made only this one world for our sake,
who could repay his grace? Where in our deeds is any repayment to him? Who first persuaded him to bring us into existence? And who pleads with him on our behalf
when we are forgotten, as though we had never existed? Who stirs our decayed remains to life? And from
where does the stirring of awareness once again enter the dust? Oh, the wonder of God’s mercy!
Oh, the marvel of our Creator’s goodness! Oh, the power of his provision for everyone!
Oh, his immeasurable kindness toward our nature: he brings even sinners back into existence!
Who can adequately praise him? The person who acted wickedly and blasphemed against him—
he raises him, motionless dust, into a glorious being endowed with knowledge and speech.
And the scattered, unfeeling dust and dispersed senses he makes into a rational nature, quick in its movements.
Even at his resurrection, the sinner cannot comprehend his grace.
Where is the Gehenna that could cause us grief? What torment is there whose fear could overpower us?
to surpass the joy of his love? And what is Gehenna compared with the grace of the resurrection? For he indeed raises us from Sheol,
and makes this perishable thing put on imperishability,
and raises in glory this one steeped in the disgrace of Sheol. O discerning people, come and marvel!
Who has a wise mind capable of wonder? Come, let us marvel at the grace of our Creator!
This is the repayment sinners receive: instead of the repayment justice demands, he repays them with resurrection.
And in return for those bodies that trampled on his laws, he will clothe them in the glory of perfection.
This grace shown after we have sinned is greater than that by which, when we did not exist, he brought us into being and formed us.
Glory to your immeasurable grace! Your favors have now silenced my words,
and no movement remains in me, not even to give you thanks. With what mouths shall we give thanks to you,
good King who loves our lives? Glory to you in both worlds, which you created for our upbringing and our delight,
from all whom you have brought into being to know your praise, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.
On the three degrees of knowledge, and the differences in their activity and movements.
And on the faith of the soul, and the wealth of mysteries hidden within it.
And on how opposed the knowledge of this world, with its methods, is to the simplicity of faith. 51.
Now a soul that travels the road of faith along the paths of its conduct, and has prospered in this many times,
if it turns back to the methods of knowledge, immediately becomes crippled in its faith
and is deprived of that power of faith perceived by the mind,
which reveals itself through various kinds of help in a tranquil soul that makes use of it simply, without investigation, in all its affairs.
A soul that has once entrusted itself to God in faith, and through many trials has tasted the help faith provides,
no longer has any concern for itself, but is held fast in wonder and silence.
Nor is it free to turn back to the methods of its knowledge and make use of them,
lest, because of this opposition, it also be deprived of divine providence,
which secretly visits it without ceasing, cares for its affairs, and constantly accompanies it everywhere,
as one that has despised providence, considering itself capable of directing itself by the power of its own knowledge.
For those in whose hearts the light of faith has dawned no longer dare even to pray for themselves:
Nor should they ask God, “Give us such and such,” or, “Take away from us
such and such,” nor concern themselves about themselves in any way, because with the discerning eyes of their faith
they continually see the fatherly care that shelters them,
coming from that true Father whose immeasurably powerful love surpasses all the affection of earthly fathers.
He has the power to do for us far beyond everything, beyond what we ask or think.
For knowledge is opposed to faith, and faith, in all that belongs to it, overturns the laws of knowledge.
I do not mean spiritual knowledge. For this is the defining limit of knowledge:
a person is not permitted to do anything without investigation and examination.
Instead, he must investigate whether what he has decided to undertake is possible.
But what about faith? Whenever “yes” and “no” approach it on equal terms, faith refuses to remain there.
Knowledge, unless it employs complications and devices, is not even recognized as existing.
This itself is a sign of its doubt concerning the truth.
Faith, however, requires a single, clear, simple mind, far removed from all cunning and searching for devices.
See how opposed they are to one another. The home of faith is a childlike mind and a pure heart.
“In the purity of their hearts,” it says, “they praised God.”
And, “Unless you turn and become like children,” and so on. Knowledge, however, is toward both these things
a persecutor and an opponent. Knowledge observes the boundaries of nature in all its paths.
Faith, however, makes its journey above nature.
Knowledge does not even allow one to attempt to approach anything that overturns nature, but instead to stay far away from it.
Faith, however, commands with authority and says, “You will tread on the viper and the adder, and trample the lion and the dragon.”
Fear accompanies knowledge, but [?] accompanies faith.
As long as a person proceeds by the devices of knowledge, he is not freed from fear, nor can he attain freedom.
But once he follows faith, immediately, like a free man and master of himself,
and like a son of God, he makes use of everything freely and with authority.
The person who has found the keys of faith makes use of all the created natures as God does.
For faith has the power even to create a new creation, in the likeness of God.
“You willed,” it says, “and everything stood before you.” And many times faith has been able to make everything out of nothing.
Knowledge, however, cannot make anything without materials.
Knowledge does not dare to venture beyond what has been granted to nature.
How so? Because the fluid nature of water does not support bodily footsteps upon its surface,
and fire burns anyone who challenges it, and venturing against
these things is dangerous. Knowledge carefully observes this.
It is entirely unwilling to command anyone to cross this boundary.
Faith, however, commands this with authority, saying, “If you walk upon fire, it will not burn you,
and rivers will not sweep you away.” Faith has done this very thing many times, before the eyes of all creation.
For if knowledge had been given a place there, it would never have permitted anyone to attempt such things.
For through faith many entered the mouth of the flame and restrained the power of the burning fire,
and remained within it unharmed; and they walked upon the surface of the sea as upon dry land.
Look, all these things are beyond nature and contrary to the restraints of knowledge.
Have you seen how faith shook the foundations of knowledge
and showed all its methods and laws to be empty? Have you seen knowledge,
how it observes the boundaries of nature? And have you seen faith,
how it steps beyond nature to make paths for its journey? For five thousand years, more or less,
the methods of knowledge governed the world.
Yet it was utterly unable to lift its head from the earth and perceive the power of its Maker,
until faith dawned upon us and freed us from the turmoil of labor over earthly things
and from empty slavery in pursuit of pointless distractions. And even now, when we have found an unfathomable sea and a treasure that cannot
be bounded, we long to cling to a poor little stream.
There is no knowledge that is free of need, however rich it becomes. But heaven and earth cannot contain the treasures of faith.
The person whose heart rests in the shelter of faith never lacks anything.
And although he has nothing, through faith he possesses everything.
As it is written: “Whatever you ask for in prayer, believing, you will receive.” And again: “Our Lord is near.”
“Do not worry about anything.” Knowledge constantly seeks ways to safeguard its possessions.
What, then, about faith? “Unless the Lord builds the house [?] and guards the town, the one who builds and stays awake to guard it labors in vain.”
The one who takes refuge in faith never makes use of schemes.
For knowledge praises fear everywhere, just as the wise man also said: “Blessed is the one whose heart is afraid.”
But what about faith? “He became afraid and began to sink.” And again: “You have not received a spirit of fear leading to slavery,
but a spirit of adoption as children, leading to the freedom that comes through faith and trust in God.”
And it says: “Do not be afraid of them, lest I break you before them.”
Fear always accompanies doubt, and doubt accompanies inquiry; investigation accompanies schemes, and schemes accompany knowledge.
Its constant inquiry and investigation reveal doubt and fear.
For knowledge does not always succeed in everything, as was shown above.
Often difficult events and many circumstances full of danger arise,
in which all knowledge and the devices of wisdom are unable to provide any help at all.
Their difficulty exceeds the full extent of the power of human knowledge.
Faith, however, has never been defeated by anything. For what help can human knowledge provide
in open battles against invisible beings and incorporeal powers,
along with many other things? You have seen how weak the power of knowledge is, and how strong the power of faith is.
Knowledge keeps its disciples from approaching anything harmful to nature.
But look here at the power of faith and what it commands its children: “In my name they will cast out demons and pick up snakes.
And if they drink deadly poison, it will not harm them.” Knowledge, for all who walk in its path,
commands this in accordance with its laws: that from the outset they should investigate the outcome of everything, and only then begin,
lest the outcome of the undertaking exceed the limits of human strength,
and they endure hardships for nothing, when it proves impossible for them and difficult to accomplish.
But what does faith say? “Everything is possible for the one who believes,” because nothing is difficult for God.
Oh, inexpressible wealth! A sea rich in its waves and in its wonderful
treasures, and the abundant outpourings of the power of faith! How full of encouragement
and how pleasant and full of confidence is the journey in its company! How easy its paths are!
And how pleasant its work is! Anyone who has been found worthy to taste faith and then turns back to the soul’s knowledge
is no different from someone who found a pearl of great price and exchanged it for a copper coin.
He has abandoned sovereign freedom and turned to the resources of poverty,
which are full of the fear of slavery. It is not that knowledge is contemptible, but that faith is higher than it.
And if we reject anything, it is not knowledge itself that we reject—certainly not!
Rather, we reject the distinctions between the different orders in which it proceeds contrary to the excellence of its nature,
and becomes allied with the order of demons. We will explain these things clearly later:
how many degrees there are through which knowledge proceeds, and what distinctions there are in each of them;
with what impulses it awakens in each of the orders while it remains in them;
in which of these orders, as it proceeds in it, it becomes opposed to faith and departs from nature;
what the distinctions are in the work within that order; and to which order, when you turn it back toward its original aim,
it returns to its natural condition and, through its good conduct, prepares steps leading to faith;
how far the distinctions of this order bring it; and how it passes from
this order to the one higher than it; and what the kinds of work are in that last order, which is first in honor;
and when knowledge is united with faith and becomes one with it,
clothes itself in fiery impulses received from it, is set ablaze by the Spirit, and acquires wings of freedom from the passions,
and is raised from service to earthly things to the realm of its Maker—along with other topics.
Therefore we ought to know that the degree at which faith works is higher than that of knowledge.
Knowledge itself is also perfected through faith.
It acquires the power to ascend on high and to perceive the One who is above all perception,
and to see the radiance of the One who cannot be comprehended by the mind and knowledge of created beings.
Knowledge, then, is a step by which a person ascends to the height of faith. Once he reaches faith, knowledge is no longer needed.
“Now,” he says, “we know only a little out of much, and we understand only a little out of much.”
But when perfection comes, even that little passes away.
Faith, then, shows us, as though before our eyes, the reality of that perfection which is to come.
Through faith, therefore, we learn about that which cannot be comprehended, and not through investigation and the power of knowledge.
All the works of [?]: fasting, almsgiving, keeping vigil, chastity,
together with the other things practiced through the body; and love for one's neighbor, humility of heart,
forgiveness of offenses, meditation on good things, investigation of the mysteries that in the Holy Scriptures
are concealed, the mind's attention to the labors of goodness, and keeping the passions of the soul within bounds,
and the other virtues accomplished in the soul—all these depend on knowledge, and it is what nourishes them.
Yet all these are steps by which the soul ascends to the exalted height of faith, and they are called virtues.
But the way of life that belongs to faith has an activity that is even above virtue.
It is not a matter of toil, but of perfect rest, and it fills the heart with consolation.
And it is accomplished in the movements of the soul. All the wondrous [?] of the spiritual way of life,
whose activity is perception through spiritual faculties, and the delight and gladness of the soul,
and love and joy in God, and everything else bestowed in that way of life
on the soul that has been made worthy by grace of that blessedness, according to the indications contained in the Holy Scriptures,
are already heaped up for it here through faith by God, who is rich in his gifts.
But someone says: “If all these good things and works of virtue mentioned above,
as well as abstaining from evil and discerning the subtle movements that arise in the soul,
and the struggle with thoughts, and the contest against enticing passions, and the rest—
without which even faith itself cannot display its power through its action in the soul—
if it is knowledge that brings all these to completion, how, then, can knowledge be thought to oppose faith?”
Resolution of the difficulty. There are three levels through which knowledge ascends and descends in a discernible way.
According to the differences between the regions through which it travels, it likewise undergoes change, and either does harm or gives help.
By three levels I mean: body, soul, and spirit.
Although knowledge is one in its nature, it takes on a body and a form according to its presence in these intelligible realms.
It also changes its means and the way its movements operate.
Listen, then, to the stages of its activity and the reasons why it harms or helps.
Knowledge, then, is a gift from God, given to rational beings as part of their nature from the beginning of their existence.
It is simple and indivisible in its nature, like the light of the sun.
Yet it acquires differences and divisions according to its activity. The First Stage of Knowledge.
Whenever knowledge follows love of the body, it gathers these resources: wealth, empty glory,
honor, adornments, bodily comforts, ways of protecting the body from things opposed to its nature,
the pursuit of rational wisdom useful for conducting the affairs of this world,
and becoming a source of new discoveries in crafts and fields of learning,
and the other things that crown the body in this visible world of its own.
Among the characteristics of this knowledge are those listed above in opposition to faith.
This is also called bare knowledge, because it is stripped of all thought of God. And it brings upon the mind a weakness that cannot
be expressed, because of its attachment to the body and because its entire concern is with this world.
As for this level of knowledge, the existence of any hidden power at all that works and governs on a person's behalf,
or of divine providence that cares for him, never enters its thoughts.
Instead, every good thing that comes to a person, his deliverance from harm, and his protection from difficult circumstances
and from the many adversities that attend our nature, openly and secretly, it considers to be the result of its own diligence and methods.
It is this level of knowledge that holds the opinion expressed by those who say, “There is no providential governance over visible things.”
Consequently, it cannot stop its continual anxiety and fear over bodily matters.
And for this reason: faintheartedness, sorrow, despair, fear of demons, dread of other people,
reports of raiders, rumors of plagues, thoughts of illnesses, anxiety over a shortage of food,
terror at death, fear of crawling creatures and wild animals, and other things like these.
And like a sea stirred by waves, it is troubled at every hour of the day and night,
because it does not know how to cast its care upon God with the confidence of faith in him.
For this reason it uses devices and tricks in all its affairs. And whenever its devices are thwarted by any cause,
because it does not see the hidden providence, it quarrels with people as though they were its obstructors
and adversaries. For in this knowledge is planted that tree of good and evil which uproots love.
It searches out the subtle faults in others, people's shortcomings and weaknesses, and viciousness in argument;
and twists of words, devious tricks, and all the other devices that dishonor a person are found in it.
In it are also boasting and pride, because it attributes to itself everything that happens, if it turns out well, and not to God.
Faith [?], however, attributes its deeds to grace.
For this reason it cannot become proud, as it is written: “I have strength for everything through the grace that helps me.”
And again: “Not I, but the grace that is with me.” And as for the blessed apostle's saying, “Knowledge makes people proud,”
he said this about knowledge that is not mingled with faith and trust in God, not about the knowledge of truth—certainly not!
For the knowledge of truth perfects in humility the souls of those who possess it [?].
Such were Moses, David, Isaiah, Peter, Paul, and the rest of the saints who were found worthy of perfect knowledge, within the limits of human nature.
And because, through various divine visions and revelations, and through the exalted vision of spiritual things,
their knowledge is constantly absorbed in inexpressible mysteries,
in comparison with these things they regard themselves as dust and ashes.
That other knowledge naturally becomes proud, because it walks in darkness
and tests its affairs by comparison with earthly things. It does not know that anything higher exists.
And all those who are carried away by pride are so because they measure their conduct by earthly and bodily things
and rely on their own activity, rather than raising their minds to things beyond comprehension.
As long as they meditate on those waves of the glorious splendor of the Godhead, and their activity is on high,
their minds do not incline to dwell on shameful things and empty thoughts.
For those who walk in the light cannot go astray.
For this reason, all those who stray from the light of the knowledge of the Son of God and turn aside from the truth walk along these paths.
This is the first order of knowledge, when it follows the love of the body.
It is this that we reject and declare to be opposed not only to faith,

but also all the works of virtue.
The second degree of knowledge.
For whenever knowledge leaves the first aim and turns toward the soul’s meditation and love,
it practices the good things described above through the movements of the soul together with the senses of the body, by the light of its own nature.
These are fasting, prayer, compassion, reading the Holy Scriptures with virtue as the aim,
and struggle against the passions, along with the rest. For all good actions and the virtuous distinctions seen in the soul,
and the wonderful rites performed in Christ’s church, the Holy Spirit brings to perfection in this intermediate degree of knowledge
through the working of its power. It is the Spirit that opens paths in our hearts that lead to faith.
Through this knowledge we gather provisions for that true world of ours. Even up to this point, knowledge is still bodily
and composite, even though it is occupied with virtue and even though it is itself the path that leads us to faith.
For there is a degree higher than this, to which knowledge can ascend with Christ’s help if it works diligently,
taking as the foundation of its work solitude away from other people, reading the Holy Scriptures, and prayer.
The other good things are brought to perfection through these. This is the measure of the second degree of knowledge,
in which all good things are practiced. It is called knowledge of actions,
because it accomplishes its activity in the outward order through actions perceptible to the bodily senses.
The third degree of knowledge, which is the degree of perfection.
As for how knowledge becomes refined, acquires spirituality, and comes to resemble the way of life of those invisible powers,
whose service is accomplished not through the perceptible activity of labor but through the mind’s contemplation—listen.
When knowledge rises above earthly things and concern with practical activity,
and begins to test its movements in the inward things hidden from the eyes,
and to some extent dismisses the memories of things from which the twisting of the passions arises,
and stretches upward and follows faith through contemplation of the world to come,
love of the promises, and inquiry into hidden things, then
faith itself swallows up knowledge and gives birth to it anew, so that it becomes wholly and entirely spiritual.
Then it can fly in realms without bodies,
and explore the depths of the unfathomable sea of God’s wonderful providence:
of intelligible and sensible natures, and to investigate spiritual mysteries, which are perceived by a simple and subtle mind.
Then the inner senses are awakened to the work of the spirit,
according to the order that prevails in that way of life without death or corruption.
For they have already received here, as in a mystery, an intelligible resurrection, as a sure demonstration of that universal renewal.
These are the three orders of knowledge within which the whole course of human life is contained: of the body, the soul, and the spirit.
From the time a person begins to distinguish between good and evil until he leaves the world,
within these three measures enters [?] until he leaves the world; within these three measures the knowledge of his soul enters,
including the full extent of all injustice and wickedness, and the utmost limit of all righteousness,
and reaching into the depths of all the mysteries of the spirit: one and the same knowledge operates within these three measures.
Within them lies every movement of the mind as it rises or falls, whether in good things, in evil things, or in an intermediate state.
The fathers call these measures: according to nature, outside nature, and above nature.
These are the three regions into which the awareness of the rational soul rises and descends, as has been said.
Either it practices righteousness according to nature, or it is caught up above nature in its awareness, in contemplation directed toward
God, or it goes out beyond nature to feed pigs, like the man who lost the wealth of his discernment while working amid the filth of demons.
For the first order of knowledge holds the soul back from the labors of pursuing good things.
The intermediate order sets the soul ablaze with the fervor of advancing through the degrees of faith.
The third order is the soul's rest from work and a foreshadowing of the life to come,
in which, through the mind's meditation alone, it delights in the mysteries of the good things to come.
But because nature has not yet been raised above the order of mortality and the weight of the flesh,
so as to exist completely in that spiritual state [?] which is above any inclination to change,
and it is impossible to practice a perfection lacking nothing in the mortal world,
and to abandon the nature of the flesh completely while still living in it, one alternates between this state and that.
At times, like someone poor and needy, the soul occupies itself in that intermediate order of knowledge,
with practicing through effort the virtues implanted in nature, because of the nature of the body.
And at times, like those who have received the Spirit of adoption as children,
In the mysteries of freedom, it delights in the gift of the Spirit, to the extent that its giver sees fit.
Then it returns again to the poverty of its world—that is, the body—while remaining watchful within the body,
so that the body does not take it captive through the temptations found in its world, by means of its turbulent and wayward impulses.
For as long as it is confined behind the gates of the flesh,
it has no assurance. For there is no complete freedom in an incomplete world.
For all the work of knowledge belongs to the world and to disciplined practice.
The works of faith, however, are not performed through toil,
because they are accomplished through spiritual movements, in the soul’s naked delight, beyond the senses.
For faith is subtler than knowledge, just as knowledge is subtler than things perceived by the senses.
For all the saints who have been found worthy of the spiritual way of life, which is wonder at God,
are led by the power of faith, in the delight of that way of life which is above nature.
By faith I do not mean believing in the distinction between the worshiped persons of the divine Being,
and in the properties of its nature, and in the marvelous saving work accomplished in our humanity through his assumption of our nature.
Rather, by this faith I mean the light perceived by the mind, which dawns in the soul through grace.
Through the testimony of the mind, it supports the heart without doubt,
with the assurance of hope that is free from all conjecture, and not through instruction received by hearing.
It shows the soul, through spiritual eyes, the mysteries hidden within it and the concealed riches of the Godhead,
which are hidden from the eyes of mortal people and revealed through the Spirit to those who are nourished at Christ’s table by meditating on his laws.
As he said, “If you keep my commandments, I will send you the Spirit, the Advocate, whom the world cannot receive,
and he will show you the whole truth.” In this way it also shows a person the holy power that shelters him at all times.
That power is the Advocate. Through the power of this faith, every part of the soul is set ablaze as though by fire,
and it boldly faces every danger with trust in God.
On wings that come from faith, it rises above the sphere of this visible creation,
and becomes like someone drunk, continually lost in the wonder of meditation on God. Through simple vision,
and through imageless insights concerning the divine nature, it trains the mind to gaze in meditation upon his hiddenness.
For until he who is the fulfillment of the mysteries comes, and we are found worthy to behold his revelation openly,
faith ministers the holy, ineffable mysteries in the house of God.
May we be found worthy of them through the grace of Christ: here as a pledge,
and there in their true reality, in the kingdom of heaven, with all who love him. Amen.
Further concise chapters on another theme: the distinctions between the movements of knowledge. Fifty-two.
Whenever knowledge occupies itself with visible things, about which it receives instruction through the senses, it is called natural.
And whenever it occupies itself with the intelligible powers within them and with incorporeal natures,
it is called spiritual, because it receives perception through the spirit,
and not through the senses. In both these cases, the material for the soul's understanding is external to it.
But whenever it occupies itself with the divine Being, it is called supernatural—or rather, unknowing, which is higher than knowledge.
The soul does not receive contemplation of this through material external to itself, as with the former kinds.
Rather, without material, it is suddenly revealed inwardly, within the soul, by grace, without being expected.
For the kingdom of God is within us.
It does not come through expecting it from some place or through watching for it, according to the saying of our Lord.
