Rather, it is revealed within the hidden form of the mind, he says, without a cause and without reflection upon it.
For the mind does not even have material with which to reflect upon it.
The first, he says, comes from constant meditation and diligence in learning.
The second comes from upright conduct and faith of mind.
The third, then, belongs to faith alone, because there knowledge will cease,
works will come to an end, and the senses will no longer be needed.
Thus, insofar as it descends below this boundary, it is called knowledge.
And the farther it descends, the more highly knowledge is esteemed.
When it reaches the earth and earthly things, knowledge is mistress of everything.
Without it, everything is crippled and ineffectual. But when the soul raises its gaze upward
and extends the range of its movements toward heavenly things, and longs for those things that, to the eyes
are not seen by the body, and the flesh has no power over them; then everything rests on faith.
Again, on the purpose of prayer, and [?] concerning those things that must necessarily be kept in constant remembrance:
and which are very beneficial if a person reads them with discernment and holds to them. 53.
Being steadfast in the petition of one's prayer through trust in God is a principal part of the gift of faith.
Firmness of faith in God is not soundness of belief,
even though that is the mother of faith, but a soul that gazes upon God's truth through the power of its conduct.
Whenever you find faith in the holy Scriptures, in passages where it is linked with conduct,
do not understand the teaching about it as referring to correctness of belief.
Faith that gives the assurance of trust is never required of the imperfect or of those whose minds are corrupted and estranged from the truth.
But firmness of faith reveals itself in the soul in proportion to its progress in conduct,
with an intention directed toward what our Lord's commandments prescribe. The light of the soul is constant study of the Scriptures.
For they imprint on the mind reminders useful for vigilance against the passions,
and for remaining continually with God in love and purity of prayer.
And they set before us a path made peaceful by the footsteps of the saints. Yet
do not rely on knowledge of the sayings when it is not accompanied by great watchfulness
and constant attentiveness to prayer at all times.
You must accept words spoken from experience, even if the person speaking them is uneducated.
Even the great treasury of earthly kings does not refuse an addition from a beggar's small coin.
And from small streams the great currents of rivers grow.
For if remembering virtuous people renews in us the desire for virtue whenever we converse with them in our thoughts,
remembering the dissolute also renews a shameful desire in our minds whenever we remember them.
For remembering each of these imprints the distinctive features of their deeds in our thoughts.
And, as though with a finger, it shows us the ugliness of their deeds or the heights of their exalted conduct, whether of the former or of the latter.
And that remembrance, with its promptings, whether toward the right or toward the left, compels us to dwell on them when our minds are unguarded,
as images of their distinctive conduct are portrayed in the mirrors of our minds, and we eagerly become spectators of them.
Thus, it is not only dwelling on evil that harms those who are caught up in it,
but also seeing and remembering those who carry it out.
Nor, again, is it only the practice of virtues that greatly benefits those who accomplish them,
but also the mental image imprinted by memories of the people who practice them. And from this
it is clear that those who are close to reaching the state of purity
are continually granted the sight of holy people in visions at night.
And during the daytime, throughout the whole day, a source of joy for them
in the inward activity of their minds is the images of the saints imprinted on their souls.
Through this they strive still more fervently to practice the virtues,
and a greater fire of love for virtue is left within them.
And they say that the holy angels take on the likeness of honorable and virtuous people
and appear to the soul in the dreams of sleep, as its movements wander, to give it joy and greater encouragement.
They also stir these images during the daytime in the mind’s vision, and their daytime labor becomes lighter through their delight in holy people.
And so they press on with greater speed. Likewise, at a time when the struggle is intense,
demons visit in the same manner someone who continually pursues evil thoughts.
They take on a likeness to appear to the soul: visions that stir up all the more, in daytime memories, the person caught up in these things.
At [?], they also appear in a terrifying vision that frightens and weakens the soul
and shows it the difficulty of a life of stillness and solitude, along with other things.
So, my brothers, let us discern the memories in our meditation: which of them we should occupy ourselves with,
and which we should quickly drive away when they approach our minds—whether they come from the activity of demons
who supply fuel for the passions, whether desire or anger,
or from the holy angels, who give an indication of joy and knowledge
and of encouragement through the thoughts they impart when they draw near us, or from the memory of earlier deeds and sensory experiences,
from which thoughts are stirred in the soul that suit one side or the other.
And let us gain experience of both through discerning knowledge, both of their appearance and of their activity.
also of the service of their deeds. And let us immediately attach a separate prayer to each of them.
Love sustained by material things is like a small flame whose light lasts only while it is supplied with oil,
and like a river sustained by rain: as soon as the source sustaining it fails, the force of its current subsides.
Love whose source is God is like a spring gushing from the depths, whose flowing stream never ceases.
For he alone is the spring of love whose supply never fails. Do you want to take delight in the singing of your worship
and to feel the words of the Spirit that you sing? Give up completing the full amount.
Do not keep track of its measured lengths. Recite the verses with the intention of praying.
Abandon habitual repetition. Understand what I am saying. As for the things expressed as narrative,
let your mind, as you recite them, attend to something belonging to God's saving work, as though you were reading,
so that, through the great meanings contained in them, your soul may be awakened
to wonder at God's saving work, and from this be moved either to praise or to beneficial sorrow.
As for the passages that are prayers, apply them to yourself.
Once your mind has become firmly established in these things, distraction has already given way and departed.
For there is no peace of mind in the service of slavery, nor the turmoil of distraction in the freedom of children.
For distraction habitually sucks away the taste of the meanings and plunders the understanding contained in them,
like a leech that sucks away the body's life through the blood of its limbs.
Indeed, distraction could rightly be called Satan's chariot, if that is possible.
For Satan himself, like a charioteer, habitually rides upon it constantly, bringing a host of passions with him.
He enters the miserable soul amid the clamor of its distraction. Understand this too with discernment:
do not become someone who delivers the words in the verses of your singing and prayer as though speaking on behalf of someone else,
lest you imagine that you are diligently carrying out the work of a messenger,
while you remain entirely outside the sorrow and joy contained in them.
Instead, speak the words pleadingly as though on your own behalf, with understanding and discerning feeling,
like someone convinced that he is truly dealing with his own affairs. Despondency comes from the wandering of the mind.
And wandering comes from neglecting labor and reading, and from prolonged conversation.
Not to use counterarguments against the thoughts that speak within us, but through supplication
to cut off their speech: this is the sign of a mind that has found wisdom and strength from grace.
Its true knowledge has freed it from much toil.
By discovering the shortcuts it has grasped, it has cut short the many windings of the long road.
For we do not always have the strength to silence all hostile thoughts by answering them.
Rather, sometimes we receive a wound from them that does not heal for a long time.
You are entering into battle against beings who are six thousand years old.
They also have equipment with which to strike you, beyond your own wisdom and training.
But even when you win, the filth of the thoughts stains your mind, and the stench of their rottenness lingers in your nostrils for a time.
But through the first [?], you are freed from all these things and from danger, because there is no helper like God.
Constant tears during prayer are a sign of divine mercy,
of which the soul has been found worthy through its repentance, which has been accepted; and through tears it has begun to enter the open plain of purity.
For unless thoughts have been lifted above concern with passing things and have cast away hope in the world,
and contempt for it has arisen within them, and they have begun preparing provisions for the day of a person's departure,
and contemplation of things beyond this world has flowed into the soul, the eyes cannot stream with tears. For tears arise from
careful, undistracted meditation and from persistent thoughts that do not turn aside,
and through some subtle recollection that falls into the mind and pains the heart with concern about it.
From this, tears flow continually. When you turn to manual work as a regular practice in your solitude,
do not make the fathers' commandment about it a cover for the love of money.
They say: Let your work be little, to counter despondency, and let it be work that does not disturb the mind.
But if you wish to devote yourself more intensely to it for the sake of almsgiving, know that prayer ranks higher than almsgiving.
And if it is for your own needs, then, unless you are greedy, what our Lord provides for you is enough to meet your needs.
He has never abandoned those who serve him to be anxious about passing things.
“Seek first God's kingdom and his righteousness, and these things will be added to you before you ask,” our Lord said.
One of the saints said: “For this is not the aim of your way of life:
so that you may feed the hungry and your cell may become a lodging place for strangers.
For this way of life is much more suitable for those who live in the world,
not for solitaries who are free from concerns about visible things and keep watch over their minds in prayer.
If you are ever found worthy of solitude, with its light burdens, in the kingdom of its freedom,
do not let the thought of fear alarm you as usual, with the many kinds of changing thoughts that accompany its fluctuations.
Instead, be like someone who believes that a guardian is with him and is firmly convinced in his understanding
that he and all creation are under one Lord, and that a single command moves them all, brings them to rest, and governs them.
Not one fellow creature can harm another without the command of the one who governs them.
And since everything is under his providential care, stand firm in this confidence and take courage.
Even if freedom has been given to some of them, it does not extend to everything. Neither demons nor destructive animals,
nor human beings acting wickedly—none of them can satisfy its will by harming anyone,
until the command is given and permission is granted within a certain limit.
Not every exercise of freedom is allowed by the divine command to be put into action. Otherwise, no flesh would survive.
For the Lord does not abandon his creation to the freedom of demons or human beings,
so that any of them may use it as they please. Therefore, say to yourself, “A guardian is with me.
Not a single creature has the power even to appear before me unless permission has been given from above.”
Thus, even when you see them with your own eyes and hear their threats with your own ears, do not concede that they dare to act.
If they had received an order by the command
of heaven, there would be no need for speech or words; action would simply follow their will.
But say to yourself, “If it is my Lord’s will that evil beings should have power over what he has made,
I will not resist this, like someone who wishes to thwart his master’s will.”
Then even in your trial you will be filled with joy, like someone who knows and perceives
that his Lord is the one who governs him. Therefore, make your heart firm in the confidence of faith in the Lord,
and do not be shaken, either by the terror of the night or by the arrow that flies by day.
For, it is said, the righteous person’s faith in God makes the wild animals like lambs and goats.
“I am not righteous,” you say, “that I should trust in God.” But be assured:
because you went out into a wilderness full of afflictions to practice righteousness, you are therefore a servant of God’s will.
Are you then troubling yourself in vain as you endure these hardships?
It is not that God desires human hardships, but that you should offer him your own sufferings as a sacrifice of love.
All who love God show him this distinction: they suffer out of love for him.
For all who wish to live in the fear of God in Jesus Christ are afflicted.
Then he gives them authority over the hidden things of his treasures. For one of the saints said:
“There was a certain venerable old solitary, and once I went to him when I was worn down by trials.
He was sick and gasping. After greeting him, I sat beside him
and said to him, ‘Pray for me, father, because I am terribly worn down by the trials brought by demons.’
He opened his eyes, looked closely at me, and said to me, ‘My son, you are young, and God does not allow trials to come upon you.’
Then I said to him, ‘I am young, but I face the trials of strong men.’
Then he said to me, ‘God therefore wants to make you wise.’ And I said to him, ‘How am I becoming wise
when I taste death every day?’ But he said to me, ‘God loves you. Be silent.
God is going to give you his gift.’ He also said to me, ‘Know, my son,
that I have been at war with demons for thirty years, and for twenty years I received no help at all.
But when twenty-five years had passed, rest began to appear.
As it came, it increased. When twenty-eight years had passed, it increased more and more.
At the completion of thirty years, rest had increased so much that I cannot tell how great it is.’
And he said, ‘When I want to stand for the prayer service, I am allowed to recite one section of the Psalms.
For the rest, even if I stand for three days, I remain in wonder with God, without feeling any weariness.’”
See what boundless rest prolonged labor has brought forth!
There was one of the fathers who used to eat twice a week.
He told us, “On a day when I speak with anyone,
I cannot keep my customary rule of fasting, but am compelled to break it.”
And we have understood that guarding the tongue not only awakens the mind toward God,
but also secretly supplies great strength for completing the outward labors performed by the body.
And the understanding is continually illuminated through hidden spiritual practice, as our fathers said:
“Guarding the mouth awakens the conscience toward God, if one keeps silent with understanding.”
Now this holy man was deeply devoted to keeping vigil at night, and he said:
“On a night when I remain standing until morning and then rest after the psalms,
after I wake from sleep, I spend that day as though I were not in this world.
No earthly thought enters my heart,
nor do I need prescribed rules; rather, I remain in wonder throughout that entire day.
“Now on one of those days, a day on which I was to eat, after four days in which I had tasted nothing,
I rose to perform the evening service and then eat. I stood in the courtyard of my cell while there was still plenty of sunlight.
I was conscious only of beginning the section of psalms at the start of the service. After that, until the next day, when the sun shone on my face
and my clothes grew warm on my body, I was unaware of where I was.
When the sun troubled me by scorching my face, my mind came back to me,
and I saw that it was another day. And I gave thanks to God for how
abundant his grace is toward human beings, and for the greatness of which he makes those who seek him worthy.” The accounts of holy men are finished.
Further accounts concerning overshadowing. 54.
Although we have spoken about this from another perspective in the preceding passages, as far as the occasion allowed,
it is no burden for us to explain it further here as well. Overshadowing is
a term indicating help and protection, and also the reception of a gift—a heavenly gift.
As in the saying: “The Holy Spirit will come, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you.”
And another example is the saying: “With your right hand, Lord, overshadow me.”
This is a request for help. And likewise the saying: “I will overshadow this city and deliver it.”
Thus we understand two kinds of activity in the overshadowing that comes from God upon human beings:
one occurring mystically and within the understanding, and the other through actual events.
And the first is the holiness received through divine grace.
That is, through the working of the Holy Spirit, a person is sanctified in body and soul.
Such was the case with Elisha and John, and with the blessed Mary, blessed among women.
But hers is beyond comparison and above the order of created beings.
Let us turn to what belongs in part to the rest of the saints, like limbs belonging to a body.
There is a mysterious kind of overshadowing, such as that experienced by individual saints, which is a kind
that works upon and overshadows the mind. And whenever a person is found worthy of this overshadowing,
the mind is caught up in wonder and drawn out into some divine revelation.
And for as long as this working overshadows the mind,
the person is above the movement of the soul’s thoughts, through participation in the Holy Spirit.
This is what the apostle said to the Ephesians in the form of a prayer,
when he wished to make this mystery known to them, saying: “May the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory,
give you a spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him, and may the eyes of your hearts be enlightened.”
And what comes of this? “That you may know what is the hope of his calling, and what are the riches of the glory of his inheritance among the saints,
and what is the surpassing greatness of his power in us who believe.”
This is one mysterious kind of overshadowing:
whenever this power overshadows a person, that person is found worthy of the glory of the new world through revelation.
This is the share that has fallen to the saints in light, of which the blessed Paul spoke,
and of which those are found worthy who have received holiness of mind from the Spirit through their holy and virtuous conduct.
There is another kind of overshadowing, whose working is known through its practical effects.
It is a perceptible power that continually shelters a person and hovers over them,
and drives away any harm or misfortune that threatens to approach their body or soul.
Without being visible, it is perceived by the mind, clear and recognizable to the eye
of faith. The saints know it more fully through experience, as it is written:
“The camp of the Lord’s angels surrounds those who fear him, and he delivers them.”
“Many,” it says, “are the trials of the righteous, but the Lord delivers them from them all.”
How the hidden vigilance within the soul is preserved,
and what causes drowsiness and coldness to enter the mind and extinguish the holy warmth in the soul,
and kill its desire for God, for spiritual and peaceful delights. 55.
The hostile power has no ability to hinder those who desire good things,
if the lovers of good things themselves do not provide an opening for his wicked schemes.
The matter is as follows: every impulse of love for anything good
is accompanied, as soon as it begins to stir, by a certain zeal whose heat resembles burning coals.
This zeal normally surrounds that impulse of love like a wall and drives every opposing force and obstacle out of its path.
It possesses immense strength and indescribable power
to fortify the whole soul against growing slack or being shaken by the assaults of any hardships.
The former is the power of holy desire planted in the soul’s nature.
The latter is an awakening stirred up by the power
of the anger naturally present within it, which God has placed in us by nature to guard the boundaries of our nature,
so that the force of its onslaught may be roused to fulfill the soul’s natural desire, which is virtue.
It is impossible to practice virtue without it. For it is called zeal.
It is what repeatedly inspires a person with zeal, stirs him, sets him aflame, and gives him courage
to disregard his body amid the afflictions and terrible trials that befall him, to surrender himself confidently to death,
and to confront the forces of the rebel, for the sake of accomplishing what his soul has virtuously come to love.
For a certain man clothed in Christ, in one place in his book, called this zeal a dog and a guardian of God’s law,
which is virtue. Virtue is the fulfillment of God’s laws.
For this zealous power grows strong, awakens, and is set aflame to guard the house for two reasons.
And again, it grows weak, falls asleep, and becomes negligent for two other reasons.
The first cause of its warmth and vigilance is when a certain fear awakens in a person,
because he is concerned about the virtues he has acquired or is yet to acquire.
lest it be plundered or corrupted by some misfortune that befalls it.
This is stirred up by divine providence in all diligent practitioners of virtue,
to keep the soul watchful and constantly zealous, so that it does not fall asleep.
Now, whenever this fear is stirred up in our nature, this dog of which we have spoken, by night and by day,
burns hot like a blazing furnace. It rouses our nature to be watchful like a cherub and to scan all its surroundings at all times.
One might say that if a bird passes around it, it is stirred up and barks with an indescribably fierce rush.
When this fear is on behalf of the body, it is satanic, because the person has become doubtful in his faith concerning God's providence,
and has forgotten how God cares for those who concern themselves with virtue, continually looking after their needs.
As the Holy Spirit said through the mouth of the prophet: “The eyes of the Lord are on the righteous,
and his ears are ready to hear them.” And, “The Lord's concern is for those who fear him.”
And elsewhere, speaking as though in his own person to those who practice virtue, he says:
“No evil will approach you, and no plague will come near your dwelling.
For he will command his angels concerning you, to guard you, and they will carry you in their arms”—along with the rest of the verses that are written.
So whenever this fear is on behalf of the soul, because of the misfortunes that befall virtue,
lest it be plundered or harmed through one of these causes, this is a godly thought and a virtuous reflection.
This distress and fear in the soul, and the dread that torments the mind with its anxiety, come from God's providence. There is also a second cause
of the dog's strength and fierceness: when the love of virtue grows still greater in the soul.
For in proportion to the love in the soul for that to which it clings
in love—that is, godly thought—this natural zeal becomes correspondingly fierce on its behalf.
As for the causes of its slackness and sleep, one of them is when this love grows faint and diminishes in the soul.
The second is when some thought of self-confidence enters and settles in the soul.
The person becomes confident and repeatedly thinks that he has nothing to fear from anything that could harm him.
As a result, he throws off the armor of zeal and becomes like a house without a guard. The dog falls asleep and neglects its watch.
Most often, it is because of this thought that most spiritual houses are plundered.
This happens when the brightness of that flame of holy knowledge within the soul grows dim.
What causes this darkening, unless some subtle thought of conceit enters and slips into the soul,
or a person falls into excessive concern for these bodily things, or frequent encounters with the world come his way?
Whenever the spiritual athlete encounters worldly people, his soul is immediately brought low, especially when he encounters a woman.
Likewise, if he meets many people, the sight of them inevitably wears down his soul through vainglory.
In short, whenever the world confronts it, the wandering mind resembles a helmsman who was sailing pleasantly on the sea,
with a gentle wind blowing for him from [?] toward the harbor, and suddenly fell among the rocks.
Excellent distinctions concerning human life. 56.
The closer a person draws to this world in his way of life, the more firmly love of material things becomes established in him.
Thinking about them keeps him constantly disturbed, and he quarrels with other people over them.
Without realizing it, he becomes attached in affection to particular individuals among them.
But when the mind advances through subtle meditation on the world to come, an incomparable contemplation continually awakens within it.
In hope it longs for the things it cannot see, forgetting the things that are here.
From time to time he forgets himself as he becomes absorbed in spiritual insights, and in his thoughts he pays no attention to visible things.
Thus, in action as well as in thought, he comes to despise all the concern he takes over them.
The mingled love that distinguishes between persons is erased from him, and a single love, independent of sight, becomes firmly established in his soul.
Little by little, the conscious remembrance of these human things slips away from his mind, and contemplation of hidden things increases within him.
It grows strong and overcomes bodily thoughts. From then on he withdraws from these perishable things as far as nature allows.
And were it not that his inward remembrance rouses him at a time of need for one thing or another that cannot be entirely disregarded—
for most of the time his mind is gathered into those things to come, through the contemplation of them in which he has advanced.
Because of them, he becomes a fool in the eyes of all the wisdom of this world.
His memory becomes weak, and he becomes foolish when judged by the standards of human knowledge.
Blessed is the person who has been found worthy of these things! Tears never cease flowing from his eyes
whenever he turns inward, remembering the things in which human beings go astray:
what they have been left to, and what occupies his own whole inner being; what toil there is, and what wandering, and for the sake of what things!
It is said of Paul that for three years, through these stirrings that ruled in his soul, tears abounded within him, and he could not bring them to a stop.
This thought counsels a person with a stirring of tears:
when he becomes aware of that future hope and turns his mind to the things of this world,
how much less natural life is worth than that hope reserved for eternity in the new life.
Through this feeling he becomes dead to all passing things and to concern about them.
All the passions of body and soul die within him. Let us remember these things, my beloved, and despise the things here,
as far as we can. In this way, little by little, we draw near in our inner movements to those things to come.
For unless a person first forces himself and repeatedly looks with contempt on the things before his eyes,
so that he gradually leaves them behind and thus advances,
and reflection and meditation on those things increase within him, he remains in this body in his way of life.
Even those traveling along a road—unless they advance by walking day after day and shorten their journey,
but instead remain where they are—the road before them never grows shorter, and they never
reach the place they are aiming to arrive at. Our own situation is like this too.
Unless we force ourselves little by little, we will never gain the strength to free ourselves from bodily things and turn our gaze toward God.
This is wisdom: because struggling with these things is so hard once a person has become entangled in any of them,
let him struggle not to approach them. In this way he also reduces his thoughts about them.
Then, as reflection on them diminishes, the mind is freed to turn its gaze toward something else.
I am not saying that we should take no care of our needs. That would be a constraint that cuts human nature off from life.
Rather, we should not make this our primary work and put this divine work in second place.
Instead, while attending to our needs in moderation, let us leave the concern about them to God.
Let us place our trust in God more than in ourselves.
And if someone should dare to disregard these needs entirely for the sake of those other things,
I do not think it blameworthy, since we have all these encouragements from the Scriptures,
which teach us to take courage through hope, as it is written: “Our Lord is near.
Do not worry about anything.” And David says, “Cast your concern on the Lord, and he will sustain you.”
“The rich have become poor and gone hungry, but those who seek the Lord will lack no good thing.”
And our Lord commanded us, saying, “Do not worry about anything, but fill yourselves with meditation on the things to come.”
And you will not lack these earthly things that are necessary for the needs of nature.
May God in his grace grant us that his love may increase within us, so that through constant meditation on him we may forget the world and everything belonging to it, being released from its bonds.
And instead of many bonds, may we be bound by one bond, which cannot be undone in those who love him.
For he is the kingdom of the worlds above. May we too be bound to him, so that we may be worthy of the mystery of blessedness.
Its fullness is kept in the world to come for those who have gained him here.
May we too gain him and become his possession through the strength that comes from him, forever and ever. Amen.
On endurance for the love of God, and how abundantly help from God is available to it. 57.
The more a person despises this world, taking care to fear [?] God, the more divine providence draws near to him.
He secretly senses its help, and clear thoughts are given to him so that he may understand it.
Even if someone is deprived of the good things of this world against his will, the more he lacks them,
the more mercy accompanies him, and divine compassion carries him.
Glory to him who shows us mercy through things on the right and things on the left, and makes everything an occasion for us to find life!
For those whose own will is too weak to gain their lives,
he leads their souls toward virtue through involuntary suffering. That poor man Lazarus, too, was not
deprived of the good things of this world by his own choice; his body was also tormented by sores.
He had two bitter afflictions, each worse than the other:
illness and poverty. Yet in the end he was honored in the embrace of the chief of the patriarchs.
God is near to the suffering heart that cries out to him in distress.
And although he sometimes leaves a person to endure these bodily sufferings for his benefit,
like a physician who brings healing through the severe pain of incisions, nevertheless the Lord shows him great mercy in his soul,
in proportion to the severity of his painful afflictions. Therefore, whenever the love of Christ has not so prevailed in you
that you remain free from suffering in all afflictions because of your joy in him, know that the world is more alive in you than Christ.
Whenever illnesses and deprivation, or bodily injury, or fear of harm to the body,
disturb your mind and turn it away from the joy of your hope and clear meditation on our Lord, know that the body is alive in you, and not Christ.
The one whose love holds the greatest power over you is the one who lives in you.
If, when all your needs are fully supplied without anything lacking, and your body is not ailing,
and there is no fear of opposition, you can then proceed peacefully on your journey toward Christ,
know that you are weak in your mind and lack a taste of the glory of God.
I am not judging you for being like this, but only asking you to recognize how far you fall short of perfection, even the
partial perfection of the way of life of the saints who came before us.
Do not say that no human being has ever been found whose mind rose entirely above weakness,
even when the body was tormented by every trial of suffering, and the power of love for Christ overcame the mind’s susceptibility to suffering.
But I refrain from bringing to mind the examples of the martyrs,
lest we be unable to stand before the flood of their sufferings:
how greatly endurance, arising from the power of love, overcame the severity of the body’s affliction and its love for itself.
But because even remembering these things is difficult for human nature,
because we are bewildered by the greatness of the matter and the wonder of seeing it, let us turn [?] to the philosophers who are without God.
From there let us learn about the weakness of our will by comparing it with their endurance.
But let this too be kept for its proper time, since we intend to explain it in its own place, knowing that this very thing is also a sign of weakness:
that we do not judge the matter from ourselves, so as to believe how low we lie and that it is possible for someone to be wholly above this.
A drunkard never believes that there are many people who do not even drink wine.
Nor does a promiscuous person believe that there are people who have no sexual relations at all.
Nor does someone tormented by desire believe that there is someone who is not tormented by it at all, even if troubled by other things.
Nor does someone who is constantly sick believe that there is a body untouched by the ravages of illness. So it is with those who cannot
completely overcome these things of the mind. Their consolation is this: they say that no human being is entirely free from being overcome by these things.
For that there are people in whom love for Christ overcame the weakness of nature,
who utterly scorned the body and love for it, whose minds were not shaken from their joy in Christ,
and who consented to being overcome by the blows of adversities affecting the body,
and that the gifts overcame nature’s inadequacy—they do not believe at all.
I am not saying that hardships cease on the path of God, or that anyone lives on this path without trials.
On the contrary, I say that anyone who lives virtuously has his afflictions increased day by day.
The further he advances, the more he is beset by troubles. And this is the sign that his journey is genuine:
he lives a bitter life in this world and departs from this body in suffering.
For this is not the world of the righteous, and it is impossible for them to be in it without trouble.
But the will can be strengthened through the gift of grace and rise above all these things,
and keep the mind untroubled through the joy of Christ’s love.
And there have been people who attained this, and even now it is possible for people to be like this,
through the abundant help of Christ’s gift. O human being, do not judge the deeds of all people by
your own circumstances, and do not weigh their conduct on the scales of your own weakness.
If you wish, set out in hope, and you will be helped.
Do not be unbelieving, lest you not even be allowed by the one who sows these things in you
to grasp how great your deficiency is in comparison with those who have completely overcome the world and its troubles.
If you do not believe the Church, turn to the philosophers.
You will see how much power the will has to rise above the body and remain untroubled in the course it chooses.
When you look at them, these people who did not even know God,
see how much endurance and strength they displayed to the world through the courage of their will, and how they showed the great power possessed by the inward nature.
If it wills, it overcomes everything. Thus, when someone reads their histories, he is filled with amazement
at how much power God has indeed placed in this nature, so that, if it wills, it can overcome everything.
But because we are unwilling, we proclaim the weakness of our nature.
And while we conceal the strength of our nature with the weakness of our will, we say:
“Who has ever been able to overcome these things?” For one of them mastered the desire of his body to such an extent,
so that he would not abandon the course he had chosen and turn away from it,
that even when a sword was drawn, his mind was not troubled, nor did the fear of death overcome the limit he had set for himself.
He had kept silent for many years, and the king of the Greeks was amazed when he heard the report of the matter:
And wishing to put him to the test, he ordered him to come before him.
But he remained silent about everything that he said to him and asked him, and gave him absolutely no answer.
The king became enraged and ordered him to be put to death, because he had shown no respect even for the dignity of his throne and crown.
But he was not shaken by this; instead, he calmly kept his rule.
The king instructed the executioners that if he abandoned his rule out of fear of the sword, they should kill him.
But if he persisted in his stubbornness, they should bring him back to him alive.
When the time came, those appointed for this task pressed him to abandon his resolve, or else he would die.
But he considered: “It is better to endure death, which lasts only a moment, while keeping intact the boundary of my resolve,
“in which I have persevered all this time, than to give way through fear of death, dishonor my wisdom,
“and prove base on account of something that I am certain to encounter sooner or later in any case.”
Through this readiness of will and courageous mind, he both escaped death and proved upright and faithful to his rule.
Have you seen the power that the will possesses? This wise man stretched out his neck before the sword and did not break the rule he had set for himself.
Others trampled on natural desire and rose above it through the oath they swore concerning it. Others, amid insults, remained unshaken
and stood firm. Others, under merciless blows, showed no anger.
And these things came from their equals, something scarcely bearable. Others endured them even from people far beneath them.
Others, when their possessions were plundered, continued without hostility or anger.
Others, in dreadful and severe illnesses, showed endurance without despondency.
Along with these things, they also added other observances. Others undertook voluntary hardships.
Others practiced complete nakedness, apart from a covering for modesty,
a solitary way of life, and a diet of plants growing wild. Thus even King Alexander,
when he once met with one of them to see him, heard nothing from him except contempt for the world.
They did all these things so that they would not be distracted from the study and pursuit of their wisdom.
If the labor of learning and training in wisdom, apart from the fear of God, the light of faith, and the hope of the world to come,
can accomplish these feats, who would not be condemned by his conscience if, with all this light of Christ poured out upon the world,
the many gifts freely and abundantly bestowed, and the hope in God confirmed by events from day to day,
As long as the hardships and pleasures of this body still overcome him, and he does not stand firm like adamant for the love of God,
and joyfully make light of everything—but even doubts how human beings can overcome these things:
that no one can do anything by their own strength is known to everyone who is wise.
But that it can be overcome with help from God and a willing resolve—this is possible.
Certain solitaries were stirred to zeal by these things. They let go and suddenly abandoned the world and everything belonging to it.
They took courage and stood against every opposing force, and through perseverance of will and the help of their Lord they overcame every hardship there is.
For they lived among them, and many of them were philosophers by training.
They said, “If pagan sages, for the sake of passing wisdom and training in the learning of this world, which comes to nothing,
outside the way of God, undertake to endure these things, even estranging themselves from the world
and living outside it in their conduct, in order to attain what their will desires, though there is no righteousness in their thinking
and no hope beyond death in their labors—and all this for an empty hope—
how much more should we endure for the love of God and triumph over every hardship for the sake of the great hope promised to us!”
They were strengthened by this thought and gained mastery over the weakness of their thoughts.
They entered the contest and did not turn back until they received the crown. They became an example even to the generations after them.
They set up a standard for the world, showing how those who pursue this path ought to enter the [?].
On those who live close to God and in a life of knowledge all their days. 58.
Blessed is the person who lives a brief life in this world!
An elder had writings on all the walls of his cell: various texts and thoughts of different kinds,
and wonderful, varied sayings expressing all sorts of thoughts. They asked him, “Elder, what are these?”
He told them, “They are thoughts of righteousness that pass through me, coming from the angel who is with me and from the upright impulses of nature.
I write them down when I am in these states, so that in a state of darkness I may occupy myself with them,
and they rescue me from going astray.” This is what a person ought to do all their days.
An elder’s thoughts were calling him blessed and praising him:
“In exchange for the world that passes away, you have been found worthy of a hope that does not perish.” The elder said to them,
“Why do you call me blessed while I am still alive? I do not know what will happen to me before my death.”
I am still on the road; my happiness is not secure until I reach my home.
Truly, this is a sound thought. We should set the day of death as the finish line for victory.
Before death, the one who is winning is not yet a victor.
For his enemies are alive, and the road still lies before him, and he does not know what he will encounter. He has not
finished his journey, after all, or reached the time of confidence.
Likewise, even someone who is caught up in evil has no sentence of [?].
For he can gain life, since he is still alive. He has hope, just like someone who lives well.
Why do you belittle the sinner, O human being? The fruits of your own trading labors have not yet entered the harbor.
The one over whom you exalt yourself has not lost his hope in God.
For he may soon surpass you in virtue and draw closer to God than you.
For death has not come and set its seal on his way of life, nor on yours. A person undergoes many changes as long as he lives.
For God looks at the end, not at what happens along the way.
There have been many truly righteous people who fell from their righteousness, while sinners rose and took their place.
Therefore, let the righteous person not exalt himself, because he is still alive. And let the sinner not give up hope, because God is near him if he desires it.
And he is ready to receive him if he changes his way of life and turns toward him.
If you have practiced virtue well but have not tasted its help, do not be surprised.
Until a person becomes humble, he does not receive the reward for his labor.
The reward is given not for labor but for humility.
Whoever withholds the latter loses the former.
Whoever first acquires the virtue of labor comes before the one who acquires
the labor of virtue. Virtue is the mother of afflictions.
From afflictions, humility is born, and to humility the gift is given.
Therefore, the reward is not for virtue or for the pains endured for its sake, but for the humility born from them.
But if this is lacking, the things that came before are empty. The labor of virtue is keeping our Lord’s commandments.
The virtue of labor is an upright mind, established through humility and lowliness.
Where strength is lacking for the former things, this is accepted in their place.
Christ, then, seeks not the performance of commandments, but the setting right of the soul.
It was for its sake that he also laid down commandments for rational beings. The body works equally on the right and on the left.
The mind, however, is rightly acquitted or condemned differently in each case.
One person produces life through a matter of the left, by wisdom from God.
Another trades in sin under the guise of divine things.
The minor shortcomings found in them in particular matters are left in them by God to safeguard their righteousness.
Thus their transgressions and deficiencies become a cause of humility for them.
And this humility safeguards their great works, not merely so that they may be protected from pride,
but so that, by remembering those failings, they may humble themselves and receive a greater reward.
Without blows, a gift cannot be preserved. A gift without trials brings ruin
to those who receive it. If you have worked well before God,
and he has given you a gift in return for your uprightness toward him, to encourage you further and make you rejoice in your work,
ask him to give you knowledge, so that you may know how you ought to humble yourself.
Or ask him to appoint tormentors over it, or to take it back from you, so that it may not become a cause of destruction.
Not everyone can preserve wealth [?] without harm. A soul that has taken up the burden of virtue
and lives with scrupulous fear of God cannot be without daily troubles.
Virtues and troubles are bound together. Whoever has departed from afflictions has certainly departed from virtue as well.
Whoever perseveres in virtue perseveres in troubles. If you have desired virtue, you have surrendered yourself to every trouble.
Virtue gives birth to troubles; troubles give birth to humility.
For God does not wish the soul to be without care.
Anyone who desires this is found to be outside God's will in his thinking.
By care, however, I do not mean care about bodily things, but the struggles that accompany the virtues.
For until we reach knowledge of the truth, which is the revelation of hidden things, we are brought near to humility through trials.
For anyone whose virtue is found to be without troubles, a door to pride has been opened.
Who longs for this: to be free from distress in his mind? It is impossible for the mind to remain humble without the occasion of afflictions.
And without humility it is impossible to persevere with serenity in prayerful communion with God.
First a person turns his mind away from thinking about his duty, and then the spirit of pride approaches him.
First he persists in this, and then the angel who watches over him withdraws from him.
As long as that angel is near him, he instills in him every thought of righteousness. But when he has wronged this angel,
and the angel has withdrawn from his side, then the stranger approaches him, and at that time there is not even one righteous thought in him.
“Pride comes before ruin,” says the wise man, “and humility before a gift.”
The amount of pride evident in the soul indicates the weight of the ruin that is about to be [?] upon it by God.
For none of our sins does God withdraw from a person, abandon him completely, and recoil from him,
until he finds his mind occupied with pride or blasphemy.
For this reason, the first also becomes a cause of the second.
Those who depart in their minds from the path of humility and are stripped of divine help
fall either into shameful debauchery, into blasphemy concerning divine matters, or into impairment of the mind.
Most of those who become proud of the excellence of their conduct fall into shameful debauchery.
But those who become proud of their knowledge and their mental discipline fall into blasphemy concerning divine matters,
or into mental derangement. Pride is not when
the thought of it passes through the mind, nor even if someone happens to be overcome by it for a time, but when he persists in it.
Clearly, the former person also experiences remorse. But once the latter has come to love pride, he does not know how to repent.
If he repented, he would no longer persist in it. It is not sinning or acting wickedly that is evil in God's sight, but persisting in evil.
The former reveals the limitations of human nature; the latter, the insolence of the will.
A person can also become deranged in his understanding through human praise and be struck with madness,
when he longs for things beyond his measure to be accomplished through him among people, so that the praise of his greatness may increase,
as though to make them perceive that he is very close to God. There were many who excelled in their conduct,
grew great through gifts from God, and were honored with gifts of miraculous signs.
Afterward they underwent a change and [?] received a blow from God—those who had previously been so greatly honored.
Because they could not bear the many gifts they had received, they were led into pride.
They were cast away from God like refuse and no longer had a place in the exalted rank they had held.
Many others, too, who were calm and composed in mind, whose words were measured and whose conduct was modest,
and who were admired for their knowledge, became a sign of terror to those who knew them and a sight that brought tears to those who saw them.
With great weeping, raise your voice to God and ask
for humility. Fill your mouth with your tears and sprinkle your head with dust.
Do not get up from the ground or lift your head from the earth until God has pity on you
and takes you from this life while you are still sound, or has mercy on you and gives you humility.
Do not cease mourning until you sense within yourself that you have received it,
lest you suddenly find yourself like one of these people. Even if you have received it, do not raise your eyes or look toward heaven.
Do not satisfy your gaze with the sight of people, and do not let your heart rest from fear and supplication.
Perhaps you will escape the evils prepared for the demons in the [?] of this way of life, full of darkness and narrow in its path,
with many stumbling blocks, resisting human nature's ability to understand and comprehend it.
Believe me, my brother, and accept my words as true: you cannot comprehend the full power of the demons,
nor is your knowledge sufficient to stand against their schemes.
Granted, for now, that abundant light has been poured into you, the light in which the love of Christ is found,
and that you are sheltered within the wall of divine mercy because of the honor accorded to the humility you possess.
If you enter the darkness of trials when this light withdraws,
and you are left to be tested in that thick darkness of soul experienced by those who are abandoned by God and handed over to the demons,
then you will know that you stand before them like a child who does not
know where to go. All your knowledge will be bewildered like that of a little child.
Your mind that is firmly established in God, the certainty of your knowledge, and your sound understanding
will be tossed about in a sea of doubts. There is one thing by which you can overcome them:
humility alone. Once you have first taken hold of it, all their power is undone.
When you move forward smoothly in your joy in God, do not suppose that your soul is healthy.
But when attachment to things does not distract your mind from love of God and your neighbor,
nor attachment to people from your meditation on our Lord.
To him be glory, and may he keep us close to him and in communion with him. Amen.
An instructive discourse. 59.
True is the word of our Lord, who said that no one can acquire love of God while loving the world,
or enter into communion with God while mingling with the world, or concern himself with the world and concern himself with God.
Now I leave aside those things that are done for empty glory.
Very often, under the pretext of meeting the body's needs, many of us are drawn into this—
those who have pledged themselves to the service of the kingdom of heaven but do not remember the promise of our Lord, who said:
“If you direct all your concern toward the kingdom of heaven,
I will not let you lack what your visible nature needs.
Instead, these things will come to you of themselves, before you think about needing them, at the time of need.
I will not even let you need to think about them.”
As for the bird that has no soul, which is for your sake [?], that you should be in need.
God cares for the bird that has no soul, which was created for your sake.
Will he neglect you who concern yourselves with righteousness? Whoever is concerned with spiritual things, even in part,
has bodily things provided for him, even without his being concerned about them, according to how necessary they are and when they are needed.
But whoever shows concern for secondary things beyond what is proper falls away from God, even against his will.
When we concern ourselves with the things that are for the sake of our Lord's name, our Lord takes care of both kinds of things for us,
according to the measure of our concern and the urgency of the need for each of them.
Nevertheless, we should not seek for ourselves proof of God's care through these bodily things as a reward for our labors.
Instead, let us direct all our work toward the hope of what is to come.
For whoever has once devoted himself to virtue out of love for his soul, and has longed to practice it completely,
is no longer concerned about tomorrow's bodily provisions, whether they will be available or not.
For God often allows those who love virtue to be tested by such things.
And not only that: he also allows many evils from every quarter to rise against them.
He strikes their bodies, as he did Job’s, and brings them into poverty.
He alienates other people from them and strikes everything they possess, provided only that no harm comes near their souls.
It is impossible for us to walk the path of righteousness without encountering sorrow,
or for the body to remain free from illnesses and pains and continue unchanged, if indeed we have chosen to live virtuously.
But if someone deliberately exposes himself to death or the destruction of his own person, or to any kind of harm, he is subject to judgment.
But if, while he is walking the path of righteousness and making his journey toward God,
with many companions, one of these things encounters him on that path, he should not turn away from it.
Rather, he should accept it joyfully, without questioning, acknowledging that God has sent him his gift:
that he has been considered worthy, for God’s sake, to be placed amid trials, so that he may share in the suffering of the prophets and apostles
and the rest of the saints, who endured afflictions for the sake of God’s path.
For God has considered him worthy to endure troubles himself for the sake of the path of virtue,
whether they come through human beings, through demons, or through the body.
These things are not allowed to come without God’s command, but so that they may become an opportunity for righteousness for you.
For God cannot otherwise bring growth in virtue
to someone who longs to be with him, except by bringing him trials for the sake of the truth.
And that no one can accomplish this by himself—to be considered worthy of such greatness, to enter into trial joyfully for the sake of
these divine things, without the gift that comes from Christ—the blessed apostle testifies.
For this is so great a thing that he explicitly calls it a gift:
that someone should prepare himself in faith to suffer for the sake of his hope in God. He says:
“This has been granted to you by God: not only to believe in Christ, but also to suffer for his sake.”
And give thanks without ceasing to him who delivered you from the dominion of this world’s darkness
and brought you into the kingdom of his Son, and made you companions of all the children of light who suffered for God’s sake,
so that you may attain the portion allotted to the saints in light.
And there is what Peter wrote in his letter: “Whenever you suffer for righteousness, blessed are you.”
so that you may share in Christ’s suffering. Do not, then, rejoice with gladness when you are at ease,
but put a gloomy look on your face when afflictions press upon you, and consider this something foreign to the way of God.
Look: for years and generations, the way of God has been trodden through the cross and death. Where did you get this idea,

that the troubles along the way seem to you to lie outside it? Do you not want to walk in the footsteps of the saints? Or do you want to blaze a separate path by yourself, from yourself and for yourself,
and travel along it without suffering? The way to God
is a daily cross. No one ascends to heaven in comfort. We know where the path of comfort leads.
As for anyone who has entrusted himself to God with his whole heart,
God never wishes to leave him without concern—that is, concern for the sake of truth.
Rather, he knows from this that God is guiding him: God continually sends afflictions upon him.
Those who are guided through trials are never abandoned by divine providence to fall into the hands of demons,
especially if they kiss the feet of their brothers, cover their shortcomings, and conceal them as though they were their own.
Anyone who wishes to be without concern in this world and to live virtuously has had enough of the path itself.
As the blessed Interpreter said in his volume on Matthew: “Those who long for virtue cannot escape afflictions.”
As long as the soul advances against opposition, its afflictions must increase.
But when these cease to trouble it, it has first ceased its own efforts.
Anyone who says that he is without concern and lives virtuously
does not even know from what—from what—virtue is born in the soul.
For we know what the guides to virtue are.
Through trials the gate of heaven is opened before the soul. Our fathers led us along this path.
May God, who made his saints victorious in the struggle, whose thoughts did not weaken in their hope for what is to come,
protect and help us through their prayers. Amen. The righteous do not
win glory only through the good labors they undertake willingly,
but also win great glory through involuntary trials, by the testing of their endurance,
because they steadfastly endure all the sorrows of this life while awaiting the wondrous reward of the world to come.
The soul that holds fast to the fear of God is not afraid of anything that harms it bodily.
On why it is right not to desire or ask, without necessity, that some sign should happen openly through our hands or be performed for us [?]. 60.
Although the Lord is always close to the saints through the help he gives them,
he does not reveal his power openly unless it is necessary, through some intervention involving a sign perceptible to the senses,
so that the things that help us may not become trivial to us and prepare us for harm.
And this is so even though he takes such great care of them that his hidden intervention on their behalf never ceases for a single moment.
But in everything he leaves them to show diligence themselves, according to their strength, and to labor in prayer.
But if there is a matter whose difficulty outweighs the measure of their knowledge,
when they have grown weak and fallen short in dealing with it, because it is beyond their natural ability,
he brings it to completion according to the greatness of his power, as is fitting and as he knows will help them. As far
as possible, he strengthens them secretly so that they can withstand that difficulty.
Through the knowledge he grants them, he causes its obstacle to be removed.
And through contemplation he stirs them to praise, so that there may be benefit in both respects.
But if the matter requires his action to be made manifest, then he does this out of necessity.
His arrangements are wise and serve necessary purposes, not distraction.
Anyone who presumptuously seeks this without necessity, or asks God and longs for wonders and mighty works to happen through his hands,
has been found to be tempted in his mind by the mocking demon. Rather, he is also boastful and sick in his conscience.
For it is right to ask for God's help in distress. But to put him to the test when nothing compels it is dangerous.
Nor is anyone who desires this truly righteous.
But the Lord's doing this when the person himself does not wish it is something experienced by many of the saints.
For someone to desire this of his own will, when there is no necessity, is a fall from watchfulness
and a departure from the knowledge of the truth. And if the person making the request is heard in this,
just as he dared to approach our Lord, he finds an opening against him and leads him on to another, greater thing.
But those who are truly righteous do not long for this. Not only do they not entertain the thought, but
they do not even want it when it is given to them—not only in other people's sight, but even when they are alone by themselves.
For consider one of the saints, who, when a gift was given to him because of his purity,
And he used to know beforehand whenever someone was coming to him. He asked God,
also urging others to pray with him, that the gift might be taken away from him.
But the fathers did not exercise such boldness even in times of distress.
Consider that blessed Ammon, a truly holy man, one of the remarkable fathers:
once, while he was going to visit Saint Antony, he lost his way in the desert.
He did not say, “God, pick me up and put me where Antony is,”
although he certainly could have done something like this because of his closeness to God and the urgency of the situation.
For it is said of that region that those who lost their way in that desert fell into danger.
Despite all this, he did not say this to God, but said only these few words:
“Lord,” he said, “do not let the creature you have formed perish.” Have you seen his humility?
Have you understood the true wisdom of the fathers? But God, in his care for the saints,
because he knew that the man was steadfast and that he would not
be weakened in his thinking by pride, acted in a way worthy of the man's greatness.
Although he had not pleaded with him, God did what was fitting. He lay down to sleep, we are told, and got up,
and saw something like a human hand suspended in the sky above his head,
showing him the way, until he went and stood above the cave of blessed Antony.
Have you seen God's care for those who belong to his household? For he could have kept him from losing his way at all.
But he wanted him to know how much he cared for him. He allowed him to lose his way, and then showed him the way again in plain sight.
And he showed it to him not through a human being, but through an angel in the air. Oh, the care God has for the saints!
Remember also the story of Abba Macarius, who was going to Scetis carrying baskets.
He became weak and exhausted and sat down, because he could no longer walk.
He did not ask God to do anything for him to restore his strength through supernatural power.
Instead, he entrusted himself to God, saying, “God, you know that I have no strength left.”
Immediately, at a sign, he was lifted up by God's power and set down where he wanted to go, together with his baskets.
But those who are truly righteous constantly reflect within themselves that they are not worthy of God.
And by this they are recognized as genuine: they consider themselves wretched.
And they sincerely acknowledge, in private and in public, that they are unworthy of his care.
And like sinners and lowly people, they show care and exertion
in everything, and entrust themselves to God in faith.
They themselves, to the best of their ability, leave undone nothing that they ought to do.
Through the Spirit they learn this wisdom: not to cease attending to their duties or toiling as long as they live.
But reserve the time of rest for the world to come.
And those in whom God dwells do not desire to have this rest here
or to find relief from their struggles, even though consolation in spiritual things is secretly given to them from time to time.
Virtue does not mean that once someone has attained it, he ceases to take care and exert himself.
Rather, the dwelling place of the Spirit is the person who continually subjects and disciplines himself,
even if there is an opportunity to accomplish the task with ease. For this is the will of the Spirit.
He does not hold those in whom he dwells in idleness or invite them to comforts, but to labors and greater affliction.
He teaches them watchfulness, spurs them on through [?], and brings them closer to wisdom.
This is the will of the Spirit: that those who love him should live amid hardships.
Those who lead lives of comfort do not have the Spirit of God within them, but the spirit of Satan.
The Spirit of God does not desire bodily comforts, nor does he find rest in a life of ease, but in a life of hardships.
Satan, however, finds rest in a life full of comforts, according to our Lord’s testimony.
But the Holy Spirit departs from ease, as was said
to the holy fathers: the Spirit of God does not dwell in a body that rests in comfort.
Rather, he looks toward those who discipline themselves, with a body under affliction and a willing soul,
and makes his dwelling with them, and teaches them how to live during this short time.
Those who loved God completed their lives amid afflictions of every kind.
For all the righteous passed through this world amid hardships.
The closer they drew to God, the more their hardships increased.
For one of them said under oath, “I die every day.”
“I swear,” he says, “by my pride in you, my brothers, which I have in our Lord Jesus Christ: I die every day.”
This is what distinguishes those in whom God dwells from the rest of humanity: they live in affliction, while the world lives in comfort.
God did not wish those who love him to enjoy bodily comfort. Rather, he wants them, as long as they live,
to be afflicted in the world, distressed, tormented, needy, and isolated.
They are naked and destitute, sick, despised, and mistreated. They have no settled home.
Their hearts are broken, their bodies brought low, and their acquaintances disown them.
Their minds are full of anguish. They look upon all creation as foreign to them.
Their way of dwelling is foreign to all humanity. Their dwelling is solitary and secluded,
deprived of the sight of the world, empty of every sign of the delights found here,
stripped of everything that brings comfort. Mourning is found there. Joy
is far from it. Troubles crowd into it. They do not even have their bodily needs fully met, as everyone else does.
The ground is their bed. Their faces burn from fasting. Their knees give way from weakness.
The functioning of their internal organs is impaired by privation beyond what people are accustomed to.
They weep, while the world laughs. They are sorrowful, while the world is joyful. They fast, while the world indulges itself.
All creation rests quietly in sweet sleep, while they keep vigil in prayer.
For they labor by day and set the night aside for struggle.
The saints live bitter lives in the world, with humbled bodies, afflicted souls, and troubles coming from every direction.
Such is God's will: that all who draw near to him should live amid hardships,
humbled and brought low in their whole soul and body. Some endure afflictions of their own choosing,
and some, torments caused by their passions. Some bear bitter pains in their bodies.
Some endure miseries and persecution at the hands of others, dangers from passions,
dangers from demons, dangers from illnesses, and dangers from poverty.
Others were persecuted. Others were killed. Others were sawn apart. Others were stoned.
Others were drowned in the sea. Others had their limbs cut off while they were still alive.
Others were handed over to abuse and ridicule. Others entered the mouth of the flame. Others
to imprisonment and terrible beatings. Others met the edge of the sword.
Others wandered about dressed in sheepskins and goatskins, and lived like wanderers in the wilderness.
The saints lived in distress, in mountains and caves and holes in the earth.
Such were the people of whom the apostle testifies that the world was not worthy of them.
And most astonishing of all, throughout all these things they were not looking for deliverance or relief, according to the words of the blessed apostle.
Glory to the one who crowns them, who himself completed this path through the suffering of the cross, after all these things,
so that his saints too might follow in his footsteps. And our Lord’s word was fulfilled in practice:
“In the world,” he said, “you will have distress, but in me you will have joy.”
Through the power of this joy, these saints gain strength to endure.
May God, by whose power the saints endured these struggles and did not grow weak in their hope—
may he strengthen hope in him within us all. Amen. Without afflictions there is no life.
God knew that two joys could not exist in one person,
and that it was impossible to persevere in love for him while enjoying bodily ease, so he kept them from this.
He strengthened their love for him in their souls by depriving them of all the world’s pleasures.
May Christ, whose love is stronger than death—and consuming fire, exile, and estrangement from family
and deprivation of life and every hardship cannot withstand love for him in those who love him—may he reveal in us the power of his love.
Amen. On the reasons why God allows trials to come upon
his friends. 61.
Through the love that the saints show God in return for the things they suffer for his name,
when they are afflicted and do not abandon the virtue that God loves,
their hearts gain boldness to look toward him without a veil and to ask him with confidence.
Great is the power of prayer, of prayer with boldness.
For this reason he allows his saints to be tested by every kind of distress on the path toward him, so that they may have boldness.
And also so that they may gain experience of his help and of how much he cares for them, when he is found to be their deliverer in the danger they encounter.
And because wisdom is acquired through trials, so that his friends may not be ignorant and deprived of training,
so that they may acquire knowledge of [?] through experience and not be easily made fools of by demons.
For if he trained them only through good things, they would lack training in other things and would be blind in battle.
And if someone says, “Let him guide them without training or knowledge of their own,”
then he wants them to be like oxen and donkeys, whose free choice determines
nothing. There is not even any savor in goodness when someone has not first been tested by experiencing evils,
and then encounters it, without making use of it knowingly and freely as something of his own.
But how sweet is the knowledge acquired through training and through the experience of hardships!
And how much strength it gives to someone who has found it through personally experiencing many things is known to those who are convinced of the help it provides.
They also learn the weakness of their nature and the help that comes from divine power
when he has first withheld strength from them while they are in the midst of trials.
Then they become aware of the weakness of their nature, the intensity of the trials, and the wickedness of the enemy:
what sort of enemy they have, what sort of nature they are clothed in, and how they are protected by divine power.
And however much they run and however high they rise, when divine power withdraws from them, they learn how they fall before every passion.
From all these things they acquire humility, press toward God, await his help, and persevere in prayer.
Where would they have acquired all these things if they had not gained experience of countless evils,
in which God allows them to become involved? And as he says, “So that I might not become exalted by the abundance of revelations,
a thorn was given to me in my flesh, a messenger of Satan.” A person also acquires firm faith through trials,
by experiencing divine help, which he has experienced many times.
From then on he also becomes fearless and acquires courage in trials because of the training he has gained. And everyone benefits from
trials. The diligent are tested so that their wealth may increase;
the negligent, so that they may be protected from harm; and the sleeping, so that they may be made ready for wakefulness;
those who are far away, so that they may draw near to God; and those of his household, so that they may enter with confidence.
Any son who is untrained cannot benefit even from the wealth given to him from his father’s household.
For this reason God first tests and afflicts, and then reveals his gift.
Glory to that Lord who, through purifying medicines, brings us to the joy of health.
There is no one who does not find the time of training difficult, and no one who does not find it bitter when he is given the medicine of trials to drink.
Yet without this, a healthy constitution cannot be acquired. Even the ability to endure is not our own.
Where does a vessel made of clay get the ability to withstand surges of water,
unless divine fire strengthens it? If we humble ourselves to ask, eagerly longing with diligence and perseverance, we receive something.
On how a person recognizes the level at which he stands from the thoughts stirred within him, which are as follows. 62.
As long as a person lives in negligence, he fears the hour of death.
But when he draws near to God, he fears the encounter with judgment.
But when he comes fully into God's presence, both fears are swallowed up in love.
How does this happen? When, in knowledge and bodily practices,
he stands, he is terrified of destruction. But when he stands in knowledge of the soul and upright practices,
his mind trembles continually at the remembrance of [?], because he stands rightly within nature itself.
In his knowledge and conduct, he moves and lives on the level of the soul.
And he is well situated in nearness to God. But when he reaches that knowledge of the truth,
through the stirring of awareness of God's mysteries, and is released through hope for what is to come, he is swallowed up in love.
The person who is bodily fears slaughter like an animal.
But the rational person fears God's judgment. The one who has become a son seeks to please love, not the threatening rod.
“I and my father's household,” he says, “serve the Lord.” For love abolishes fear.
Not only does he have no fear, but he even longs to depart. Love brings temporal life to an end.
The person who has reached the love of God no longer desires to remain here.
My beloved, because I have become a fool, I cannot bear to keep the mystery in silence.
Instead, I become foolish for our benefit, [?].
For this is true love: it cannot hold back in matters of love from those who love it.
Many times, while I was writing these things, my fingers stopped on the page.
They could not withstand the sweetness that fell into my heart and silenced the senses.
But blessed is the person who constantly occupies himself with God and withdraws himself from all worldly things [?].
He remains with God alone, occupied with knowing him. Even if he must be patient, he will not have to wait long to see fruit.
Joy in God is stronger than this present life.
Whoever has found it not only pays no attention to sufferings, but no longer even concerns himself with his own life.
From then on he has no other awareness, if he has truly been found worthy of this. Love is sweeter than life.
And understanding concerning God, from which love is born, is sweeter than honey and the honeycomb.
What is the sweetness of love that surpasses life? Love does not grieve at accepting ten thousand deaths for those who love it.
Love is the child of knowledge. Knowledge is the child of the soul's health.
The soul's health is a strength that is born of endurance over time.
And what is knowledge? Awareness of immortal life.
What is immortal life? Awareness of God. Knowledge concerning God is king over everything desirable.
For the heart that has received it, the sweetness of everything on earth is superfluous.
For nothing compares with the sweetness of knowledge concerning God.
Lord, fill my heart with eternal life. Eternal life is consolation in God.
For whoever has found consolation in God, the world's consolation is superfluous.
How does a person recognize that he has received wisdom from the Spirit? By its teaching him the ways of humility,
in his inner life and in his senses. It is revealed to him in his understanding how humility is acquired. And how does he recognize that he has attained
humility? By finding it repugnant to please this world,
whether by his conduct or his speech, and by finding the praise of this world hateful in his eyes.
What are the passions? They are impulses rooted in the things and affairs of this world,
which stimulate bodily activity to meet its needs [?]. Their impulses do not cease as long as the world exists.
But when a person has been found worthy of divine understanding and has tasted and experienced something superior to these things, the impulses toward these things do not enter his heart.
For a longing superior to theirs has taken the place of these impulses.
The impulses toward material things, and those born from them, do not approach his heart. Instead, they remain outside, inactive.
This is not because the impulses of the passions themselves no longer exist, but because the heart that receives them is dead to them and alive to something else.
Not that he has slackened in vigilance and the work of discernment, but that there is no struggle in his mind.
For his consciousness is satisfied with the delight of something else.
It is like someone who has eaten his fill of delicious, rich food, and whose consciousness is filled with its richness and delight.
Afterward, however, he sees repulsive food, befouled with filth:
not only does his consciousness then need no careful attention to restrain it from craving,
nor any struggle in his mind to keep him from looking at it with desire,
but his whole consciousness is also shaken and disturbed at the sight of it. Not
merely because of its filthiness—for perhaps he even used to live on it before—
but still more because of the comparison with the excellence of that other food,
which filled his consciousness with every delight. This is how it is with the health of the soul.
The heart that has truly gained an awareness of spiritual things,
and contemplation of the world to come—its consciousness is in this same state when it remembers the passions.
And just as someone may lose his wealth and fall into poverty,
and be deprived of that splendid, excellent food on which he used to feast at the royal court, and forget its pleasure and taste,
