and those splendid dishes may no longer be available to him, and his stomach may be empty of the delight of their [?],
he is inevitably obliged to turn even to much inferior food.
So it is with someone who has been granted health of soul. If he is deprived of that divine delight,
through neglecting his duty and falling into the sleep of carelessness, he is once again enticed by that repulsive food,
befouled and spattered with every kind of filth; and his consciousness makes no distinctions, because the soul’s stomach is empty.
“To a hungry soul,” it says, “even bitter things are sweet.” And again: “No one is entrusted with a treasure and sleeps.”
But if he observes the rule of vigilance and the work of discernment, and with understanding
draws life from them, the struggle with the enticements of the passions does not approach his mind at all.
It is not through combat that those enticements are prevented from entering the heart.
Rather, it is the satisfaction of the soul’s consciousness, filled with knowledge,
and the longing for wondrous visions found within it, that keep them from approaching to engage him in conversation.
Not that he has withdrawn from vigilance, as I said, and the labor of discernment,
which guard the knowledge of truth and the soul’s light, but that his mind has no struggle, for the reasons that have been explained.
The food of the poor is distasteful to the rich, and the diet of the sick to the healthy.
Yet wealth and health themselves are maintained by vigilance and diligence. Nature itself bears witness to this.
As long as a person [?], he needs vigilance and diligence, and watchfulness to guard his treasure.
But if he relaxes his discipline, he becomes sick and wastes away, even though strength from his former health remains in him for a long time.
But whenever he receives no replenishment, he slips into weakness and deficiency.
Does not nature itself also teach us about these things? What heavenly thing is there
for which we cannot find an example in our own nature to illustrate it? Indeed, our Lord too, in the case of all spiritual things,
used natural things to confirm them and establish their power in our souls.
Not only those belonging to the small pledge we have here, but also those belonging to the true substance, the fulfillment and reality that await us. Do not
be amazed at what I have said. Labor is needed not only until the fruit appears; even until it is gathered in, labor is still needed.
By gathering in, I mean the grave. Sometimes, when the fruit has grown plump, hail suddenly strikes it.
Anyone who becomes entangled in affairs and gives himself over to social interaction cannot be confident that his health will remain with him.
I mean enjoyment and vision. Jesus Christ, King of the ages, make me worthy to long for you.
Great is the person who perseveres in communion with God and mingles his life with him,
greater than every person on earth and every service performed by rational beings.
When you pray to God, say this one thing to him: “Lord, make me worthy truly to die to involvement with this world.”
In this you have included every petition. Strive to bring this to completion in yourself through action.
But if action also accompanies your prayer, you truly stand in the freedom of Christ.
Being dead to the world does not consist merely in withdrawing from involvement in its affairs.
Rather, this is true death to the world: not to desire the world’s good things in the activity of one’s mind.
But if we become accustomed to good meditation, we are hidden from the passions when we encounter them.
Those who have gained experience within themselves know this.
And we are ashamed to approach the things that give rise to them. Whenever, in place of action, something
Do you long to pursue the love of God? Set death as the limit of your desire for it.
In this way, and by this very act, you become worthy of the rank of martyrdom,
through every suffering and injury that befalls you short of that limit, if you endure it to the end without giving up.
Dwelling on a weak thought weakens the strength to endure.
But a firm resolve gives even strength beyond nature to the person who follows its meditation.
Lord, make me worthy to hate my life for the sake of the life that is in you.
Life in this world resembles a written page that can still be erased.
For whatever a person wishes, and whenever he wants, he can add to it or take away from it and alter what is written on it.
Life in the world to come resembles documents entered on scrolls and bearing the king’s seal,
in which no addition—no addition or subtraction—can be made. While we are still in the realm of change, let us examine ourselves.
And while we have authority over the book of our lives, and our book is in our hands,
let us make an effort to add to it through good conduct and erase from it the shortcomings of our former conduct, which lacked freedom.
We have authority to erase debts from it as long as we are here. And God takes account of every change we make in it,
so that we may become worthy of eternal life before it is brought before the King and he places his seal upon it.
As long as we are in this world, God does not place his seal either on our good deeds or on
our evil deeds, until the hour of departure, when we have finished our work in our own country and set out on the journey.
From now on, we ought to act as blessed Mar Ephrem said: our soul should always resemble a ship ready to sail,
which does not know when the wind will come for it; and an army that does not know when the horn will summon it to march;
and a lodger who does not know when the owner of the house will order him to move out.
And if, he says, these are so prepared for a brief separation, though they may return and come back again,
how much more ought we to be prepared and ready before that great separation on the day of departure!
May Christ, the mediator of our life, grant that we approach prepared that great bridge and the gate of the new world.
To him be glory forever and ever. Amen.
Why people whose knowledge is natural perceive spiritual things in terms of bodily solidity.
And how the mind can rise above this, and what causes us not to be freed from it.
63. When and by what means the mind can remain without images during prayer.
Blessed be his glory! May he open the door before us, so that we may seek nothing except to desire him. For in this way, when we let go of
everything and our mind goes out in search of him alone, it will contain no thought of anything that sets [?] a barrier before it, before that vision of the Lord of all.
My beloved, the more the mind abandons thought of visible things and reflects on that hope which is to come,
the more, in proportion to its elevation above thought of bodily things and its occupation with that hope, it becomes refined and clear in prayer.
As the body is freed from the bonds of material things, so too the mind is freed.
And the more it is freed from the fetters of cares, the clearer it becomes. And the clearer it becomes, the more refined it becomes.
And the more refined it becomes, the more it rises above the impulses of this world, which bears the mark of coarseness.
And it knows [?] to gaze upon God as he is, and not as we are. Unless someone has first been found worthy of revelation, it is impossible for him to know this.
And unless he attains purity, the movements of his mind do not become clear enough to gaze upon hidden things.
And until he is freed from everything visible in his possession, he is not freed from the impulses concerning these things either,
nor does he become empty of thoughts that darken the mind. And wherever there are darkness and tangled thoughts, the passions are there too.
For unless someone is freed from all these things I have mentioned, and from their causes, he cannot perceive the hidden things of the mind.
For this reason, before everything else, our Lord commanded us to embrace renunciation,
withdrawal from the disturbances of the world, and release from concern about anyone.
He said, “Whoever does not leave all his relatives and everything he has, and deny even himself, cannot be my disciple,” so that in anything
the mind may not be harmed by seeing, hearing, or concern for possessions, their loss or their increase, or by anyone.
And by binding our mind to hope in him alone, he directed the whole reflection of our thoughts toward himself.
And by releasing us from everything, he bound all the concern of our mind to himself.
Thus we may be drawn to communion with him through our constant attention to him.
Prayer also requires practice, so that through spending a long time in it the mind may become wise.
For after renunciation, which releases the movements of our mind from their fetters, prayer requires perseverance.
Through perseverance and time, the mind will also gain practice in knowing how to put its thoughts in order,
and in learning through many experiences things that it cannot receive from others.
Every way of life grows out of the way of life that precedes it, and that preceding way of life is necessary.
for attaining what follows it. Solitude precedes prayer.
Solitude itself is also for the sake of prayer, and prayer is so that through it we may acquire love of God.
For through it we find reasons to love God.
We should also know this, my beloved: every inward act of communion that exists,
every beautiful meditation of the mind on God, and every contemplation of spiritual things comes within the bounds of prayer,
is included under the name of prayer, and falls within the scope of this designation. Whether it is reading with discernment
that you speak of, or words spoken by the mouth in praise of God, persistent meditation on our Lord, bodily prostration, chants of praise, and the rest.
For from these we receive instruction concerning true prayer, and from prayer love of God is born.
Love itself comes through prayer, and prayer through dwelling in solitude.
Solitude itself serves this purpose: that we may have a place to commune with God alone.
Solitude, in turn, is preceded by renunciation of the world.
For unless a person first leaves the world and gives up everything he has, he cannot live in solitude.
Likewise, renunciation of the world is itself preceded by endurance.
Endurance is preceded by hatred of the world, and hatred of the world by fear and desire.
For unless fear of hell terrifies the mind and desire for blessings draws it, hatred of this world does not arise within it.
Unless a person hates the world, he cannot endure being deprived of its company and comfort.
Unless endurance first comes to his mind, he cannot choose a dwelling that is utterly deserted and empty of inhabitants.
Unless he chooses a solitary life for himself, he cannot persevere in prayer.
Unless he constantly communes with God and persists in those inner movements mingled with prayer,
and in the kinds of instruction within it that have been mentioned, he does not experience love.
Thus love of God comes from communion with him; the communion of prayer comes through stillness, and stillness through giving up possessions.
Giving up possessions, in turn, comes through endurance, and endurance through hatred
of pleasures. Hatred of pleasures comes through fear of hell and expectation of blessings.
The person who hates pleasures is the one who knows their fruits: what they prepare for him, and what blessedness he is deprived of because of them.
Thus each of these practices is bound to the one before it, receives its growth from it, and reaches toward the others above it.
And if one of them is missing from the middle, the one after it cannot stand. It becomes clear that they all fall apart and perish.
On the many changes that affect the mind and are examined through prayer. 64.
Choosing what is good belongs to the good will of the person who desires it.
But bringing the choice of that virtuous will to completion belongs to God, and it requires much help from him.
For this reason, we accompany the desire for good that awakens in us with continual prayers.
This is not only to ask him for help, but also to discern whether that desire agrees with his will.
Not every desire for good enters the heart from God, but only one that is also beneficial.
There is something good that a person desires even though it does not help him.
Such a desire can also come from Satan, while appearing to be helpful.
Often, however, it is beyond the person's capacity, and he devises his own harm by forcing himself
to seek it, although he has not yet reached that way of life, or it is foreign to the order of his calling.
Or again, it is not the time appointed for him to accomplish these things.
Or he is unequal to the task, whether in knowledge or bodily strength, or because the circumstances do not permit it.
In any case, under the guise of good, he either confuses the person, harms his body, or hides a trap in his mind.
Therefore, as I said, we accompany the apparently good desire that awakens in us with continual and earnest prayers.
Each of us says, “Let your will be done in me, so that I may carry out in practice
this good thing that I have chosen for myself and desired to practice, if it agrees with your will.
To desire it is easy for me, but I cannot accomplish it without a gift from you.
Yet both belong to you: both willing and doing.
For it was not without your grace that I consented to the impulse that arose in me or was moved by it.”
This is the practice of someone who desires good with a discerning mind: to labor continually in prayer for it,
and to receive strength from above as help for his work, and wisdom that distinguishes truth from falsehood.
Through many prayers and labor, vigilance and unceasing longing, the good is discerned,
through continual tears, humility, and heavenly help, especially since it has an opponent:
proud thoughts, which keep God's help away from us. These too we put an end to through prayer.
Fine instructions that teach vigilance and the rules of a way of life, through which a person acquires a fitting order for himself. 65.
Repentance is the mother of life. She opens her door to us
through flight from everything. The grace that we lost after baptism through lax conduct—
repentance renews it in us through the discernment of the mind.
Through water and the Spirit we put on Christ, without perceiving his glory.
Through repentance we enter into his delight, through the knowledge of discernment that dawns within us.
Anyone who lacks repentance lacks the delight that is to come.
Anyone who is close to everyone is far from repentance. Anyone who withdraws from everyone with discernment is truly repentant.
As soon as a person withdraws from other people and gathers himself inwardly, stirrings of repentance are immediately imprinted on his mind.
He receives the seed of life from grace, and a feeling of discernment stirs within him like an infant.
And the remembrance of life in the world to come, the expectation of the resurrection, and the thought of judgment flutter in his heart.
Do not suppose that a feeling enters the mind without divine grace.
For through a gift, by divine mercy, he secretly receives piercing remorse, together with a longing for life.
As the blessed Evagrius also said, “Fervent remorse of soul is a cleansing medicine,
which the Lord, through the holy angels, providentially gives to those who repent, to purify them from the passions.”
And again he says, “Fervent remorse of soul is the fire of a furnace,
which comes to the soul through the grace of Christ at the time of prayer, and the memory attains contemplation.
But living waters heal the lack of it.” The beginning of repentance is humility without pretense.
Adornment of clothing is a distraction from repentance. The way to wisdom is the discipline of the limbs.
Bodily dissipation is a distraction from wisdom. True wisdom is gazing upon God.
Gazing upon God is the silence of thoughts. Stillness of mind is tranquility of discernment.
Confusion of the senses is a spring of thoughts. Awareness of God is the depth of humility.
True contemplation is the death of the heart. A heart that has truly died to the world is wholly awake in God.
True death is the stirring of life.
It is better to spend one's life resting from everything than to build a life by moving away from the marketplace.
Better is someone who builds himself up than someone who builds up the world. It is better to make life sweet than to impart life.
When someone's outward limbs are subdued, his inward movements are alive.
Someone whose outward limbs are alive has put the limbs of wisdom to death. Humility born of discernment is knowledge of the truth.
Knowledge of the truth is a spring of humility. Someone who is gentle in heart is humble in body.
Someone who is preoccupied with his body is insolent in heart. Someone who is disturbed in body is disturbed in heart.
Someone who is disturbed in heart is reckless in mind. Someone who is reckless in mind follows evil paths.
Someone whose path is evil is dead while alive. If you love humility, do not love adornment.
A person who loves adornment cannot endure being despised, and he finds it difficult to hurry to perform menial tasks.
And he is ashamed to submit himself to someone beneath him. A servant of God does not adorn his body.
Know that anyone who loves adorning his body has a feeble conscience, even if he possesses virtues.
And anyone who loves visible gain cannot acquire genuine love for another person.
And anyone who pursues honors is a slave of this world. If everyone who does these things is hateful to you, keep yourself far from those things.
One and the same kind of being despised helps both humility and chastity.
And do not look for the genuine practice of these things in someone who loves honor and adornment.
If you love chastity, do not love distraction.
The encounters that press upon you through distraction do not allow you to preserve chastity within yourself vigilantly.
Anyone who loves distraction is not chaste. And do not believe that anyone attached to worldly things is humble.
And everyone who loves God loves seclusion. A distracted person cannot preserve truth within himself unstained.
Many display repentance, but no one truly possesses it except someone whose heart is sorrowful. Sorrow of heart—many
strive to find it. No one truly finds it except someone who has acquired constant silence.
Everyone who is a servant of God loves sorrow.
Know that anyone given to many words is empty within, even if he recounts wonderful things.
Inward sorrow is a restraint on the senses. If you love truth, love silence.
This makes you shine like the sun in God,
and frees you from ignorant musings. Silence unites you with God himself.
When kneeling is pleasant to you, do not hurry to bring it to an end.
If only it could continue uninterrupted as long as you remain in this life! When your mind is collected, do not interrupt your prayer.
Do not consider the time spent in collected prayer to be idleness because the psalms have ceased.
Love kneeling in prayer more than reciting verses.
Whenever this is possible for you, it will take the place of the service for you.
Whenever the gift of tears is granted to you during the service itself:
Do not consider delighting in them to be neglecting the service. The gift of tears is the fulfillment of prayer.
Do not be surprised if sometimes, while you are kneeling in prayer and your mind is collected in it, your mind becomes silent and ceases praying.
You can experience this both during the service and during reading.
When your mind is scattered, spend more time reading than praying.
Let the character of your reading agree with the aim of your way of life. Not all books are suitable for collecting the mind.
Many books contain instruction, but for purity they are not
suitable. Books on miscellaneous subjects leave you with a distracted mind.
Know that not every book that teaches the fear of God is also suitable for purity of conscience and the collecting of thoughts.
Do not argue about the precise nature of these things with someone who does not know the truth. Love stillness even more than ascetic labors.
If possible, value reading more than standing in prayer, for it is the source of pure prayer.
But do not despise it altogether. Beware of the snare. Psalm-singing is the root of the spiritual life.
But know this: verses recited with a distracted mind are useful chiefly as bodily exertion.
The suffering of the mind is more excellent than bodily weariness. In times of listlessness, make a habit of stirring up a little zeal.
For the heart is greatly awakened by it, and it also warms the impulses of the soul. Just as against desire,
so also in times of listlessness, the natural power of anger is helpful, for it drives coldness out of the soul.
This usually comes upon us in two circumstances: from a stomach weighed down with food, and from excessive weakness caused by exertion.
Orderliness in spiritual practice is light for the mind. There is nothing like knowledge.
Let every prayer you offer at night be more precious in your eyes than all your labors during the day.
Do not weigh down your stomach, lest your mind become confused and you be troubled by distraction while standing
you at night, and your limbs are slack, and you are completely filled with weakness.
But your soul is darkened, and your thoughts are confused, and you cannot gather them around the verses at all because of the gloom.
Everything will taste bland to you, and the words of the psalms will not be sweet to you,
whose different meanings the mind is accustomed to savor with pleasure because of the agility and clarity of its understanding.
Whenever the order of the nighttime service is disturbed, the mind will also be confused during the daytime service and will wander in gloom.
It takes no pleasure in reading as it usually does, for the gloom rests like a fog over its thoughts,
whether they are stirred in prayer or in meditation.
The delight granted to the ascetic during the day flows over the pure mind from the light of the nighttime service.
Do not expect to learn anything more about the blessings of ascetics from anyone who has not had long experience of solitude,
even if he is very wise, is a teacher, and has many accomplishments.
Be careful not to weaken your body excessively, lest listlessness gain strength over you
and cool your soul's desire to taste its labor. A person should weigh his way of life as though in a balance.
When you have eaten your fill, be a little wary of taking liberties with yourself.
Let your sitting posture be modest, even when attending to your bodily needs. Be especially modest and pure when going to bed,
not only in your thoughts, but also by keeping your limbs guarded.
Beware of presumption when changes for the better occur. But your weakness and your ignorance in the face of
its subtlety—make these known to our Lord in earnest prayer, lest you be left to be tested by ugly things.
For sexual immorality follows pride, and error follows presumption.
Work with your hands only as much as your needs require, especially during your confinement in solitude.
Do not grow weak in your hope in the one who cares for you. God's provisions for the members of his household are wonderful:
even in a desolate wilderness he provides for those who dwell there in hope of him, without human hands.
But if our Lord attends to your bodily needs without labor on your part, while you concern yourself only with the soul,
then, through the murderer's schemes, the thought arises that there must somehow be some reason
on your part for all this providential care. And with that thought, God's care for you ceases.
At that very moment ten thousand trials spring up against you, whether from the neglect of those who care for you,
And even when the pains and illnesses that stir within our body recur.
God does not withhold his care merely because of an impulse, but when the mind persists in it.
But God does not chastise or judge anyone for an involuntary impulse.
Not even if we consented to it for a moment, but immediately sorrow pierced us and remorse overtook us.
Our Lord, too, does not hold us accountable for a transgression like this, but for one that the mind deliberately pursues.
That is, in the case of those who regarded it without sensitivity and as though it were a duty,
and did not consider it an evil thought. Let us constantly offer this prayer to our Lord: “Christ, the fullness
of truth, make your truth shine in our hearts [?], so that we may know how to walk in your way according to your will.”
Whenever an evil thought presents itself within you, either for the first time or as one of those that have been recurring frequently for a long time,
know for certain that it seeks to hide a snare for you. Be alert to it in time.
But if it is one of those that belong to the right side and to goodness, know that the Lord wishes to give you some share in life.
That is why it stirs within you with unusual frequency. But if it is an obscure thought,
and you are uncertain about it, because you cannot clearly discern whether it is a member of the household or a thief,
and whether it is a helper or an ambusher hiding under a good appearance,
prepare yourself to face it with fervent prayer night and day, together with prolonged vigil.
Do not drive it away from you, nor consent to it, but pray earnestly and fervently about it.
Do not stop calling upon our Lord, and it will clearly reveal itself and where it comes from.
Love silence more than anything else. It brings you close to a fruit that the tongue is too weak to describe.
At first we force ourselves to be silent. Then, from our very silence, something is born within us that draws us toward silence.
May God grant you the awareness of what is born from silence.
If you begin this practice, I do not know how much light will dawn within you as a result.
Do not suppose, my brother, that what is said about that admirable man,
Arsenius—that when the fathers and brothers gathered to see him, he would sit with them without speaking and dismiss them in silence—
was merely a matter of his own will, although at first he forced himself to do this.
After a time, a certain sweetness is born in the heart through the exercise of this practice;
and forcibly compels the body to persist in silence. Abundant tears are born in us through this way of life:
through the wondrous vision of various things that the heart perceives distinctly, sometimes with sorrow and sometimes from wonder.
For the heart becomes small and becomes like a child: as soon as it begins to pray, it bursts into tears.
Great is the person who, through the endurance of his bodily members, acquires wonderful habits within his soul.
If you put all the labors of this way of life on one side and silence on the other, silence will outweigh them.
There are many instructions from the fathers which, when a person approaches silence,
make the labor of observing them superfluous for him, since carrying them out has become unnecessary.
He has risen above them because he has approached the goal. For silence also supports stillness.
For, in any case, while we live among many people, it is impossible for us not to have someone encounter us.
Not even that angel of God, Arsenius, who loved stillness more than anyone, could escape this.
For we have meetings with fathers and brothers, unexpected encounters, and the journey to church.
When that man, worthy of blessings, saw that it was impossible
for anyone to escape these things as long as he was near a place where people lived,
even though his own dwelling was many miles away from human gatherings,
and even from the solitary monks who lived in those places, he learned this means from grace: constant silence.
Thus, even when it was sometimes necessary for him to open the door to some of them,
they were delighted merely to see him, while conversation and the use of speech were unnecessary among them.
Many fathers were trained by this sight to be watchful themselves as well,
so that their spiritual wealth might increase through the instruction they received from seeing the blessed man.
They constantly saw him keeping silent, so that many of them
would put a stone in their mouth, while others would tie a rope around their waist underneath their clothing as a reminder.
Others would afflict themselves with severe hunger, more than usual.
Whenever one was about to go out among people, he would impose the affliction of hunger on himself.
For hunger greatly helped those who embraced humility to subdue their senses.
They did many things like these to acquire this watchfulness, which is delightful to behold and gives life.
I have found many fathers, my brothers, great and wonderful men, who, more than with other ascetic labors,
were concerned with disciplining the senses and with the bearing of the body, because from these there also arises the disciplining
of thoughts. Many circumstances confront a person against his will and cause him to pass beyond the bounds of his freedom.
And if he is not watchful over his senses, because of the persistent habit that has already taken hold of the soul,
they keep him for a very long time from returning to his senses and finding his former stillness.
Nourishment for the heart is meditation on its hope. Nourishment for one's way of life, however, is
release from everything. Remembering death is a good restraint for the outward members of the body.
The soul's absorption in life is the joy that springs up within the heart through hope.
Knowledge is watered by the constant trials arising from both kinds of change, which the mind receives inwardly every day.
The heart's flourishing is the assurance about the resurrection that it receives inwardly through the faith of hope.
Make me worthy, my Lord, to see your compassion in my soul before I depart from this world,
so that at that hour I may experience consolation within myself, together with those who have departed from this world in good hope.
Open my heart, my God, through your grace, and cleanse me from fellowship with sin.
And trace in my heart a path of repentance, my God and my Lord, my hope and my glory, my strong refuge,
so that through it my eyes may be enlightened and I may understand your truth, Lord. Make me worthy, my Lord, to taste that delight of the gift of repentance,
through which the soul is separated from involvement in sin and from every desire of flesh and blood.
Make me worthy, my Lord, to taste this sorrow, in which the gift of pure prayer is placed.
May I reach, my Savior, this wonderful passage through which the soul leaves the visible world,
and in which new stirrings begin toward entry into the spiritual world, along with experiences of new perceptions.
Whoever begins and finishes well lays this foundation for his way of life.
And without ceasing he implores God to make him worthy to experience this,
through which knowledge of that future state is stirred into life, in an imperishable hope,
which, by God's grace, is kept for human beings after the end of this world.
But whoever begins in the opposite way comes down from above to below. That is, he begins in joy and ends in weeping.
He becomes empty of knowledge and hope, like an unformed body and like a physical frame not fully developed enough to receive a soul.
Because he was not brought to maturity through the process of growth in the womb, and came to the fullness of the life of [?].
Disdain for involvement with the world is a sign of a soul that has become aware of its hope.
Hidden wakefulness is sleep toward visible things.
The heart’s armor is faith in Christ, which, through its longing for hope, dares even to face death.
Death is regarded as nothing in his eyes, nor does he regard exile from his country or attacks from demons,
or estrangement from other people, or deprivation of the world’s consolation.
What is the consolation that comes from visible things and involvement with them,
compared with the delight of hope felt in the heart? He is like someone transported out of his body through the intoxication of his joy,
through the blaze of faith that sets the heart alight; and hidden
from him are all visible things. He does not know that he is in the created world, because of the warmth of his body together with the stirrings of his soul.
Through the faith of his mind, he seems to himself like someone already standing in that kingdom.
For although we sometimes experience discouragement because of solitude—perhaps this is allowed to happen providentially—
we also have the consolation of hope, beyond words, through the faith of our heart.
Through this hope, we regard afflictions as nothing, and death likewise.
One of those clothed in God spoke well when he said, “The love of God is enough to console the believer, even when he loses his life.”
“What harm,” he says, “can afflictions do to someone who even despises the pleasures of comfort for the sake of the good things to come?” This too:
My brother, I urge you: in your whole way of life, let the scale of compassion outweigh everything else,
so that through it you may become aware of the compassion God has for the worlds.
These things in us become a mirror for us, in which to see that true delight in the qualities that belong by nature to that Being.
Through these things and others like them, we are enlightened, so that we may turn our thoughts toward God with a clear mind.
A harsh heart never becomes clear. A compassionate person is the physician of his own soul,
driving the cloud of darkness out from within himself as though with a powerful wind. This is a good pledge with God, according to the saying
of the Gospel of life: “Blessed is the merciful person, for mercy will be shown to him.” Besides what happens in the world to come, this also happens mystically here.
What mercy is greater than this: that when he is moved with compassion for his fellow human being and shares in his suffering,
our Lord saves his soul from the gloom of darkness, which is the spiritual Gehenna itself:
And he brings her near to the light of life for her delight.
Blessed Evagrius rightly said, “A smooth road comes from compassion.”
Therefore, as I said, let a compassionate heart prevail over all your conduct, and you will find peace with God.
Take care that harm never comes through your hands to anyone, not even to an evil person.
Whenever it is in your power to rescue a wrongdoer from harm, do not neglect to do so.
This does not mean that, if the matter is far removed from you, you should go and throw yourself into affairs like these.
For this is not your task. But if the matter is placed in your hands and you have authority over it,
as when a matter comes before you as a trial through an adverse encounter,
and God brings you into a test by leaving you on your own, take care:
Do not become an accomplice in the wrongdoer’s bloodshed by failing to make an effort to deliver him.
Instead, with all your soul, find a way to rescue him, even if it means dying for him.
At that moment you are truly a martyr, like the one who accepted death on the cross for sinners.
And implore God that this should not come from you yourself. Rather, even if he deserves harm, through the hands of
others let him receive judgment for his deed. It is not your task to consider what his deeds deserve.
Through your own hands, let good come to him.
Remember the one who bears with everyone, while everyone’s deeds lie before his eyes
and shine before him more brightly than the sun. If he wishes, he can destroy everyone with a breath from his mouth.
But you have not been appointed to exact retribution for deeds and those who do them, but to ask for mercy upon the world,
to keep vigil for the salvation of everyone, and to share in everyone’s suffering, both the righteous and sinners.
And know that if that person deserves it, whoever he is, it will not be long
before justice binds him through the hands of others suited to the deed. But you will save your soul and become a living martyr.
Yet you should not even desire or dwell on this. Instead, ask God in his compassion on that person’s behalf
that he may be changed and become as God wills, and that he may depart this life in righteousness, not in punishment for wrongdoing.
Instead of an avenger, be a deliverer. Instead of an accuser, be a comforter. Instead of a betrayer, be a martyr.
Instead of a quarreller, be a peacemaker. Instead of a reprover, be an advocate. Plead on behalf of sinners, that they may receive mercy.
Pray also for the righteous, that they may be protected. Overcome evil people with your kindness.
Astonish the zealous with your goodness. Put those who love justice to shame with your mercy.
Share inwardly in the distress of those who are distressed. Love everyone, and keep your distance from everyone. Death—
remember it, and prepare for your entrance into it. Adorn the course of your life.
Remember that everyone’s sins go ahead of them to the court of judgment. Do not lose hope when you stumble.
I am not saying that you should not grieve, but that you should not think these things are beyond healing.
For it is better to be broken than [?], since even the broken person has a physician:
the one who asked for mercy on his crucifiers while on the cross, the one who forgave his killers while he hung on the cross.
“All sins and blasphemies will be forgiven people,” he says—that is, through repentance.
For a little weeping, he forgave Simon, who had denied him. After his resurrection, he appointed him to be head of his flock.
Three times he asks him, “Do you love me?” corresponding to the three times he denied him, so as to confirm his forgiveness.
Christ came for sinners, to heal the brokenhearted and bind up their wounds.
“The Spirit of the Lord is upon me,” he says. “For this reason he has anointed me, to [?] to the poor. He has sent me to heal the brokenhearted,
to proclaim release to captives and sight to the blind, and to set the crushed free.”
And the apostle says in his letter, “Jesus Christ came into the world to save sinners.”
And his Lord testifies, “For I did not come to call the righteous.”
“The healthy do not need a physician,” he says, “but those who are seriously ill.”
“There were two debtors,” he says, “who owed one creditor. When they had nothing with which to repay him, he forgave them both.”
That is, when they pleaded with him. Our frail nature is weak if repayment is demanded
by God’s justice. Therefore he deals with us in mercy: we are always held under debt.
Do not sin, O human being, in expectation of repentance, and do not let yourself fall because you are confident of forgiveness.
Remember that death does not delay. Do not cunningly scheme to approach the pleasure of sin.
God is not mocked. His knowledge precedes your thoughts. For distress will overtake you suddenly,
and you will call, but he will not answer you. When you approach your bed because the time has come to sleep,
say, “O bed, perhaps this very night you are to become my grave, and I do not know it.”
Could it be that instead of a temporary sleep, that eternal sleep will fall upon me tonight?
Yet I am thinking about preparing for days and months that I will not see.
While you still have feet, run after the practice of righteousness, before that shackle falls upon them
which can never again be undone. While you still have hands, stretch them toward heaven in prayer,
before the time when your arms fall from their sockets, and you want to raise them but cannot.
While you still have fingers, raise them toward God in supplication.
For the time is coming when the firmness of their finely woven structure will loosen. While you still have eyes,
fill them with tears in prayer, weeping over your sins, before the hour
when a film covers the pupils and they remain fixed in an unfeeling stare toward one corner, without your knowing it.
While the heart, the wellspring of thoughts, is governed by the power of discernment, think about the things that will awaken your life [?],
before the soul becomes troubled about departing from it, and it becomes a house deserted by its inhabitants.
O wise one, do not let a thought deceive you with the expectation of a long life.
Just as a flower withers when hot wind blows upon it, one of the elements within you blows upon you from inside.
Suddenly, without your knowing it, your knees grow weak. And while you think it is nothing,
while you are still nursing the illness, suddenly that tireless one draws near, the one who mocks the wise.
Oh, the misery of our nature! How firmly we cling in love to that in which God does not wish to leave us!
Set your heart on preparing for departure, O human being. Like a wise person, always be expecting the journey,
thinking every day, “Look, the messenger who has come for me has reached the door.
Why am I sitting here? This is a departure forever; I will never return here again.”
Spend every night with this reflection, and meditate on this thought every day,
so that when he comes, you may rejoice to meet him: “Welcome! I knew that you would surely come,
and I have neglected nothing that I need for the journey.” Gather provisions for your long journey, wise one.
Lift the weight of sleep from your heart, you who have been summoned. Put your belongings in order for departure, you who dwell here.
The appointed time of morning is near, guest. Why are you sleeping? Get up and prepare yourself, sailor traveling on the sea.
Get up and ready your ship’s equipment, for you do not know when the wind will rise for you.
Prepare yourself and be ready before the one who destroys your features comes. For it is said, “Sheol will wear away their form.”
They will be driven away from the splendid glory of their nature, and their bodies will be left to decay.
At all times, call to mind that destruction, dreadful to behold, that unrecognizable scattering of your senses,
and that collapse of the structure of your body—that pure composition which becomes mud in Sheol.
Blessed is the person who joyfully welcomes the remembrance of that destruction!
Blessed is the person who awaits with good hope that event full of mystery, in which the wonder of the Creator’s great power is hidden!
The aforementioned meditation on what is expected after the resurrection is a spiritual exercise.
The culmination of repentance sets this movement in motion in the mind.
Constant reflection on things to come sustains repentance in the soul.
Whoever has been moved to repentance has moved in hope to the world to come.
Whoever has forgotten this has kept his mind in this world. Whoever loves communion with Christ loves to be alone.
Whoever loves to remain among many people is a friend of this world. Repentance
is the heart’s constant sorrow as it meditates on that great, indescribable order:
“How, then, shall I attain that indescribable entrance?” If you love repentance, love stillness too.
For without it, repentance is not brought to completion.
If anyone disputes this, do not argue with him, for he does not know what he is saying.
If he knew what repentance is, he would also know its place, and that it cannot be perfected amid turmoil.
If you love stillness, the father of repentance, also love to accept gladly the small bodily losses and the reproaches that arise.
Without this readiness, you cannot live freely in stillness, undisturbed.
If you disregard these things, you honor stillness according to God’s will.
If you are wronged, deprived, mocked, and so forth, and are not disturbed because of your love of stillness.
Love of stillness is the constant expectation of death. Whoever enters stillness without this exercise,
while having something else in mind, cannot bear the things that must be endured on its account from every direction.
To die for God’s sake and to live in God. “The perfection of life,” it is said, “is meditation on death for God’s sake.
For this brings our mind close to being united with God,” says Evagrius.
Know this too, discerning one: the life we live by ourselves, in solitude, stillness, and seclusion,
we choose not in order to undertake greater exertion in the prescribed practices. For it is well known that living in community
with many others lends greater support to this, because of the constraint it places on the body.
If this alone were necessary, those devout men, the holy fathers, would not have abandoned conversation and human company,
with some living in tombs and others choosing confinement in a solitary cell,
which greatly weakens the body and hinders the fulfillment of the prescribed practices.
Despite all that bodily weakness and debility, and the severity of the illnesses that overtook them,
they gladly persevered throughout their lives, even though they could not stand on their feet,
or offer their customary prayer, or praise God with their mouths.
Nor could they recite a psalm or perform any of the things carried out bodily.
Bodily weakness and stillness alone, together with this intention, sufficed for them in place of all the prescribed practices, throughout all the days of their lives.
Amid all this apparent inactivity, not one of them longed to leave his cell
and, because he was resting from the exertions of the prescribed practices, wander outside or enjoy the sound of others’ praises in the assemblies.
Better, then, is someone who has become aware of his sins than someone who benefits the world through his visions.
Better is someone who has sighed once in solitude than someone who raises the dead through his prayer while living among many others.
Better is someone who has been found worthy to see himself than someone who has been found worthy to see angels. The latter
shares in this through the eyes of the body, but the former through the eye of the soul.
Better is someone who follows Christ alone in mourning than someone who celebrates him in an assembly.
Let no one bring forward that saying of Paul: “I myself would be accursed and cut off from Christ,” and the rest.
Whoever has received Paul’s strength is also permitted to do this.
But Paul was guided by a divine command addressed to him to benefit the world,
as he himself also testified that he was not doing this of his own will: “Necessity is laid upon me,” he says, “and woe to me if I do not proclaim the good news!”
Moreover, the purpose of Paul’s election was not directed toward repentance, but toward proclaiming the good news to humanity; he also received extraordinary strength.
Therefore we love stillness, [?], so that this world may die away from our hearts and we may constantly remember death.
Through this very meditation, may we draw near to God in our hearts.
And let us despise the emptiness of the world, and let its pleasures become contemptible in our eyes.
Let us gladly endure in this wretched body the continual inactivity that [?] in stillness,
so that we may be worthy of delight with those who, in caves and hollows of the earth, await the glorious revelation of our Lord from heaven.
To him, to his Father, and to the Holy Spirit be praise and exaltation forever and ever.
A letter that he sent to his beloved friend, in which he explains various things about the mystery of stillness,
and how many neglect it because they do not understand this wondrous practice.
Most of them maintain their residence in a cell merely out of habit, because of the tradition current among those of later times.
Together with a collection of brief sayings useful for meditation in stillness. 66.
Because, my brother, you have laid on me the obligation to write to you about the things that are necessary,
I make them known to you, my beloved, through my writings, in accordance with the promise I made to you.
For I found that you were determined to pursue a life of stillness with exactness in your conduct.
I too, gathering together the meaning of their words, take what I have heard from discerning people about this practice,
along with closely related experiences in actual practice, and set it down in plain language to remind you.
You too will benefit from meditating on this letter, through the diligence you possess,
since you approach the reading of the concise words of this letter of ours with wise understanding, rather than merely following your usual routine.
You take them as a kind of illumination for the rest of your reading, because of the abundant meanings and the power hidden in them.
For the mind is greatly strengthened by readings like these and receives from them a weapon against distraction of thought
and against the discouragement that commonly arises from the severity of the labors and the prolonged time spent in stillness.
It casts the world and concern for its affairs behind it, through the fervor with which it is clothed by what it reads,
in keeping with the aim we have set ourselves in this letter: what residence in stillness and its practice are;
what mysteries lie hidden in this way of life, concealed from many;
and what discoveries diligent people strive to attain in stillness;
and why they reject the righteousness practiced among people and flee from the sight of the world,
choosing instead the afflictions and struggles of a quiet and solitary dwelling.
Through understanding these things and what they encounter in this letter, they call those who live in solitude blessed.
Those who spend their lives in this world dwelling in collected solitude, alone with themselves.
For those who have not perceived these things, admonition, together with all the warnings about the disciplines of solitude, is superfluous.
Here, however, I write as to wise people, and I offer counsel in love.
If you wish to find incorruptible life within your few days, brother,
let your entry into solitude be made with discernment, so that you may find the benefit that the wise expect from the practices of solitude.
Investigate its work, and do not chase after the name. Enter, go deep, persevere boldly, learn, and acquire.
Train yourself in all the wonderful and noble distinctions between the kinds of work practiced in solitude,
so that, with all the saints, you may comprehend what is the height and depth and length and breadth
of this boundless way of life, because of the boundlessness of that wealth which its merchants strive to acquire.
Do not rest until you have trained yourself in all the paths of its practices.
For every human undertaking, at the beginning of its execution, some benefit expected from carrying it out
moves the mind toward laying the foundation of the undertaking.
This goal strengthens the mind to endure its difficulties, and the mind receives some consolation from it by looking toward it.
Like a kind of bond, it holds the mind until the undertaking is completed.
Likewise, in the precious work of solitude, the harbor of mysteries, discerning people have a goal
toward which the mind looks from the time it lays the first foundations until the building is finished.
Throughout all its long and difficult labors, like the eyes of a helmsman looking at the stars,
so the solitary fixes his inward gaze, throughout the entire course of his journey, on that goal which he adopted in his mind
on the first day when he gave himself to sailing the difficult sea of solitude,
until he finds that pearl for whose sake he plunged into the sea’s unfathomable depths.
Looking toward what he hopes for lightens for him the whole burden of the work and the hardships, bitter with danger, that he encounters on his journey.
But anyone who, at the beginning—at the beginning of his entry into solitude—has not set himself this goal for the benefit to be gained from his work,
but labors in mere busyness, like someone beating the air, will never be free from the spirit
of discouragement throughout his life. One of two things will happen to him:
either, unable to endure the unbearable burden, he is overcome and leaves solitude altogether.
Or if he stubbornly persists in it, his cell becomes a prison in which he is tormented,
because he does not know how to wait for the consolation born of the work done in stillness.
Consequently, he cannot even ask with an aching heart, seek with fervent prayer, or yearn
for those things about which our fathers, full of compassion and love for their children, left us instructions in their writings so that we might find life.
For one said: “For me, this is the benefit of stillness: when I withdraw from the community where I live,
my mind is emptied of its preparations for battle and turns toward the work of virtue.”
Another saying. Stillness cuts off the causes that renew distracting thoughts.
Within its walls, it makes memories of former things grow old and fade.
When the old contents of the mind have worn away, the intellect returns to its natural uprightness. Another saying.
“But I hasten toward stillness for this reason: so that the words of reading and prayer may become sweet in my heart.
When my tongue falls silent through delight in their meanings, I fall into something like sleep, with my senses and my inner movements stilled.
And when, through remaining long in stillness, my heart is again at peace from the turmoil of memories,
waves of joy continually surge over me, gushing unexpectedly from inward stirrings,
suddenly bringing delight to my heart. When these waves beat against the ship of my soul,
they sink it away from the world's talk and the life of the flesh into the deepest abysses of stillness in God.”
Another saying. You can understand the measure of your hidden inner states from the differences in your inner movements.
I mean those that persist, not those that chance stirs up and time sweeps away.
There is no one clothed in flesh whose house is not visited by a guest from both kinds of change, good and bad.
If he is diligent, he is visited by states of deficiency, because of nature—that is, the parents of offspring.
And if, on the other hand, he is negligent, he is visited by states of elevation,
because of that leaven of grace placed in our nature, because of the one who was given a lineage in the family of the kingdom above.
Another saying. Choose for yourself a delightful practice: constant vigilance through the nights.
Through it all the fathers put off the old person and were found worthy of renewal of mind.
It is at these times that the soul perceives that immortal life; through its awareness of that life,
it takes off the garment of darkness and becomes receptive to the gifts of the Spirit.
Another saying. It is impossible, when a person sees many faces
and hears various voices foreign to his spiritual meditation, and speaks and converses with such people,
for his mind to have the leisure to look inwardly at himself, remember his sins, and put his thoughts in order,
and keep watch over things to come and occupy himself with hidden prayer. Again, to bring
these senses under the soul’s authority is impossible for a person without stillness and separation from other people.
For the knowing soul is united and intertwined with them in its very being,
and is carried along with their movements unless it remains vigilant in hidden prayer. Again,
how keeping vigil, with its wakefulness accompanied by prayer and reading, refreshes, delights, gladdens, and brightens the soul
is understood especially well by those who have practiced these things throughout their lives in strict ascetic discipline.
But you, a person who loves stillness, set these indications drawn from the meaning of the fathers’ words before you as a target,
and direct the course of your labor toward the goal they set.
Before everything else, learn to discern which things are especially suited to the aim of your labor,
without which you cannot be instructed in the knowledge of truth; and strive all the more to show your perseverance in them.
Silence is a mystery of the world to come. Speech is an instrument of this world.
A person who fasts is training himself to resemble the nature of spiritual beings.
A person who perseveres inwardly in divine service is distinguished by his silence and his constant fasting.
Through these mysteries there is also performed by those invisible powers
that service, full of holiness, of the Being who is Lord of the worlds.
People, too, who were at times set apart to enter into the divine mysteries
were marked with these seals. Some of them were entrusted with governing a mighty people.
Others were even given authority over the elements, and, in a great wonder, the natural forces of creation obeyed the command of their words.
Still others were entrusted with revealing, for inward renewal, the hidden things concealed in the secret silence of the Lord of all.
For it was not fitting that, with a full belly and a mind distracted by indulgence,
such mysteries should be celebrated, or that those holy people should dare to converse with God
and rise to the hidden depths of his mysteries, except with weakened limbs and a complexion grown pale from the suffering of hunger.
And this is one whose mind is calm through being emptied of all earthly thoughts.
For when, through the long time spent within your cell, through strenuous labors and hidden watchfulness,
and through keeping your senses still and away from every encounter, the power of stillness overshadows you,
you first encounter that joy without a cause which reigns in your soul from time to time.
Then your eyes are opened to see the power of God's creative activity and the beauty of created things,
in proportion to the degree of your purity. And when the mind is drawn into wonder at this vision,
night and day become one for it from then on, in wonder at the glory of God's works.
From this point, awareness of the passions is gently stolen away from the soul by this vision. Through it the soul enters the regions
of the stages of intellectual revelations, which are arranged in order after this, from purity upward.
An explanation through illustrations of the distinctions between intelligible things, and of what meaning each of these has. 67.
The understanding is a spiritual sense, made to receive the power of sight, like the pupil of the bodily eye,
into which perceptible light is poured. Sight [?] is natural knowledge,
which was blended into it potentially along with the constitution of its nature, and which is called natural light.
The holy power is grace, the sun that makes discernible the things placed between light and sight.
Natures are the things lying in between, made discernible to sight by the light.
The passions, however, are like certain opaque substances,
which, whenever they come between light and sight, prevent sight from distinguishing things.
Purity is the clarity of the intelligible air, within which the spiritual nature in us flies.
The converse. If the understanding is not healthy in its nature, knowledge does not work in it.
It is like the bodily sense: whenever it is damaged by ailments, sight is taken away from it.
If the understanding is healthy, but knowledge is absent,
the understanding cannot distinguish spiritual things without it. It is like an eye that is healthy in all its parts,
yet is sometimes deprived of visual perception. If, then, all these are preserved in their proper qualities,
but grace is not near, they all remain inactive, unable to perform their work of discernment.
It is just as it is during the hours of night, when, because of the sun's absence,
They remain inactive, even though they are all sound and complete in themselves.
I mean the eye, sight, and the things seen: they neither distinguish nor are distinguished.
This is what is meant by the saying, “In your light we see light.”
But even if grace is an intelligible sun, near at hand, enticing, drawing, working, and awakening,
if there is no purity in which, as in air cleared of dense clouds and darkening matter,
the sun’s rays can readily extend toward us, and in the delightful light
from which we take pleasant delight in the wholly spiritual vision of this universe, sight is impaired in its discernment;
nature is inactive, and the soul is deprived of experiencing the delight of the second sun, which shines upon everything,
because of the bodily disposition in which the radiance of truth is dissipated, so that it does not stream toward us.
Therefore, all these things that have been mentioned are indispensable.
And because all these things are scarcely to be found without deficiency in a single person,
not many are found who attain even a partial completion of spiritual knowledge.
Such deficiency comes from the mind’s inadequacy, from a lack of focused purpose,
from the will’s lack of readiness, from insufficient purity, from the unavailability of paths, and from the withholding of grace.
For it is said, “Wealth does not suit a fool, nor does it suit a slave to exercise authority over great affairs.” It also comes from the obstacles of time, place, and person.
Concise Chapters. 68.
You know, my brothers, that the physical eye, solely through its power of sight,
which flows toward it from the brain as though through a channel,
cannot perceive the distinctions between things unless that power participates in another light.
All the perceptible things of nature are arranged in parallel with the [?] of the spiritual way of life, according to this analogy.
And the mind’s natural power, which is also called the knowledge of the soul—
unless it receives divine light, the soul cannot participate in truth through its contemplation.
This light, through excellence of conduct, after the part of the soul subject to passions has been built up in natural health,
is acquired. Many, that is to say, have ventured, while still having passions of soul and body,
upon the philosophical course, relying on this alone, and have strayed even from the truth they held.
And they lost their accustomed vision. Like eyes that see mirages in the air,
because of the weakness of their sight, which is deprived of the moist substances within them, each one of them regarded a single
image that was imagined before him as reality.
And when all their images were gathered together, many images appeared there instead of one, taking the place of reality.
This happened to them because they did not seek the rays of grace, which shines through the purification of the soul.
Truth is an awareness of God that, through the perception of the mind’s spiritual senses,
a person experiences for himself. The blossom of spiritual knowledge is divine love,
which comes about through the inflaming insights that are found through the Spirit in prayer.
Love is the fruit of prayer, which, through contemplation of its content, draws the mind insatiably toward love of it,
when we persevere in it without interruption, whether in prayer expressed perceptibly through the body,
or in prayer offered fervently and intensely through the quiet movement of the mind.
Prayer is the death of the movements of the will to the life of the flesh.
For to pray genuinely and to die to the world are the same thing.
This is what it means for a person to deny himself: to be constant in prayer.
Those who know the Scriptures know what genuine prayer asks for.
And it is known that those who have undertaken this solitary disposition,
to acquire single-minded prayer in their petitions, do not [?], contrary to their desire,
so as to stir up disturbances in their souls because of the opposing passions that, after prayer, in their souls
are set in motion. Therefore, love of God is found through self-denial.
Just as the ear of chastity sprouts from the seeds of the sweat of fasting,
so recklessness springs from satiety, and obscenity from a full stomach.
But base thoughts never beset a hungry stomach.
Every food that we take into ourselves increases the fluids of the natural semen that accumulates in our bodies.
And when the reproductive organs have become filled with the fluid that comes there from the whole body,
if someone happens to see a body, or some memory stirs involuntarily in the heart,
Along with the thought, pleasant material is immediately stirred from there and rushes throughout the whole body.
Thus, even if the mind is very strong, chaste, and pure in its movements,
through that sensation in the bodily members, its discernment is immediately thrown into confusion,
and it is brought down from where it stands, as though from some height. The stillness of its thoughts is disturbed,
and its pure chastity is defiled by the confusion caused by that passion which stirs in the heart through the burning of the bodily members.
Immediately, half its strength is brought low, so to speak, and it forgets the original goal of its hope.
Before entering the contest, it finds itself defeated, without a struggle and without any effort on its enemy's part,
and condemned to submit to the degrading will of the body. All this is forced by nourishment
in abundance and continual fullness upon a person's good will, so that, while he is being guided properly in the harbor of chastity,
he is inclined to surrender to something that he had never before been inclined or willing even to let enter his mind.
While he lies alone, a crowd of thoughts clothed in shameful images surrounds him.
They have turned his pure bed into a theater and a brothel,
as he acts and speaks with them in the drunkenness of his thoughts, defiling his holy bodily members,
though no woman is near him. What sea is so disturbed and battered by storms
as the upright mind is disturbed by the force of the waves stirred up against it in the sea of its body
by the fullness of the stomach? O chastity, how brightly your beauty shines through sleeping on the ground and suffering hunger,
from which sleep flees because of the body's emaciation and the emptiness of the stomach,
which has become a deep hollow between the ribs for the intestines because food is scarce!
But from the food and rest that we take into ourselves, hateful likenesses and disgraceful images are formed and come into being.
They come forth and appear to us in the hidden place of our mind,
and entice us into secretly joining them in filthy acts. But the emptiness of the stomach
makes the mind a deserted place, empty of thoughts and quiet from all the turmoil of imaginings.
But a stomach that is full and satisfied makes it a place of spectacles and a theater, even if we are in the wilderness
and alone. As the saying goes, fullness craves many things.
You who through divine grace have been deemed worthy of freedom from passion in the soul, understand:
Not from the fact that evil thoughts do not pass through you, or that bodily impulses do not stir—for that is impossible.
Nor from the fact that you overcome them easily, while your mind remains entirely undefiled and undisturbed, although this is a very exalted state.
Rather, from the fact that, because of the mind’s excellent activity, the intellect is not even allowed to engage them in battle and destroy them.
Instead, as soon as the thoughts appear, it is snatched away from them by the compelling force of something beyond its own will.
For through habit and grace, leaven has taken hold within the heart, which is the dwelling of the mind.
The intellect that struggles is one thing; the priestly order is another.
For the mind that has died to the world through heavenly affections, thoughts about things are merely ordinary thoughts,
without the clash of combat. And if they arise from the movement of the bodily members, there is sensation without a mental image.
Perfection that is bound to flesh and blood does indeed rule over the things that spring from flesh and blood,
but it does not abolish the properties of nature, while the movement of its life still stirs within the life derived from the elements,
and the foundation of its existence undergoes changes at every moment from the four humors.
How discerning people ought to dwell in stillness. 69.
Listen, my beloved, to what our love tells you. If you want your labors not to be empty and your days not to be wasted,
and do not want to be deprived of the benefit awaited by discerning people in the practice of stillness,
let your entry into stillness be made with discernment, and not, as with many people, through the mere momentum of habit.
Rather, let a goal be set before your mind, toward which it will direct the labors of its way of life.
Ask those who understand well through experience, and not through reading alone.
Train yourself in all the wondrous and noble distinctions of stillness.
Do not rest until you have become skilled in all the paths of its practices.
With every step you take, examine whether you are traveling along the road,
or have strayed from it onto one of the paths that lead into trackless country.
Do not believe that the sound practice of stillness is perfected through outward labors alone.
If you wish to attain in your own experience what our fathers discovered,
let there be indications and signs hidden within your soul at every step you take,
through which you can recognize the truth of our fathers or the deception of Satan.
Here are a few of them, so that you may become wise in your way.
Whenever, during your time in stillness, you see that your mind can freely direct its movements toward what is right,
and there is no compulsion in its control over any of them, know that your stillness is sound.
And again, if, while you perform your service with discernment, keeping as free from distraction as possible,
the words suddenly cease on your tongue, and the restraints of involuntary silence are laid upon your [?],
and this continues persistently, know that you are advancing in your stillness, and its simplicity has begun to become twofold.
For mere stillness is contemptible in the realm of righteousness.
And every practice pursued on its own is regarded by those skilled in discernment as a single limb separated from [?].
And again, if you see that, with every thought stirred within your soul, with every remembrance and vision that comes in stillness,
your eyes fill with tears, and you shower your cheeks with them without forcing them, know
that a breach has begun to open before you in the enemy's camp. And if you find
that from time to time your mind sinks within you, without your deliberately attending to it and outside its customary pattern,
and remains there for part of an hour, however long it may be, and afterward you see that your limbs seem very weak,
and peace reigns over all your thoughts, remaining continually the same, know that the cloud has begun to overshadow the tabernacle.
But if, after spending some time in stillness, you find that disruptive thoughts dominate your soul, and that
it is continually driven by them as though by force, and its mind is constantly drawn toward the things with which it was formerly occupied,
or is eager for empty investigations, know that you are toiling in stillness in vain, and your soul is being corrupted by distraction.
It has occasions for this from outside, or there is neglect of its inward duties,
especially keeping vigil and reading. Set your affairs straight and put them in order.
But if, as soon as you enter upon these days, you do not find peace from the sting of the passions, do not be surprised.
For even in the world's expanse, after the sun's rays have withdrawn from it, their warmth remains for a long time afterward.
And the smell of aromatic substances and the fragrance of perfumes poured out into the air remain for a long time before they disperse and fade.
How much more will the passions, which, like dogs beside a butcher, have become accustomed to licking blood,
when the things that feed their habits are withheld from them, stand barking at the door until the strength of their former habit dissipates.
Whenever negligence begins to creep secretly into your soul and to envelop it in darkness from behind,
And the house is close to being filled with darkness. You secretly sense these approaching signs within yourself.
You will grow weak in your faith, become absorbed in visible things, and lose confidence.
You will fail your neighbor, and your soul [?] will become full of accusations, in your mouth and in your heart, against every person and thing
and the matters you encounter in your thoughts and through your senses, and even against the Most High himself.
You will fear bodily suffering, and because of it, faintheartedness will rule over you constantly.
From time to time your soul will tremble with fear, so that you will be startled and terrified by your own shadow.
For by faith I do not mean the faith that forms the foundation of the common confession,
but that spiritual power which supports the heart through the light of the mind
and, through the testimony of conscience, stirs up great confidence in God within the soul.
The soul no longer worries about itself, but casts its care upon God, entirely free from anxiety.
When, on the other hand, you advance in spiritual understanding, here too there are these clear signs:
You will feel them closely [?] within your soul. Hope will strengthen you in everything, and you will become rich in prayer.
Your mind will never lack material for spiritual benefit in anything you encounter.
You will recognize the weakness of human nature. On the one hand, this will protect you from pride;
on the other, your neighbor’s shortcomings will become insignificant in your eyes.
Departure from the body will become desirable to you, because you long to draw near to the things in which we are destined to live.
As for all the distressing events that assail you, openly or secretly,
you will find that they all come upon you justly, with complete certainty, free from delusion. And for
everything you will offer thanksgiving. These signs are for those who are watchful,
who persevere in stillness and wish to attain precision in their way of life.
The lax, however, have no need of subtle and hidden signs of falling,
since they are also far removed from hidden virtues. Whenever one of these things begins to stir within your soul,
observe at once which way it has begun to incline, for you will immediately recognize which group it belongs to.
On understanding the measure of our way of life from the changes in our mind,
and on not relying childishly only on the many different forms of our labors, but knowing the measure of our soul as wise people do.
From the joy that he feels inwardly day by day. And on the subtle order of knowledge. 70.
Examine yourself continually, my beloved, and consider, amid all your relentless labors and pressing afflictions,
the desolate place where you live, the subtlety of your mind together with the sharpness of your knowledge, and the long duration of your solitude,
along with the many medicines of trials administered continually by the true Physician for the health of the inner person:
sometimes through demons, sometimes through the illnesses and sufferings of your body,
sometimes through the terrors that stir your soul as you remember the dreadful things awaiting you at the end, and sometimes, again, through the soothing treatments
and bandages of grace: fervor, sweet tears, joy of spirit, and the rest—not to prolong the discussion.
Now, through all these things, do you see any sign at all that your wound has begun to close? That is,
have the passions begun to be wiped away? Set yourself a marker, and continually enter into yourself:
which passions do you see have grown weak before you? Which of them have come to an end and disappeared entirely?
And which of them have begun to become quiet because your soul is healthy, and not because the things that provoke them have gone away,
and because your mind has grown strong, rather than because occasions for them are lacking?
Consider: in the healing of your wound, do you see any sign at all
that healthy flesh has begun to grow—that is, peace of soul? Which passions oppress you continually, and which only from time to time?
Are these bodily passions, passions of the soul, or a mixture? Do they stir faintly in your memory, like sick people,
or do they rise forcefully against the soul? And do they act like masters,
or stealthily? How does the mind, the king and ruler of the senses, regard them when they knock? Does it fight against them and bring them low by its strength,
or does it no longer even look at them or give them a thought? Which are remnants of the old passions,
and which have newly taken shape? Are the passions stirred through images,
or is there awareness without an image, remembrance without passions, and movement without incitements? From these things, too,
it is possible to know the soul’s measure and where it stands. In the former case, even if they do not prevail,
the soul still has a struggle, even though it shows itself stronger than they are.
The latter, however, can be understood through an illustration, as Scripture says:
“David settled in his house, and the Lord gave him rest from everyone around him.”
Do not understand these things as referring to only one passion, but also to the natural passions of desire and anger:
And also the passion of love of praise, which pictures faces and stirs up thoughts and desires.
And again, the passion of love of [?], whenever the soul secretly participates in it, even if it is not persuaded to put it into practice.
Love of money paints images of things in the mind, with materials for amassing wealth,
and persuades the soul to dwell on them and urges it to acquire them, along with the other things.
Not all passions wage war through desires. For there are passions that make the soul endure nothing but distress.
Weariness, despondency, and sorrow do not work through desires or pleasures, but merely lay a burden on the soul.
The soul’s determination is tested by victory over those passions that wage war through enticements.
A person ought to have precise knowledge and awareness of all these things, so that he may perceive, with every step he takes,
where he has arrived and in what place his soul has begun to tread:
whether in the land of Canaan or on this side of the Jordan. Consider this too:
whether, because of the soul’s brightness, its knowledge is sufficient to make these distinctions,
or whether it distinguishes them dimly, or is entirely devoid of such things. Can you, then,
[?] at all whether your thoughts have begun to grow calm?
Does distraction give the mind any room at the time of prayer? And which passion causes disturbance when the mind approaches prayer? Do you perceive within yourself
that the power of stillness has overshadowed the soul through the unusual tranquility and peace it produces in the mind?
Is the intellect continually carried away, beyond its own will, through movements without bodily form, toward things that the senses are not permitted to interpret?
Does a joy [?] suddenly within you, silencing the tongue with its incomparable delight?
Does a certain sweetness continually well up from the heart, drawing the whole person completely toward itself?
Sometimes, without your being aware of it, does a certain delight and gladness come over your whole body, which a tongue born of flesh cannot express,
so that you consider all earthly things ashes and dung, even at the memory of it?
The first of these occurs sometimes during prayer and sometimes during reading.
Sometimes, again, it comes from meditation in which the mind engages persistently and at length, while the intellect burns with fervor.
This last experience generally occurs apart from these activities, and quite often during prolonged work,
and on most nights in that same state, between sleep and wakefulness: asleep, yet not asleep,
and awake, yet not awake. And the delight that courses through the whole body seems this way to the person at that time:
As though the kingdom of heaven were nothing other than this. And see also whether the soul has acquired
