the strength to disregard memories of things perceived by the senses, through the power of that hope which has settled upon the heart
and strengthens the inner senses with an indescribable assurance. And whether the heart has become accustomed, without any effort on its part,
to being carried away from earthly things through uninterrupted communion with our Savior.
But acquire an understanding of the distinctions in reading about this communion whenever you hear of it.
Uninterrupted stillness, together with its constant practice, readily gives the soul a taste of these things.
Yet after they have been found, they are lost again through the negligence of those who receive them, and for a long time they are not found again.
Through these things a person dares, with the testimony of his mind, to say confidently what the blessed Paul said:
“I am convinced that neither death nor life, neither things present nor things to come,” and the rest, “can separate me from the love of Christ.”
Or can affliction of both body and soul, or persecution, or hunger,
or nakedness, or enticement, or imprisonment, or danger,
or the sword? No, not even Satan’s angels, nor his powers with their wicked schemes,
nor passing glory with its compelling enticements, nor oppression and abuse through undeserved blows.
If these things, my brother, have not begun to appear in your soul to a greater or lesser degree, your labors, your afflictions, and all your stillness
are wasted effort. Even if miracles are performed through your hands
and you raise the dead, they are nothing compared with these things. From now on you must rouse yourself and plead with tears with the giver of life to all,
to remove the doors from your heart and roll away the darkness of the clouds of the passions from the inner sky,
so that you may be counted worthy to see the radiance of daylight and not sit in darkness forever like a dead person.
Constant vigil with reading, and frequent kneeling interspersed between them,
do not take long to bestow these blessings on the person who strives. For those who found them found them through these practices.
And those who find them now can likewise find them through these practices. When we persevere in stillness while practicing these things,
with the mind bound to nothing and no one outside itself, through the acts of virtue practiced inwardly,
through those very acts we find some of these things within ourselves, directly and with certain awareness, and we also gain assurance concerning the rest.
Those who, by living in stillness, have experienced God’s sweetness do not need much persuasion.
Nor does their soul grow sick with the affliction of unbelief, like those who doubt the truth.
The testimony of their own understanding is enough to convince them, more than ten thousand words without experience.
On the workings of grace themselves. 71.
Continually take note within yourself and observe. And at the time when you sense within yourself
that God’s providence has begun to reveal itself to the soul, understand then that you are near the harbor of purity.
When a person begins to rise above the passions, this holy power immediately attaches itself to the soul
and does not leave it, either by night or by day. It shows the soul God’s governance.
For even the smallest details of everything that exists and happens, every yes and no, of the things that befall a person secretly and openly,
and in the creation of this world, are revealed to the soul by that power which accompanies it. It reveals to the soul the power of God’s creative activity
and shows it the divine providence that unceasingly accompanies and cares for everything in this creation,
and how it accompanies a person at every moment and, though he neither perceives nor knows it, always protects him from adversities
and guides him toward what brings salvation and rest to his soul and body, and provides for his livelihood.
Then this very divine power, which carries out all these things,
reveals itself secretly to the person, through a revelation perceptible to his spiritual nature, which is the mind.
When a person has been found worthy to receive this power within his soul, he has nothing left
but wonder and silence, and tears that flow continually like water. From then on the person ceases
from all activities. And then, in this vision of God’s constant providence toward the work of his hands, you continually see:
the mind absorbed in wonder; the senses at rest; the mortal person lying face down in prayer,
with no tongue to speak, and with a heart no longer able to pray.
Rather, because of wonder at these workings, even prayer itself ceases—that cessation which is more excellent than activity—
while the person simply remains still in all his senses and movements, continually lying prostrate on his face before his Lord.
Even his bones offer praise to God in their silence, in that apparent inactivity,
as the prophet said: “All my bones will say, ‘Lord, who is like you?’”
At that time, more than all the other passions, you will find the demon of pride bound and lying beneath the soul’s feet.
Through this gift, as they say, a person is found worthy of the love of God and of perfect humility.
This gift itself is first tasted in stillness.
And those who have entered fully into stillness through spiritual practice and watchfulness cannot fail to know this.
But when a person leaves stillness and gives way to laxity, it withdraws from him.
And when he enters again, takes care of his soul, and diligently perseveres in his accustomed practice, it opens out again and shows its power to the soul.
Therefore, when someone has become completely perfected, this power accompanies him both within and outside, and he does not cease for a single hour
from sighs and tears and the rest, provided that he does not depart from the vigilant order of his practice.
Even now, there are people who have attained this in part.
From this partial experience that they possess, they recognize the characteristics of its fullness.
For when someone tastes a small measure of wine from a large wineskin, he then knows the whole of it:
what it is like even when others drink it, whether in part or in its entirety.
But someone who possesses it in its fullness is not readily found, except with great difficulty.
For this power is a gift of the observance of stillness.
And because no one in this broken [?] holds to complete stillness and perfect watchfulness, they are also lacking in gifts.
But someone who has acquired these insights through marks made in ink, while they are not present in him through practical experience,
is like a person carrying on his arm a harp that is adorned and fitted with tightly stretched strings,
but whose fingers do not know how to strike them and are not trained to produce different melodies for his soul’s delight.
He possesses only the harp, not the skill to play it. He needs others to play it before him and delight him.
Do not rejoice when you become rich in knowledge of many things. Rather, rejoice when you find that what you know is present in you in practice.
The first, without the second, gradually turns backward and also leads to pride because of inactivity.
But when you apply yourself diligently to the second, you will certainly be enlightened in the first as well, without instruction.
The eye of knowledge is experience, and its nourishment is constant practice.
Let this be a clear sign to you of your soul’s purity:
when, upon examining yourself, you find that you are full of mercy toward all people,
and your heart is stirred with compassion for them and burns as though with fire, without distinction between persons.
Through these things, the image of the Father in heaven is continually seen in you.
Understand the measure of your way of life not from the different kinds of your labors, but from the changes that your mind undergoes.
The body is accustomed to bathing in tears whenever the mind contemplates spiritual things.
They flow from the eyes as though from streams and wet the cheeks, without force and without any act of will.
I myself know a man who, even in his sleep, was seized with wonder at God while contemplating something
from the subject of his evening reading. His soul was amazed as it pondered that contemplation.
He seemed aware that he had spent a long time pondering it in the movements of his sleep and reflecting on the wonder of that vision.
For it was the middle of the night, and suddenly he awoke from sleep, with his tears flowing like water
and running down to his chest. His mouth was full of praise,
and his heart continued in contemplation for a long time, with a delight that could not be satisfied.
Because of the abundance of tears pouring without measure from his eyes,
and because of his soul’s astonishment, which had left all the limbs of his body slack,
and because a certain sweetness was stirring within his heart, he could not even complete, as he usually did,
the night service. Instead, he barely managed a single psalm at the appointed time for morning prayer.
He was so overcome by the abundance of tears, which the fountain of his eyes poured out against his will, and by all the other things.
Let us also make an effort, my brothers. When we intend to sleep, let us spend a long time beforehand
engaged in praises, songs, and the reading of the Holy Scriptures,
guarding ourselves against evil memories and every shameful thought. Let us stock our treasury with every good thing.
Let sleep overtake us while we are filled with the remembrance of God and our soul is aflame with a great longing for good things,
because of the grace of God, which surrounds us in our sleep and pours its gifts upon us even while we are asleep.
It examines us to see whether our body is clean of every kind of impurity and whether the impulses of our heart are free of shameful things.
Because of it, those under the authority of darkness cannot approach us, because of the sword and armor of grace that surround us.
But if they find us as they wish, so that grace withdraws from us,
recoiling from us and driving our souls away from its presence like corpses devoid of life,
then they approach us with all their wickedness.
They tempt us with every repulsive and terrifying impulse, according to the desire of their shameful will.
Whenever we find something like this happening to us in our sleep, let us immediately understand, remember, and take notice:
For on that night divine protection had withdrawn from us. And how could the demons not have swallowed us up? But
the divine command, in whose hand rests the life of all flesh, gave them permission only to approach us in this way,
so that we might wake up and examine ourselves. They cannot approach us whenever that protection is near.
On knowledge of the truth, and on trials.
And on the need to know with certainty that not only people who are weak, deficient, and untrained,
but also those who have been found worthy of temporary freedom from passions and have attained perfection of understanding,
and have approached the appointed measure of partial purity that is bound up with mortality, and have attained a position above the passions,
as far as God permits in this world, in a life bound to flesh that is subject to suffering,
have a struggle and are battered by the passions because of the body.
They also continually experience merciful abandonment, because of the danger of pride in particular circumstances.
And how often they fall into transgression, and through repentance restore [?] themselves, and grace receives them. 72.
For susceptibility to change runs through all rational nature without distinction, and changes come upon every person at every stage of life.
Although a discerning person can understand this from many things, the trials that come upon him every day
can make him especially wise, if he is watchful and guards himself.
And how many changes between rest and alarm the mind experiences every day,
and how it suddenly turns from its peaceful state to turmoil, though it has no cause for this from anywhere,
and comes into great, indescribable danger. The blessed Macarius clearly records this very thing
with great care and concern, as a reminder and instruction for the brothers,
so that they may not turn to despair at times of adverse changes—
those who stand in the rank of purity—when they experience a change like that of the weather.
This is provided that it does not arise from negligence and laxity, but that, while they are following their rule, experiences of suffering befall the resolve of their mind.
And the blessed Evagrius also bears witness to this from sure experience,
and sets it down in his book to provide further confirmation,
so that no one may suppose that the blessed Macarius set it down in his letter casually, rather than on the basis of genuine testing. Thus, in every way,
on the testimony of two such trustworthy witnesses, the mind may accept it without doubt, for its comfort in time of need.
What, then? “Changes,” he says, “happen to everyone, just as they do to the air.”
Understand the words “to everyone.” For human nature is one and the same. Do not suppose that he is speaking only of the imperfect,
while the perfect are free from changes and remain unwavering in a single state, without any stirring of the passions,
as the Messalians say. This is why he included the words “to everyone.”
“How does this happen, blessed one?” “For example,” he says, “there is frost, and a little later, warmth.
And perhaps there is hail, and a little later, clear weather. It is the same with our spiritual training: warfare, and help from grace.
Sometimes the soul is in a storm, and fierce waves rush against it.
Then a change happens again, and it is visited by grace.
And joy fills the heart, together with peace from God and chaste, peaceful thoughts.”
His explicit mention of chaste thoughts here points to the brutishness and impurity of the thoughts that preceded them.
He therefore warns us, saying that after these chaste and peaceful thoughts,
if adversities assail the mind, we should not grow discouraged and lose hope.
And in a time of rest granted by grace, we should not become conceited. Rather, in a time of joy, we should look ahead to affliction.
When he says that we should not grow discouraged if adversities assail us, he does not mean that we should not resist them,
or that the mind should welcome them gladly, as though this were now natural and they belonged to us.
Rather, you should not fall into despair like someone who had expected a state beyond struggle and a complete, unchanging rest,
in which he would no longer experience contests or hardships,
and in which none of the opposing forces would stir within him. For it did not please the Lord our God
to grant this to our nature in this world: that we should be entirely free from toil.
Otherwise, through this way of thinking, you will grow slack in despair and stop running your course.
“Rather,” he says, “know that all the saints are engaged in this very toil as long as we are in this world, although, along with this, we have abundant consolation
in secret. For every day and at every moment we are required to give proof of our love for God through our struggle against temptations.”
This is what “we should not grow discouraged” means: we should not lose heart in our contest. This is how our path has been prepared.
For anyone who turns us away from this is prey for wolves. We should marvel at this holy man: with just a few words,
how firmly he has established this statement, so rich in meaning, and completely removed doubt from the reader’s mind!
“Whoever strays from this,” he says, “is prey for wolves”—that is, whoever intends to travel without a path.
This means someone who holds this intention in his mind and wants to travel alone along a path not trodden by the fathers.
For this reason he is in danger of becoming prey for the ancient wolves wrapped in sheep’s clothing,
to steal foolish souls away into their wickedness under the guise of truth.
The saying that we should look toward affliction in a time of joy means this:
Whenever, through the working of grace, great stirrings suddenly arise in your soul,
and wonder at the mind’s vision of things beyond nature—as the blessed Evagrius said,
“Whenever the holy angels approach us, they fill us with spiritual vision,
and all the opposing powers withdraw, and there is peace and inexpressible wonder”—
when you are in such a state, he says, when grace has overshadowed you and the holy angels are near and surround you,
and because of this all those who tempt you have been driven away from your company, do not become proud
and suppose that you have now reached an unshakable harbor and an unchanging atmosphere,
and have risen completely above this gulf and the onslaught of the waves within it,
and that there is no longer any enemy or any harmful encounter. For many have thought these things
and fallen into danger, as Evagrius said. Nor, again, should you think that you are greater than many others,
and that you deserve to be in this state, while others, you say, because of the deficiency of their conduct,
or because their knowledge is inadequate, are deprived of such things.
“I,” you say, “am where I ought to be, and have now attained perfect chastity, the rank of spirituality, and renewal without change.”
Instead, bring to mind the unclean thoughts and shameful images that became fixed in your mind during the storm,
and the turmoil and disorder of the thoughts that assailed you a little while ago in that dark gloom,
and how easily you inclined toward the passions and engaged with them when your mind was troubled,
and felt no shame before the divine gaze or at the gifts and blessings you had received.
Know that God’s providence brought all these things upon you to humble you, for it cares for each one of us in whatever way benefits us.
If you become proud because of its gifts, it abandons you, and you fall completely into actual deeds,
the very things with which you are tempted in your thoughts. Know, then, that the fact that you are still standing,
It is not yours, nor is it due to your virtue. Rather, it is grace that carries you on
the palms of its hands, so that you will not be shaken. Bring these things to mind in times of joy,
when your thoughts become exalted, says our holy father. Weep and shed tears,
and roll in the dust as you remember your lapses during the time when you were left to yourself,
so that perhaps you may be saved by gaining humility from them.
Nevertheless, do not let your soul lose hope, but obtain forgiveness for your sins through humble thoughts.
Humility, even without labors, brings forgiveness for many sins.
Labors without humility, on the contrary, are not only useless,
but also prepare many evils for us. Therefore, obtain forgiveness for your sins through humility, as I have said.
As salt is to every food, he says, so humility is to every virtue.
It can break the power of many sins.
Therefore, it is necessary for the mind to remain continually in humility and discerning sorrow.
If we persevere in this, it makes us children of God, and without works it sets us before God as virtuous people.
Indeed, without it, every work, every virtue, and all our labors are empty.
Therefore, it is a change of mind that God seeks. Through our mind we become virtuous, and through our mind we become contemptible.
This alone, then, is sufficient, without assistance, to stand before God and speak on our behalf.
And give thanks to God without ceasing: although the nature you possess is so weak and so prone to going astray,
to what heights you are raised from time to time through the help of grace, and to what gifts! And in what ways
do you rise above your nature? And whenever you are left to yourself, to what depths do you sink,
and acquire the mind of an animal? Remember the wretchedness of your nature and the susceptibility to change [?] that clings to you.
For one of the holy elders also says, “Whenever a proud thought comes to you,
that is, when you remember your virtues, say, ‘Old man, look at your fornication!’”
He means the fornication with which one is tempted in thought during a time of being left to oneself,
which grace arranges for everyone, whether struggle or assistance, according to what benefits us.
Have you seen how plainly this admirable elder expressed the matter? “Whenever,” he says, “a proud thought comes to you,
“Because of the excellence of your conduct,” the elder said, “look at your lust!”
For it is clear that this elder was saying this to a great man, since it is impossible for people to be assailed by thoughts of pride
unless they stand in an exalted rank and lead a life worthy of praise.
For this passion attacks the soul after virtue has been practiced, to strip it of the fruits of its labor.
You can also learn, if you wish, from one of the blessed Macarius’s own letters
at what stages the saints stand when particular trials are allowed to come upon them.
The letter is this one: “Abba Macarius wrote to all his beloved children.”
There he clearly explains how struggles and the assistance of grace are dispensed by God.
Through these, God’s wisdom has been pleased to train them, as long as in this life
they are engaged in the contest against sin for the sake of virtue, so that their gaze may always remain fixed on him.
Through their constant gaze toward him, holy love for him will grow within them.
Thus, as they continually run to him from the onslaught of the passions and the danger of going astray, they will be strengthened in faith, hope, and love.
These very things, then, are not said of those who constantly remain among other people and wander about everywhere,
and continually give themselves freely to activities and impure passions.
Nor are they said of those who practice righteousness through outward deeds apart from stillness, and are constantly ensnared through their senses,
while the unavoidable things they encounter against their will, through unforeseen events, continually place them in danger of falling.
For they cannot fully guard even their senses, let alone their thoughts.
Rather, they are said of those who guard their bodies and thoughts with great vigilance,
and keep far away from disturbances and dealings with other people, and, having abandoned everything, even themselves,
have devoted themselves to guarding their minds in prayer, and receive the varied provisions of grace in complete stillness.
They are nurtured beneath the arm of the Lord’s knowledge and are secretly taught wisdom by the Spirit,
in stillness away from activities and the sight of things, and have acquired a mind dead to the world. The passions do not die.
But involvement with them dies through distance from things and the assistance of grace.
The section’s condensed meaning, together with explanations of what has been said. 73.
The condensed meaning of this section is:
To make us know that at all times, throughout these twenty-four hours of night and day, we need repentance.
The meaning of the term “repentance,” according to its actual practice, is this:
a continual, sorrowful plea offered to God in prayer full of remorse, for forgiveness of past deeds,
and a petition for protection from those yet to come. For this reason our Lord, too, gave our weakness the support of prayer.
“Stay awake,” he said, “and pray, so that you do not enter into temptation.” And, “Pray, and do not grow weary.”
And, “Keep watch and pray at all times.” And he said, “Seek, and you will receive. Ask, and it will be given to you.
Knock, and it will be opened to you. Everyone who asks receives, and whoever seeks finds,
and to whoever knocks it will be opened.” He confirmed his word still further and urged us all the more,
by telling the parable of the friend who went to his friend at midnight and asked him for bread.
“Truly,” he said, “I tell you: even if he will not give him anything because of their friendship, because of his shameless persistence he will get up and give him as much as he needs.
You too must pray and not grow weary.” Oh, the inexpressible encouragement of the Giver,
who invites us: “Ask me, and I will give you a gift!” He himself also provides everything that is helpful,
as he knows best. Indeed, these words are full of encouragement and great assurance.
And because our Lord knew that he had not removed our susceptibility to change before the cup of death,
and that as long as it remains, a person is liable to change from virtue to deficiency,
and that human nature is subject to unforeseen events, he urged us to continual supplication.
For if there were a place of security in this world such that, once a person reached it,
from then on his nature would be raised above need and his conduct above danger,
he would not have warned us about prayer and urged us to it so earnestly.
Similarly, in the world to come people do not offer prayers to God with petitions for this or that,
because in that place of freedom our nature will not be susceptible to change or confined under the threat of opposition,
but will be perfect in everything. For this reason, not only concerning prayer and vigilance,
but also because of the subtle and imperceptible things that constantly assail us and defy our power of understanding—
things in which we find ourselves continually caught, very often even against our will.
And even if our mind is very firmly established and desires what is good, how often his providence has cast us even to the very edge of trials!
As blessed Paul said: “So that I would not become conceited because of the abundance of revelations,
a thorn was given to me in my flesh, a messenger of Satan, to strike me.
Concerning this, he says, I asked my Lord three times to take the trial away from me, so that I could freely carry out the work he had commanded me to do.
And he said to me: ‘My grace is enough for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.’”
Then, my Lord, if this is your will, and our immaturity has such great need of a tutor who disciplines and admonishes,
so that even when someone is as absorbed in your love as I am,
and so devoted to goodness that the whole world disappears from his sight because he is intoxicated with you,
because of which you have even brought me to this—to revelations and visions that no fleshly tongue is permitted to describe,
so that I might see and hear the sound of worship from the ranks of spiritual beings, and be considered worthy in the Spirit to see you in your abundant holiness—
even with all these things, I am still unable to keep watch over myself, though I am a mature man in Christ.
For there is still something that, because of its subtlety, eludes the power of my understanding, even though I possess the mind of Christ.
Then, my Lord, for this reason I rejoice in my weaknesses, in afflictions, in imprisonments, in chains,
and in hardships, whether they come from nature, from my fellow creatures, or from the enemy of nature.
Therefore I will gladly endure my weaknesses—that is, my trials—so that the power of Christ may overshadow me.
If, despite all these things, I still need the rod of trials, so that through it your protection may increase
over me, and I may be kept close to you, I know that you have no one dearer to you than I am.
And this is clear from the fact that you have exalted me above many, and from what you have given me,
namely, knowledge of your glorious powers, which you have not given to any of my fellow apostles.
And you [?] me as a chosen vessel, trusted to preserve the order of your love.
And because of all these things, and because the work of proclaiming you would make even greater progress
if I were free from the bonds of trials, I know that you would have given me freedom for all these reasons, if it had been beneficial to me.
But you did not wish me to be without affliction and without anxiety in this world.
You were not as concerned that the work of proclaiming your good news should increase more abundantly in the world
as that I should benefit from my trials and that my soul should be kept sound in your presence.
Then, discerning one, if all this [?] gift,
The higher a person rises and the more exalted he becomes in spirituality, like Paul,
the more he still needs fear and vigilance, and he reaps benefit from encountering trials.
Who has reached a place of security in this world of mortality, so full of robbers,
and received the inability to fall—a gift not given even to the holy angels, so that they should not be made perfect without us?
Has this man received it before the entire company of spiritual and bodily beings, that he wishes to be utterly beyond change,
and that not even a temptation in thought should approach him? But the order of this world, according to the understanding of all the holy Scriptures, is this:
even if we receive blows a thousand times every day, we must not lose heart and stop running in the arena.
It is possible that through one small occasion we may seize victory and receive our crown.
This world is a competitive race and an arena for runners. This time is a time of combat.
In the place of combat and at the time of the contest, no law is laid down.
That is, the king sets no limit for his soldiers until the contest is over.
Then everyone gathers at the gate of the King of kings, and there it is determined who persevered in battle and did not accept defeat,
and who turned his back. For how often it happens that a person who was of no use at all,
who was continually struck down and laid low because of his lack of training, and was always in a state of defeat,
snatches the army’s standard from the hands of mighty warriors, and his name becomes more illustrious than those of the valiant,
the [?], the skilled and the knowledgeable, and he receives a crown and gifts more honorable than those of all his companions.
Therefore, let no one remain in despair. Only let him not neglect prayer,
and let him not fail to seek help from our Lord.
Let us keep this in mind: as long as we are in this world and dwell in this body,
even if we rise to the vault of heaven, it is impossible to be without toil and weariness, or free from care.
This is the conclusion. Forgive me. Anything beyond this is repetition.
A question about the distinction between the virtues and the goal of the entire course,
and about the greatness of love for humanity, and about the spiritual aim that brings all the saints to perfection
and establishes the divine likeness in them through his abundant love, which he poured out upon the human race. 74.
The goal of the entire course consists in these three things: repentance, purity, and perfection.
And what is repentance? Ceasing from former deeds and grieving over them.
And what is purity, in short? A compassionate heart toward every nature in creation.
And what is perfection? The depth of humility, which is the abandonment of everything visible and invisible.
The visible: everything perceived by the senses. The invisible: every thought about these things.
On another occasion, this same elder was asked, “What is repentance?” He said, “A broken heart.”
“And what is humility?” He said, “A twofold voluntary death to everything.” “And what is a compassionate heart?” He said:
“The heart burning for the whole creation—for human beings, birds, animals, demons, and everything that exists.
“At the remembrance and sight of them, his eyes stream with tears through the force of the mercy that presses upon his heart out of great compassion.
“His heart grows tender, and he cannot bear to hear of or look upon any harm or even slight suffering in anything in creation.
“Therefore, even for irrational creatures, for the enemies of truth, and even for those who harm him, he continually offers prayer with tears
“that they may be protected and forgiven. He does this even for creeping creatures,
“because of the great compassion poured without measure into his heart, in the likeness of God.”
“And what is prayer?” He said, “The mind being emptied of everything here,
“and the heart turning its gaze entirely toward longing for that future hope.
“Apart from this, the one who sows is sowing mixed seed in his tilled field; it is like driving a plow with an ox and a donkey together.”
“How is humility acquired?” He said, “By constant [?] remembrance of one's failings,
“by expecting death soon, by poor clothing, and by always choosing the last place;
“by hastening in everything toward lowly and humble work, by avoiding contentiousness, and by constant [?] silence;
“by not loving to attend gatherings, and by being unknown and disregarded;
“by holding exclusively to one of our practices until its completion, by hating social dealings with people, and by not loving material gains.
“All these follow this. His mind then rises above finding fault with or accusing anyone, and above jealous zeal.
“His hand must not be against everyone, nor everyone's hand against him. Rather, he should be solitary, keeping to himself and living alone.
“He should not take on concern for anyone in the world except himself.
“In short: living as a stranger, poverty, and solitude in one's dwelling.
“These give birth to humility and purify the heart. As for those who have reached perfection, this is their distinguishing mark:”
Even if they are handed over to be burned ten times every day out of love for humanity, they are not satisfied with this.
As Moses also said to God, “If you do not forgive the Israelites, erase me from your book that you have written.”
And as the blessed Paul also said, “I wish that both worlds, with all the glorious and delightful things in them,
may be unable to separate me from the love of Christ.
I wish to be separated from Christ, and for the Israelites to be brought near to the faith that gives life,
if, by things happening this way, it is possible for them to believe in Christ through this and enter eternal life,
and not be estranged from the living God.” And likewise, “I rejoice in the sufferings I endure for you Gentiles.”
And like the rest of the apostles, who accepted death of every kind out of love for the lives of human beings.
And the culmination of all these things is God, the Lord of all, who, out of love for his creation, handed his Son over to death on the cross.
For, it says, “God so loved the world that he gave his only Son for it.”
It was not that he could not have redeemed us in some other way,
but that in this way he could make his immense love known to us more fully: by bringing us near to himself through the death of his only Son.
And if he had had anything more precious than his Son, he would have given it to us, so that through it our race might be won for him.
And because of his great love, he did not even wish to constrain our freedom by force, although he was fully able to do so,
but wanted us to draw near to him through the love of our own minds. And our Lord himself obeyed his Father because of his love for us,
joyfully accepting humiliation and suffering, as Scripture says: “In place of the joy
that he had, he endured the cross and disregarded the shame.”
For this reason, on the night when he was handed over, our Lord said, “This is my body, which is given for life, for the salvation of the world.
And this is my blood, which is poured out for everyone for the forgiveness of sins.” And, he says, “For their sake I consecrate myself.”
In the same way, all the saints also reach this fulfillment when they have become perfect:
to become like God in the abundance of their love and compassion toward human beings.
And this is the sign of likeness to God that they seek for themselves: to become perfect in love for their neighbors.
This is also what the solitary fathers used to do,
so that they might constantly bear in their own persons that life-filled likeness of Christ, the Lord of all.
The blessed Anthony, it is said, never decided within himself to do something that benefited him as much as something that benefited his neighbor.
When he had this hope, his work for his neighbor’s benefit became more excellent.
And as is said of the blessed Agathon: “I would like to find a leper and give him my body and take his.”
Do you see perfect love? Even in matters external to himself, he could not bear not to give his neighbor greater comfort than himself.
For example, he had a knife, and a brother saw the object and liked it.
And, it is said, he did not let him leave his cell until he had taken it. And likewise,
if he had something and saw someone who needed it, he no longer considered it his own.
Why do I speak of these things? Many of them even surrendered their bodies to wild beasts, the sword, and fire for their neighbors.
No one can reach this degree of love unless he has inwardly perceived something through his hope.
Those who love this world cannot acquire love for other people.
When someone acquires love, he clothes himself in God himself along with it.
Necessarily, someone who has clothed himself in God will not consent to possess anything else along with him, but even strips off his own body.
But if he is clothed in the world or in this present life through his love for them, these things do not allow him to clothe himself in God.
For he himself testified: “Whoever does not abandon and hate everything, even his own life, cannot be my disciple.”

And he must not merely abandon them, but also hate them. And if he cannot become a disciple, how can God dwell in him?
Questioner.

Why is the practice of hope so pleasant, its labors so light, and its exercise so easy for the soul?
Elder.
Because natural desire is awakened within the soul, and this cup gives them drink and makes them drunk.
From that moment onward, they no longer feel weariness and become insensible to afflictions.
Throughout the entire course of their journey, it seems to them
as though they were traveling through the air, without human footsteps, while there is no sign
to them at all of the difficulty of the road, nor even of the valleys and heights ahead of them.
Instead, rough ground becomes smooth for them, and difficult terrain becomes a plain, because they are always looking toward their Father’s wing.
It makes all these distant and invisible things certain to them, as though they were actually present,
so that they contemplate them with wonder through the hidden eye of faith.
For all the parts of the soul have grown hot, as though in fire,
with longing for those distant things, as though they were near them. From then on, the entire reach of their thoughts stretches toward that place.
And they hurry to arrive; and whenever they approach each one of the virtues
to practice them, they do not practice them partially, but comprehensively, each one in its entirety, all at once.
For they do not make their journey along the king’s highway like everyone else, but choose shortcuts for themselves,
those traveled by the strong and the nimble, who easily reach their resting place.
For hope itself sets them ablaze as though with fire, and in their joy they cannot cease their urgent, constant running.
And what the blessed Jeremiah said happens to them: “I said that I would no longer remember him
“or speak in his name. But it became in my heart like a burning fire, blazing in my bones.”
So the remembrance of God becomes in the hearts of those who journey in hope of the promise [?].
By “shortcuts” I meant the comprehensive virtues,
in which there is no circuitous wandering along the many paths of conduct, passing from one thing to another,

requiring place, time, and exertion. Instead, they take their stand upon a virtue and immediately fulfill it.
The questioner:
“What is freedom from passions?” And the elder answered: “Freedom from passions is not being unaware of evil things, but being unreceptive to passions.
“Through the abundant virtues they have acquired, both outward and hidden, the passions have become weak in them,
“and cannot easily attack the soul. Nor does the mind need to keep watching them constantly,
“because it is always active in the meditation and consideration of virtuous thoughts, which arise with understanding in the intellect.
“And when a passion begins to stir, the mind is suddenly snatched away from it by some insight that appears in the intellect, and the passion is left inactive.
“As the blessed Evagrius also said: ‘The intellect that, by the grace of God, completes the works of virtue
“‘and draws near to knowledge is scarcely aware of the irrational part of the soul.
“‘For its knowledge carries it away on high and estranges it from everything in the world.’
“And because their intellect has become refined through their purity, it has become light and keen.

“Through ascetic discipline, too, the intellect has been polished, because the body has dried out, and also through the freedom from occupation afforded by stillness and the length of time spent in it.
“For this reason it readily [?] settles upon one thing after another, whose contemplation [?] draws it into wonder at that thing. And for this reason
“they also abound in contemplations, and their minds never lack material for insights.
“Besides this, the Spirit himself stimulates his fruits in them. And habit itself, over a long period of time,
“has erased from the heart those memories that stir up passions in the soul and are Satan’s chief strength.”
But whenever the soul has not joined itself to the passions by dwelling on them,
because it is continually occupied with another reflection, the force of their claws cannot touch its spiritual senses.
The questioner: What are the characteristics of humility? The elder says:
Just as conceit scatters the soul through the fantasies of its wandering,
with an impulse that drives it to fly on the cloud of its thoughts and roam throughout creation,
so humility gathers it into itself in stillness of thoughts
and the soul’s withdrawal into itself. And just as the soul is unknown
and cannot be seen by the bodily eye, so the humble person is unknown among people.
Like the soul within the body, he is concealed from sight and from association with everyone.
The truly humble person not only has no wish to be seen and known among people, because of his concealment and withdrawal from everyone,
but wishes, if possible, to be submerged and concealed even from himself, deeper within himself,
in stillness and the cessation of his movements and his senses, entirely and completely, like something that does not exist in creation and has never come into being,
and does not exist at all, in any way. He does not even wish to be known or perceived by himself.
And the more he is concealed, hidden, and withdrawn from the world, the more completely he is with his Lord.
The humble person never finds rest in seeing gatherings, the tumult of a crowd, commotion, or noise,
nor in extravagance, adornment, and finery, which give rise to dissipation; nor in talk, conversation, noise, and the scattering of the senses.
Instead, above everything, he chooses inward concentration and withdrawal into himself,
remaining quiet, collected, and unified, resting by himself in a still atmosphere empty of everything, and keeping silence toward all creation.
In everything, smallness, moderation, scarcity, and poverty are dear to him.
He does not favor many affairs and numerous activities, but always remains unoccupied and free from anxious thought,
without being disturbed by the things of this world, so that his thoughts do not go outside himself.
For he is convinced that if he becomes involved in many things, it is impossible for his inner movements to remain undisturbed.
For many affairs mean many concerns,
and many concerns are a gathering of reflections and mingled thoughts.
He has then ceased to be free from concern for earthly things in the peace of his thoughts.
Apart from the small pressures imposed by necessity itself, and the mind that has taken up solitary meditation, tranquil in its movements.
And from then on, even if his mouth is restrained from speaking, they do not leave him alone—
the pressures. He even comes to the point of being harmed and harming others. From then on, the door to the passions is opened for him.
The serenity of discernment departs, humility flees, and the door of peace is closed.
Because of all these things, then, he constantly guards himself against involvement in many things.
And you always find him calm, gentle, modest, and peaceful.
In a humble person there is never impetuosity, haste, or agitation, nor heated and flighty impulses.
Instead, he always dwells at rest. Even if heaven were to collide with earth, the humble person would not be shaken.
Not everyone who is calm is humble, but everyone who is humble is also calm. There is no humble person who is not modest.
But you can find many modest people who are not humble. This is the gentle and humble person of whom our Lord spoke:
“Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls.”
The humble person is always at rest, because there is nothing that disturbs his mind.
Just as no one can move a mountain, so the mind of the humble person cannot be moved, if one may put it this way.
And perhaps it is not even improper to say this very thing: that the humble person is not even of this world.
For he neither loses heart and becomes disturbed by afflictions, nor becomes dazzled and carried away by joyful things.
Instead, all his joy and true gladness are in the things of his Lord.
Humility is accompanied by patience; self-recollection, which is modesty; a subdued voice; little
speech; a low opinion of oneself; humble clothing; a measured walk; a gentle gaze; abundant compassion;
readiness to weep; a collected soul; a broken heart; freedom from the stirring of anger; senses that do not dart about;
few possessions; little need for anything; forbearance; endurance; fearlessness;
courage of heart born of hatred for this temporary life; perseverance in trials;
deliberate rather than hasty movements; the quieting of thoughts; keeping secrets; chastity; modesty; concealment.
And above all these: remaining constantly silent, and constantly taking refuge in not knowing.
The humble person never encounters a necessity that causes him to become agitated.
Even when the humble person is alone, he hides himself even from himself.
I wonder whether anyone is truly humble and yet dares even to pray to God when he approaches prayer,
or considers himself worthy of this, or dares to ask him for anything, or knows what to pray.
Rather, he simply stills all his impulses and waits only for mercy,
wondering what decision concerning him will come forth from that worshipful Majesty.
His face is bowed toward the earth, while the inward gaze of his heart is fixed on the door of the Holy of Holies of the Most High,
whose cloud of indwelling presence dazzles the eyes of the seraphim, and whose radiance strikes terror into the legions of their ranks.
Silence rests upon all their orders, and they await the dawning of mysteries from within what cannot
be seen, in a space without air, with movement without sound, with senses without a body,
with a perception without likeness, of the invisible essence of the revelation that comes upon them,
while the strength of their movements is too feeble to endure before the waves of his mysteries.
He dares only this much: “As you will, my Lord.”
As for these things thus far, to set them down for you in plain sentences,
so that the mind might grasp them without investigation because of the clarity of the expressions, has been my concern:
things which, merely by reading them, cause the mind to forget its conduct and activities in this world and its bodily life,
and already to pass in thought into its true and more excellent world.
I implore you, beloved, when you encounter these mysteries,
do not leave them without benefit, so that they prove to be dead words to you.
Let them not be for you as they were for those who were invited to that spiritual banquet but excused themselves from entering it.
Look, the table is prepared, and spiritual dishes are arranged upon it; all the delicacies are ready.
The bridegroom is waiting for us to enter and enjoy ourselves with him.
Let us no longer make excuses, lest the same declaration that was made concerning them be addressed to us as well.
What declaration, then? “Truly I tell you, not one of those who were invited will taste my supper.”
On the hidden measures, and the powers and operations within them. 75.
Be assured of these things, my brother: the working of miracles, the foretelling of future events,
relief from trials, rest from battles, and victory over each individual passion:
and the attainment of each of the virtues, and the consolation that sometimes fills one through grace;
and purity of prayer, fervor of spirit, spiritual joy, and all the other requests there are;
when a person labors for a time for each of these
with a good purpose and heartfelt longing, God eventually inclines toward his desire.
And when he sees his purpose and eagerness, he grants his request and gives him rest.
But as for the mysteries that belong to the Spirit, namely, the stirrings experienced in spiritual prayer,
the mind’s entrance beyond the veil of the Holy of Holies, and the perception of the inheritance of incorruptibility,
unless a person pays their due, God will not be persuaded to grant them, even if the whole creation pleads on his behalf.
Their due is purity of soul.
But when a person reaches purity from the passions, then those things that no eye has seen and no ear has heard,
and that have never entered the human heart to ask for in prayer, purity itself reveals before him,
never ceasing for a moment from mysteries and spiritual visions. And what the power of April is
accustomed to do to the nature of the earth, grace does to the soul through purity.
For its power stirs even the fine roots that sprout in the depths.
Like fire beneath a cauldron, it makes the earth seethe, so that it brings forth the treasures of growing things that God placed in its nature,
for the delight of creation and for his own praise.
In the same way, grace brings to light all the glory that God [?] in the soul’s nature,
revealing the soul to itself and delighting it with its own beauty. For when it sees the great and indescribable treasures that God placed within it,
which had been hidden from it beneath the stained robe of the passions, without its knowing,
and which he has now revealed to it, since it has torn off the garment of the passions, its joy will carry it away from earthly things in love for him.
It no longer remembers the body, which hid the beauties of its own being from its sight.
Then it sees heavenly beauties within itself, like a clear mirror that, because it is so highly polished, reveals the beauty of faces.
For holiness is fitting for the holy. Every virtue, whatever you may name,
and every work of righteousness through which it is perfected, can be practiced, acquired, and brought to completion outside stillness.
But there is no possibility of acquiring freedom from the passions and purity outside stillness.
Chapters on Salvation. 76.
Blessed Paul teaches us when he says, “Take off the old person,
and put on the new person, who was created in God in holiness and true piety.”
He did not say, “Put on the new over this old person.” For he knew that this was impossible.
See how wisely he gives his command. He did not say, “Put on the new person, who is renewed through the knowledge of God.”
Instead, he first says, “Take this one off,” and then he says, “Put on that new one.”
As he also said explicitly elsewhere, “Flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God,
nor does corruption inherit incorruptibility.” By “incorruptibility” he means the knowledge of that world.
“Corruption” and “flesh and blood” are names he gives to the corrupting passions of soul and body,
whose movements have their seat in fleshly thinking. He calls purity “the new person.”
By “the kingdom of God” he means the lofty, intelligible contemplation of the blessed movements of the rays of divine being,
which only the devout soul is permitted to enter, through its incorruptible movements that have been raised above corruption and flesh and blood.
If the little pupil of your soul is not purified, do not dare to gaze at the sun,
lest you be deprived of your ordinary sight and be cast into one of those intelligible places, namely,
Tartarus, which is an image of Sheol. This means the darkness outside God.
For those who depart from nature in the movements of their minds wander there in the intelligent nature they possess.
For this reason, the man who dared to enter the banquet in filthy clothes was also ordered to be thrown into this outer darkness.
The banquet means the vision of spiritual knowledge.
Its provisions are the abundance of divine mysteries, [?] joy, gladness, and delight for the soul.
He calls the robe of purity “the banquet garment.” The filthy clothes, however, are the passionate movements that stain the soul.
“Outer darkness” means being outside all the delight of knowing the truth and of intimacy with God.
For anyone who, while wearing such clothes, dares to ponder in his mind the heights of God,
and to bring himself in and seat himself amid the spiritual contemplations of that holy banquet, which shines forth only in the pure,
and wishes to share in its delight while steeped in the delight of the passions,
is suddenly swallowed up as though in a quagmire, and is driven away from there to a place without light.
That which is called Sheol and destruction, which is ignorance and wandering away from God.
For it is said that the things of God come of themselves, if the [?] is pure and undefiled.
The statement that they come of themselves means that purity naturally has the capacity for heavenly light to shine within it,
without investigation and toil on our part. In a pure heart, it is said,
a new heaven is imprinted, whose appearance is light and whose realm is spiritual. Likewise, in another place:
Just as a lodestone possesses, through its natural power, the ability to make particles of iron cling to it,
so spiritual knowledge comes to a pure heart. Yet it is firmly acknowledged by trustworthy people
that no mind is entirely free from the disturbance of passionate impulses in this life.
But I say this confidently, and I have no fear concerning the truth established by experience:
a person whose mind is wrapped in the garment of mourning is not merely invincible against the impulses of the passions,
or mighty and victorious in battle against them, nor is it merely that they do not dare show themselves at all with the intention of fighting;
rather, they do not even dare pass before the soul at a distance. For wherever there is a mourning soul,
which has made for itself a place of dancing amid varied lamentations over its sins,
and, as the blessed Jacob said, makes its dwelling in the grave until he meets beloved Joseph again [?]—
wherever the bitterness of mourning is present, I am not persuaded to say that the sweetness of the passions can enter.
But I say that this person's practice is marked by vigilance and confidence, and is above fear:
the person who perseveres in mourning because of fear—that is, because he does not know where the end of his course will lead—
more so than the person who perseveres in a joyful way of life because
he has already begun here to perceive the hope of his labor. You whose city has been captured by the passions within,
arm yourself with the weapon of mourning and pursue them, and rescue your children from their hands.
For this weapon is always invincible and dependable, and has been tested by trustworthy people.
This chapter is full of life. 77.
Weak human being, do you want to find life? Hold fast to faith and humility,
for through them you will find mercy and help and speech within the heart from God, together with protection in [?] and in [?].
Do you want to acquire these things, which are a fountain of life? Hold fast to simplicity from the beginning.
Walk before God in simplicity, not in knowledge. Faith accompanies simplicity.
But presumption accompanies subtlety and the shifting thoughts of knowledge [?].
And estrangement from God accompanies presumption. Whenever you fall down before God in prayer,
be like this in your own estimation: like an ant, like the crawling creatures of the earth, and like a beetle.
Babble like an uneducated person, and do not speak before him with knowledge.
Approach God with a childlike mind and walk before him, so that you may be worthy of that fatherly care
which fathers have for their little children. It is said, “The Lord watches over little children.”
A little child approaches a snake and takes it by the neck, and it does not harm him. A little child goes about naked all winter.
While others are clothed and covered, the cold penetrates all their limbs.
Yet he is unclothed and [?] on a day of bitter cold and frost, and feels no pain.
For their childish bodies are covered with another garment that cannot be seen,
provided by that hidden care which protects the fragile limbs of childhood, so that no harm from anything may come near them.
Do you now believe that there is a hidden providence, when a tender body, so delicate and vulnerable to every injury,
because of its tenderness and the weakness of its constitution, is nevertheless protected amid hostile conditions, which do not hurt it? For it says, “The Lord watches over little children.”
Do not understand and believe these things only about those who are children by nature, but also about those who, though wise in the world,
abandon their knowledge, rely on that wisdom which is sufficient for everything, and become children of their own free will.
Then they learn the wisdom that cannot be learned through the labors [?] of study.
The blessed apostle, who was wise in divine matters, also spoke well when he gave this exhortation:
“Whoever thinks he is wise in this world must become a fool, so that he may become wise.”
But implore God to grant that you may attain the full measure of faith.
If you experience the sweetness of faith in your soul, it is not too much for me to say
that nothing will any longer keep your soul from Christ. Nor will it be difficult for it
to be carried away from earthly things at all times, and to forget this feeble world and the memory of its affairs.
For this reason, pray without growing weary, seek faith with tears, and plead fervently.
Entreat with great diligence until you receive it, for then you will no longer grow weary.
But you become worthy of this if you first compel yourself
to cast your anxiety upon God in faith and exchange your own care for his care.
Then, when he sees that you have willingly trusted God with your affairs in complete sincerity of mind,
and have compelled yourself to rely on God more than on yourself,
then that power of which you are unaware will overshadow you, so that you will distinctly feel, without any doubt, the power that is with you.
It is through sensing this power that many enter fire without fear,
and walk on water without their thoughts wavering over whether they might sink in it.
For faith weakens the senses of the soul,
as though the soul perceived within itself some invisible assurance, so that its thinking does not grow weak
or look at the sight of fearful things, but instead looks with a vision that is above the senses.
Take care that you do not suppose at all that spiritual knowledge can be received through this knowledge of the soul.
Not only can that spiritual knowledge not be received through this knowledge of the soul,
but those who strive to train themselves in the latter cannot even be found worthy to perceive the former. And if there is
someone among them who wishes to approach that knowledge of the spirit, unless he renounces this knowledge, with all the convolutions of its subtlety and its entanglements,
and takes his stand in a childlike state of mind, he cannot come even a little closer to that knowledge.
Indeed, its habits and its twisted impulses become great obstacles to him, until little by little he forgets them.
That spiritual knowledge is simple, and it does not shine forth amid the thoughts of the soul.
Until the mind is freed from the multitude of thoughts and comes to the single simplicity of purity,
it cannot even perceive spiritual things. Now this order of knowledge,
by which a person perceives, even here, the delight of life in that world, rejects a multitude of thoughts.
But this knowledge of the soul, apart from gatherings of densely crowded thoughts, cannot know anything else
that is received in serenity of mind. And the word of our Lord cannot prove false:
“Unless you turn and become like children, you cannot enter the kingdom of God.”
Yet, look: there are many who do not attain this ignorance,
but through their good deeds a share with our Lord in the kingdom of heaven is reserved for them.
As is also evident from the meaning of the Beatitudes that he explicitly set down in his Gospel.
For in the Beatitudes he made known variations, together with the many distinctions between dwelling places.
For everyone, at every level, whatever road they take toward him, the gate of the kingdom of heaven stands open before them.
But the saying, “Unless you turn and become like children,” refers to this: that already here
a person should experience the delight of the kingdom—this is what he means. They say that the kingdom of heaven is spiritual contemplation.
This is not found through the labor of thoughts, but is tasted through grace.
Until a person is purified, they cannot even bear to hear of it, for it cannot be acquired through instruction.
But if you attain purity, my son—the purity acquired through faith of heart and through stillness away from other people—
and you forget the knowledge of this world, it will suddenly be found within you without your being aware of it, without your searching for it.
“Set up a pillar,” it says, “and pour oil over it.” And you will find your treasure within you.
But if you become caught in the entanglements of natural knowledge, I do not hesitate to say:
It is easier for you to escape iron chains than to escape it, and you are never far from the snares of error.
And you will never be able to gain boldness and confidence before our Lord.
You are always walking on the edge of a sword, and you cannot be entirely free from suffering.
Take refuge in weakness and simplicity, so that you may live well before God and be free from anxiety.
For just as a shadow accompanies bodies, so mercy accompanies humility.
Therefore, if you wish to live in this way, give no ground at all to feeble thoughts.
If every kind of harm, evil, and danger surrounds
you and frightens you, do not trouble yourself by looking at them or thinking about them.
If you have once trusted God to be able to protect and guide you, and have followed him, no longer concern yourself with anything of this kind.
Instead, say to yourself, “The one to whom I have entrusted myself once and for all is sufficient for everything.
I am not involved; he knows.” Then you will see God's wonders in action:
how his salvation is always near to those who fear him, and how his care surrounds them without being seen.
Do not doubt that the guardian who is with you exists merely because he cannot be seen with bodily eyes.
Sometimes, moreover, he is revealed even to bodily eyes, to strengthen your own assurance.
But when a person casts aside all visible help and human hope,
and clings to God in faith and with a pure heart, grace immediately attaches itself to him and reveals its power in him through various kinds of help.
At first, through its care for him, grace shows him its help in outward and bodily things,
since through these he is better able to perceive the power of God's care for him,
so that, through understanding visible things, he may become firmly convinced about hidden things, as suits the immaturity of his mind and his inexperience.
How, for example? As one might say, what he needs is provided for him without effort, while he is free from worry.
And grace turns away from him many misfortunes
that have repeatedly come near him, full of danger.
While he is unconcerned because he is unaware of them, grace drives them away from him in a greatly wondrous way,
along with all the other things that suddenly arise when he is not expecting them, which can often harm the soul, and some of which can harm the body.
Grace protects him from them like a mother who shelters her young and spreads her wings over them so that harm may not come near them.
At that very time, it makes him aware of what has happened, showing him with his bodily eyes what would have caused his destruction,
and how God quietly helped him in those events,
and the loss of his life that had drawn near, from which God rescued him. In this way, grace also trains him in hidden things.
It lays open before him the ambushes of thoughts and reasonings that are difficult to perceive,
so that he may readily understand their meaning, their connection with one another, and their deceptiveness,
and which follows which, and how they arise from one another and destroy the soul.
It exposes before him every ambush of the demons and the disguise of their thoughts,
and what follows each of these. It gives him understanding so that he may discern what is happening.
And a hidden light dawns within his simplicity, enabling him to perceive everything, including the power of the movements of subtle thoughts.
Grace shows him, as though pointing with a finger, what would have happened to him if he had not known this.
Then, as a result of this, he is moved to ask his Guide in prayer for everything, small or great.
And when, through all these things, grace has firmly established his mind in trust in God,
then it begins to lead him into trials, little by little.
It allows trials to rise against him whose hardship is within his capacity to bear.
And during the trial itself she offers him her help in a perceptible way, so that he may take courage.
Until, little by little, he becomes trained and gains wisdom, and looks down on his enemies with trust in God.
For without these things a person cannot become wise in spiritual battles, know his guide, and become aware of his God,
and be inwardly strengthened in his faith through the power of the trial he has personally undergone.
And whenever she sees that a slightly presumptuous thought has begun to stir within him,
and he begins to think highly of himself, she allows trials to press upon him and grow stronger against him, so that he may recognize his weakness,
flee, and submit to God in humility. Through these things a person reaches the stature of a mature man,
through faith and hope in the Son of God, and is raised toward him in love.
For God's help toward a person becomes known in a wonderful way
when he finds himself amid circumstances full of despair; there God shows his power by delivering him from them.
No one has ever learned to know divine power in comfort and ease.
Nor has he ever shown his care in a perceptible way except in a quiet place and in the wilderness,
and in places free from the dealings and turmoil of life among people.
Do not be surprised if, when you begin to practice virtue, severe afflictions spring up against you from every direction.
For a practice unaccompanied by hardship and toil is not even considered virtue.
For virtue itself takes its name from this, says Saint Evagrius.
This [?], he says, is accustomed to having hardships press upon it.
And virtue itself, he says, is despised when it is yoked to comforts, says the blessed Mark the Solitary.
Every virtue that exists is called a cross, because it fulfills the commandment of the Spirit.
For all who wish to live in the fear of God in Jesus Christ suffer affliction.
“Whoever wishes to come after me,” he says, “must deny himself, take up his cross, and come after me.
Whoever wishes to preserve his life in comfort will lose it, and whoever loses his life for my sake will find it.”
This is why our Lord first placed the cross before you: so that you would pronounce a sentence of death upon yourself and then prepare yourself to follow him.
Nothing is as powerful as giving up hope. It knows no defeat from anything, whether from the right or from the left.
When a man has given up hope of his life in his own mind, no one is more courageous than he.
And there is no enemy who can confront him, and no affliction whose news can weaken his resolve.
For every affliction that exists is less than death.
And he has resolved to accept death. If everywhere, in every undertaking, and at every time,
in everything you are about to do, you set your mind to expect toil and hardship,
you will not only always find yourself courageous and unflagging in confronting every difficulty you anticipate,
with the strength of your thoughts driving a fearful disposition away from you—
the disposition that usually arises in a person because his thoughts are directed toward ease—
but all the hardships and difficulties that befall you will also seem easy and light to you.
And often your situation is [?] the opposite of what is expected, since perhaps they will not even assail you.
For you know that the expectation of ease always deprives people of great benefits and excellent good.
For even those who are in this world do not attain the fulfillment of their desires in their bodily activities
unless they resolve in their minds to endure difficulties. And since experience bears witness to these things,
there is no need for persuasive words. For in every generation before us, right up to our own day,
there is nothing else that causes people to falter in pursuing victories and to fall short of excellent deeds,
and, to put it all in a word, to disregard entry into the kingdom, except the expectation of a little ease close at hand.
And not only this, but often this very expectation
prepares difficult circumstances and severe trials for anyone whose mind is fixed upon it
and whose thoughts move toward its promise, because he is governed by the will of desire. Who is there
who does not know that even a bird approaches the snare in the expectation of ease?
Could it be that our knowledge is far inferior even to a bird's, by comparison,
concerning the hidden things and circumstances concealed in affairs, undertakings, places, and everything else?
For Satan too, from the beginning, has hunted us with promises and thoughts of ease.
But because my thought has run toward the subject of desire in this discussion, I have strayed from the aim I set earlier in my discourse:
that we should always set before our minds the expectation of afflictions in everything we wish to begin on the road to our Lord's house,
so that its final outcome may bring you successfully to your goal.
How often, when someone wants to begin some undertaking for our Lord’s sake, he asks whether there is any comfort in the matter:
whether it is possible to proceed easily in it without toil, or whether there is something in it that puts the body under strain.
Is there not talk of comfort everywhere? What are you saying, man? You want to ascend to heaven,
and to receive the kingdom there, and to attain fellowship with God and spiritual rest,
and that blessedness, and companionship with the angels and with [?] who do not die,
and you ask whether there is toil along this road? What an astonishing thing!
For those who long for the things of this world, for wealth that perishes and authority that comes to an end,
cross the sea’s fierce waves and tread fearful roads.
They endure a long journey full of toil and suffering, along with all the other
terrible things that people habitually do because of their desires.
They give no thought at all to whether there is toil in the undertaking or exhaustion in what they want to do.
But we inquire about comfort at every turn.
But if we always keep the road of crucifixion in our minds and always think about crucifixion,
what hardship would not become easy in comparison with it? Or is there anyone at all who is not convinced of this:
that no one has ever won a victory in battle and received a perishable crown,
or carried out divine works, or succeeded in any of the glorious achievements of virtue,
or obtained what he desired—even something not praiseworthy—without first bracing himself for toil and suffering
and driving away from himself the mindset [?] toward comfort that gives birth to despondency and cowardice,
from which comes weakness in everything. But when the mind is zealous for virtue,
the outward senses—smell, touch, hearing, sight, and taste—do not know defeat from harsh encounters with foreign influences,
even beyond what they are accustomed to and beyond the limits of their natural strength.
At the time when anger naturally produces its effects, bodily life is then regarded as worth less than dung.
But when the heart is filled with spiritual zeal, the body takes no notice of suffering and does not shrink from terrifying things.
Instead, the mind makes it stand against every trial, like adamant in its endurance.
Let us too be zealous with spiritual zeal for the will of Jesus, and all despondency will be driven away from us.
For it produces slackness in the mind. Zeal, on the other hand, gives birth to courage,
determination of soul, and diligence of body. What power do demons have
when the soul rouses its zeal against them with natural fervor? Resolve, too, is called the offspring of zeal.
It establishes in the soul all the unshakable strength that arises when the soul puts its powers into action.
Even those crowns of confessing the faith which the victorious martyrs receive through their endurance:
through these two powers, zeal and resolve, which are born from the force of natural anger,
they become insensible to the violence of the suffering inflicted by tortures.
On the benefit of fleeing from the world, and how the fathers devised this practice through wise discernment. 78.
For the struggle that arises through proximity to things is truly fierce, difficult, and very hard.
However agile and strong a person may be, when the occasions that provoke battles and conflicts are near him, danger accompanies him.
And he is more liable to fall than if Satan himself were to confront him openly in battle.
For as long as a person does not distance himself from the things his heart fears,
the enemy continually has an opening against him. And if he happens to doze even a little, the enemy easily destroys him.
In the former case, the body fears being injured, but the person is in any event far removed from sins.
Here, however, it is the soul that receives an invisible wound, and it does not put its adversary to the trouble of fighting against it.
For the things themselves are enough, on their own, to stir up the turmoil of battles against it at any time.
It willingly lets itself be led into captivity by them, though no one outside it is drawing up battle lines against it.
Instead, it is itself a contest for itself, through the enticements of the things arrayed before the bodily senses,
as it is said somewhere: “When the soul is caught up in the harmful encounters of the world, those very encounters become slippery places for it.”
And likewise: “It is naturally overcome when it encounters them.”
And so, because the saints of old who walked these paths were convinced
that the mind is not always sound enough to remain unwavering in a single state and keep watch,
since there are times when the soul is in darkness and cannot be on its guard against harmful things, they exercised wise discernment
and clothed themselves in renunciation as in armor, for it frees a person from many struggles.
As it is written: “There is one who escapes sins because of his poverty.”
And they [?] to the desert, where there are no things that give rise to the passions.
Thus, even when a time of weakness comes upon them, they will find no occasions for falling. I mean anger,
desire, resentment, and glory—these are slight compared with the rest, because it is a desert. There they hid themselves as in an unconquerable fortress.
Then each one of them was able to complete his struggle in stillness, where the senses could find no help
to become adversaries through harmful encounters. Death in our struggle is better for us than a life of falling.
On how hidden impulses undergo change along with changes in outward conduct. 79.
As long as a person lives without possessions, departure from this life constantly stirs in his mind.
He meditates continually on the life after the resurrection, and is always devising the preparation needed for that life.
Disdain for every honor and bodily comfort is sown in his mind,
and the thought of the world's worthlessness constantly hovers in his mind.
He is courageous in his thinking and always possesses a brave heart in the face of every terror and life-threatening danger.
For he does not fear even death, since he continually looks at it close at hand and awaits it.
His care is cast upon God, with complete and unwavering trust.
And if afflictions confront him, like someone who knows and is firmly convinced that crowns are prepared for him,
he endures them with complete joy, while his soul rejoices and exults at receiving them.
For he knows that it is God who arranges their coming to him for benefits arising from causes
that are unknown, through arrangements that are not revealed. But when it happens that, for whatever reason,
something among these passing things falls into his hands and he acquires it through the activity of the one skilled in every evil,
immediately love for the body begins to stir in his soul, and he thinks of a long life.
Thoughts directed toward bodily comfort continually spring up within him. He protects his body so that, if possible, it may suffer no hardship at all.
He devises every means by which things conducive to our body's comfort may be secured.
He becomes estranged from that freedom which is not enslaved to any fearful thought.
From then on, in everything, he ponders and considers impulses that produce anxiety and occasions for fear.
For that courage of heart has been taken from him which he possessed in his soul when, through his lack of possessions, he was raised above the world.
And because he has become an heir to the world, so, in proportion to the amount of property he holds,
Accept fear, too, as a law and an arrangement ordained by God.
For whichever side we prepare our limbs to serve,
we become its slaves, in submission with complete fear, as the apostle says.
Before all the passions comes self-love, and before all the virtues comes contempt for comforts.
Whoever nourishes his body with comforts will suffer distress even in a place of peace.
“Whoever is pampered in his youth,” it says, “will become a slave, and in the end he will groan.” Just as it is impossible
for someone whose head is submerged in a dense mass of water to breathe in the thin air spread through this open space,
so it is impossible for someone whose mind is immersed in the concerns of this world
to draw into his soul a perceptible breath of that clear air of the new world.
Just as the smell of poison disturbs the body's constitution, so an indecent sight disturbs the mind's peace.
Just as health and sickness cannot exist in the same body without one being destroyed by the other,
so money and love cannot exist in the same house without one destroying the other.
Just as glass cannot remain next to a stone and stay intact,
so a holy man cannot constantly meet with a woman to look at her and speak with her, and have his purity remain undefiled.
Just as trees are uprooted by the constant force of rushing waters,
