so love of the world is uprooted from the heart by the onrush of trials that come upon the body.
Just as purgative medicines clear harmful humors from the body, so the severity of afflictions clears evil passions from the heart.
Just as a dead person cannot perceive the affairs of the living, so a solitary who is buried in stillness as in a grave—
his soul is spared the storm that usually arises from awareness of the affairs going on among people.
Just as someone who spares his enemy on the battle line cannot remain unharmed, so it is impossible
for an ascetic to spare his body and have his soul escape destruction.
Just as children, when frightened by terrifying sights,
run and take refuge in their parents' laps, so also the soul, whenever it is distressed by the terror of trials,
hastens toward God to take refuge in the persistence of its supplication.
The more frequently trials come, the more it increases its supplication. But when it finds relief, it [?] in distraction.
Just as those who are handed over to judges to be flogged for their evil deeds:
if, as soon as they are brought forward for flogging, they humble themselves and immediately confess their offenses,
their flogging is reduced, and they are readily released after only slight suffering.
But if some of them act foolishly and become stubborn, their floggings are increased,
and in the end they confess unwillingly after many lashes, with their sides torn, and gain nothing.
So too with us: whenever, because of our faults in which we persist without correction,
we are handed over from the hands of divine mercy into the hands of justice, the judge of all,
and justice orders us to be stretched out beneath the rod of trials so that our floggings in the world to come may not be severe:
if, as soon as the rod of judgment approaches us, we humble ourselves and remember our offenses,
and confess before the one who calls us to account, we are readily delivered through slight trials.
But if we become stubborn in our afflictions and do not acknowledge that we ourselves caused these things and deserve even more
than these, but instead blame other people, sometimes demons, and at times even God's justice,
and declare ourselves innocent, thinking and saying that our deeds do not deserve such things,
and do not consider that God understands and knows us better than we do ourselves, and that the Lord's judgment extends throughout the whole earth,
and that no one is chastised without his command, then, as time goes on, our troubles come in ever closer succession,
and our affliction grows fiercer. They hand us over from one to another, as though by a rope,
until we know ourselves, humble ourselves, and become aware of our sins. For without becoming aware of them, we cannot even begin to correct ourselves.
And in the end, after being distressed by many afflictions, we then confess our sins—a confession without benefit,
since we receive no comfort from it. Even this very thing, that a person becomes aware of his sins,
is a gift from God that enters the mind when he sees that the person has been battered by many kinds of trials,
so that he may not depart from this world amid all these troubles and afflictions without having benefited.
And it was not out of stubbornness, but out of ignorance, that we failed to understand.
Some depart from this world even amid these very things, without acknowledging their guilt, but instead arguing and blaming others.
But the merciful God watches to see whether they will humble themselves, so that he may forgive them and give them relief,
and not only provide a way out of their trial, but also forgive their sins through a small confession from their hearts.
Just as someone who presents a great gift to a king wins a cheerful welcome from him, so
the person who sheds tears in prayer before God, the great King of all worlds,
wipes away the whole extent of his sins and also wins a cheerful welcome from him.
For just as a sheep that leaves the fold and, while its shepherd is distracted, goes and stands beside a den of wolves,
so is a monk who separates himself from fellowship with his companions under the pretext of living alone,
yet constantly keeps company with apparitions and the distractions of village life.
Just as someone who carries a very valuable pearl on his shoulder,
and travels along a road with a bad reputation, is always afraid of being robbed,
so is someone who carries the pearl of chastity and travels through the world along the road of enemies:
until he enters the chamber of the grave, which is the place of safety, there is no assurance that it will escape bandits and robbers.
Can that man avoid being afraid? In the same way, this man too does not know
in what place, from what direction, or at what time they will suddenly attack him and strip him of his hope.
Some are robbed at the door of their own house—that is, in old age.
Just as someone who drinks wine in a time of mourning becomes drunk and forgets all the anguish of his grief,
so whoever becomes drunk with the love of God in this world, which is a house of weeping,
forgets his pain and all his distress, and because of his drunkenness becomes insensible to all the passions of sin.
The soul of someone whose heart is sustained by hope in God is a swift winged creature.
For his mind is always lifted above the earth, and in the meditation of his thoughts he flies above heaven. Whoever has
unceasing prayer is like someone who has the wind for his mount, whom his enemy cannot overtake.
For whenever he wishes, he flies away from him.
Someone who shows compassion to those in distress is like someone who has an advocate in court.
Just as someone who is in danger amid storms at sea throws his belongings out of the ship,
so does someone who disregards hindrances on this road to the house of God, in this world, which is a sea that drowns people.
There is no shortage of hindrances. Why do you labor over a house that is not yours? Let the sight of a dead person teach you about your departure from here.
Why do you multiply bonds for yourself? Save your life before your light grows dark and you seek help but cannot find it.
This life has been given to you for repentance. Do not waste it on excuses.
The cross is the gateway to the mysteries. Through this gateway the mind enters into knowledge of the heavenly mysteries.
Knowledge of the cross is hidden in the sufferings of the cross.
As one shares in those sufferings, so one becomes aware of it, according to the apostle's words.
For as the sufferings of Christ increase in us, so our consolation in Christ increases in proportion to them.
He calls contemplation “consolation.” Contemplation means the soul's vision. Vision gives birth to consolation.
Our soul cannot bring forth the fruits of the Spirit unless our heart is dead to the world.
The Father, it is said, raises the soul that has died Christ's death into contemplation of all the worlds.
Another saying. Unless you die to the world, it is said, there will not rise
within you the spiritual Adam. For, it is said, when a person dies through spiritual self-sacrifice to the whole way of life of this existence,
and entrusts his life to the life after the resurrection, grace rests upon him, and his way of life is [?] in the Spirit.
And when he hates the world, then he becomes aware of that way of life of the new person
which is above the filth of human existence, and he is deemed worthy of divine revelations.
We cannot be in the world and dead to the world as long as our mind desires comforts,
and the world, through its material things, lies before our senses, renews its memory through sensation, and rouses the body to seek it,
through proximity to those things, through sight, hearing, touch, smell, and taste.
The soul's death to the world is the heart's freedom from dwelling on memories of it,
the soul's restraint from thoughts of its material things, and the will's severance from the love of thinking about them.
For our heart cannot be in a peace that is above disturbance, and in the serenity of a love that is above the world,
while memories, renewed by encounters with material things through the senses that receive them, are poured into it.
The soul's death to the world cannot be acquired unless the body too is beyond sensing and seeing material things.
On keeping vigil at night, and on the many different kinds of labor involved in it.
And on how the aim of our labors should not be to fulfill a fixed quantity, but to labor freely and with discernment,
like children of God who work with their Father in the freedom of love.
And on how precious the labor of keeping vigil is, above all other spiritual practices.
And what is required of those who choose this labor, and how they should proceed in it.
And concerning the gifts they are deemed worthy to receive from God, and the struggles brought against them by the rulers of the world. 80.
When you wish to stand for the service during your night vigil, do as I tell you, with our Lord’s help.
Set out incense as usual, and stand up. After that, do not immediately begin your service.
Rather, when you have finished praying and have marked your heart and your limbs with the living sign, stand silently for a little while,
until your senses have settled and your movements have become peaceful.
Then lift your inward gaze toward our Lord, and earnestly plead with him to support your weakness,
and to make the words of your tongue and the movements of your heart pleasing to his will.
And say quietly in the prayer of your heart: “My Lord and my God, who watches over his creation,
to whom our passions, the weakness of our nature, and the strength of our adversary are known: protect me from his evil.
For his power is mighty, while our nature is frail and our strength is limited.
You, therefore, the kind one who knows our weakness and bears the hardships
of our infirmity, guard me from the turmoil of thoughts and the onslaught of passions, and make me worthy of this holy service,
so that I may not spoil its sweetness through my passions and be found presumptuous before you.
Rather, may I stand before you with radiant thoughts and a clear mind,
as befits your holiness, whose radiance that chariot of seraphim cannot bear,
who, with their swift, fiery movements, proclaim holy and praise the holiness of your being, which is their garment.”
With these thoughts, your heart is immediately opened by grace, and you shed tears at the beginning of your prayer.
Your thoughts become radiant through remembrance of the Lord, and your soul receives serenity and radiant modesty.
With your mind collected and clear, you begin your service without anxiety and proceed pleasantly through it to its completion.
We ought to carry out our service in complete freedom, apart from every anxious, childish thought.
But if we see that there is little time and that dawn is breaking before the service is finished,
let us willingly and knowingly leave out one or two of the customary divisions of the Psalter,
and give anxiety no opportunity to spoil the sweetness of our service and disturb the morning psalms as well.
If, while you are performing the service, a thought whispers to you and says, “Hurry a little!”
That is, “Let us increase the work, and you will finish quickly.” Do not pay attention to it.
But if it presses you about this, immediately go back over a few sections of the Psalms.
And every verse whose meaning carries the purpose of prayer,
repeat many times. And if it troubles or presses you again, stop chanting,
and kneel in prayer and say, “I do not want to count miles;
rather, I seek to reach the lodging place. Whatever path leads me there quickly, that is the one I will take.”
Those people who fashioned the calf in the wilderness walked for forty years, wandering in the wilderness,
climbing up and down mountains and hills. Yet they did not see the promised land even from a distance.
And if standing overcomes you during your vigil because it lasts so long, and you grow weak from exhaustion,
for your thought—or rather, the schemer who speaks through your thought as he did through the serpent—says to you, “Finish now,
since you have no strength to stand,” say, “No, not so! Let us sit down instead; that is better than sleep.
For even if I do not recite a psalm, let my tongue be silent while my mind is occupied with prayer and conversation with God.
Wakefulness is in every way more beneficial than sleep.” A vigil does not consist entirely of standing,
nor, again, only of reciting psalms. Rather, one person spends the whole night in psalms;
another in kneeling, heartfelt prayers, and rolling on the ground;
and another in weeping, tears, and lamentations over his sins.
It is said of one of our fathers that for forty years his prayer consisted of a single saying: “I have sinned as a human being;
but you, as God, forgive me.” And the fathers and brothers used to hear him
repeating this verse with sorrow, weeping without ceasing.
This prayer alone served him in place of the prayer service, by night and by day.
There is also someone who chants psalms for a little while in the evening and spends the rest of the night in responses, praises, and teaching hymns,
and other delightful songs. And there is someone who divides the hours of the night into sessions.
Between one session and another he lights a lamp and takes pleasure in reading a book while he rests.
There is also someone who sets himself the rule of not bending his knees at all,
not even during the prayer at the end of a section of the Psalms, as is customary for those keeping vigil. Instead, he passes the whole night in one uninterrupted stretch.
It is also said of one of the saints that, because the demon of sexual immorality was fighting against him
and would not leave him alone by any means, he devoted himself to the labor of keeping vigil.
He set himself a rule never to bend his knees at all. Instead, he stood throughout the night with his eyes open.
He did not kneel down until morning. All these different practices belong to the labor of keeping vigil.
Through them the diligent strip off the old person, corrupted by deceitful desires, and put on Christ and are saved.
Through these kinds of strenuous labors of wisdom, the saints are made worthy of the wonder of divine revelation, which rises above fleshly thinking.
When the diligent find delight during their vigils in these and similar kinds of distinct practices, they pass without weariness through the whole
span of the long hours of the night. Their soul rejoices and is glad, forgetting the tunic of flesh, woven of passions, in which it is wrapped.
Because of the delight and exultation in their hearts, they do not remember sleep.
They are like people who think they have stripped off the body and are already living the life that follows the resurrection.
Because of their great joy, from time to time they leave off the psalms
and fall on their faces, overwhelmed by the joy welling up in their soul.
The whole length of the night is like daytime to them, and the darkness like the rising of the sun,
because of the hope that lifts their hearts and intoxicates them as they ponder it, and because of the fervor of their mind, which burns with the remembrance of the good things to come.
While the tongue continually plays upon the harp of the Spirit, the mind, meanwhile, attends to its own tasks.
Sometimes it moves toward understanding the verses, and sometimes it drives out an adulterous thought that presses upon it.
Sometimes, when it grows weary here, it turns back to the subjects of the day's reading.
At these times it stirs into activity the memories it has stored up from there in its treasury
and takes delight in them, so that there may be absolutely no room for foreign thoughts.
Then again it quickly springs back, bringing the mind to the meaning of the prayer and the singing,
lest, by lingering there—even though reflection on those things is beneficial—it be deprived of conversation with God and the light of contemplation
that the mind is accustomed to receive from undistracted prayer, when, alone, through the secrecy
of the heart, it speaks with its Lord in the humility of its thoughts. In this way, and in these practices, they spend the whole time of their lives.
Each one of them pleased his Lord through his labors, according to his measure and his strength, with complete readiness of will [?].
But if anyone wishes to rest his body a little, he finishes and sits down facing east.
And while he is sitting, he does not let his mind remain idle.
Instead, he meditates, reflects, and thinks about the greatness of this way of life:
what it is, how demanding its work is, how great its crown is, and how glorious the fruit of its labors is;
how much vigilance it requires, how those of former times conducted themselves in it, and what they were found worthy of at the end of their struggles;
and how the mercy of Jesus brought him out of the world, where he had been wearing himself out with fruitless labors,
whose outcome is destruction from God and disgrace from sins, and brought him to this service of angels,
whose hope is a sure hope, and whose joy is a joy over which sorrow has no power,
and whose assurance is an assurance that does not prove false. For however much a person labors, his labors are small
compared with what he is to receive at the end, as a pledge of blessings for the delight of his soul.
As he ponders these and similar thoughts in his heart and marvels, he then urges his mind onward in a chariot of the spirit and makes it fly,
letting it wander with all the holy fathers of every generation, those
whose way of life he has inherited: how each one of them fulfilled this spiritual service in different ways;
and how they left behind ease and human company, and removed themselves from the entanglements of the world and from a life of turmoil;
and went and hid themselves in mountains, caves, and remote and solitary places,
because they saw that this way of life could not be perfected among people because of the many obstacles. They became dead during their lifetime for the sake of life in God,
wandering in desolate places and among cliffs like people who had lost their way:
men whose glory, even that of a single one of them, the whole world could not equal.
Some of them lived on lofty, sheer cliffs, and others at the foot of mountains and in deep ravines.
Others lived in hollows in the earth and in holes like those that foxes dig to hide in.
Others lived in tombs and among the crags of the mountains.
One pitched a little shelter for himself in the wilderness and spent the rest of his life in it.
Another built himself a small enclosure on a mountaintop, or a little hut,
and lived in it contentedly, as though in royal palaces. Their concern was not how to stay alive,
but how each one of them could please God and finish his struggle well.
And what kind of life did these holy men live in these places? Did they live in the body, or rather in a life higher than
Flesh and blood? Did the soul not grow faint in all that desolation? Did the strength to endure not fail over all that long time?
Did the body not languish throughout that entire span of time,
deprived of everything needed to meet nature’s demands? How, then, was human life preserved in them? And besides all this, what struggles they endured!
And what afflictions! How resolutely, how unwaveringly they endured the hardship of the various battles
that evil spirits brought upon them! And how they did not slacken throughout the whole span of their lives, right to the end,
in their harsh and exhausting labors! How their spirits did not become discouraged in all that solitude,
deprived of visible consolations! And can all this strength really exist in human nature?
And how, again, divine power kept them unharmed through all those various trials!
And how, through various means of provision, he made ready for each one of them, according to the place where he lived,
what was needed to supply his necessities! Some of them he fed by means of a bird.
“Look,” he said, “for sixty years I have been receiving half a loaf from this bird.”
Others, again, from some tree or palm tree, in a manner beyond nature, as one of them said.
That is, the bishop who was doing penance in the wilderness.
“I have now been in this wilderness,” he said, “for forty-nine years.
God has given me my livelihood from this palm tree.” Likewise, again,
that holy man who had remained in a fallen state for six months in his monastery
and fled into the inner wilderness to repent of his sin.
That is, the man whose liver lobe was hurting, and an angel came and healed him.
Some, too, were provided for through animals, like that blessed man who lived in a cave in the wilderness of Sodom.
But where the wilderness was near inhabited country, he provided for them through people.
For example, that resolute man whom Serapion saw, and that blessed Martinian who lived on that secluded island,
whom a merchant visited twice a year.
For where there was neither inhabited country nor any roads nearby, he visited them through an angel.
As is said about the blessed Apollo: he lived, it is said, in a small cave on the slopes of the mountain.
This, it is said, was his practice: he offered prayer to God all day long, and a hundred times during the night.
His food, it is said, used to come to him in the wilderness through an angel, without his having to worry about it.
He wore a tunic and had a small shawl over his head.
These remained on him in the wilderness without wearing out.
Do you see how God cares for his servants in everything? Others sustained themselves on roots.
Others lived on edible greens that grew by themselves.
Others ate soaked seeds and pickled greens, which were cultivated with care. Others lived on the fruit of trees.
There were also some for whom an infusion of celery and crushed cress [?] sufficed for the needs of this
fleeting life—just enough to keep the body's natural constitution alive.
On the other beneficial recollections that grace stirs up at these times to comfort a person.
When a person's mind is occupied with these and similar matters,
he then becomes intoxicated as though with strong wine and forgets himself. Then he looks at himself again and marvels
that, throughout all that journey through the wilderness and those encounters with the saints, he suffers no harm at all in his mind.
Rather, at that moment it seems to him that he is already with those saints and sees them clearly.
And from this recollection of the saints' way of life, which the mind ponders as it recalls their stories,
and from this meditation on them, despondency ceases and listlessness is driven away.
The limbs are strengthened, sleep is driven from the eyelids, and the mind takes courage.
It casts fear away from itself; distraction is forcefully overthrown, and the thoughts are gathered together.
A burning fervor blazes in the heart, and inexpressible joy awakens in the soul.
From this come copious tears that soak the cheeks [?], and spiritual delight that intoxicates the mind;
consolations beyond explanation, which the soul receives; and hope that supports the heart and gives it courage.
Then, during that vigil overflowing with good things, the person feels as though he were dwelling in heaven.
These and similar things come to meet those who labor with discernment in keeping vigil.
For nothing so purifies and gladdens the mind,
illuminates it and banishes evil thoughts, and brings the soul joy, as persistent keeping of vigil.
For this reason all the holy fathers persevered in this labor of keeping vigil.
And they kept this rule of keeping vigil at night throughout the whole course of their lives.
Especially because they heard our Savior, in many places, carefully warning us about this through his living word:
“Always keep watch and pray,” he said. And, “Wake up and pray, so that you do not enter into temptation.”
And again, “Pray, and do not grow weary,” and so on. He was not content merely to give us warnings in words,
but also gave us an example in his own person, always honoring the practice of prayer above everything else.
And he would constantly withdraw for this purpose—for prayer—and not carelessly.
Rather, he would choose the nighttime and a deserted place,
so that, when we are free from all bustle and disturbance, we may have the opportunity to pray in stillness as we ought.
Also, all the revelations concerning various matters that came to the saints, whether for their own enlightenment or for the instruction of everyone,
usually came to them at night and at the time of prayer.
For this reason our fathers too, having received from our Savior himself this exalted teaching about prayer
and watchfulness in it, also in accordance with the apostle’s commands, would choose stillness and freedom from everything
first of all, so that they might remain unceasingly near God through constant prayer.
They fled into stillness not only so that nothing would hinder their constant devotion to the practice of prayer,
but also lest something foreign should confront them from outside and disturb their pure mind,
and their joyful vigil, which is the light of the soul, should be disrupted.
They also ate in measured amounts, so that the smoke rising from a full stomach would not darken the intellect,
disturb its serene discernment, and deprive it of the spiritual delight bestowed through prayer.
In short, they made every effort in everything
to be able, as far as possible, to speak with God without a veil, with their mind entirely unhindered by anything.
For Satan himself also understands that all these good things are stored up within this wonderful practice,
which serves as the soul for all the constituent limbs of the body of virtue,
and so he attacks it more than any other practice. Everyone knows this from experience as well.
For in nothing else is he so provoked and enraged against a person, or so ready to struggle with him,
as during the night vigil, whether that person is a solitary, a monk living in a monastery, or a layperson.
Here he can no longer bear not to show himself openly, in open battle against him, without an intermediary. Although he is entirely unaware
of the gifts secretly received by those who keep vigil, he nevertheless envies them because of the modest bearing with which they stand,
and because of their perseverance against sleep, keeping awake with praises and singing, and prayers with bowing and stretching out,
with prostrations and rolling on the ground, and heartfelt supplication throughout the night.
He envies them all the more because, while others lie on their beds like the dead,
and he toys with them as he pleases through the loathsome and shameful visions of his imaginings,
and rolls them about as though in mud, amid various fantasies, in the heavy sleep brought on by the fullness of their stomachs throughout the night,
these people, by contrast, already depict in themselves the wakefulness of the resurrection.
He sees that, although they are still confined behind the gate of the flesh, and the waves of mortality continually assail them,
and they are restricted to a limited life under the dominion of the air of this world,
they display in their mortal nature a pattern of that way of life which is to come.
Prayer offered during the hours of the night possesses great power, greater than prayer offered during the day.
For this reason all the righteous used to pray at night, fighting against the heaviness of the body
and against the sweetness of sleep, forcing nature away from its own inclinations.
As the prophet also said, “I am weary with my groaning, and every night I soak my bed,”
as he groaned with the anguish of prayer from the depths of his heart.
And again: “At midnight I rose to thank you for your judgments, O righteous one.” And for every request that they urgently
asked of God, they armed themselves with prayer during the night vigils, and immediately received what they requested.
Nothing is so terrifying even to Satan as prayer offered while keeping awake at night.
Even if it is offered distractedly, it does not return empty-handed, unless perhaps what is requested is entirely inappropriate.
For this reason he wages a fierce battle against those who persist in this practice, to hinder them from it if possible.
But those who persevere for a little while against the wickedness of his schemes, and taste the gifts of God that are given during the vigil,
and personally experience the greatness of the help God provides them,
then utterly despise him—both him and all his devices. Therefore, more than the whole congregation of the church,
this order of solitaries engages in battle against him through the struggle of prayer and vigil.
One reason is their freedom from visible things; another is their perseverance in stillness.
Since they are free from occasions for distraction, he can no longer divert their thoughts from meditation on God,
or disturb their continual supplication by waging war against them.
Thus, from the beginning of their discipleship until their old age, they never neglect the labor of keeping vigil.
Rather, this is their accustomed practice: standing continuously throughout the night,
as we also learn from the recorded accounts of each of them.
For Saint Athanasius says in his account of that mirror of monks:
"He would keep vigil so thoroughly that on many nights he reached the dawn without sleeping."
Indeed, Satan found in this an occasion to launch his first battle against the victorious man. This happened while he was still young.
We also find repeatedly in many [?] that he never neglected keeping vigil throughout his life,
not even when he was meeting with others, as when he went to visit the blessed elder Paul:
after they had eaten the meal brought by the bird, they stood, we are told, in prayer throughout the night.
Which monk who neglects this, even if he possesses all the virtues together,
would not be considered idle without it? For it is the light of the mind.
Through it the understanding is raised up, thought is gathered together, and the intellect soars and gazes into spiritual things;
it is absorbed in prayer and filled with wonder. Through it are given pledges of the blessings of the life to come,
and the bestowals of gifts whose mysteries are depicted in the Holy Scriptures.
For this reason, our fathers did not neglect this labor from the beginning of their discipleship until they reached the full measure of perfection.
Thus, not even in extreme old age, when they could scarcely stand on their feet,
did they allow weariness to gain control over them and prevent them from persevering in wakefulness through the nights,
so as to give their bodies rest through a little sleep. We also learn this from
the accounts told about that perfect image of virtue and of every spiritual beauty—I mean the blessed Arsenius.
After withdrawing himself completely from all contact with other people,
and establishing his dwelling a great distance even from the brothers in that famous desert of Scetis,
he devoted himself entirely to this wonderful practice of keeping vigil.
His standing in vigil, too, was exceptional among all the fathers of his time.
As the account of his life also testifies, on the evening ushering in Sunday, it says, he would leave the sun behind him
and stretch out his hands toward heaven until the sun rose before his face.
And again, in another place: “He would spend the whole night in vigil,” it says.
And whenever, toward morning, he wanted to rest because of his natural needs, while struggling against sleep,
he would say, “Go away from me, you wicked servant!” Then he would snatch a little sleep and wake up.
And this despite his great old age, for it is said that he was bent over because of his age.
And so that his diligence in keeping vigil may be better known, let us hear another account about him:
how he persevered despite all that old age and weakness—a man ninety years old.
Once he called two of his disciples, who
were great fathers, and said to them, “Because the demons are fighting against me, and I do not know whether they may catch me asleep,
struggle with me tonight by keeping vigil. Watch over me and see whether I doze during the vigil.”
They sat, one on his right and one on his left, from evening until morning.
They said, “We fell asleep and woke up, but we never saw him doze at all.
When it began to grow light, perhaps he did this deliberately to make us think he had dozed, or perhaps sleep really did overcome him—
we do not know. Three times the sound of breathing came from his nostrils, and he got up.
He said to us, ‘I did doze off, didn’t I?’ We answered him, ‘We do not know, Father, because we were asleep.’”
Those guides in our way of life took delight in these pleasant labors of keeping vigil.
And what benefit, one may ask, did the illustrious Arsenius gain from this torment,
with which he was afflicting his body so much? Clearly, he did not endure all these things without purpose.
For we see that not only was his inner self illuminated, to his delight, by that heavenly radiance,
but it also clothed his outer self, whose nature is opaque and subject to decay, in glory—
the glory in which all the saints will be wrapped at the end, in the transformation that the nature of the entire human race will undergo.
And how do we learn this? Once, it says, one of the brothers went to the cell of Abba Arsenius.
He peered through the window and saw the old man standing, his whole being like a blazing fire.
For that brother, it is said, was worthy of this vision. That is, he was not one of the lesser ones,
but one of the great ones who went to see the elder. The blessed man had a reputation
because of his outstanding way of life, and all the fathers longed to see him.
And because they saw him only at very long intervals—as Abba Macarius said to him,
“Why do you flee from us?”—for this reason even the visitors who came to Scetis
wanted to see him first and receive his blessing. So when that brother knocked, the elder came out
and saw that he was astonished at what he had seen. He said to him, “Have you been knocking for a while? Perhaps you saw something?”
He said to him, “No.” Thus he dismissed him. And what shall I say about that blessed Pachomius, who was this man's equal,
outstanding in other respects, a wrestler in the contest, eager and mighty in the watchfulness of his vigil?
He spent a long time fighting demons like a victorious athlete, after the example of Saint Antony.
Because they came against him on many nights—that is, while he was keeping vigil—he asked God to free him from sleep,
so that he might remain sleepless night and day and be able to bring down the enemy's power. As it is said, “I will not
turn back until I have destroyed them.” For they are powerless, it is said, before faith in the Lord.
And this gift was granted to him for a certain time, just as he had asked.
And because his heart had grown tender—that is, because his soul's sight had been cleansed through night vigils, solitude, and prayer—
he saw the invisible God as though in a mirror.
These are the fruits of keeping vigil; these are the blessings of those who practice it; these are the crowns of its contests.
You too, brother, if you long to share with these saints and inherit their way of life,
persevere in solitude without losing heart, so that you may also be able to practice the work of prayer without interruption.
Endure its afflictions so that you may reap its benefits. And if circumstances weaken your body and it ceases its labor,
and you cannot carry out the practices of solitude as usual, and you then begin to be reproached by your conscience, to lose heart, and to be distressed—
since this is the work of conscience: never to stop rebuking and pricking, especially those whose intention is upright—
do not say, “Alas, I am idle! It would therefore be better for me to be outside and engage in some activity,
rather than have the empty reputation of living in solitude and seclusion while being idle in practice.”
Or again, “I am a solitary and a hermit, yet I am far from fulfilling the duties required of me”—do not say this.
This. But the kind God holds the scales of our weakness: he asks of a person according to what that person has.
He knows us better than we know ourselves, and knows how much strength we have. Do as much work as your strength allows.
And if you cannot do even a little, gladly accept your inactivity in stillness, and persevere.
Know that if you leave stillness, not even this thought will remain with you, so that your conscience might rebuke you for your inactivity.
On the contrary, many troubles will press upon you through distraction and the unrestrained activity of the senses,
which ruin even what you have already accomplished, because the grace of stillness is taken away from you.
You fall into trials, and many troubles that you do not expect come upon you.
If you fall into trials, do not lose hope. For there is no merchant who travels by sea and along the roads
without suffering losses, nor any farmer who does nothing but gather in his entire harvest,
nor any athlete who is not struck and beaten, even if he wins the victory in the end.
So it is with the things of God's household, with the merchants of this invisible [?]: there are gains and losses in it,
wounds and victory. When you are beaten, do not turn your back. Forgive me.
An explanation of the question addressed to the brother who asked him: Why, when our Lord established mercy as the measure of likeness to the greatness of the Father in heaven,
do solitaries honor stillness more than mercy? And a spiritual explanation of this,
and that we must not neglect those in distress and the sick when they are nearby [?]. 81.
You have done well to bring an example from the Gospel and a discerning comparison for the great practice of stillness,
as though we stood opposed to mercy, or rashly ventured to dismiss it as something superfluous.
You say, “Our Lord established mercy as the means by which those who practice it draw near to likeness to the Father.”
This is true. Nor do we solitaries honor stillness apart from mercy,
when we strive to withdraw as far as possible from anxiety and disturbance.
It is not that we would resist necessary duties when they press upon us. Rather, we take care to preserve stillness
so that we may persevere in solitary communion with God. Through it we can more readily become clear of turmoil
and draw near to serenity of mind, even a little. And whenever necessity arises, we do not neglect mercy either,
as we constantly compel ourselves to be inwardly filled at all times with compassion for every rational being.
For this is what our Lord's teaching commands, and this is the distinguishing feature of our stillness, not of busy activity, although to it too
to the inward one, whenever the time is suitable for action and circumstances require it.
None of us neglects to show his love openly through deeds.
Especially those who have not bound themselves to solitude under an absolute restriction
that they must meet no one, but whose solitude follows a rule of days and weeks.
For people such as these, from deeds of mercy toward their neighbor,
would not hold themselves back even during the periods prescribed by their rule.
Unless someone is utterly foolish and maintains solitude outwardly and in people's sight.
For we know that without love for one's neighbor, the mind cannot be enlightened through communion with God and divine love.
And so, which of the wise solitaries, having food and clothing, has seen his neighbor hungry and naked
and persisted in withholding them from him? Or who, when his fellow human being is sick, suffering, and without anyone to care for him,
has, because of his love of solitude, valued the rule of his seclusion more than his neighbor's life? But where circumstances such as these are not at hand,
we preserve love and compassion for our neighbor in our minds.
But whenever an opportunity for action is at hand, God fully requires us to carry it out in deeds as well.
For it is clear that if we possess nothing, he does not
permit us to become involved in anxiety and turmoil for the sake of the poor. Rather, we are held accountable for what we have.
And again, if we live far away from human habitation, and from mingling with people and seeing them,
we are not required to leave our retreat and our secluded, solitary dwelling
and give ourselves over to going out and wandering about in the world, visiting the sick and attending to such matters.
For it is clear that someone who does this moves from what is greater to what is lesser.
But if he lives in a community and is close to people through continually dwelling among them,
and also benefits from the labor of others, both when he is healthy and when he is ill,
he is required to provide this same care himself, rather than merely demanding it in full from others.
But when he sees his fellow human being, who shares his monastic way of life, in distress—or rather, Christ himself lying there suffering—
he runs away and hides, intent on a false solitude. Someone like this is merciless.
Do not bring up John of Thebes to me, or Arsenius and others like him.
“Who,” he says, “has devoted himself to deeds like these,
or cared for the sick or the poor, and despised stillness?” Do not concern yourself with their affairs.
For if, like them, you keep far away from every comfort and from contact with people,
you are permitted to disregard such things. But if you are far from the way of the perfect,
and are constantly occupied with bodily distractions and dealings with others, why do you despise the commandment suited to your measure,
taking refuge in the exalted way of life of the saints, which you have not approached? For my part,
I will not neglect to recall the account of Macarius the Great, which is recorded to admonish those who despise their brothers.
Once he went to visit someone who was sick.
When he asked him whether there was anything he wanted, he told him, “I would like a little soft bread.”
For those hermits generally baked their bread for the entire year.
Such was the custom in those regions. And that man, worthy of blessedness, went—
a man ninety years old—from Scetis to the city of Alexandria, more than forty miles,
carrying dry bread in a cloth. He exchanged it [?] and brought the sick man what he had requested.
But another man, his equal, did something even greater than this: a certain Agathon,
the most distinguished of all the hermits of that time, a man who valued stillness and silence more than anyone.
Once he went to a fair to sell his handiwork. He found a stranger lying sick in the marketplace.
He rented a house and stayed with him, working with his hands, providing for him, and paying the rent for the house.
He cared for him for six months, until that sick man recovered.
This man, as the account relates, used to say, “I wish I could find a leper and give him my body,
and take his.” Here is perfect love! Let us imitate our fathers, so that we may be found worthy of grace as they were.
My beloved, those who fear God undertake without distress the task of keeping our Lord’s commandments,
even though they accomplish it through toil and danger is expected on its account.
Christ bound their fulfillment to two commandments and made it depend on them; these encompass the whole of them.
I mean love of God; and he made love toward his image the likeness of this.
The first has spiritual contemplation as its aim; the second has contemplation and action.
Therefore, because the divine nature is simple and not composite, and is both invisible and not [?] in its nature,
the conscience, in its communion with it, has no need of any activity, bodily work, or movement of [?].
Its service is simple, performed by a single faculty in the mind, in keeping with the simplicity of the Cause,
which is worthy of worship and is above sensory and bodily perception.
But the second commandment, which is love for humanity, requires a twofold fulfillment, corresponding to the twofold character of human nature.
I mean that we should fulfill it invisibly in the conscience, and also visibly in the body.
But also in secret, through things accomplished in vigils, together with what belongs to the conscience.
For just as a human being is constituted of two parts, namely body and soul,
so everything concerning a human being requires twofold attention, corresponding to
the twofold character of his constitution. Since practice everywhere precedes contemplation,
it is impossible for anyone to rise to that exalted [?] unless he first completes the lower part in practice.
Therefore no one should dare to say that he possesses love for his neighbor within his soul
if he neglects the part fulfilled through the body, according to his strength and the time and place that afford an opportunity for action.
Then that aspect of love which is held and known in the conscience is shown to be trustworthy.
When we have been found faithful and steadfast in these things, as far as we are able,
then, toward the great realm of exalted and divine contemplation,
the soul is given strength to reach out through simple movements free of images.
But where someone has no opportunity to fulfill love for his neighbor through visible actions,
through material things and bodily activity, it is enough for God that we preserve love for our neighbor in our thoughts alone.
This is especially so if we are able to devote ourselves to practicing that all-embracing part which is superior to this one.
But if we fall short of the fullness of that all-embracing part, let us make up its deficiency through the commandment that follows it,
which consists in outward activity. According to the demands of the time,
let us accomplish [?] relief for [?] through the labor of our bodies, so that our freedom does not become an opportunity for
the flesh, while, under the name of solitary communion, we [?] in empty things.
For it is well known that it is not permitted for someone who is entirely cut off from human company
and wholly absorbed in God, being dead to everything through his detachment from it, to require such a person to serve other people.
But someone whose rule of solitude is limited to days and weeks, and who, after completing his rule,
meets and mingles with other people and enjoys their company, yet neglects his brothers in their distress,
thinking that he is keeping the rule of the week [?]—such a person is accursed.
For it is clear that it is out of a lack of compassion, presumption, and deceitful thoughts
that he will not stoop to involve himself in matters like these.
May whoever neglects the sick see no light, and may the daylight of whoever turns his face away from someone in distress become dark.
May the household of whoever despises the cry of someone afflicted grope in darkness. Let us not ignorantly dishonor the great name of solitude.
Every way of life requires a time, a place, and discernment. Then its labor is acceptable to God, who knows everything.
Apart from these things, the labor that strives for perfection in every degree is empty.
Anyone who expects to be comforted and visited by others in his lowly condition
should humble himself also to serve his neighbor at the very times when that neighbor is being tested,
so that his labor in solitude may also be joyful and free from presumption and the deception of demons.
It was said by one of our holy fathers, Evagrius,
a man of knowledge, that nothing saves a solitary from the demon of pride
and helps him attain chastity when the passion of sexual immorality flares up
like visiting people who lie on their beds, languishing in bodily suffering.
Great is the angelic labor of solitude when discernment of this kind is joined with it,
because of the need for humility. For we are being robbed without knowing it.
I have said these things, my brothers, not so that we should despise and scorn the solitary way of life—we who everywhere urge it upon you.
It is not that we now find ourselves opposing our own words. Let no one pull an isolated statement out of our discourse
and, leaving the rest aside, seize on it without understanding.
I remember that in many places I have insistently said
that not even if someone happens to be completely inactive in his cell because of the compulsion of a weakness that has overtaken him,
should he on that account prefer leaving it altogether and working outside to remaining inactive there.
I meant going out altogether—not that, if a necessary matter should sometimes present itself, offering certain opportunities
through which a soul or the life of one's neighbor might benefit, we should consider this a waste of time.
If someone considers himself perfect and raised above everything here through his constant devotion to God
and his distance from every visible activity, he is rightly
called upon even for these things. Great is the labor of discernment for someone who receives God's help.
May he in his compassion grant us the ability to fulfill the word of the one who said:
“Whatever you want people to do for you, do likewise for them.”
To him be praise and honor from all creation forever and ever. Amen.
On how much honor humility possesses, and how great its rank is. 82.
I want to open my mouth, my brothers, to speak about the exalted subject of humility, but I am filled with fear,
like someone who knows that he is about to speak about God in the account he gives.
For it is the robe of divinity, because the Word who became human clothed himself in it and spoke with us through our body.
Everyone who has truly clothed himself in it becomes like the one who descended from his height, concealed the radiance of his majesty,
and covered his glory with humility, so that creation would not perish at the sight of him.
For creation could not even have seen him unless he took a part of it and spoke with it through that part.
Only then could it hear the word of his mouth face to face. The Israelites could not bear to listen to his voice
when he spoke with them from within the cloud. Could creation have endured seeing him openly?
For they were so distressed that they said to Moses, “Let him speak with you, and you tell us his words. But let him not speak with us
himself, so that we do not die.” The sight was so terrifying, it says, that even the mediator himself said, “I am afraid and trembling.”
For the radiance of his glory was revealed on Mount Sinai, and the whole mountain smoked and shook in fear of his revelation upon it.
Even the animals that approached the foot of the mountain died.
All the Israelites made themselves ready and prepared themselves at Moses' command,
that everyone should purify himself for three days, so that he might be worthy to hear the sound of God's speech and to see his revelations.
Yet when the time came, they could not endure the sight of his light or the force of the sound of his thunder.
But now, when he poured out his grace upon the world at his coming, it was neither with an earthquake nor with fire,
And not with a terrifying and mighty voice; instead, he came down like rain upon a lamb’s fleece,
and like quiet showers falling gently upon the earth.
He saw fit to speak with us in another way: namely, by concealing his greatness under a covering of flesh,
to speak with us through us, in that robe which his command wove for him from the Virgin’s womb,
so that, when we saw that the one speaking with us was one of our own kind, we would not be terrified at the sight of him.
Therefore, whoever puts on this covering in which our Maker appeared, through that body filled with holiness, has put on Christ himself.
For he has longed to put on, over his inner
self, that likeness in which he appeared to his creation and lived among them, and to appear in it to his fellow servants. Instead of an outward garment of honor and glory, he adorns himself with it.
Therefore, anyone whom creatures, both speechless and speaking, see clothed in this likeness,
they bow down before as before their Lord, because of the honor of their Lord, whom they saw when he [?] and lived in it.
Which creature is not abashed at the sight of a humble person? Yet until the glory of humility was revealed to everyone,
that appearance, filled with holiness, was despised by them.
But now that its greatness has shone out before the eyes of the worlds, everyone honors this likeness wherever it appears.
For through this intermediary, creation was found worthy to receive the sight of its Creator.
Therefore, it is not despised even by the enemies of the truth. Even if the person who has acquired it needs help from all creation,
the one who has learned it is honored through it as though wearing a crown and purple robes.
No one ever hates a humble person, attacks him with words, or despises him.
Because his Lord loves him, he is loved by everyone. Everyone loves him; everyone cherishes him.
Wherever he goes, people look upon him as an angel of light and offer him honor.
A wise and learned person may be speaking, but they silence him to make room for the humble person to speak.
Everyone’s eyes are fixed on his mouth to see what word will come from it. Everyone waits for his words,
as for words from God. As they listen to his words, they examine their meaning as they would a philosopher’s statement.
His words are sweeter to the ears of the wise than honeycomb to the palate of those who eat it.
He is regarded as like God, even if he is untrained in speech and lowly in appearance.
Anyone who speaks contemptuously of a humble person is no longer regarded as living, but as someone who opens his mouth against God.
And the more he is despised in his own eyes, the more honors from all creatures come pouring upon him.
The humble person approaches dangerous animals, and as soon as their gaze falls on him,
their wildness is calmed, and they approach and cling to him as to their master.
They wag their tails and lick his hands and feet.
For that scent which came from Adam before he transgressed the commandment,
when they gathered around him and he gave them names in Paradise, they smell on him.
This scent had been taken from us, but Christ renewed it and gave it back to us at his coming. He is the one who made the scent of the human race pleasant.
And if he approaches deadly [?], as soon as the touch of his hand reaches their bodies,
the fierce potency of their deadly venom grows cold, and he crushes them in his hands as though they were locusts.
And if he approaches human beings, they look upon him as upon a lord. But why do I say human beings? For despite all
the wickedness and bitterness of demons, and all the arrogance of their minds, when they encounter the humble person, they become like dust.
All their harshness loses its force, their schemes unravel, and their tricks come to nothing.
But now that we have shown the greatness of the honor humility receives from God, and the power hidden within it,
let us now show clearly what humility is, and when a person becomes worthy to receive it fully as it truly is.
And let us distinguish between someone who is humble in outward appearance and someone who has been found worthy of true humility.
Humility is a mysterious power that the perfected saints receive after bringing their entire way of life to fulfillment.
This power is given only to those who, through the power of grace, have brought virtue to complete fulfillment in themselves,
as far as nature is capable within its limits, since virtue encompasses everything.
For this reason, we cannot indiscriminately consider everyone humble,
but only those who have been found worthy of this rank of which we have spoken.
Not everyone who is naturally peaceable, quiet, gentle, or innocent has reached the degree of humility.
Rather, the truly humble person is someone who, though he secretly possesses something worthy of exaltation, does not exalt himself.
Instead, he is like dust in his own thoughts. Nor, in the case of someone who is humbled by remembering his faults or lapses—
recalling them so that his heart may be broken and his mind brought down from proud impulses through their memory—do we call him humble, even though
this is praiseworthy. For he still has proud thoughts, and humility has not taken possession of him.
Rather, he brings it close to himself through deliberate methods. And although this is praiseworthy, as I said,
he does not yet possess it. Rather, he is seeking it, and it is not his.
But the perfectly humble person is someone who does not need to devise a reason for his mind to become humble.
He has fulfilled all these things and possesses humility effortlessly, as something natural.
Thus, even when a great gift, which the whole creation cannot contain,
is received within his own nature, he considers himself a sinner and an ordinary person in his own eyes.
And although he has entered into the mysteries of all spiritual beings and is mighty in the wisdom of all created things,
he knows with complete certainty that he knows nothing. And this is not through deliberate methods; rather, this is how he is in his heart, without forcing himself.
Can a human being really become like this? Does nature have the power to transform him in this way? No. Then do not doubt:
it is a mysterious power that he has received, and this is what perfects him effortlessly in every virtue.
This is the power that the blessed apostles received in the appearance of fire.
It was because of this that our Savior commanded them not to leave Jerusalem until they received power from on high,
which is the Paraclete, meaning the comforting Spirit. He is also the Spirit of visions.
This is what Scripture says about them: “Mysteries are revealed to the humble.”
That is, this Spirit of revelations and revealer
of mysteries—the humble are deemed worthy to receive him within themselves.
This is why holy people have said that meekness perfects the soul through divine visions.
Therefore, let no one dare to think of himself that he has personally attained the full measure of humility
because of a single thought of repentance that arose in him at some time, or because of a few tears that he shed,
or because of one good quality that he has by nature or maintains in himself by force,
as though that which is the culmination of all mysteries and embraces every virtue
were something he had acquired within the limits of a few small labors, which he counts as equivalent to this gift.
But if a person has conquered all the opposing spirits, and not one of the paths of all the virtues has escaped him
without his having labored for it and acquired it, and he has conquered and brought low all the rebellious strongholds,
and afterward has perceived in his soul, through the Spirit, that he has received the gift:
When the Spirit itself bears witness to his spirit, according to the apostle’s words, this is the height of humility.
Blessed is the person who has acquired it, for he always embraces the bosom of Jesus. But someone asks:
“What should I do? How can I acquire it? By what means can I become worthy to receive it? For look, I force myself.
Yet when I suppose that I have acquired it, I see that, without my being aware of it, impulses opposed to it are stirring within my mind.
And then, because of this, I fall into despair.” To the person who asks this,
this answer is given: “It is enough for the disciple to become like his teacher, and for the servant to become like his master.
Look at the one who commanded this and who gives this gift: see how he possessed it, and imitate him yourself, and you will be able to acquire it.
For he himself said, ‘The ruler of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me.’
Do you see how humility is acquired through the fulfillment of every virtue, so that we may emulate in it the one who commanded it?
He says, ‘Foxes have dens, and the birds of heaven have shelter, but the Son of Man has nowhere to rest his head.’
To him be glory from all who have been perfected, sanctified, and brought to completion in every generation,
together with the Father who sent him and the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.
With the help of our Lord, the first part of Mar Isaac, bishop of Nineveh, is finished.
[?] This part was copied for Rabban David [?] in the village of Alton, that is, [?] Welatu, in the cell on the cliff [?]. And thieves came [?] and took his books [?], and this one was found
by the brothers who were living in the cell in the village of Tyareh. And after [?] sixteen years [?], it was completed by a man
whose name was Paul, in the year one thousand five hundred and forty-six of the kingdom of the Greeks, and in the [?], six hundred and thirty-three.
